Like a lot of others, I really really wanted to like this game.  I've always enjoyed the dark vampire mystique and setting a lot, and stealth games are one of my favorite genres.
However the game has lots of repetition to it, and some very simple mechanics which don't add to it's overall variety.  My character has maxed out around 6 skill trees now, and still only has a single primary attack (outside of the basic melee attack).  You sneak around, try to get into position to either kill an enemy or drink their blood without alerting others, rinse, repeat..  ad infinitum.
It does have a story, passable enough to keep you in tune with what is going on.  And it has some really nice visuals - vampire vision is one of those.  On the whole however the sum of the parts doesn't quite make a whole that is enjoyable and engaging enough to keep you entertained.  You will either be bored of repetition, detatched while watching cutscenes, or frustrated due to the difficulty changing between levels.. often from overly easy to horribly hard.  And most objects in the game world aren't something you can interact with, which gives it all a very sterile and pale feeling.
Combine those elements with a save system that (on normal difficulty) only gives you two saves per area, which can be maddening if you save too early and have to end up playing a large chunk over and over due to mistakes, without benefit of a save.
If you can get it on the cheap like I did in a bundle, it might be worth looking at.  Or if you're just a complete vampire nut and need one more thing to consume (pun intended).  Otherwise buy with caution - watch a few let's play videos first.  Chances are what you see in the first ten minutes will be what you see through to the end of the game.

OK, I really don't understand the negative-lukewarm reviews of the new Thief. I'm a die-hard Thief fan, and I've been eagerly awaiting the Thief reboot for ages: this is possibly my favourite game franchise ever. That doesn't make me an impartial reviewer, but I think Square Enix has successfully retained the feel of the original Thief games, an important element of which is the variety of arrows at Garrett's disposal (using water arrows to create darkness through which Garrett can slip unseen, for example, is still a brilliant gameplay strategy), as well as Garrett's dry vocal intonation. I'm not that far in, but thus far I am very much enjoying the exploration, pickpocketing and blackjacking that made the original so captivating. As far as the comparisons to Dishonored go, I feel like perhaps I am the only gamer on the planet who thought Dishonored brought dishonor to the original Thief games it referenced. I felt profoundly disappointed by Dishonored. It felt too easy, it was unchallenging, the exploration elements were made boring by the Blink ability, and the ending was a letdown (as was the silly revenge narrative). I still think the Thief franchise - including the new one - is a better game. But perhaps I need to play it a little more first to see if my interest in the game is sustained. Nevertheless, when the reviewer for IGN complained that the arrows were 'extremely limited in where they can be used - particularly the fire, water, and rope arrows that only work on very specific objects like open-flame lights and leaking oil barrels', I did think that they missed the point. Just like in the original games, the ingenuity lies in precisely this use of the right object with the right target. At this point, I'm ignoring the haters and making up my own mind - and so far, I'm very much engrossed in the exploration and treasure-hunting, and I'm impressed with the way the game has stayed true to the originals that I loved so much.

So it's been 30 hours so far, and even though I'm having such a blast, the collecting of EVERY SINGLE LOOT (OCD) is starting to get to me. I just had to get that out of the way, here and now! Surely Garret is content by now?! Moving on...
This reboot of the original Thief will not be suited to all, in fact I wouldn't be surprised if only 1 in 10 people actually will enjoy it, as the taste is a rather specialized one. If you are a diehard fan of the original series you may or may not enjoy this one, since while it still captures the essence behind Thief, the whole openworld experience is quite hampered with long loading times, awkwardly placed transitional zones and poor openworld map layout, other than that it is everything you could want from a Thief game!
If you're used to running around and killing everything without repercussions then I suggest you look elsewhere. As the original games, Thief is very unforgiving in all but stealth actions. And rightly so, for this is a fully stealth based game, and thieves are no match in combat. Thief, not Rogue, there is a difference. They're light footed, they get in and out, that's all there is to it.
A lot of people seem to want to compare this game to Dishonoured, and while the two may share similarities I can honestly say from playing both that Thief is the one to go for a complete stealth experience and a very dark storyline whereas Dishonoured you can get away with pretty much anything you do, without a real challenge (unless you impose one on yourself).
All looting and thieving aside, Thief has one of those rare atmospheres that manages to draw you into the game world, and that is thanks to the talented developers at Square Enix, the driving force behind Deux Ex: Human Revolution which also had such an amazing atmosphere to get absorbed into. The story in itself is quite an interesting one, and later on towards the end the game starts taking a turn for the horror/paranormal reminiscence of Outlast which both terrified and excited me since at least in Thief you have a chance (emphasis on YOU, not me, as playing on Master difficulty with instant fail on taking damage/being seen is what I've condemned myself to).
While the graphics in Thief never was an issue since it's such an old game, I can't help but feel that they limited themselves quite a bit by using the Unreal Engine (though I've seen much better looking games with the same engine). But to be honest, it's not about realism (though it does get that across), but about the dark noir/steampunk feel which goes hand in hand with its rugged graphics display. The audio is what really makes the game come to life though, with footsteps perfectly positioned and the rest of the sounds matched correctly more often than not you'll feel like you're really in the game until you're stuck humping a wall because it's not a predefined climb spot.
Take all this and add the ability to start a custom difficulty game where YOU get to decide how the game will play out, if you can use healing items, if you are allowed to take damage or use specific items amongst many other modifiers makes for a completely unique experience tailored to your own playstyle! Think you're a Master Thief? Prove it!
For those who haven't played any of the Thief games and are looking for something new which doesn't heavily rely on combat (though it is available) a la Metal Gear Solid/Splinter Cell then I'm sure you'll find something of value in Thief.
For those of you who are Thief fans, or have played any of the older Thief games then for nostalgia sake you will enjoy being a Taffer once more, causing mayhem for the guards, racking up loot, finding the secrets and generally just being a badass.

Oh, there's a DLC preorder starting? Please, take my money. Ignore the tears.
Full disclosure:
Thief: The Dark Project - 8/10 - Replaying once a few years
Thief II: The Metal Age - 10/10 - Replaying at least once a year
Thief: Deadly Shadows - 7/10 - Replaying once a few years
Thief - 4/10 - Will not touch ever again
Thief has that "Be glad it happened at all" feeling about it. You felt it while following development, all the way to the release date. I hope the story of all the hoops Thief had to jump to get greenlit will become public domain one day.
Now let me rant for a bit.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Non spoilery review part:
- Story 4/10 - Garrett shines as a smart protagonist at the start of the game by saying "This doesn't look good - lets get out of here.” I fell in love right there. Finally, a man driven by common sense. But that was a trick as I quickly learned, as Garrett quickly plunged into saying one thing, and agreeing to do another.
- Main mission level design 3/10 - (7/10 for one later level in the game that glittered with greatness ("The mansion"). If you followed the trailers, you may remember a point where the narrator from Square Enix comes up to an off path and says something along the lines of "There's a side area down there, we wont go there right now", well you know... I went there... Theres just two pieces of loot laying on a barrel down there, and nothing. This approach plagues most of the environments, you often see a myriad of possibilities, but the closer you get, the more often it will unfold as a linear A to B line. We don't want anyone to get confused now do we?
- Side mission level design 6/10 - I had more fun with the smaller, more thought trough levels than the main ones largely for the more unique and more interesting stories presented with them. Clockwise? Brilliant room design!
- Secrets design 8/10 - These are got to be some of the most well hidden collectables ever, great job whoever hid them.
- The tone of the game is grim and serious. Everything is blue and grey. All the lights have two colors. Even the more luxurious level don't come off as anything remarkable. Color is good. Use colors.
- Quicktime events that instantly kill you even if you turn around to see what's happening. Oh the anger I experienced.
- Yes, yes. If you're making a game that has enemies and you can interact with them, you must have the option to kill them in some brutal fashion. I can understand the need. But I'm afraid the scales were tipped towards the killing when designing this title. Im sorry killing sells.
- Amazing ambiance, whoever did Moria sound design deserves a medal.
- Marketing guys! Good work, you did everything by the book and then some.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Start of spoilery review:
Garret - "These cultist look like to be using some magics to summon something weird, lets get out of here"
Orion - "Hey, can you help me find these artifact items that those guys were using to summon something weird?"
Garrett - "Aw yeeah, lets do zis. Cant see why not."
Garret - “Stop killing people damnit!”
Annoying teenage lady - “You don't understand me dad! Leave me alone!”
- I get it that you wanted to top off the Cradle, but all the weird♥♥♥♥♥♥that went on in there had a great explanation of "house having a consciousness of its own". You guys just made a billion jump-scare scripts, added some anomalies from Stalker and added some weird story tie-in. It boiled down to "Oh boy, I wonder what scary thing is going to happen when I pick up this loot!", which is a little disappointing. I gotta hand it to you though, I was glad to see a human after the first major part, even if that human was a corpse. And thank you for the nightmares. Those are the best.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Lets have a look at my crystal ball, shall we?
- At some point in the future a DLC with "challenges" will come out.
- After that, a DLC with Armored guards that cannot be knocked out and hard to kill will come out.
- After that, with a small chance, a DLC with mechanical men as adversaries will come out.
Hopefully like in other projects, someone else will take the producer seat and make some great DLC's out of them. Just dont let the guy afraid to make hard decisions at the wheel again. “Mediocre? Please everyone equally? Sounds like a plan!”
Children who grew up playing these games have gotten jobs, got married and even had kids by now. They became someone who can afford to buy the games they love. Im sad to see that companies don't see this group of people as financially viable and still try and target the younger generation with their products.
Arcane Studios were probably on the edge of a chopping block when they launched Dishonored, but it turned out amazingly, became financially successful and kept the spirit of the true stealth genre. Im disappointed that a bigger company with great track record with Deus Ex fell so short with Thief.
I’m sure there will be sequels and sequels of sequels to Thief. And I'm sure I'll still be here. Waiting. For that childhood perfection. Or just replaying the old ones.

While this isn't a good "Thief game", it certainly is a good game.
Let me explain why:
First, the bad parts of the game:
1.) The story is generic and forgetable. You never get any twists, any surprises, characters are way too generic, and voice acting is pretty bad.
2.) The sound levels are all over the place. Sometimes they arre high, sometimes you can barely hear conversations. Sometimes you hear a guard that sounds like he is just next to you, but in reality he is pretty far away from you.
3.) Sometimes the maps aren't as open as previous thief games.
4.) There's barely any incentives for exploration. While in previous thief games you had to find your own way around to complete any objectives, in this there are waypoints. Sure, you can disable them. But you get no clues as to where to go or where the objectives are at.
5.) There are boss fights. In a thief game. /facepalm
6.) The "scary" level is just a rehash from a previous thief game and it had a lot more to live up to. It was average.
7.) There's no freeform mantling or use of rope arrows.
Now for the good parts of the game:
1.) The level design is good. You get multiple solutions to sneaking past some guards.
2.) There's the city hub. It's huge.
3.) The graphics in this game are great. If you have tesselation enabled, the road looks beautiful with it instead of flat.
4.) Sidequests are pretty good.
5.) Overall, the gameplay is fun. Completed it on master difficulty first time around, and I had a blast.

This War of Mine is a game that attempts to replicate the difficulties of war. It's premise is designed around choosing a character and playing out the war in that characters shoes. As you progress, there will new characters available to choose from. Some characters comes with perks, such as one guy might be a fast runner while one guy may be a cook. When you first start off, you'll have three characters at your disposal. To move these characters, you simply click their face on the bottom right hand corner or click literally on them, then click where you want them to go. You can also tell them to double time it (sprint) if necessary. There will be actions available throughout the game. This may include cleaning up rubble, breaking down a garrisoned door, pick locking a door, opening/searching through cabinets or even fighting with other survivors. In your own house, you can build things from beds to stoves all the way to shovels to lock picks.
Upgrading these work station will give you access to better weaponry. Upon ending your day, you will be prompted for further action. As you end the day, you will be asked whether you want to send someone to scavenge, allow someone to sleep or allow someone to guard the door. Just because you have a guard wandering the house doesn't mean you're completely fool proof. When selecting a person to scavenge, you may choose different areas of the city to check out. More locations will open up with their own unique challenges. For example, there is one area where there is a sniper watching over a location. If you don't take the appropriate steps (or cover), you will be shot dead or injured. When scavenging, it is wise to take the proper materials. Most of the time you will need a shovel with you and a few lock picks. Keep in mind though, not all scavengers can carry as much as the other so making use of space is really key. Sneaking around in someone's house does provide a challenge but is more of a waiting game than anything. Red markers that appear in circles will display the location of potential enemies (or even rodents making noise).
Fighting is pretty basic and can turn into a gun or knife fight if the proper material is available. Some opponents are a lot stronger and tougher than others due to this fact. There is a bit of a thrill while raiding homes but can become redundant after doing it a hand full of times. The game is really minimal when it comes to being immersive in it's works. Meaning, you will be using the mouse a lot in this game and not much else. What provides the pleasure in playing is watching the characters act out what you've told them.
The graphics are pretty good and the animations do their best to ensure every detail is nailed. When someone is breaking down a barrier to access another room VIA door, you will see material being broken off of the door as your character gets closer to breaking through. The sounds are actually not too bad and the sniper gunshots will initially shoot a shock down your spine.
Although this game is seen extremely positive, I think it's an OK game. It's neither good nor bad, just there sort of thing. I am not recommending it as it's really not my cup of tea as I'm not a huge fan of point-and-click type things. I also found the game play lacking as they could have given the player more control in sneaking around, fighting or even shooting. There may be some cool RPG elements in it but it wasn't enough to keep me satisfied.

Verdict: Avoid at all costs.
WARNING: Does NOT work as advertised on Win 8.1 or Win 7 64-bit.
Do not let my Steam-recorded 'playtime' fool you: all time I've spent on this was purely trying to get it to just start successfully, which it did not, not even once, on neither of the tested rigs.
Not after following the community-offered fixes of deleting the video files (seriously, *video* files make the game crash? That should be a first hint right there), manually editing the config files from the default just to get a reasonable screen resolution, crafting a special shortcut to prevent it from running on more than one CPU core (how many PCs these days have a single-core CPU anymore?), and disallowing Steam updates to avoid a standard mechanism from undoing all the required fixes.
Not even after following unreadable non-translated Russian quintuple-redirected patch download links on pure faith. I almost stopped clicking through after the fifth redirect level, way more than my sense of computing security wanted to allow me to, and now it is justifiably nagging at me from the back of my mind for running the risk with zero reward, since even the acclaimed community-created patch did not make things work (no offence to my Russian co-gamers, but clicking through links one cannot read that keep redirecting away to yet more sites one cannot read, is just not safe Internet practice, and I am sure many non-Russians are stopped from downloading the patch because of that. Even a purely Google-translated blurb with a direct download link would go far at making it at least 'feel' safer, warranted or not).
The devs themselves, despite obviously being very much not dead as shown by their posts, and despite feeling quite ok about still asking money for their broken product, are unwilling to either fix their own product or to validate the community-created patch by making it an official part of the Steam download.
This game should plainly NOT be advertised as working on Win7/8, and should definitely not be sold as such. That creative and persistent community members managed to (sometimes? mostly?) make it work through more effort than is warranted for a paying customer, does not mean you are allowed to advertise something for what it is not.
Which in the end is a damn shame, because the videos make it look like good fun. I went into this eyes open since I always read forums before-hand, and it looked fun enough to warrant some effort to get a clearly abandoned game to work. That 'some effort' unfortunately turned out to be more time than I have spent on fully playing through other very enjoyable games, to get zero results. I had one last workaround in mind (creating a dedicated WinXP VM to run the game in) but frankly I have not found any further energy to try anymore. Money totally wasted, since the devs show no signs or initiative of fixing this, not even by admitting defeat and accepting community help.
Avoid at all costs unless you have an old pre-win7 system lying around; and considering the types and severity of the crashing bugs, maybe not even then, but I cannot vouch for it either way. Others obviously are having more success, but it's far from guaranteed to work for you and more effort than many will want to spend.

The Battle of Mogadishu, more commonly referred to as Black Hawk Down or, locally, as the Day of the Rangers (Somali: Maalintii Rangers), was part of Operation Gothic Serpent and was fought on 3 and 4 October 1993, in Mogadishu, Somalia, between forces of the United States supported by UNOSOM II, and Somali militiamen loyal to the self-proclaimed president-to-be Mohamed Farrah Aidid who had support from armed civilian fighters.
A U.S. Army force in Mogadishu, consisting primarily of U.S. Army Rangers from Bravo Company, 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment; C Squadron, 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (1st SFOD-D), better known as "Delta Force"; as well as Air Force Combat Controllers and Air Force Pararescuemen and helicopters from 1st Battalion, 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment, attempted to seize two of Aidid's high-echelon lieutenants during a meeting in the city. Shortly after the assault began, Somali militia and armed civilian fighters shot down two UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters. The subsequent operation to secure and recover the crews of both helicopters drew the raid, intended to last no more than an hour, into an overnight standoff in the city. The battle resulted in 18 deaths, 73 wounded, and one helicopter pilot captured among the U.S. raid party and rescue forces. One Pakistani soldier and one Malaysian soldier were killed as part of the rescue forces but other resources claims there were more loss of life. American sources estimate between 1,500 and 3,000 Somali casualties, including civilians; SNA forces claim only 315 killed, with 812 wounded. The battle is also referred to as the First Battle of Mogadishu to distinguish it from the Second Battle of Mogadishu of 2006.

On the whole there is much to recommend this game, but I think it is not in any way a racing game for the novice or hobby racing aficianado.  Tracks are beautiful, the sound is fantastic, race modes are surprisingly diverse and engaging, course layout is well-balanced and challenging, but there are a few significant shortcomings that easily-frustrated racers will struggle with.  AI is atrocious and will run you over in the pursuit of their racing line, any collision with AI vehicles will remove all steering capacity from your car until you disengage (meaning you will have to brake as the AI won't do so to disentangle itself), and the game's inexplicable career decision to constantly shift you between disciplines and vehicle classes will rapidly grow weary.  It is almost impossible to develop any kind of racing groove when you are boomeranged between track toys, drift cars, and heavy upper class vehicles that steer like couches.  And then the shuddering camera - evidently set that way to give the sensation of car vibration and sway - will give you fits if you suffer from any kind of motion sickness.  In the chase view, and especially racing at night, the sway becomes infuriating and actively impedes developing skill and consistency.  The handling can be an issue, too, but with practice you will get a solid handle on how cars respond to steering inputs, and indeed the (unalterable) steering sensitivity comes to make sense with time.
In the end, the game is excellent, but is perhaps not suitable (re: fun) for gamers not familiar with its quirks and oft-puzzling handling/viewing designs.  The difficulty slider can only help with the competitiveness and timing of the AI and cannot help with those issues that are most likely to cause the greatest frustrations: camera shudder, collision detections, and erratic career arc.
Mac-specific notes: the game performed fine - and indeed better than most Codemasters titles have for me! - crashing to desktop only 1 time.  Menus are easy to negotiate and understand, although there is no slider to adjust steering sensitivity and linearity.  On just a few races there was significant screen-tearing as well as general hiccups on loading screens, but for the most part these did not influence the game negatively.
EDIT: after further time with the game, new issues which have resulted in its removal from my installed library - without finishing the game campaign - have popped up.  The WSR in Asia section offers a mix of race types with restricted car selection; many of these vehicles are "grip" RWD which behave in unpredictable ways.  The light track toys, for example, will sometimes drift as instructed and on other sweeping turns will not.  Combining unpredictable handling response with downhill driving at high speeds and ridiculous amounts of camera shake ended with me terminating the game.  Speeds that would result in my car being unable to steer were met by the AI with no issue at all, in fact the AI gained speed on some corners!  The difficulty spike is understandable, but I have zero desire to grind seconds off of long, twisting races where I cannot guarantee that handling will remain the same upon application of braking and throttle.  And elimination races with drift cars became simply tedious; starting in 9th with a drift car that you can not drift with - because contact with any other racer causes you to lose all steering regardless of contact point - makes it less a race and more a demo derby.  The game is still recommended, but only to racers of sufficient patience and understanding to deal with the game's plethora of puzzling design schemes.

The goal of Orbital, is to defend the specified planet from all incoming asteroids. Players start out as a single rock (such as the Moon) in the game, and can destroy smaller asteroids, or deflect larger ones via contact. You start off with 3 lives and 5 different abilities, all listed on the bottom of the screen.
It has a basic concept, and the controls pretty much meets its simplicity at that. You, as the rock, will always be moving in one direction, whether it’s left or right and cannot stop. I find that overtime, the difficulty does not increase nor do we get any upgrades, promos or hints and suggestions to the game. This easily leads to boredom, if a new objective is not presented, or if the level does not vary.
The art has the flat, 2D cartoon appeal to it, similar the Dumb Ways to Die game for those who are familiar with that. It’s simple, and easy to the eye when you put aside factors such as textures and strong detailing.
I don’t know where to start with the music. It’s like something you would hear from an old Galaxy film, and when the movie is at its climax. I find it humorous, but not in a bad way. That is consequently forgotten and followed up by exceedingly boring slice of life of the blandest kind. Seriously. You don't advertise "You're a boy crossdressing at a female school!!" and then do literally nothing with that. Your target audience isn't normals. It's weebs. You get three routes, two of which are nearly identical, railroaded, and filled with so many lame timeskips and things like the game telling you this character you've seen twice is suddenly your best friend. It even offers a Mass Effect-style ending decision node. Really?
Story aside, this game has next to no art assets. There are 18 event CG in the entire game, and several of that number are literally the same scene, just with different underwear on. The main character is drawn as a girl and called a guy (No, seriously, he has childbearing hips and wears eyeliner in your first look at him). There are three characters that have sprites, three expressions for each, and three sets of clothes: School, Casual, and Underwear. Oh, I guess the Principle has a yukata too. The game frequently forgets that the characters actually have multiple expressions to choose from; past the halfway point no one will react to anything visually again.
The background CG is horribly limited too. For instance, in one scene everyone starts commenting how it's night time and the fireworks going off are beautiful. There's no firework CG, no firework effects, no firework sounds, and the background is still bright with a blue sky like it's 1 PM. In another scene, you're supposedly in the gym showers getting mud and sweat off of yourself....and the background shows you in the school's entrance, by the shoe lockers. What?
Art isn't the only type of asset lacking in this game. There's no audio. The only sound you get is the repetitive soundtrack, which seems as limited as the Art in variety as well. Inappropriate music plays several times, setting a mood that doesn't reflect the text in the slightest.
And then just like that, the game's over. After nothing happens for an hour, you suddenly choose one of the girls and, if you chose to hang out with them a lot, you end up marrying her. It's bad. It's literally "Which do I choose?" [Hoshi] [Selina]. Oh, and [Lea] is only an option if you answered the first decision in the game correctly. Yes, the best route (with most of the CG and noteworthy scenes) is completely locked out if you express dismay at the idea of crossdressing to stay in the school. If you go full weeaboo and express some interest in crossdressing, Lea hops all over you. her route is the only one that's got any entertainment value in it, and I only enjoyed it because I could skip all the scenes without her, as I'd already completed most of the game at that point.
I unlocked all 18 event CG and had seen all scenes in this game, while streaming, in 2:41:00. This game is short, shallow, and unimaginative. It doesn't even play with its premise. By all means, send it as a gag gift to people. That's how I got it. But for your own sake, don't buy it and expect even a passable time. I'm surprised that the developers canceled their kickstarter to develop this privately; it really feels like they'd put something out just to say they did it. Even Katawa Shoujo is leaps and bounds ahead of this one.

I initiallly played the game back in January of 2012, so I'm sure the game has changed somewhat since I last played it due to updates, but I imagine my comments still apply. Battle Academy is a turn-based tactical WWII strategy game where you can command various infantry, tank, transports, etc across a tile based battlefield. The UI and clear presentation make it approachable for players without a lot of war game experience. Even though war is a serious subject, the story in the campaign is presented in a pretty light-hearted comic book / graphic novel style.The game has three campaigns covering North Africa, D-Day and the Ardennes.
I enjoyed my time with Battle Academy. Movement, line of sight, and morale, along with detailed combat factors make for interesting battles. When I initially played the game the UI shrouded many of the details factored into combat, but the easy-to-mod data files and scripts do offer up all of the juicy bits. I actually modded the game so the UI exposed more of the factors (and I'm not a big modder, although I do have  a software development background). This lack of information was the biggest drawback for me, but more data may now be exposed by the UI without modding because according to the patch notes some more advanced tool tips were added. The scenarios provide enough of a challenge for victory with the option to try for more difficult achievements, accommodating a variety of skill levels. Ambushes and bombardments keep the tension up as you fear for the virtual soldiers traversing the open ground. Expansions, user-created content, and multi-player options should extend the game's shelf life. If interested you can visit my full
.

This game is absolutely amazing. It completely draws you in, your heart will be beaten, mashed and crushed but you will feel some of the deepest emotions you've ever felt in a video game.
My own personal story:
I had a small group of survivors. We'd been fairly cohesive and effective for the first couple weeks of the war, then we got a new survivor to the group. She was badly hurt and sick but I felt this deep compassion after reading her story. She's barely escaped with her life when soldiers (Never learned if they were government or rebel soldiers) burnt her village and killed her family. I knew we needed to help her, so I sent Marco out to gather some medical supplies so we could nurse her wounds and treat her infections.
Marco crept through an abandoned hospital to find our desperately needed supplies. There was a chance there would be soldiers but that was the only place left with medical supplies. Marco found the last of the supplies that were desperately needed. He made his way towards the exit when suddenly, a group of soldiers burst in from the way he came. Panicking, Marco sprinted towards the other exit as gunfire and curses were shot in his direction. The exit was within arms reach as two bullets lodged themselves in Marco's back. He collapsed dead on the floor.
I was in shock. This character, this person, I had grown attached to and heard their story was now gone, forever. I sat there and read as everyone in the group tried to come to grips with Marco's death. They cried the entire day, no one could be motivated to do anything, I cried with them. For a solid ten minutes I sat in front of my computer weeping over Marco, this friend I'd felt I'd known as lost. All the while the song from the soundtrack "We keep going" played in the background.
I cannot recommend this game enough to people but be forewarned, this game will leave you feeling some of the deepest emotions a game has ever made you feel.

One of the greatest games i have ever played, takes the entirety of war simulation games and simply says "you're all a bunch of posers, this is how its really done".
During the game you take control of a selected band of survivors each ranging in their skills from their capability to withstand emotional trauma to their skill at crafting and carrying and even down to their basic combat prowess and overall involvement with wartime activities, you as the player need to guide and manage this small group by collecting resources such as food and water as well as scrap materials and electronic components to try and improve your shelter, you can only scavenge for so long as the game readily reminds you so you will need to start producing some of your own things if you want any hope of survival.
Each of the differeing playthroughs has entirely new aspects and storylines to reveal to the player, on one playthrough the hospital has been seriously bombed but is still barely running thanks to the kind doctor there and in another it could be the hideout for a ruthless band of heavily armed thugs, not only that but you have to deal with the changing weather as winter is just around the corner and sitting in a ruin freezing to death is currently not on your survivors wishlists for their future's.

Hard Truck Apocalypse (HTA) is a game that harkens back to Elite / Wing Commander: Privateer type game. You're a lone trucker, prowling the highways, moving freight, and killing enemies. You can be as good as as bad as you wish, but if you enrage a faction none of their towns will let you enter and their units will shoot you on sight, leading to further bloodshed. As you upgrade your truck wtih better weapons and better models, you will become an unstoppable force of the highways... As you search the world for the killer of your father, are you prepared for the truth? And perhaps, find what caused the apocalypse? And if given a chance, what will you do about it?
As the game was released almost a decade ago, the graphics are a bit dated, and out of the box (or fresh install) it has several bugs but all of that can be easily worked around with a few easy edits of config.cfg file. The game is not very stable. There are two notable bugs: 1) sometimes when game's loaded the key commands won't work. You may need to load a game multiple times to make the keys work, and sometimes going into town (not gas station) may resolve it. 2) the game often crashes when transiting between regions (about once very 4-6 transits). You should save or quicksave just before you exit the region.
Despite the simple graphics, the game is much deeper than one would suspect. There are trade goods from each town and prices drop as you brought more in, and prices rise as you buy more. Enemies often drop loot which you can sell for profit. Trucks can be customized with various models of "cabs" and "beds", of various qualities. Some cabs and beds have additional weapons hardpoints and enhancement hardpoints so you can customize your truck. With dozens of weapons, from little 5.45mm MGs all the way to 20mm quad cannons to plasma cannons, lasers, mortars, and so on, you can customize the vehicle into your personal killing machine.
Bad parts about the game? No "autopilot" or even "cruise control". You have to hold down "w" to move forward, and you can't lock the view to "front" for driving, as the game relies on mouse-look for aiming your weapons, which is independent from your driving. This makes some driving quite tedious, esp. at the beginning when you have a relatively slow vehicle. Also, the game is in essence, a FPS where you "circle-strafe" the opponent. Depending on the vehicle, there will be a point where most guns can point toward, and that is where you want the enemy to be. Also, the game's translated from Russian, so there are PLENTY of translation errors here and there, typos, even a few "missing references". The plot is also quite... cliche.
Still, if you like Mad Max style games this will be right up your alley. Even if it's not, if you like the "lone wolf roam the world" genre you should give this game a try, esp. if you get it cheap.

You're probably familiar with the budget tactical shooter series called Delta Force. Black Hawk Down is the 6th installment of the series and inherits all the good things about the previous titles and executes them pretty well. Unlike the previous titles all your campaign missions take place in one country: Somalia.
The Visuals.
BHD has it's own engine and runs at DirectX8, 4:3 aspect ratio resolution. I managed to get it up to 1200p, it refused to go above. All widescreen solutions stretch / cut off the screen. Considering that it's budget titles made in 2003 the visuals are fine. Decent textures, fine poly count and nice drawing distance (like in every other DF title). Framerate is unlimited. Game is compatible with pretty much all Windows versions.
The Mechanics & AI.
You can switch between first and third person. You can lean around the corners, crouch, go prone. Before the mission start you have a loadout screen where you can choose your equipment (depending on the mission sometimes it's limited to 2-3 weapons). You have a map/radar that shows friendlies and items. There's no health regeneration, you can be killed in 1-3 shots. You can't pick up weapons from enemies, but you can use ammo and health boxes that are scattered around the map.
The enemy AI is simple. it gives as soon as a hostile sees you it gives a few seconds to react. If you don't eliminate the hostile during those seconds, then the hostile will start shooting at you. The enemy accuracy has been nerfed, but you have a high chance of getting killed if you simply stand without taking cover.
The Audio.
BHD is the first title to feature a lot of chatter between teammates and music tracks during mission.
The Gameplay.
There are 16 campaign missions. Your goal is to follow the orders, complete objectives and eliminate hostiles while avoiding any friendly or civilian casualties. You're given waypoints to help you navigate through the maps. Unlike previous titles BHD doesn't have much of long range fights in open areas like fields and mountains. During the campaign you'll be advancing through villages, cities and even bunkers. For each mission you're given a limited amount of saves.
Delta Force series are not for everyone. I'd recommend to actually trying one of the titles to see if a tactical shooter is your thing. It doesn't have fancy visuals or AI, but it's fairly enjoyable.

All in all, Thief is decent, but far from great. I would not necessarily recommend that someone who isn’t already a Thief fan buy this game at full price, rather saving it in their wishlist until it goes on sale. Anyone with an immediate desire to play a story-driven stealth role playing game should pick up the (by now) cheaper Dishonored, which told a better story in more ways than one. Or, if you are inclined to take your punk “cyber-” rather than “steam-”, Eidos’ own other classic PC reboot, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a better stealth role playing game, as well.
Here are some things to ask yourself as you consider whether or not to swoop out of the shadows and snag a copy of Thief:
Do you like fancy graphics? Thief definitely has these. The world is richly modeled and textured, and the lights and shadows of The City make for a deep, if claustrophobic visual experience.
Are you sick of “grimdark” reboots and grey-brown game worlds? If so, stay away from Thief until you’re prepared for its grimy, lifeless, violent world, and un-ironically moody, flat characters.
Do you love stealth games? Thief is a mixed bag where its stealth gameplay is concerned. On one hand, the “pick your path” element is deeply flawed due to the relationship between level design and the game’s oddly restrictive movement system, which results in obvious paths that are very linear. On the other hand, the AI is better than in most stealth games, and if you find that the game lacks challenge, there are extensive built-in difficulty mods which will also earn you higher standing on a global leaderboard (if you’re into that kind of thing).
Are you looking for a great story? You will absolutely not find that here. The pacing is off, the cutscenes are of poor quality, the characters are unlikable, and all in all it doesn’t really feel like the protagonist has that much to do with what’s going on in the world.

If you're a hardcore Thief-fan, this game is definitely not for you. I was more than a little disappointed with all the deviations this game makes from the original Thief-series. Already at the main menu, you can hear the music is more like that of an action movie, rather than the fearful noises and tunes found in Thief. The next thing you notice is that they're using a new voice actor, which is really a pity, but as you play you'll find that this new Garett does a real good job in mimicking the original Thief voice. However the language of the previous thief games is gone, replaced with a more modern and American linguistic. Next, the character of the City. The city atmosphere is completely different, more akin to a medieval city with christian chapels, rather than the conflict between hammerites and pagans. The city's secret order seems to be completely gone, replaced by an old blind lady in some ruins - a poor and cliché-like replacement. Finally, the levels. It seems each map is divided into sealed compartments. You only get one chance to loot each compartment, and each compartment can only be progressed from one entry, and left by one exit. What was once open maps, and an open city, is now more or less a straight path on rails (at least that's the feeling I got while playing). Still, for people who can accept some deviation, this game represents a good addition to the stealth game genre. Voice acting is good, cut scenes are well-made, and maps are very well designed. The game looks stunning, and there's definitely some fun to be had, which is why I can actually recommend playing this game.

"If you're not dreading every single monster encounter then its not horror is it? You're just setting up a failing pest control bussiness."
If you're a fan of survival horror this is something you're gonna wanna grab.
The monster population is actually surprisingly but pleasingly small - it means its still an event as well as surprisingly and worrying when you actually run into one or two of em - instead of mowing them down by the dozen with a sword or machinegun.
Every enemy type (but some more than others) can cause a serious amount of damage and even poison or make you bleed. Going into sneak mode and trying to get by unoticed is possible but if you get caught, panic and open fire any nearby enemies are gonna start smashing down doors and running about looking to finish your weakened♥♥♥♥♥off.
On top of this the cold is quite a serious problem - lose track of time while out scavenging for food or meds and you can find yourself after hours, in the dark, in minus twenty degrees celsius snowstorms with about five feet of visibility. You see a crumbling structure up ahead and head inside hoping to find some shelter and maybe somewhere to set up a fire and sleeping bag - only to hear the growls and footsteps of the current ocupants. Which would you prefer: sitting there next to the fire all night staring at the doorway and hoping they don't find you, or go off and try and clear the building out in both the cold and dark?
Included in the game are skills which can be upgraded with points found while generally looting or sometimes on the corpses of slain monsters. Skills include resistance (cold, posion) crafting (more items to make) strength (bare fist damage, carry weight) and more.
Also, bases. Technically a player can make any building they found and clear out their home sweet home but they also have the option of crafting four different buildings (ascending in size) almost anywhere they want. In the same "buildings" tab "homely" craftable items are avilable such as crafting tables, storage boxes and torches to spruce up your new home or refurbish your current one, and fotifications such as wooden walls and spike barricades.
Oh and did I mention that like in project zomboid and one or two other games that enemies don't appear on your screen unless you are facing them? That means to make sure a building is completly secure, every cuboard, toilet, nook and cranny much be searched. This also means that you may not notice an enemy was hiding around the corner until its picking its teeth with your bones, or that the enemies chasing you were a lot closer than you thought but didn't know until you stopped running and turned around to check.
Cons: (In order of nit-picky-ness)
Player controls, movement and combat, are pretty clunky - its next to impossible to defeat an enemy using melee without taking a few hits.
More craftable items needed - walking around with a cart full of transistors, insulation, paperclips, light bulbs etc. that sound like they may be useful in some contraption but at the moment seem to have no purpose in crafting.
Player appearence doesn't change - may seem mild but I dislike when your character doesn't change when equipping new armour/clothes. It shows clear progression and looks silly in this game when in reality you are wearing several polar bears to brave the winter colds but your character appears to be knocking about wearing jeans and a t-shirt.
I could continue nitpicking but many of these will likely be fixed after a few months or when out of early access and if, like me, you're a fan of survival horror this is a game you are gonna want to keep your eye on.

11/27/14 Edit:
This game is not without its problems, but overall, I would highly recommend it. If you are looking for huge improvements over Far Cry 3, you will probably be disappointed. The gameplay is virtually identical with its frat-boy protagonist, outposts, hunting and crafting, and missions that seem like a chore that takes you away from the real fun of the game. The real reason to purchase this game is for the co-op. Drop-in/drop-out (with a reload) co-op allowing full access to the map in its entirety with all missions and events fully accessible takes this game from an ok sequel to an awesome evolution of an already great game. It adds a level of polish that makes it everything Far Cry 3 should have been.
Now, the things that annoy me. For one, they still have not fixed the "black screen" crash issue. I know it has been fixed for some but it hasn't for me, despite Ubisoft's patch and insulting comments about making sure I meet the minimum requriements. I can get the game to run but only after several launch and crash attempts do I actually get to the main menu.
Also, eagles. Ubisoft, why? You cannot walk anywhere in the game without being spontaneously assaulted from the air every five minutes by a random bird. These do not provide the game experience with any additional challenge whatsoever but serve only as a nuisance. I often find myself spending more time looking up at the sky while trudging around in the bushes than looking for men on the ground with machine guns.
Mouse acceleration. This game has it BAD. It cannot be disabled, despite editing game configuration files and trying just about every fix one can find on Google at this point. There is a workaround if you have a mouse with adjustable DPI which is not a fix in any sense but works quite nicely as a temporary workaround until (hopefully) Ubisoft fixes the issue. If you set the in-game mouse sensitivity all the way down and set the DPI on your mouse to max (or whatever is comfortable to you), the mouse acceleration will be saturated each time you move the mouse and in turn, it will be negated. However, when entering menus, your mouse will be far to sensitive so this works best with mice that have on-the-fly DPI adjustment.
There are many other small bugs, such as ropes getting embedded in rock faces and not allowing you to scale any higher while grappling. These things are annoying but can be dealt with. Overall, I would definitely recommend this game if you plan on playing co-op. There's just something hilariously awesome about tromping around and exploding things with a friend, or tag teaming outposts after formulating a long, thought out strategy that never seems to go as you planned.
TL;DR: It has its annoyances, but it's way too much fun to pass up. Highly recommended.

I wanted to like this game. I wanted to recommend it. I really did... but I can't. I just can't. When I first heard about DARK, prior to it's release, I was extremely excited. It was a promising concept... a vampire game that focused more on stealth than outright combat, but alas, it was not meant to be.
DARK is a short, clunky trek through 6 chapters of repetition. It took me about 12 hours to complete the game my first time through (which I did on Hard), but I took my time through the chapters trying to kill every enemy, and left the game sitting paused several times, so my real time was probably closer to 10 hours or so. Again, that's my first playthrough, and on Hard, so make of that what you will. The game is exclusively single-player, and there's really no incentive whatsoever to play through the game a second time as there are no branching paths or decisions, and the individual "challenges" accessible from the main menu are pointless unless you're interested in leaderboards.
The game features no real combat system. It's allllllllll stealth and stealth kills, unless you use your vampiric powers, but those are intended to be used from stealth as well. Speaking of powers, while they're fun to use for a while, they're largely irrelevant. You could make it through the game fairly easily without using any of them. When you do use them, they're incredibly powerful when maxed out (which can be done rather fast) despite having cooldowns, and make the game very easy. The AI is very, very simple and easy to out-maneuver throughout the entire game, and they all follow a set patrol pattern with no real variation.
The story is poorly written and honestly barely even there. You're a vampire, with classic hero amnesia, and you have to find the person who turned you (or a powerful elder vampire) in order to avoid a horrible fate. Between the opening and the ending, there's very little else. Almost no character development whatsoever, not even for the main character, and a forced sort of last minute romance between your character and only other person in the game you know more than 2 or 3 things about. It's an odd feeling to listen to these characters and know that they're voiced by talented people, but have the writing be so bad. The protagonist Eric is voiced by none other than Doug Cockle, who voiced Geralt in the Witcher games, but even he can't hide the terrible writing. It's all rushed, vague, short, and flat out generic. Not to mention there is a colossal plot hole at the end of the game. Huge. I won't say it here for obvious reasons, but it's such a huge plot hole it's astounding they didn't notice, or didn't care. The other sounds aren't anything too special, but nothing really stood out as bad to me, except for a couple character's voices. Music is very meh, and I can't remember a single bit of it except for the same song that plays on a loop in the pseudo-hub you enter in the beginning of the game. It also features probably the lamest, easiest, most pathetic final boss any game has ever had ever.
The graphics are stylized in a comic-book style, but are pretty bland outside of 3-4 fairly interesting areas. Outside of those limited sections, most of what you'll be going through are large rooms of offices or similar obstacles connected by small hallways or elevators. That is most of the game. The animations are absolutely atrocious. Your character's walking, crouching, running, etc animations aren't that bad, but everything else is. It all feels and looks clunky. Anytime you stealth kill a character it's there. If you feed on someone, every. single. time. you can see that Eric's lips aren't anywhere near the victims neck. It's just bad. Lip sync is also pretty off. With that said... I really liked the vampire vision. It's hard to describe, but the world is viewed in shades of white, purple, and black in this view, and you can see living things through walls and such as red silhouettes, and it kind of looks almost on fire, with everything moving and... well, it just looks cool. It also slows down time when you're using it, and there's no limit to it. It's probably the best thing about the game, but as cool as it is, that's kind of sad.
Lastly, I have to mention the save system. The game auto-saves at certain parts thoughout the game, but it also gives you the option of manually saving a limited number of times. Two times, actually. Seems like a strange number of saves, but hey, once you get the hang of the game it's not too hard to rely on the auto-saves. Granted, it can be annoying to redo sections of the map because you made one mistake, but it's not too hard and with only two manual saves, what can you do? Well... press F5, actually. Yeah. Despite you having a limit on how many times you can save through the pause menu, you have unlimited use of the F5 quicksave. The game never tells you about F5, and it isn't anywhere in the options. Why? Why are there two separate ways of saving the game manually? Why is one way obvious and limited, and the other completely hidden but unlimited? It's a mystifying decision on the part of the developers and just another indicator of a rushed, sloppy game.
Overall, DARK is a very underwhelming experience, and very disappointing to me personally. It's not necessarily a bad game... but it's very, very sub-par, and not worth anywhere near what it's priced at. I did have fun at some parts, but it was almost in a trance like state, like I had been tricked into not being bored. It's hard to describe. I can say that I don't regret my purchase, as I do like stealth games and vampire lore quite a lot, but I can't recommend anyone purchase it unless the game is around $10.

A decent game with some flaws.
This is one-of-a-kind game, you drive a truck, fight other trucks, collect and trade gear, go on missions, talk with people in cities, buy new gear and trucks in said cities, visit several lands, all the while trying to discover who killed your father.
It sports one of the best soundtracks ever, which adds to the post-apocalyptic atmosphere.
Combat is against other trucks, generally you'll have three adversaries which spawn and try to chase you.
Pathfinding is ridiculous. Merchants carry goods from city to city, but mostly try to climb up trees or manouver in circles. Baddies are a little bit more intelligent, they'll follow you but they never reach full speed, so it's very easy to just outrun them. There are also some scripted ambushes and boss battles.
The plot is nothing new, but it gives a thread to follow, and opens new areas to explore.
Trading goods generates good money - and you'll need it to buy more powerful trucks - but the best way to strike it rich is through combat and gathering of the remains of your enemies.
The game lacks polish, the translation is approximative and it has its lot of annoying bugs, but it can be quite rewarding when you buy a new truck, new gun or discover a new area to explore. Even the plot becomes interesting after a while.
Give it a try, it's worth your time.

I really don't write reviews for games/titles that don't deserve them so this is a gem...
If you're looking for an unforgiving, tense and fun title then Frozen State ticks those box's. At first there is a learning curve but the experiance and self achievment pays off.
So far it contains a good fair sized map that is explorable through the style of point and click to pick locations then entering those areas to explore, loot, hunt, build and die in... and once you die you are dead for good, yes this game is perma-death... which is one of it's great characteristics.
Other features include:
Crafting weapons, food & drink, traps, medical items and building supplies.
Building structures for living in, home defences, storage and decoration.
Hunting & Tracking of animals for food and materials.
Transport in the form of a Truck (Only found it myself, yet to get that thing running.)
Skills to pick from through leveling up by finding a specific drug.
Medical system in which you can suffer burns, poisoning, bleeding, fractures etc.
Weather system in which the majority of the time you will be needing to keep warm (as the game is based in a fictional siberian city)... along with some blizzards for visual effect that hinders your visibility.
A.I in this game is so good for a title in it's early stages... it's possible to steath around and use distractions which is probably your best bet to survive but it's possible to win fights against even the hardest of mutants through using tactics.
Has more, I know this but I have not fully tried every feature/mechinic myself.
A title to support/keep on your radar for future release.

The art was cute, more or less "aesthetically pleasing" from MY point of view (although some might disagree), and the characters were fairly interesting with seemingly different backgrounds and personalities, albeit I suppose it would've been appreciated to branch a bit more on their characters-- It may've made them a bit more 3D in a way, but beggars can't be choosers.
Aside from all the interesting options, the semi good music (it wasn't bad but it wasn't overly good & the changes weren't all that in 'sync', if that makes sense, making it a bit off to listen to-- More or less, overly joyful music & suddenly a dreary tone slips in. Otherwise it was pretty good for the most part), and the pretty cute characters (ngl Shoji has wormed "her" way into my heart among the other characters), the gameplay itself was....lacking to say the least.
As many others have stated, the game was far too short and I honestly would've appreciated a lot more, maybe some other characters and various scenes which would've made it a bit more fun! (There were some scenes that were described but didn't have a picture which was a tad bit upsetting to say the least-- For further clarification, i'm not talking about the scenes that progressed soon after one of the CG's showed up or the small tidbits describing certain things progressing around the main character).
There were a few grammar mistakes & some of the CG's weren't necessarily linked up to what was being said, for example, Shoji would mention something about putting his shirt back on but in the CG he'd still be in a bra or whatever-- Just nitpicky things, nothing that detracts from the overall gameplay and nothing to really, you know, fuss about.
Aside from the cons to this game, i'd really only recommend this to people who're looking for short gameplay and very FEW characters (as well as choices). Can't really complain about the price as it wasn't OVERLY expensive but not TOO cheap to be considered a rip-off of it's worth.

Magic Duels is the most cost effective way to play Magic in a way that feels like the real game. There are a number of negative reviews and, while there are some valid concerns (the game interface is no Hearthstone...the animations slow the game down way too much - even the card playing ones -, and there are a number of cards and game modes you simply cannot play that you could with MTGO or the actual cards), the good FAR FAR outweighs the bad. Advantages as follows:
1) The game is absolutely free to play and is not riddled with advertisements. While you do not start with amazing cards and people who pay will get better cards much sooner, earning cards is much more efficient than Hearthstone and feels, to me at least, to be worth the grind. I have not paid a cent for the game (though I may in the future) and probably have close to half of all the cards you can get from all 5 expansions, including many powerful mythic rares and planeswalkers. Yes, my "hours played" is closing in on 300, but it should be noted that I have left the game on many times, including overnight multiple times that has artificially inflated that time when I haven't been playing. You could get all the cards I have with significantly less play time.
Even if you choose to buy cards out of the gate, this game will NEVER approach the costs of real Magic (which can be cost prohibitive if you really want to play with the best/most powerful cards)
2) The deck building is real! Unlike all prior duels games except 2015, you can make your own decks as you want. This was what really held the old duels games behind real magic in my mind. I didn't care as much about different game modes, but I wanted to make my own decks and try my own combinations. You can do that in duels and it keeps getting better, more nuanced and more interesting with each release.
3) Great way to learn magic. This has been talked about before, but introducing new people to Magic via Duels is the best way for them to learn, as the game can really hold your hand if you want it to.
4) All the great things about Magic remain true. Best CCG there is...beautiful art...fun interactions. Just a great game.
I wish that there could be more interaction with online opponents and that the game could be a bit faster, but overall, there is no other way to feel like you are playing real deal Magic for as low a cost. Love it!

This game will give you an exact and thorough evauluation of 'Is MtG for me?' without spending a single penny.
In my case, the answer is no - because i'm too invested in 40k to turn around and make Magic work as well. As such I can only review based on the digital component.
This product was excellent in showcasing, teaching and demonstrating everything that there is to enjoy about the game at a basic and intermediate level, and I would recommend it to everyone who hasn't had a chance to give Magic a try.
On top of everything else there is a genuinely good multimedia experience to be had from this - the music is solid, the narration and CGI is done in a way that neither intrusive or overblown, and the general atmosphere of the game experience is very good, to the point that ( as a table topper) I sincerely doubt the full meatspace product would compare favorably given the typical playing venues.
The FtP model is executed marvelously in that if you just want a casual diversion, you won't be drowning in intrusives or obnoxious power gaps. On the flip side, the premium component is a bit questionable since laying even £10 down on it wouldn't really give you all that much of a return on investment.
Try it, enjoy it, move on (if you can). This is not typical for FtP.

While I am not too big on this type of game (mostly do to issues with getting into matches), I do have to say: This is how you do it.
Compared to Rise of the Incarnates (at least when I tried it, I heard there have been changes, and thus might check it out again down the road), the tutorial is optoinal (though encouraged), and they give you enough in game cash to buy at least one fighter and a costume (or even a couple of fighters with standard outfits).
While the game shows only the controls for the keyboard and mouse, a controler is an option (a little trail and error and you can get it down)... but oddly, despite being a 'consoletard', the keyboard and mouse controls (aside from the placement of the 'special'... being 'alt'... kinda wonky when using wasd controls if you ask me) are actually rather smooth and make the odd angles many attacks take easier to work with.
I am a little bugged by the choices in character outfits and representation... but I'm not going to harsh as it's the standard array and not really anything too terrible (I mean, anything I would say on that end would apply to so many other games). Still would have loved a Heavy blade using woman as well as the guy.
Still, bonus points for giving us  hand to hand fighter that is an ice user too. Was just talking with a friend about the rarity of Ice powered pcs. Better yet? If I'm reading things right, the Ice version of 'Renny' came out BEFORE the flame version. Kudos on something a little different.
... So why don't I recommend this game? My friend said it best: There is nothing to hook me. Sure the characters are interesting and varied, the tutorial non-invasive (and repeatable too in case you come back later and forget how to control things), they let you try all the characters in the training mode, they give you a lot to look forward to in unlocks, and even the 'all access' dlc is damn reasonably priced given what you get out of it (some would even say damn generous)... but then that's it.
This is an arena style game. That is, you have to que up for matches, and some can even be on the training ground, which seems to futz up how the point earning works... on top of that there is this 'queen' version 'seven' thing that is -not- expalined, no mission mode, no adventure mode... just the arenas. Nothing else.
And worse? It feels like there aren't many folks even playing right now.
There is something here, there is a good game wanting to be made. But right now, it's not quite there yet. And this isn't early access. This really feels like a half finsished game to me. The controls could use some tightening, there could be a lot more to the modes... Basically, I get this is free to play, but it feels like there needs to be more here. If they promised to go more in the direction of more modes and what not and decided to run a kickstarter or something like that, something that would get them extra cash beyond just the all access pack, I would probably back it. There is a kernal of awesome here... there just isn't enough to recommend.
In sort: there is fun to be hand, but your mileage may vary.

Look, if you say combat-driving-rpg I am THERE, but if you have Windows 7 (or presumably above) this game is going to fight you at every step.  Particularly, it's impossible to leave the first area of the game, it crashes on the level transition 100% of the time.  There are supposed workarounds but none of them have solved the problem for me, so I'm just through with it altogether.
Besides... the actual driving physics aren't fun at all.  You feel like you're just sliding along the ground rather than actually driving.

The good:
Not much. Just to be clear I am going to slam this game long and hard below because I believe in being brutally honest, but there is actually some enjoyment to be had here. It may have its problems and be quite generic even for a game made in 2005, but the combat is not poorly done and overall the game is not poorly done. If you do not get bored easily and can appreciate that this game was released during the prehistoric age of gaming (2007 or before) and don't go into it with high expectations, you will find that it runs perfectly smooth with no technical issues (for me anyway) and is done competently enough that, as I said, a fair level of enjoyment can be gleaned from your time spent.
The bad:
Terribly generic and old. Anything 2007 and older (this is 05) is the prehistoric age of gaming and the farther we get away from those times of depressingly basic PC game programming equivalent to cavemen drawing on walls, the better. I became a PC gamer back in 1997 but I can admit that until more recent years gaming was just never very satisfying because technology has only finally become what gamers have been waiting for. Driving within five feet of a rock causes a collision even if you can visibly see you aren’t touching it. Collision detection/being stuck is a real problem: there is a unstuck key (O) but it only works selectively. It worked once earlier in the game for me, but recently it would not. I was fighting a truck and I wasn't watching where I was driving because it is tough to do while also having to aim at a enemy, and I rammed into a tree, broke it and it fell over, and it left behind an invisible stump underneath my truck that I was teetering on and could not get off of so I had to reload my game which thankfully I had just quicksaved a minute earlier. That's another thing about this game: no autosave whatsoever. F2 is quicksave and F3 is quickload, so be ready to press F2 constantly. Textures are poorly done: the graphics generally look like absolute garbage and I have seen on several occasions patches of grass floating a few feet above the ground. All textures also pop in and out: if it is going offscreen it will disappear until you move the camera in that direction and it will pop back in. This one is hilarious: your minimap has a N at the top meaning of course “North” but it also has a S at the bottom meaning of course “South”. The first couple hours playing this game I assumed it was a dollar sign because I do not recall ever seeing any game with more than just a N on the minimap, which if you have a N on the radar to show you which way is north, why the fk would you need an S at the bottom? Just astonishing. Probably the most intolerable part of the game is that it has the worst music in the history of gaming. But without the music on you are driving through miles of barren, lifeless, boring wasteland with nothing to do, no other cars to kill usually, so without the music all you are going to hear while driving is the hum of the engine, which is a poor sound effect at that. I suppose I could turn off the game's ear-bleedingly bad music and play my own music on windows media player but that still won't change the fact that you are going to be driving miles upon miles through nothing while doing nothing. You will have a TON of that in this game: driving through a wasteland with nothing to do but try not to fall asleep at the wheel. Sometimes you get to kill other cars, sometimes... You can't touch anything while driving or you will rack your repair bill up the @ss and repairs are not cheap: I broke through a wooden fence and it dropped my durability from 850 to 810 lol are you kidding me. It gets worse too: I was driving past a piece of fence and was clearly about 5ft away from it and it sort of snagged my truck and made it whip around and slam into a second row of fence beyond it, reducing my durability on my truck big time. Some of the worst programmed AI I've ever seen: enemies get stuck on objects sometimes and you just blast the ♥♥♥♥ out of them. Sometimes friendly AI vehicles will repeatedly try to slam through an unsmashable gate to get into the quest area where you are waiting to advance the game, whereas if they would just back up and go to the left or right a little they can get in. But no! ♥♥♥♥ that! Lets keep backing up and try to repeatedly ram through this solidly programmed gate! I suppose that can be added to the "good" section I have above since it really is pretty funny.
Overall, 6/10

An old rusty truck, whole lotta oil, a gun, and your journal. Shrouded in mistery your life is filled with numerous puzzle pieces that lead to a much bigger picture. Who are you? Who are these people? Where am I? What is this all about? Seek and you shall find, even learn more than the storyline is telling. Old worn out roads, telephone lines, monuments, secret places, biomes, the world of HTA just doesn't seem to have an end, and the story will put you in the right post-apocayptic mood for many hours.
Pros:
-Many hours of gameplay.
-Well designed open world (for an old game that is)
-Role play fun.
-Many quests, items, characters to reveal.
-Unique gameplay experience, very rare for this kind of game.
-A chilling storyline.
Cons:
-No autosave, if you don't save manually every now and then you will be left stranded. The manual saving works very well though.
-Few annoying bugs, they can be bypassed though.
-Lack of storyline detail in some quests, ie, could use more cutscenes and speech.
-Can get exhausting in travel at times.
-No multiplayer. If only this game had full-blown MP support!
Conclusion:
HTA is my second indie open world favorite for a very good reason. I've just replayed it for 7th-8th time after many years of not playing this game, and I can assure you the experience is memorable to say the least. My first indie open world favorite is A.I.M 1 and 2, which were developed and published by the same authors, and inhibit similar open world and post-apocalypse setting and storyline like HTA, albeit with a lot more detail and story telling. I strongly recommend both games and their sequels HTA: Clan Wars and A.I.M 2. If you treasure unique gaming experience look no further.

Overall it's actually a pretty good game. I was honestly surprised. It has some problems but it's also got a lot that makes it very interesting as a game. An easy way to describe the game is a mix of the
series,
series and trucks. It's a post-apocalyptic Privateer game where you control any sort of truck complete with weapons of all sorts.
Pros:
-Well designed gameplay. Good controls that do give you some of the heft of driving a truck.
-Plenty of weapons, that are even more realistic with varying penetration and degradibility.
-Large open world to explore.
-RPG elements, mostly in the form of quests.
-Trading system that where you can use coins gathered from quests, bartering or loot to get new weapons and supplies.
-Accurate damage modeling. I love when games do this because it makes it feel like you actually took damage. Your cab and your hold both take independent damage, and things such as damage tires and even bullet holes in where you were shot show up. However, damaged tires don't seem to affect the performance of the truck which I thought was weird.
Cons:
-Bad voice acting, if not downright wooden. You can tell that it's been translated literally from another language.
-Poor AI, at least on easier difficulties. I know that AI isn't supposed to be so grueling on easier settings, but I can honestly run into one with a consistent spray of machine gun fire and destroy it in a few seconds.
-Graphics are a little bland. Although most post-apocalyptic games are like this due to the lack of lush life so I don't have a major problem with it.
Overall, it's a fun game and I've barely gone down the rabbit hole in two hours. I see a lot of content in this one, and with all the decently-priced cards to sell you'd be hard pressed not to get it while it's on sale.
8/10

Who should watch “In Search of the Most Dangerous Town on the Internet: Where Cybercrime Goes to Hide”? Every politician, every business person, every internet user in the world, that’s who. If you want to know just how evil and blind huge sums of money can cause people to be, or how much justice and honorable behavior such utterly contemptible greed can bring out of those on the other extreme, this is a documentary NOT to be missed. (Did I mention it’s FREE?!)
ISotMDTotI:WCGtH is about “bulletproof” servers, the places that criminals and terrorists go to be permitted to steal, kidnap, grape(sic) and pillage the worlds PC and banks, citizens, and even governments, and to a lesser degree it’s about those who see no problem with allowing such for-profit activity to occur. It’s about those who knowingly host ISIS (even on servers IN America), and are "dedicated" to protect them…..for money. As well, about those who may or may not be aware, and essentially just turn a blind eye. It’s about nuclear bunkers that could not easily be breached by the world’s armies, and offshore “nations” and simple apartments that are nearly as safe, due to the nature of the internet.
“In Search of the Most Dangerous Town on the Internet: Where Cybercrime Goes to Hide” also features organizations such as Anonymous that use their immense skills to protect the world, and those innocents that may yet inhabit it. The computer savvy “good guys”, those just as able to profit from their skills, but who would rather do good, despite the cost.
There are those saying it’s nothing more than a strategy to sell a product, but it’s professional standards tend to negate those complaints. As well, no product or company is mentioned, and only one employee is briefly interviewed, and clearly with no marketing agenda. Besides, a company only interested in promoting their own skills and products would have a MUCH narrower focus, and would not likely offer the degree of hope this feature offers to balance the genuine fear generated by what we see every day is clearly the truth, and is growing at a vastly geometric progression. While short (23 minutes) it gives a hard, fast punch, then offers a hand up for the future.
See it……because WHY THE HELL NOT!?!?
