The concept is really interesting and different. A 3D fighter action game. But this game fails in execution in a few ways.
Visual Design and Audio: I actually very much enjoy the design of this game, the visual style of each character is very unique which is important because even if you're new, it's unlikely that you'll get confused as to which character your opponent is playing as their sillouettes are all fairly recognizable. With the exception of Remmy, which if you happen to be blue/red color blind, you'll have a rough time telling the difference between the two unless you see them attack. The music is actually pretty nice, it's upbeat which helps get you in the mood for fighting. You can find some of the tracks on youtube if you want examples. I probably wouldn't listen to it without the game but it's all right to say the least.
Gameplay: You control one of the champions in the game, each champion has a different light and heavy attack, you can "combo" with these attacks which is just simply light attack a couple of times then heavy attack, maybe sometimes you jump after you launch them into the air. Each character also has 2 special attacks bounded to your Q and F key by default, these attacks take up meter that is built up by simply fighting other players. These moves have the potential to change the tide of the fight but actually don't feel too overpowering in some situations. Now if the gameplay worked all the time then it would be much better, many times I would find myself directly in front of players and my punches look like they are going through the enemy but they don't "hit". But then there are times when punches clearly are not landing but are still "hitting." This brings me to my next topic
Development: None. This game failed to meet the expectations of the devs and thus the company had to let this game go. There is no more support for this game, absolutely none. Found a bug on a map that keeps bothering you? I guess you have to deal with it. Think this character is overpowered or not fun to play against? Well tough nuts because it's staying like that. Do you want more content? Ha, good one. I point this out because this is something that can turn off A LOT of players. The idea that their game will literally never change is something that grow stale really quickly and deter a lot of players. For example, there are only about 7 or so maps if you don't include the training room, how many times can you play in the exact same map in an FPS before it gets old? Many of these maps have some glaring design flaws but these are the only maps you have so you better get over it. Speaking of which
Community: Nobody plays this game, absolutely no one. There are about 20-30 servers and only 3-4 of them will actually have players on them. Now people in this community can be split into 2 categories, 1. People that were browsing the F2P games section on Steam and decided to give it a shot, and 2. The people that REALLY play Archeblade, these people are nuts, while I give them credit for being fantastic at the game and putting a lot of practice into it. It causes this issue in games where the new players constantly just get pub stomped by these players who have been playing for a really long time. But when the match is over, you're going to hit that rematch button anyway and get stomped again because there are no other servers and they might even be full, so this might be the only game that you CAN play, which plays once again into that issue of limited map selection, maps on servers never rotate, so if you're playing during off hours and only one server has people, you better hope it's a map you like cause it's not changing. And the community doesn't have much time to actually communicate. The post game lobby will kick you if you don't hit rematch right away so you can't really type there except for a quick gg. But the times I've spoken to some players, many of them did seem pleasant. Even some players who have been around for a long time. I suppose out of fear of losing players to an already dying game.
The shop: So because this game has been out of development, there isn't really much of a "cash shop." After each game you earn in game currency which you can use to purchase more champions to play as, costumes, and even cosmetic accessories that you can custimize your character with. If you play this game and you find that you really enjoy it and want to support it. There is DLC on the Steam page for 10$ that will unlock ALL CONTENT. This includes characters, costumes, accessories, etc. Which if you've ever played FTP games you'll understand really quickly that it's a great deal if you find yourself playing more.
To sum up: The reason I don't recommend this game, is simply because there is no support anymore, while playing, I crashed a couple of times. A LOT of my hits didn't register despite the enemy standing perfectly still, many times while playing one character Renoah, I would be scoped in, the enemy wouldn't be moving, the crosshair will be directly over them, I click, nothing, no damage, no hit stun, none. This isn't me whining about "being bad" I know I'm bad, which leads to my next complaint that every single game has 2-3 players who play this game really often and are still loyal to it, hence they proceed to just walk all over me. If this game didn't have the buggy combat and small community, I would probably find myself playing this more. But since this game will no longer be getting support and I don't feel like doing a huge uphill battle of trying to become skilled at this game when there are already a lot of really strong players. I feel like it's just too discouraging for new players.

You know, I really wanted to like this game. Civ is what got me into gaming, and the idea of a redone alpha centauri had a lot of appeal. However, it suffers hugely from two things. First, Firaxis' DLC strategy, wherein they release a game that's mostly there, then introduce new core mechanics and major improvements in high-price DLCs afterwards. Second, there have been a lot of 4X competitors in recent years, and they've really shown up how poor the Civ series has become.
While Rising Tide fixes various issues, it makes others worse. Diplomacy is notionally more sophisticated, but very easy to farm. The factions don't really feel different, and the technologies are just confusing. In particular, the world doesn't draw you in, even with the new additions - they're basically controllable barbarians. Thjere's very little of the replay appeal that's given by Civ's history, or other game's meaningful differences between factional playthroughs.
Buy Endless Space instead, or Galactic Civilizations.

The game is a good strategy just like Civ 5. There are a few things that are good and annoying.
I like the idea of different planets, aliens, colonizing, Unit upgrades, and water bases. The planets have different look and feel to them which makes the unique. The aliens add a layer of challenges and even have the ability to capture them for your own use which is cool. Colonizing now is more challenging due to needing to protect your new found colony before it becomes a settlement. It gives the aliens a chance to take out a weak addition to your empire. The unit up greats gives you a chance to pick how you use you units based on different stats to choose from at the time of upgrade. My favorite addition is water colonies. You can found a settlement on water and even move it around the ocean tiles to expend your empire quickly. It adds a few cool things to the mix and keeps it fun.
Some of the annoying things are the limited units, aliens, artifacts, and exploration. After a while, the units just feel lacking and depth is missed. I liked the air and ships in Civ 5, but here you only get one air unit and 4 ships, but 20 different land units. Aliens are a cool addon, but at same point, it is like the spawn like no tomorrow. Most of my end games are just filled with them in spots I haven't colonized which make exploring hard. The thing I find annoying with artifacts and exploration is the lack of in game information on it and makes it hard to do the achievement for the artifact wonders.
Over all with the expansion, I wouldn't pay $40 for it like I did. I would say about $25 worth of entertainment since most of it felt reskined Civ 5 with a few new features that aren't explained well in the game. Still is a decent strategy turn based game. If you like achievements, there are some challenging ones with this game.

There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're minimalistic. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio. The visual and audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
"This War of Mine" from the developer 11 Bit Studios. It places, the players, into a position that they never thought to find themselves in.
a civilian in a war torn country.
Simulates what its like to be a civilian to be trapped in a war torn country. Survival becomes very critical because there's danger lurking at every turn. Everyday resources become ones' prized possession. As crimes runs rampant, the rule of logic and order, no longer exists.
There are plenty of pre-generated events for the players to choose from. The players can even create their own events and shared them with other players.
Morality is heavily present in the game. This gives the players a freewill to choose whether they want to be a good person and help out or a bad person and not help out. The choices that the players makes it can have either a positive or negative influence on the civilians.
There are multiple endings to this game it's heavily affected by the players' morality and the course of action they've decide to take.
There's a downloadable content called "War Child Charity." It features various artwork from various graffiti artists. These artworks are scattered throughout game for the players to find them. They are to reflect the condition of civilians in war torn countries.
[Please do note that there are different pricing for this downloadable content but they all have the same content. It depends on how much you want to spend on the downloadable content. It's a charity donation.]
There are twenty-two different achievements can be earned from the game. Each of these achievements has certain requirements to completed before they can be obtained.
There are total of six different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam's Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it's Booster Pack Creator.
Final thoughts, I felt that this is a really great game to play and enjoy, it can really draws you into wanting more out of the game. As for the game's replay value it's definitely high. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

I love this game!
The character customization is a nice feature, as it allows you to make your own avatar from built-in parts.
The arenas are nicely designed and not too large and barren or cramped. 4-8 players can make for some crazy multiplayer matches.
When it comes to the weapons, I like how there are two sets of abilities - one for mostly offensive weapons and another for tactical items, both of which you can use at anytime. The weapons are easy to pummel opponents with, but the tactical items take some getting used to. There's missile launchers and beam weapons, swinging ropes, traps, rocket boots and other cool toys to play around with. People will definitely have a favorite set of items in this game. I'm fond of the launcher+shield combo. The cool thing about the items is that they have limited ammo, forcing you to pick up other stuff and keeping other players from being too powerful.
It'll take some time to get used to the game's controls. They might feel a bit overwhelming at first but after some time practicing it can be pretty awesome dodging bullets all the while ramming into other players and knocking them into pits. Even when you have your default weapon which is pretty weak, it doesn't mean you're easy prey to other players. This makes the game pretty balanced no matter what items appear.
Overall Gem Wars is easy to pick up and really fun! But, it is challenging to master all the different moves and items at your disposal. The good thing is that learning the ins and outs of the game isn't required to have fun. But once you do, it opens up a whole new world of offensive and defensive strategies, which makes the game even more fun. A tournament scene can easily grow around this game.
Cheers to the developer, it can only get more awesome from here! Put a lot more content in and the game will be a must buy on Steam with the $4.99 price point.

I know, I know I don't usually play these games. Actually I kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥talk them on the podcast a lot. Not the individual games themselves, but the concept of local multiplayer on a PC. It's just not my cup of tea. However, I mentioned the release of Gem Wars on the last episode of the podcast(here's the exact spot on the video version -
and was contacted by the developer with a key and asked me to check it out. So I obliged.
I'm glad they reached out to me. This game is just oozing charm. From the upbeat soundtrack to the hand drawn sprites.  The music, in particular, plays right into a frantic back and forth co-op game, high energy and fits the gameplay. The art shows in the detail of the level design and character design. The character design in particular allows you to customize your eyes, mouth, head, tail and a few other options. Giving you the ability to separate yourself from your friends and make your character unique to you.
The gameplay control is a tried and true platforming. What separates this game is again it's charm. All the weapons you pick up feel and control differently. The shooting aspect just feels really good. You will also have access to a tactical set of items that change the playing field by dropping bear traps or placing temporary walls. I can't speak to the actual multiplayer portion, however, I have to imagine it plays just fine.
My only gripe is the way controller support is handled. Having to map my own controller seems odd and kind of out dated. I'd love to see an update that would recognize the controller when plugged in and maybe a tutorial that shows what those buttons do. It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥trying to remember which button is the "Advanced" key.
Keep an eye on this one though, the developer plans to roll out an Adventure Mode which will be more single player focused and a Colosseum Mode that will be an online campaign that will allow you to make friends, have rivals, and wager bits on matches. (Bits are the currency you earn from playing to purchase some of the character customizations)
Overall, Gem Wars is a low cost co-op platformer with so much charm you'd think it was a picture of a cat on the internet.

I can understand if people are nervous about paying for an Alpha game, however few alpha games are as good in there early states as this one. This is an Alpha game that has tremendous content very early on.
It is a survival game but very few games make winter an enemy. Cold weather can kill you if your not paying attention to your temperture and if you decide to take on a hybrid, (the current enemy in the game) you have to be fast because some will kill you without thinking about it. This game is not a complete rougelike but if you die, you restart, and about ninety percent of the items and objects are procedural generated. Plus (as I said above) the enemies are as deadly as the weather itself.
Now the game is early so it has it's fair share of bugs, but from my experience I didn't come across any game breaking bugs and I play this game on a laptop with an Intel hd graphics 4000 (I did have to reduce some graphic settings). There's not much that I dislike about this game, the enemies are done right so far, keeping track of your characters health (food, water, etc..) isn't too bad, and having the random generation changes things up a bit.
The issues that I do have, is that there is no sprint button. So it takes a while to do certain things such as gathering wood to build your cabin. There's no map, so it's very easy to get lost if you don't keep track of what your doing. Also there's only three enemy types and there's only one that I try to avoid (fortunately more are going to be added soon). Besides that there isn't anything else that bothers me, I would highly recommend you try this. The Developer is very nice and he listens to people on the forums. Most devs don't do that. :)

Soooo this game... it is enjoyable in my opinion. Is it worth $8? I would say no which is why I bought it when it was on sale. I began on the hardest difficulty just to see what the game had in store for Chopin (Hardest difficulty). These are the difficulties in sequential order (should go without saying, but just in case): 1. Too Easy  2. Normal  3. Hard  4. Chopin. Honestly I could not see the difference between Hard and Chopin as they looked the same to me. People who are saying that "Too Easy" is difficult surprise me. ESPECIALLY when they've only played the game for 0.1 hours. If you're one of these people.... please.... shut up. Give it at least an HOUR before bashing on this game's controls and saying that "Too Easy" is hard.
Now as for the controls.... the default ones are pretty weird and uncomfortable. I never used the mouse so I have no idea what other people are talking about. I changed my controls to make the game easier. I left ASDF alone, but changed the black keys to IOP since it made the game easier. That being said, the controls still were weird and take some time getting used to. I do not play the piano nor have I ever used you in a serious manner, yet the game was still fairly easy. So do you need experience with playing a piano to be good or decent at this game? No. Would it help if you did?.... Well I cannot answer that since I do not play the piano.
As for the story, I felt that it was slow paced. No I don't mean there was filler, just it seemed like there were many awkward pauses between dialogues. I came into this game hoping to get a few laughs in, but that did not happen. I would say it was mainly due to the long pauses between dialogues. Think of it as a joke in real life, your friend builds you up and towards the end he just pauses too long and by the time the punch line is delivered, you go, "Eh/ Meh" since they took too long. A poor analogy probably since I did not feel any build up from this game to begin with. Story was good for the price paid though and the graphics were great, like the art style.
Now for the music in the game, I personally only liked the music from Falcon's, Villain Mike's, Russian Robot Dancer's, and the final boss's battle. All of the other songs did not really appeal to me or feel like they fit in with the person you were competing with.
Also here's a tip for you people who think "Too Easy" is hard... try playing Geometry Dash, Super Hexagon, The Impossible Game, Melody's Escape, or Audiosurf 2 (Fast paced songs) . Those games will help improve your reflexes for those types of games and games like Frederic: Evil Strikes Back. I highly recommend Geometry Dash out of all of these though since it really helped me with my timing. And play levels on Hard, Insane, or even Demon to really improve. If you stick with the easy levels, you'll be wasting your time..... though you're wasting your time regardless if you play easy or not.... whatever do what you want in your "valuable" life. Hope this helped or got a smirk out of your depressing face. (If you take offense to this then............ I don't know how you handle the real world if you cannot handle some sarcastic internet crap.)

Defeat famous opponents in musical duels. Immense yourself in fantastic story of Frederic's endeavors. Catch all the Easter Eggs and subtle parodies hidden in the background. Practice your skills until perfection and become the Master of the Piano.
The world of music is once again threatened. The art of soulful music, the kind that touches your heart, is in grave danger of disappearance. The evil forces that you fought so bravely are back! And they are even more powerful and desperate. Once again you'll need to step into Frederic Chopin's shoes and face opponents that have only one agenda - to enslave the musical world, mass produce soulless artists with their same-sounding radio hits, and reap enormous profits, hindering any creativity in the process.
This time around, Frederic is almost insufferably full of himself, not to mention extremely modernized. This could have worked if some amount of time had passed, but the story is supposedly set immediately after the ending of the last game. He frequently trades substance for style, which seems to be running theme of this game this time around. It's still entertaining, it's just sad to see the hero, who was so lovable the first time around, turn into something rather obnoxious with little reasoning for it.
The part that was disappointing to me, however, was the story. The first game was quirky and charming, with clever satire mixed with other jokes and jabs at pop culture or random silly bits strewn about. Frederic himself was a somewhat smug, if charming, fish out of water, what you would expect of a composer who had been dead for a century and a half being brought back to life in today's world, trying to adjust to modern musical trends while keeping his own legacy alive and learning the reason for his return
All in All

I had a strange relationship with Cook Serve Delicious! 2!!
When I bought it, I was incredibly excited for another CSD game. Then, as I started to play it, I found myself getting bored near the beginning, wondering what the point of everything was - if my restaurant wasn't upgrading with every star level, what was I even working toward the top for? Then I realized I was living in CSD nostalgia, and that this was a different game.
As I began to play it more, I realized that it was a different CSD, but for good reason. What CSD2 has done is given me CSD, but better. The original CSD game is basically still available in your CSD restaurant, which is dope. Sure, the restaurant doesn't get nicer looking as you get closer to 5 stars, but even *better* than that, you can design your own restaurant. It's kind of boring at first, but once you hit like, 1 star, your designing options become so much larger and designing your own restaurant is it's own interesting part of the game. On that note, the designing system is one that is very difficult to learn, and is an incredibly touchy one. It's by no means easy to use, but understanding that this is a game created by literally like one dude, it's a system that only takes once or twice to actually learn.
The addition of all of the other restaurants you can work in was an excellent choice. This is the whole point of CSD2. It's incredible. R.C. Bot Inc.
Blue Budgie Studios
Blue Budgie Studios
Physics Simulation
R.C. Bot Inc. is a physics-based simulator of sorts that received a lukewarm reception since it’s relatively unpolished in its current state. Keep in mind though that this is the dev team’s Steam debut and the game itself is still work-in-progress. I’d say it most certainly fits the niche for those interested in game engine manipulation and a cutting-edge simulation of tech engines such as Nvidia’s PhysX or Epic Games’ Unreal Engine 4. So if you’re not interested in abstract playtesting, this might not be the game suited for you. It’s not very expensive for what it offers so that is exactly why I’m not going to mark that as a con. The lack of a UI, is something I can’t overlook though. I do hope the game will continue receiving support from the devs and perhaps even a spin-off/sequel.
+ Beautiful graphics.
+ Excellent game mechanics and simulation.
+ Steam Achievements.
- No Steam Trading Cards.
- Complicated control scheme and next to no tutorial.
- Lack of a proper User Interface.

This unique physics-based title is a very hard one to review so I'm afraid this is going to take a while. On the upside, if this review looks too long to bother with then it's a fair indication that R.C. Bot Inc. isn't the game for you, since time and patience are both required in abundance.
The gameplay is easy to describe: a third-person physics-based game where you (barely) take control of a quadrupedal bot and two support vehicles - a carrier truck capable of transporting the bot and a drone that can quickly survey the area and establish custom camera angles. The bot's task is to parachute into an environment and collect, capture or fight targets with the aid of on-board tools including harpoons and a cannon. However, this is somewhat secondary to the
hook of the game which is the way you control the bot. All input from the controller acts upon real-world concepts modelled with nVidia's PhysX engine; for example, the rotation of a joint or the exertion of force by a thruster. The entire game consists of manipulating these real-world concepts to drive the bot and achieve the goal.
This is going to be a divisive title. Some will love it, some will hate it and even those in the former camp should be prepared for a steep learning curve and a lot of frustration while picking up the basics. It took me over an hour to master the art of merely standing up; in any normal game, standing up is not an art to be mastered - you generally just start that way. But R.C. Bot Inc. is not a normal game, it's barely even a game but rather a very detailed physics simulation with some objectives thrown in to challenge your mastery of the simulation.
Typically I'd clock up far more than 6 hours before reviewing a game of this nature but it's already clear that this is a very unique title that has taken considerable skill to create and has a lot to offer to technically-minded fans of physics-based gaming, if they can rise to the challenge of a deep and all-encompassing simulation. This is likely to be a relatively small niche of players but the game certainly deserves better than the 0% positive rating it holds at the time of writing. This is based on two reviews totalling 0.6 hours playtime combined; I can empathise, I hadn't even managed to stand up after 0.6 hours! Casual gamers beware, this is
a pick-up-and-play game. The controls are so complicated that the developers have documented them in an on-screen overlay that you can keep open and refer to while playing. It really has to be seen to be believed:
You know you're in for a rough ride when it's a challenge to even comprehend the control scheme. Notice in the background there are further instructions printed on large boards - this is the tutorial map where there are several of these to augment the help overlays. Did I mention there's another help overlay accessible from the main menu? Well, there is!
Despite all the information in the game, its presentation is rather lacking. The menus are cluttered and chaotic and the tutorial is minimal, throwing you in at the deep end with little more than the gloriously mind-boggling control overlay and a few tips scattered around the map. On parachuting into the level you'll immediately topple over and writhe around randomly for 20 minutes before taking up the game's offer to press Return and display the control scheme. You'll then spend another 20 minutes staring blankly at the control scheme - this may be enough to break you. If you insist on persevering, give it another 20 minutes and you'll realise that you're an hour into the game and barely any better than when you first started.
However, with sufficient hand-eye coordination and a growing understanding of the mappings between controller inputs and the PhysX-modelled devices they actuate in-game, determined players should begin to see some method in the apparent madness and the control scheme starts to feel oddly natural. Patterns of input become increasingly apparent, for example the pattern required to actuate the various joints on the bot's legs to achieve a walking motion. It's still difficult to master because you have so many controls to oversee; the bot has four legs and two arms, each articulated in two places (hip and knee or shoulder and elbow respectively). With L1 held down, the left stick controls the shoulder joints and the right stick controls the elbow joints. With R1 held down, the left stick controls the hip joints and right stick controls the knee joints. This may remind you of gag games like OctoDad that have deliberately difficult or imprecise controls, but the comparison doesn't stand; the control scheme isn't deliberately abstruse, it's necessarily complex.
R2 fires thrusters on the bot's four feet which allows for limited flight or instantly flips you over if the bot isn't perfectly balanced. And it never will be, so flight is a literal balancing act that requires perfect control of all four legs and both arms simultaneously. You may find yourself working two or three buttons and both analogue sticks at the same time so dexterity with the controller is a must. The game provides some assistance here but not by simplifying the simulation; the developers clearly want to remain as close to real-world physics as possible, so to aid with flight they've modelled another real-world construct - a gyroscope. This works exactly as you would expect it to (i.e. maintains balance but only while the force of its angular momentum exceeds the force of gravity trying to displace it). This is a small touch but it impressed me, as it demonstrates the developers' dedication to maintaining an accurate simulation. There are no compromises here, no artificial aids, no scripting and no subversion of the core physics simulation to make the gameplay more forgiving. The result is an extremely hard game but an extremely accurate simulation.
There's a lot more to be said about this ambitious title; I haven't even mentioned bot customisation (allowing part variants that affect the simulation accordingly), but this review has gone on for long enough and hopefully served its purpose. This is
a game for everyone, it caters to a fairly niche audience of physics-based gaming enthusiasts, but the reviews to date are an unfair portrayal of a very competent game. If you don't think you can muster an hour or more with it then don't buy it because you
leave with a bad impression. But if it resonates with you and you're willing to put in some time and bear some frustration it can be very rewarding. It took me an hour just to stand up but by the 6 hour mark I was effortlessly back-flipping the bot into a handstand and walking upside down on its arms. Mastering the simulation can be arduous but the pay-off is immensely satisfying.
Obligatory pros and cons:
(+) Built with best-in-class middleware (UE4, PhysX).
(+) Amazing value for money (currently on sale for $1.99).
(+) One of the most uncompromisingly accurate physics simulations ever to grace a game.
(+) Solid graphics and performance.
(+) Auto-configured itself perfectly on my system but still has...
(+) Plenty of graphics settings to tweak (press space in-game).
(+) A very rewarding experience to master - if you can.
(-) Rather bewildering and inaccessible to new players.
(-) Steep learning curve that casual players are unlikely to surmount.
(-) Cluttered menus/UI that lack finesse and can be unintuitive to navigate.
(-) Certain UI conventions are ignored, adding to the navigation issues; e.g....
(-) The Escape key immediately quits to desktop (menu please, everyone expects it).
(-) Some camera issues, e.g. reset (R3) positions it directly above your bot looking down (a totally useless viewpoint that you'll immediately have to adjust).
Highly recommended to some, but only you can say whether you fit the niche.

This review is probably not very positive and some people will probably say something like: Hey you just had wrong expectations!
While I will say something about the whole expectations thing later, let us just look at the plain facts.
Let us start with the most obvious thing, how does thief look? Well it does look pretty well if you ask me. Well of course it is not the most colorful game, but hey it is a about sneaking in a dark city with steampunk elements. Thief is actually pretty good at this task. The city does look nice and so I can clearly say that thief is a good looking game.
However trouble is easy to find, or in that case easy to hear. The sound of the game is pretty much underwhelming in all aspects. While the voice actors are okay (not great and not terrible) I do miss the old voice actor of garret. However there is more trouble ahead. The entire soundscape is underwhelming and is often schockingly silent. The attempt at a dynamic music system ranges between annoying and broken and I have to say it has been a long time since I actually actively hated the ingame music of a game.
Well sound and graphics are obviously not everything so what about the gameplay and the story? Sadly those two departments show the biggest flaws. Gameplay is pretty linear and often not very interesting, of course there are some alternative routes here or there but they are neither elegant or interesting. While you can roam around the city and do some sidemissions you always feel how limited your routes and by that your options are. It does not help that the enemy AI is pretty stupid and that the guards are awful at their job. So gameplay wise the game is pretty linear and not really challenging. Of course you can raise the difficult in the settings and customize a lot of things, but that does no really make the gameplay itself more interesting and fun.
The story of Thief is also sadly pretty boring and dull. Beside that it is full of logic holes. I dont expect a story to make 100% sense and of course there are things in a story that happen because the story must go somewhere. However a a story most have its own logic and if things stop making sense inside that logic, then you have problems getting engaged in a fictional story.
So much about a look about what I would call the facts. Thief is not a terrible game, I think games with a big budget can hardly be completly terrible, but just having a big budget mean you produce a ace game. Thief is far from being a ace game. I spoke about expectations earlier and this game wants to be a thief game. The problem is that in nearly no aspect it is one. It may sound a bit extreme but this game could have been released under a completly different title and some people would only call it a part time rip off of the original thief.
Can I recommend this game? Well not really. This game claim to be something that is is not and beside that it is only a average game.

After a huge amount of speculation and suspicion about the title before it's release, it has finally got out after long periods of delays.  I got to thank Eidos Montreal for not rushing with THIEF and listening to the fans and making changes to the game they desired.
First off; the PC port is superb. You can adjust the difficulty settings and basically anything related to either the UI, interfaces or just general game experience and playstyle. Not to mention all those fancy graphics options out there aswell.
The game looks and sound very good. The city takes a very dark and moody grip on you and the athmosphere is amazing. The City itself is a fully explorable Hub area, much like in Thief: Deadly Shadows or Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
I think  the biggest thing that really made me love this game, were all the detail and little things around the City, including tons of secret areas, environments to exploit, dark corners and streets, hideouts, passages and the list goes on. This can also turn in to a real OCD hell, if you aim to hunt as many items as there is to be seen (or not to be seen) :D.
The story is actually quite good in my opinion, yet icluding a bit typical theme of a dystopic/depressing world. Also do remember that this is a reboot: Not everything can be the same like in the good ol 90's.
Garrett is not voice acted by Stephen Russell anymore, but the voice actor is no joke. He really reflects Garrett's materialistic, kleptomanic and cynical personality really well and gives a good immersion to the game.
I like how the game doesn't hold your hand if played on master custom options. You have to find those switches yourself, figure out the puzzles alone and plan your movements when doing housecleaning and anything in stealth.  I highly recommend Master difficulty for the best and longest game experience. (this game hasn't got a 12h linear story like in Bioshock Infinite.)
THIEF can be played with more aggressive gamestyle, but it's not regarded to be the most original way to play the game and it is not so fun compared to all the sneaking, lurking around and running on the shadowy rooftops. Also kinda funny when you think about Garrett's negativity about killing and positivity about stealing :).
Compared to Skyrim, I didn't find almost any bugs or glitches, apart from repeating conversations and AI NPCs that sometimes just decide to stand all night long at the same place. Even with those, the AI is extremely intelligent when it comes to sneaking.  ---->You will use load/save alot.
I did NOT like:
- Some ridicilous obstacle restrictions that even an eight year-old could climb.
- Getting stuck on finding a way to rare loot or avoiding randomly patrolling guardsmen.
THIEF is a reboot done well, even with all the negativity amongst some of the oldest fans and people with too spesific expectations.

Very very disappointed with this game. At first I hated it, then I loved it, and then by the end I hated it again. The story is subpar, generic, and predictable, nothing like the original games were. The only reason this could possibly be considered part of the "Thief" Universe is that they call the main character Garrett. There are no Hammerites, no Pagans, and there's one level where you infiltrate an abandoned Keeper library, but they never actually identify them as "Keepers." There are no Burricks, no Zombies, no Haunts, it's basically just a Steampunk game called "Thief" in order to bring in more customers. In my opinion, the coolest part of the Thief games was the universe, the mythos, and all the different factions. Of course, this Thief game doesn't have any of that. The best part of the whole game is the graphics and ambiance, it certainly feels "Thiefy" and looks "Thiefy" and the sneaking gameplay is actually pretty good, but it all comes down to level design. That is where this game fails miserably. It suffers from what most AAA games suffer from these days: very linear, tiny, and cramped levels, and not a lot of emphasis on exploration. Of course, previous Thief games (Even Deadly Shadows) have been the opposite of this: huge, exploration based levels with no real path you're supposed to take. The whole reason that the original games were fun was because you spent time figuring out how to manuever around the map and not get noticed by the guards. They were built to be big and confusing, which is what makes the entire experience challenging and tense. This Thief game is nothing like that. The majority of the levels are small, linear, and boring. The few levels that are someone exploration based are VERY small and eventually lead to another linear portion, probably accompanied by explosions of some sort. The reason I liked it halfway through playing it is because I was hit with a few levels in the middle that were actually relatively large, nonlinear, and required you to choose your path. But then, after those levels, I was again greeted by linear, trigger-based, explosion riddled levels that just didn't feel like Thief.
So overall, this game is slightly above average if you're just looking for another game to play and haven't played the original Thief games. 6/10 from that point of view.
But if you're a huge fan of the originals, don't even buy this game. It's a waste of time and money. The only good I could see coming from this game is if someone rebuilt the original Thief games in this one. That would be cool as♥♥♥♥♥♥ But anyways, as a hardcore Thief fan, I am forced to give this game a sad 3/10. Very disappointed.

DARK is ostenisbly a game in the same vein (ha! puns) as Troika Games 2004 "
". To the point it borrows heavily in both premise and gameplay.
, while buggy and shipped too early, is arguably one of the greatest shooty RPGs ever, along with Deus Ex. It featured a deeply woven narrative, excellent writing, strong characters, intrigue and politics - all dark themes with just the right amount of black comedy.
There was a heavy emphasis on character customisation allowing for numerous solutions and pathways, from combat to stealth to social interaction.
DARK is essentially the stealthy bits of VTM:B made into a full game - and it doesn't
work.
It's a serviceable stealth game, many of the powers aid strongly with traversing and avoiding enemy line of site, and there's some "updates" to the mechanics of VTM:B that tailor it heavily in this fashion, eg the Auspex ability in DARK blows Bloodline's out of the water.
There's even a
-style teleport jump to close in on enemies and get around their line of site, and all attacks from stealth are a 1-hit-kill.
But without the "other options" of social, straight combat, etc that VTM:B had, there's a lot of redundancy in the playstyle and this is especially typified in the skill tree.
An example - for the same investment of experience points, you can have an ability that insta-kills an enemy and hides the body. Or that puts the enemy temporarily to sleep.
Unlike VTM:B there's no in-game benefit for sparing lives, and greater experience rewards are earned from killing enemies, especially unalerted enemies. So why take the power that lets you sneak up on an enemy to kill them, when you can just kill them outright, stealthily, AND hide the body?
Little lack-of-thought moments like this are rife through the game and many of the stealth-sections are arduous guard-watching. Not a lot of thought or planning, just wait the seconds until the guard turns his back and snap his neck before continuing.
The voice acting's terrible, the plot is weak, the characters are one note and the general format is borrowed so heavily from VTM:B that it might as well not be its own game but a mod and collection of maps.
On the positive, the art-style's nice and overall the stylized toon-shader gives the whole thing a comic-book feeling, and when the stealth works, it really does work, it just so rarely works.
Really, it isn't a
game, it's just that there's better out there. Play through VTM:B as a Nosferatu instead and get a better game experience overall.

Cook, Serve, Delicious was a surprisingly fun game when I first played it.
Had all the charms of a first true game given life:
Charming style (graphics aren't much for some, but it still had it's thing going)
Addictive gameplay (that got even better the more you were pro at it)
Excellent writing (Okay okay, maybe excellent stretches it, but there's always something nice to read here and there for a chuckle).
The game eventually felt like you're basically in a constant rhythm of getting orders done right while working under the clock, and with a right set of balance, a couple of harsh moments to tell you to take things to the next level, and basically what you have is literally a delicious game.
...So of course I went ahead expecting the same fun out of the 2nd one when I instantly bought it, no sales or whatevs.
Now I'm sad I did.
CSD2 is no doubt an improvement on the old formula. In some ways.
This time, besides running your own place the old catering and cooking shows oddjobs are replaced with themed restaurants with different foods thrown in the mix. Basically the weekly / strike challenges.
Except now there's a hundred of them. In addition? You also decorate your own restaurant, which is nice if you ever get tired of the themed pressure (if you're an achievement hoarder like me, you'll grudgingly go through them anyways). Oh yeah, and there's like over the hundreds in available foods this time. Minus food upgrades, but nonetheless an impressive feat of items to choose from.
Because the actualy game mechanics SUUUUUUUUUUUUUCK. Ugh. Wish I could put it more lightly...
Basically, throw in the mix a bunch of bad game designs=No one's having fun tonight.
Just to list them all, here's some differences:
While in CSD1, As it'll be called from now, the days simply came and went, in CSD2 You feel like time barely moves about on the first shift job. While in a sense it's nice, you basically don't have to worry about too many customers, but for a CSD1 veteran it's not fun at all, as you're thrown in to a pretty slow start.
It's basically just that you're thrown in, and each hour feels like the most boring minute of your life, a poor choice to simply make time slower this time around. Especially since the buzz is causing you to have even LESS customers until the rush hour, by which you have to prepare dishes and hope you got eonugh or else the stress will get to you. More on that later
In the first game, for the most part it's common to at least mess up some meals. Nobody's perfect. However as you slowly progressed the gmae and got familiar with the flow of cooking, the buzz and the recipes, perfects would just be natural as long as you're not out of beat or under too much stress. You had room for mistakes with the first challenges the game threw at you as preparation, while at the end game you had to put up your best.
While I could understand if some players felt it too easy at some point, it's truly an off putting choice to have it immediately thrown at you that only perfects are allowed if you want that golden medal. Which maybe wouldn't have been a problem if the shifts at least felt more living instead of the slow approach they decided on this time around...which brings me to:
Simply put, now instead of having one order per customer, now drinks are simply refillable (in some cases), and you may make side dishes for extra patience and perhaps a generous payment. While it's nice and all, the problem is that now basically it's just a game of slow cooking, should you have to suffer through the foods that require that (most of them do). Basically you do less careful order with ingredients, and more just preparubg ahead of time, which, at most feels odd for restaurants to just have prepared dishes. at worst, it just makes the entire experience too slow to start with.
In addition to holding stations, you now don't have to choose the correct menu in order to put the right ingredient. Utterly useless for pro players, as by the point you know what the buttons are switching menus just feels slow and unnecessary. The fact it's mandatory now thanks to poor choices and the "Universale Keybinds"(at first not a bad idea, but with more than 8 choices...) basically make it feel even slower than it already was.
And don't get me started on the rest of the daily chores...I mean, in addition to sanitizing you have to press the "enter" key?! But why? you're done with the chore, you don't need to push a button to confirm that and move to the next! Again, EMPHASIS ON SLOW.
Just by going off a few reviews here and there, sneaking a look at achievements, it seems the main goal now is just to git gud as they say and get a bunch of perfect days on slow conditions instead of actually feeling like every event was something special, how every challenge was secondary, yet felt greatly satisfying when you could prove yourself to do it. Aiming for full completion was a goal like this, sure, but it felt like you had progress. From humble starts to blazing glory.
Kind of feels forgotten here when it's made clearly away that you just have to be good from start to finish to feel the same satisfaction of the achievements, which, feel even less exciting to get now with more focus on getting medals or doing a few super shifts rather than filling a checkbox of all the interesting things you got to accomplish and experience.
The first CSD felt like a labour of love, which made me legitimately regred my choices in the steam awards when there was time. It was a fun game with its share of challenges though not flawless.
CSD2 Unfortunately, while improving greatly in some aspects, simply just doesn't feel as smooth as the first game, and feels like more mandatory, as foods have to be unlocked via golden medals, rather than simply working hard every day to get your restaurant to glory. While you still could in this game, it just kinda feels like you don't have a reason to. And since it's too slow to get through a single shift day, you'll feel less motivated to do that either since it's just so slow that you'll no doubt mess up even on the first day, just because it's really hard to get motivated as every hour feels like forever.
My recommendation? Buy CSD1. But not this game. This game is simply Overcooked it's mecahnics to a slow death.

I loved Cook, Serve, Delicious 1. I've put many hours into it and grew my restaurant to 5 stars and enjoyed the progression and got a sense of accomplishment out of it. CSD2? Not so much. Tons of new recipes and added cooking dynamics have been added, and they're fun. There are many challenges to complete for achievements in the form of medals. The problem here is something feels missing from the running your own restaurant portion. You can earn furniture to decorate the same space you look at every day you play in the game, and you can earn new items to put on your menu...but there's not real sense of progression. You're not making headlines in the local papers. There aren't people clamoring for you to be a chef at their restaurants in exchange for rare recipes. There isn't any form of "leveling up" so to speak. There technically is. But it doesn't earn you anything tangible aside from a notification. You just kind of play. Which is ok, the gameplay is fun. But what really kept me going in CSD1 was my sense of immersion in really having pride in having a good job to bring my restaurant to fame. I don't get that feeling of immersion at all in CSD2.

I'm going to catch hell for this review.
Let me preface this review by saying that I believe the dev is responsive and working hard to improve the game.  I bought the game at launch and waited until the 1.12 update to post this.
Here. We. Go.
Have you ever listened to the song "De Do Do Do, De Da Da Da"?  It's a song by the 80's rock band, The Police.  The point of the song is how the simple can be so powerful.  This game is a bag of beauty wrapped in a unwelcoming UI.
I'm going to compare CSD and CSD2 for a moment, so bear with me.  CSD was a fun little game with a steady progression to help build muscle memory for the later stages.  CSD2 is a slap to the player on the difficulty from the start.  I know some folks will scream, "Git Gud", but c'mon.  If you want a franchise to be accessable to the masses, you don't go Dark Souls out of the gate.  This is coming from someone who loves CSD and appreciates the work in building a steady progression.
The visual representations of the foods and kitchens are awesome.  I feel like the dev put a lot of time into making a wide variety of foods and challenges.  I just think that perhaps more time should have been spent on making the game fun.   I have a thing for good a good UI, and this game feels clunky.
If Steam didn't have this archaic UP/DOWN rating, I would give this a 5/10.  It's not rubbish, but it feels almost thrown together at the last minute.  Nothing about this title makes me WANT to play it, outside of the positivity I have for the Developer.  Something is missing and I hope the dev finds an answer.

This is a very nice game that can be thought of as a free-to-play introduction to Magic and competitive play.  It is the evolutionary sequel to a series called Duels of the Planeswalkers, in which you slowly unlock a set of playing decks that are pre-determined with limited customizability. In Magic Duels, the notion of pre-set decks has been abandoned and players are free to build a deck suiting their preferences within the selection of available cards. The best part is that the developers are continuing to add additional cards to the selection pool with very few removals, meaning you really can design the deck that you want. There are downsides of course, such as lack of chat support, lack of two headed giant, and a matchmaking system that seems to fail as often as it succeeds. However, my general takeaway about the game is that is under-rated and could easily contend for the top spot in online card games with a bit more publicity and awareness in the community. It is free, it allows you to play exactly how you like, and there is more skill than luck involved.

Having been a huge fan of the first game (I played it to near completion), I was eager to play the second.
The second CSD changes many small but notable things from the first. It introduces a wide variety of other restaurants that you can do 'guest chef' shifts in, whilst still allowing you to do days in your own CSD customisable restaurant. I began playing after v1.1, so the humorous emails are there as in CSD1, which give me a chuckle from time to time. The keyboard shortcuts and recipes of the foods are slightly different from CSD1, but not so different that you can't pick them up easily and get back into the CSD 'flow'. As in CSD1, the art style is great, and playing this game always makes me hungry. Plus, I learn about new types of food I didn't know existed.
There are a few nitpicks I have with the game. One is the Designer interface to customise your restaurant. You can place objects, choose your seating, wall design, floor design, and so on, to make your backdrop unique. This concept is great for people who like to fiddle around with interior design. You unlock new items through playing the game, as rewards for earning a certain amount of bronze/silver/gold medals. They are randomly unlocked as far as I can tell. Unfortunately, the interface to customise your restaurant is one of the worst things I have ever come across. In order to place items, you must go through the Create submenu, and select the category of the item you want to place (seating/art/objects/etc). That's fine. But if you accidentally place an item you didn't want to, you then have to go out of the Create submenu, into the Edit submenu, select delete, select the category of the item you want to delete, and then delete it. Then go back out and into the Create submenu to continue on what you were doing. This is so incredibly uninituitive. It would be far better if you could simply click on the object and press delete without going in/out of different submenus. Even if you were using a controller it would be easier to press a button to switch to delete mode and then cycle through the objects rather than selecting each one by category. It's frustrating as I do enjoy customising my restaurant but the interface is so poorly designed I have given up on it.
On a related note, if you are uninterested in designing your restaurant much of the sense of achievement and progression is taken out of the game. After each day/shift you will usually unlock some items for your restaurant as a reward, depending on how well you did. The items tend to come in batches, so you're sitting there clicking through them which can be pretty tedious if you're not interested in what particular bar counter you unlocked. Occasionally you'll unlock a new type of food, which is great, but this is rare. Along with the change from progressing your restaurant from 1 star to 5 stars, and instead progressing yourself (as a chef) from 1 start to 5 stars, I feel that much of the sense of progression has been taken out of the game. That's likely personal preference, but I enjoyed seeing my restaurant in CSD1 become more upper class as I completed more days. If the items for your own restaurant weren't so randomised, maybe it would be different - i.e., if you started off unlocking 'lower class' items like a plastic set of chairs, and as you went on you started unlocking more stylish items - maybe this is the case already, but if it is I can't tell?
In CSD2, your restaurant is always the same - you do unlock more menu slots, but otherwise there is nothing special that changes about it. Because the main progression (apart from the designer items) is unlocking new guest restaurants, I find myself only playing the new guest restaurants and rarely touching my own restaurant, which makes me sad. Maybe it would be a cool idea to play through the guest restaurant and then unlock a food from the guest restaurant as a result, as if the guest restaurant gave you their recipe to reward you. You would still have to buy it from the pantry, but it would mean that guest restaurants served more of a 'purpose'. At the moment, some foods are locked in the pantry until you progress further in your chef stars, which is a good idea, but it's unclear how and when these will be unlocked and clarification on this (e.g. 'unlocked at 4 stars') would probably give more of a goal to work towards. Or even have the locked foods silohuetted, so you have to guess what exactly it is and creates a sense of mystery.
If the upgrading your own chef versus upgrading your restaurant thing is to work, I think it would be nice if there was some element of customising your chef too. Unlocking new clothes, or a new hat, or even new hairstyles. I know your chef icon plays a very small part in the game, but that would make it seem more coherent. Or perhaps improving your appearance of your chef; they start off looking a bit raggedy and then end up looking like a pro chef?
As a further tiny nitpick, and this is almost certainly personal preference, I don't like that after every day I'm unlocking lots and lots of guest restaurant levels. I feel that there are too many levels unlocked after each day for me to feel like I can focus on one at a time. It would be better (in my opinion) for me to complete the majority of "Max Weiners" before, say, "Chilly Bowl"'s first level unlocks. Then to complete the majority of Chilly Bowl before another restaurant unlocks. Maybe not as restrictive as that, but more restrictive than the current setup. It doesn't feel like accomplishment because there's just too many new levels for me to keep track of. It feels like there's no point going back and doing the harder levels of the easier restaurants when I've unlocked "Far East"'s first level, so I feel like I only do one level of each restaurant before moving onto the next.
All those aside, this is still a great game. I think I enjoyed CSD1 more, simply because of the better sense of progression, but CSD2 has more scope. CSD2 is definitely worth picking up if you have completed CSD1 like me and found that there wasn't much to do in the end game. CSD2 almost feels like an extension of CSD1's end game than its own game, although I think CSD2 does have the potential to become its own solid game. I applaud the developer and artists for their hard work and their new ideas on how to differentiate CSD2 from CSD1. Despite my nitpicks and suggestions for improvement, I do think they have done a great job.

Do not buy this game. It contains 8 levels, and none of them flow together. They have different focuses, there are two that involve you stealing things, two that try to be spooky, atmospheric, and have you walk in a straight line for the story to progress. There are two that mostly focus on the environment exploding around you, requiring you to use awkward climbing mechanics that shift to a jarring third person perspective with bad keybord controls (featuring a dedicated drop down button not used anywhere else in the game,) and the usual first person parkour to navigate. There are two boss fights in the game, but with Garret being made of paper, and the gameplay not being suited for combat, they are not fun in any way, and rely more on luck, as you have to physically touch enemies to get an attack in, where they have much greater range than you.
Stealth kills, and I do mean kills, you cannot knock people out in melee in this game, will cause loud noise, attracting guards. I often found the difficulty coming from their line of sight, more than how they behaved. Once detected, their AI is poor, and they lose you if you jump over tables and crouch, or hide in a (large) closet, if there are crates, you can jump onto them and kill them one at a time as they enter to investigate the dead bodies at your leisure. The combat in detected mode is sluggish, and often not worth it. Garret had a sword and blackjack in previous theif games, in this one, you have a claw, used both for stealth kills and combat.
I played on Master difficulty, each level taking about 30 minutes to complete, not counting cutscenes of course. There are a lot of them, and they are often a disjointed mess, not just in the writing, but how they flow with the game. Garret will be standing in a different place, sometimes an entirely different area when the FMV cutscenes kick in, and then dump you in a third location. The pacing is off, and by the end of the game, I was not sure what had happened in the story.
Speaking of the difficulty levels, you are only penalized for killing civilians on Master, so if you are not playing on it, go nuts, take everyone out, it's not like it matters.
Garret does not act like his old self, but it is a minor problem with all these gameplay issues in mind, the level design changing so much in tone and intent reminds me of another game.
In short, I bought Duke Nukem Forever: Stealth Edition, and you shouldn't.

Having never played the Thief franchise before, but being a fan of stealth genre of games (having previously played Dishonoured, Hitman, Splinter Cell etc) I can't base my review on how it compares to the previous games from this franchise, and I feel a lot of buyers may be in this same category with me so I can't comment on how it
play like, only what it does. Nonetheless, I boarded the hype train and had this game pre-ordered a month or two in advance.
First thing I'd like to say is that the ambience in this game is
. The shadows and light from objects really have been polished wonderfully, and the city as a whole really immerses you in the game straight away. You can tell it is a graphics intensive game and as such, this leads me to my first bad point;
.
To go from area to area, you can either interact with a glowing orb which leads to a loading screen and (thankfully short due to my SSD) a small wait to get into the next area, or you can end up having what I'll call a
where you bash E to open a window or lift a wood beam out the way of a crawlspace to pass forward. This took away some of the depth to the game I feel, where I'd be really into robbing houses yet to escape I'm having to bash a key to subtly load the next area. I expected Batman Arkham City/Origins level of freedom; it didn't deliver. There are no expansive rooftops to climb, only what you're let to climb.
The second bad point is the AI.
. Sometimes the denziens of the city will react to you and run to guards, sometimes they will not, it took me a while to realise this. They do not talk to you or react to you unless you're throwing bodies at them, which makes Garrett seem a bit like an invisible person really. I've noticed guard chatter just gets recycled and doesn't seem fresh or new. You could kill a guard right infront of a group of them and after their alert has 'timed-off' they no longer care about this corpse on the ground. Very iffy.
Sadly, the combat seems to have also been neglected,
that the developers said to themselves "oh, wait, what if the player can't escape?" and then just threw some silly mechanics at it. You're given (apart from your bow and the plethora of arrow types) a blackjack to knock them out, or just dodge around and try and smack them till they die. I can understand this game is not actually designed for you to be running around beating people up, but it would be nice if I could do it properly if I'm caught, instead of infuriating me and I inevitably just reload an autosave.
It's not all doom and gloom though, which is what you think I think of this game now. I actually reall enjoy it though. The optional objectives on missions reward bonus gold for upgrades/resources and really do push you to complete them, such as remain undetected (see paragraph above as to why you should always have this done), X number of knockouts, X number of pick pockets etc, and the difficulty settings at the beginning really make this game replayable for the challenge. I can see videos of player made challenges already in my head.

Buy this game for the single-player or playing rounds with your friends, *not* multiplayer with random people. You will find that there are not always people playing online, and if you pop into a session, then you may wait for the current race to finish just to be kicked from the lobby once the host returns to the lobby, and if you do manage to get into a race and then do well in it, you may get kicked at the end of a race. That just happened to me twice: I won but I guess the lobby host was angry so I got a message saying I was kicked from lobby, did not even receive any EXP or Cash -- the grinding is slow in multiplayer, which makes this even more frustrating. The first time, it was in a lobby doing 5-race demolition derby mode, 10 laps per race, and so I'd spent something like half an hour, so when the thing ended and I had won, I was very annoyed that I had just spent so much time just to receive nothing because the lobby host was acting like a small child. The second time, I played against 2 people who both had much better cars (they were higher level) and since they kept crashing and going off-track I got past them, but when one caught up to me because his car was faster he tried several times to ram me off of the track. I don't mind that, it's part of the game. Anyway, he failed miserably and I still won, but unfortunately it seems Codemasters has given the power to lobby hosts to kick players mid-race. Clearly, that's easy to abuse, and although it would be great if they'd patch the game to at least give EXP/Cash when you're kicked, I seriously doubt that will ever happen because this game has been around for a while already.

was wrong, so I googled it.
Apparently, an unsupported USB device (read: pretty much every USB device ever, except perhaps storage drives) is causing the crash. For the record: this is 2014, nearly 2015. USB technology has been in fairly common use since ~1998, and was on the market as early as '95. While my computer still retains a PS/2 port for a keyboard, it does NOT have one for a mouse, and after disabling every USB driver possible without losing the keyboard and mouse, the game STILL crashes on startup.
Ubisoft has really dropped the ball on this one, I'm sad to say. However, they claim to be aware of the problem and promise a fix in a "future" patch. I may change my rating then, but I'll be remembering this.
I've tried it 12 times, therefore the game currently rates at -2/10.
TL:DR Spent 2+ days preloading it and $80+ on the gold version, just so I could look at a black screen.

This game is a lot of fun and rekindled my love for Magic which I played religously as a teen and then kind of got away from over the years. This game introduces the rules in a great way where you can not only read how abilities work, but actively do a small tutorial on it (literally like a 1-2 minute quick play of the mechanic) which makes understanding things much easier. If you're familiar with the rules you can skip over it, but there are small rewards for completing each small tutorial in the form of coins. You use coins to purchase in-game booster packs.
There's story mode and battle mode. Story mode is a mixed bag. You are given pre-made decks to play with. A lot of the games you are in are pretty evenly matched but there were a few that I found to be annoyingly one sided where your deck was inferior to the computer's. Each completed match in the story mode yeilds more coins for boosters and the rewards are worth the time put in.
Battle mode is where you can face the computer or another person with decks you make yourself. You can face Easy, Medium or Hard AI for 5, 10 or 15 coins respectively.
Booster packs start at 150 coins for a single pack of 6 cards. I can't remember the rest of the coins per packs ratios but it gets up to several thousand coins for decent amounts of packs. By completing story mode, I was able to buy approximately 15 or so booster packs. Once that's done, it's up to you if you would like to grind out coins for packs or straight up spend your cash for coins.
All in all, I can say my time with the game has been enjoyable, without spending any money and I recommend it to anyone who may have been out of the game for a while.

An intriguing and intense surivival game.
Survival games as of late have drifted away from their core ideas, with many games being produced with points on action rather than pure survival, while others such as DayZ or Survivor Stories are often focused on multi-player. With Frozen State, produced by Snow Arc Studio, normally known for Mobile Apps, we see a clear return to the genre's roots.
Taking control of one of 3 characters, (only 1 available as of now), the player is thrust into an icy, post-apocalyptic world with meager supplies, and no bearing on their goal or object. Using a classic top-down view, the player must venture through the cold, and traverse numerous randomly placed 'Zones', complete with decrepit buildings, and the crumbling tenents of of former society. The wind and snow constantly blow, quickly chilling you to the bone, giving you the choice to to run for cover, or start a campfire to preserve your body temperature.
Supplies, food,  water, and sleep are constantly an issue, forcing you to scavenge every cabinet, fridge, chest, and pantry in order to survive your body's constant needs. Mutants also roam the wasteland, presenting another threat to survive, making you use found weapons to fight back against their presence.
All in all, a fantastic survival game that looks very promising.

Mac version works well. I played on an Early 2009 Mac Pro, 16 GB RAM, Radeon 5870.
No bugs / glitches during play. I really liked the audio in the background, it provided a lot of atmosphere. Enemies were tough if you don't have good weapons. On my first play through I died fighting a monster with my fists. On the second playthrough I was able to find a lot of supplies raiding a 3 story apartment building (with a yeti monster inside). I was able to take out several enemies with either an ax or a firearm at range. The only thing I had to worry about was finding a place to sleep. I am glad you are including a sleeping bag because that was going to be one of my first suggestions.
The movement was different from what I expected (I thought you would use the mouse to change direction), but I found it actually provided some advantages such as running backwards and firing at enemies. The crafting is easy to use and intuitive (combining elements to make a meal, then putting them on a fire to cook them and make them edible). I like the different outfits (coats and hats) providing different defensive and temperature protection.
One big request is to get the map working. Moving through the different maps worked well, but it was hard sometimes to remember where the nearest bed is. One issue I noticed was going to one area then going back to a previous area, but your perspective was rotated 90 degrees. The camera could be rotated back, but since you don't currently have a map it was occasionally difficult to find my bearings. Also, if you could add notes to the map that would help.
Sometimes I would find a building / house with something blocking one of the doors outside (like furniture) and you are unable to cut through it. The only thing you seemed to be able to destroy were locked doors.
Some feature requests: key remapping - everyone has their favorite keys to perform actions. A save game feature - I had to finally kill myself in one game because I was bored and could not save it. Since you start out in the same house every time, how about adding a home base to store items and protect yourself?
I have been following this game since its Kickstarter campaign and I am very impressed with the progress the team has made. You have laid a solid basis for a great game.

Frozen state does a wonderful job of portraying lonliness, the fight for survival, and a creeping sense of dread as you peer around every corner, and into every room. The game has randomized loot, crafting and survival elements, as well as monsters that remind me very much of the creatures from 'The Thing'. While the game is still in alpha and early release, I believe it is fully worth the pittance you pay for what could be hours of fun. As a plus, the developers seem to really listen to the comments people make, and take a keen interest in player suggestions to further develope and refine the gameplay. If you are like me, you'll love helping give the developers more ideas and create the game to be what you want it to be, unlocking the potential of community development.
If you enjoy "breaking & entering / Treasure hunting" games based around survival of the elements and unknown enemies, as well as unforgiving consequences to every action and 'Permadeath' roguelikes, this is the game for you. If you prefer a more casual gaming experience, this may not be your cup of tea.
In closing, I highly recommend this game to the more 'hardcore' crowd- Players which enjoy games like Project Zomboid, State of Decay, and DayZ.

[TIME OF REVIEW] [05/07/2014] [EARLY ACCESS BUILD 9]
Frozen State is one of the most interesting games I have seen in a while and after an hour of play I am ready to give out a review but first let me tell you some of my experiences in this game.
Day 1...
It's cold and i'm out of paper, I need to go out and find some if I am to make a campfire to survive.
I was attacked by some sort of infected known as a gaunt, It took a good hit on me but I am ok...I think.
It's getting dark and cold but I still have no paper I guess my only choice is to press on and hope for the best.
After searching around I found a run down house and saw something walk past the shattered window, I raised my gun and readied myself and slowly stepped towards the house. Before I got through the door I saw the horrific monster walking towards me, I fired a few bullets but I have had little experience shooting a gun so I missed 2/3 shots. I put it away and raised my axe and lunged at it taking a few good swipes at it knocking it down killing it. Once I had caught my breath I slowly walked into the same building when something more horrifc crawled across the ground at furious speed. I ran back terrified taking more shots but missing, I did as before and raised my axe slashing at it killing it. I'm not sure what it is but I really didn't want to know. I pressed on still looking for the paper I needed...
I found a supermarket but inside I found no paper although on my way out around the back something huge chased me, i'm not sure what it was but I ran and managed to escape.
Thankfully I was struck with the best of luck, a building full of apartments. I ran inside checking every drawer and cupboard but nothing until I checked an oven...And there it was, the one thing I had spent my journey looking for...Paper...I swiftly crafted myself a fire and crouched next to it, feeling the warmth as it brushed my skin...I am now in that appartment hoping that by morning I will still be alive...
I have decided to leave the room I was in, in search of more supplies. After a few minutes of searching I hear a loud crash as a wooden door breaks down, I stop dead in my tracks swiftly checking my surroundings...Suddenly a monster crawls along the ground towards me, I raise my axe once again and give it a few slashes but it keeps coming I try to give it another but a Gaunt begins his approach so I back into a small bathroom and whip out my pistol and fire an entire magazine at them...They are dead...I am now cold and dying...I rush around looking for the fire I left on so I could know where I was. I enter a room and see the thing I saw at the supermarket, it turns and begins its chase. I turn and run now looking for the exit. I run into a room hoping to find stairs but all I find is another exact same monster. I turn and run but he is right behind me. I manage to duke him out and continue my escape. Quickly I close a door to block them and run into another room...Empty...I turn back and see them already coming towards me, I try to doge him but to no avail, with one foul swoop he slices my neck cutting it open and I drop dead...
This was all in one small hour session and was a great thrillride, there was alot more I could have explored and seen but that would take far too long and be far to dangerous as I'm sure there are alot more terrifying creatures out there.
Things to improve/add:
Multiple saves - You can already do this by just copying the data folder and then deleting its contents except settings but it would make it alot easier than having to do that.
Getting around objects - I have seen various objects and such placed infront of doors and such and with no way to get around it, I think being able to climb over it or push things out of the way would be cool.
More crafting??? - I'm sure it will improve and add more but there isn't much atm anyway unless I just haven't found the right things although some things are there that I don't have but Idk.
More open worldy - Although the zone traveling does help FPS ALOT you can easily escape enemies by using zones when being chased which is a bit silly. Unless you can combat that with a sort of 'enemy nearby' system.
Mods - Of course mods 'cause why not?
Multiplayer - Although it's a big leap I think this game would be extremely good for MP as the core gameplay elements that are in the game such as lockpicking would make for some fun gameplay.
That's about all I can think of right now but my rating for this game as it is, is an 9/10.
The games concept is very unique and fun and even now I can see myself spending SO many hours in this game. Definately recommend this game!
