CSD2 got off to a bit of a rocky start, but since the more recent updates I no longer have any reservations about recommending it.
If you haven't played the original, Cook Serve Delcious is mostly a reflex-based game.  Though you do get to run your own restaurant and choose which foods to serve, there's not much of what might be considered strategy or business management here, instead the focus is placed entirely on fulfilling the orders of the customers who come through your doors.  Cooking food most commonly boils down to selecting ingredients from a list to match the customer's order, potentially with brief pauses to let food cook, but you'll have to be both fast and accurate, because your customers won't wait long to be served and aren't terribly forgiving with mistakes.  It's fairly simple in terms of execution, but each one of the many, many different types of food you can prepare has its own little nuances, and it can really get hectic during "rush hour" when a ton of customers come in all at once.
Compared to the original, the most obvious improvement in CSD2 is that the graphics are vastly better.  The original had a certain charm to it, but the graphics in the sequel look fantastic by any measure.  Playing this game makes me want to learn how to cook more things because everything always looks so good.  There's also an entirely new game mode where rather than running your own restaurant, you work for other restaurants with preset menus, which is actually a great way to encourage you to explore the full food catalogue rather than just sticking with simple foods that are easy to prepare.  Finally, there's a new holding station mechanic that allows you to fully or partially prepare certain foods ahead of time, or offer side dishes that add precious seconds of extra patience for your guests.  It's not really a vastly different game at its core, but it feels different enough to be worth revisiting.
The game is not without its flaws, however.  The most obvious one is that the difficulty ramp up is much less gradual than the first game.  In CSD1, when you first learn a new food, the recipes available are all very simple, for example, when you first get ice cream, you only have 2 flavours and a couple toppings, then as you progress through the game you unlock progressively more options that makes food preparation more and more complicated.  This concept is entirely absent in the sequel, all foods are at maximum complexity right off the bat, so even the early game of CSD2 feels somewhat comparable to the endgame of CSD1.  For this reason, if you're new to the series, you might want to play the original first, or at least stick to preparing simple foods until you get the basics down.  Secondly, I'm not a huge fan of the progression system.  As you complete days at either your own restaurant or others, you'll gain experience and level up, unlocking new foods and decorations for your restaurant, which is fine.  However, the levels you can challenge in the Chef For Hire mode are also tied to the levelling system, and they unlock in a seemingly random order, which I find to be somewhat annoying.  Want to cook more Sushi?  Too bad, come back in a few levels and the next stage might be unlocked.
Overall, though, this is still a pretty solid game.  It's very simple, but that also makes it great to pick up and play, it's easily one of the best games on Steam if you've got a few minutes to kill while waiting for your friends to get ready for another game or something.  There's also a pretty substantial amount of content to the game and it's got a sort of quirky sense of humour that helps give the experience a bit more personality.  The original game didn't become such a sleeper hit for nothing.

Block King is a simple game: Make your friends and enemies fall out of the map.
As a port coming over from the Xbox Live indie market place, I can say this is a great port of the original version of all who loved it there. It's great fun to just hop on and play with a couple of friends on an online "game-night."
There are many different block types, such as the rainbow and ice blocks. The rainbow block instantly launching you into the air. Whether that helps you or not, depends on your situation.
On the other side of the spectrum there is the ice block, destroying all of your hopes and dreams by taking away your ability to jump, creating situations where you have to run around like a mouse under a glass bowl as other players in the game try to snipe you like an MLG.
This game is overall a great experience, as long as you can get over the somewhat wonky perspective, you'll be glad to buy this after you are put into tight situations, where the outcome is only decided on your skill, and a little bit of luck. Have fun!

"Block King" is an online, high paced shooter? I'm not too sure. The main concept of the game is you play against enemies and shoot out the blocks beneath them to end their lives. Blocks are a one shot kill - if you are unfortunate to be standing on one whilst an enemy is shooting in your direction, prepare to be booted out to the main menu. Speaking of which, the design is incredibly clunky. Upon launching the game I was greeted with audio being blasted down my ear canal, and with no volume controls in-game, I had to result to editing this in the Windows mixer.
Gameplay is relatively boring - the clunky controls and unsightly graphics are a turn-off for any hardcore gamer interested in a new action shooter game. I purchased this game during a special promotion for 47 pence, however the regular price is slightly more.
In conclusion, this game is fun for about 2 minutes, then you want to close and let it lie in your Libary forever more, and hope your Steam friends didn't see you launch the game in the first place.

I remember back in the day when games weren’t the super huge multi million dollar productions with million dollar advertising budgets.  When you wanted a game, you looked at the box, the pictures on the back and decided if you wanted it.  That’s how my life with Civilization started.  I was at the Video Game Exchange shopping the Super Nintendo section and I ran across published by KOEI called Civilization.  The back stated “What would you do if you were emperor? With Sid Meyer's (yes, its spelled wrong on the box) Civilization, you are the emperor. You control your own personal civilization. And build it any way you want. Don't like schools? Don't build any.
Think the Romans were crude? Wipe them out. And when your advisors tell you what to do, you tell them where to go. Attack your enemies like a ruthless warlord. And if they're really a pain, make'em. You've got the power to take on the greatest leaders in history.”
THIS SOUNDS AMAZING!  It looked similar to SimCity, so I was in.   And it was AMAZING!  I can’t imagine I would have ever played a Civ game now if I hadn’t played it before.  I mean, what do you say?  Well, you click a few times, wait a bunch of turns, explore the planet, and occasionally attack other units, and than wait a bunch of turns…  It sounds boring..  And unfortunately, it is.  I was really hoping that a new setting would spice up the formula.  It seems that everything about Beyond Earth is a step back.
The first issue is the personality of the leaders in this game.  There are no more historical figures, theres just a handful of Civilizations called “Sponsors” with some generic figurehead running the show, as opposed to previous games with historical figures running historical civilizations.  If the Mongols were in your game, they were run by Genghis Kahn, and as you could imagine, they were ruthless war mongers.  If you played India, it was Gandhi and they wouldn’t really mess with you.  They would play very peacefully.  In Beyond Earth, you run into Kavithan Protectorate, run by, well, ya know, that one lady.  And they just, kinda sit there. And there’s Polystralia, and they’re led by, uh, that guy in the suit.  But they at least, well, kinda do nothing.  It’s just a huge step back from all the historical figures.  Don’t get me wrong, they try to achieve victory, and they will occasionally get hostile, but it’s not really as strong as previous games.  Most of the interaction with them is them scolding/praising your choice for an ally, or your choice in Affinities.  But that’s about it.
I goaded a civilization into attacking me after I got caught spying and stealing from them 6 times.  I crushed their military in 3 turns and they were pleading for a ceasefire.  I had 4 military units at the time they declared war.  And I still crushed them.  It was really disappointing.  I was ready to start giving away the farm to keep them from wiping me, and they couldn’t manage a run at me.  Why declare war if you don’t have the military to back it up?  I would have rather seen more dynamic personalities from the sponsors, and I would really love to have seen alien personalities that maybe took the role of aggressor as humans tried to take over their planets.  Anything to vary the stale personalities.
Beyond the personalities, something else that really bothered me was the way the tech web was designed.  It was very bland and difficult to decipher.  A far cry from the bright and vibrant and clear tech tree in past games.  The way the web works is there are branches and on each branch are leaves.  You have to research a branch to get the leaves, at which point you can research any leaf on the branch.  Which at most is 3.   It’s supposed to give you a feeling of being able to have more freedom to research what you want.  But I didn’t feel that way.  It seemed slightly less restrictive, but a lot of the later techs require certain levels of affinity, so there isnt a point to research them anyways until you research other techs.  I’m not the only one apparently as there are several mods already to try and add some life to the web and make it a little less confusing.
I spoke earlier of Affinity.  Beyond Earth features three different Affinities, Purity, which emphasizes the desire to make the new Colony like Old Earth, Harmony, which attempts to coexist with the aliens and Supremacy, which is the attempt to enhance humans genetically and cybernetically to become an AI like consciousness and free people from their physical form.  Really, though, it just affects how you upgrade your units, and what special units you can acquire.  It also affects how the other sponsors see you as well, but it didn’t do much but bring up a message for me saying that I need to get out of my old ways.  Even near end game, no one really gets angry about the way you treat the wildlife or what affinity you are.  I was hoping that near end game the planet would segregate itself and we would have makeshift alliances, but no one really seems to care.
I did really like the feel of the planets.  They felt not Earth like, but believable that they could be inhabited by humans.  These planets are inhabited by aliens that basically replace the barbarians from previous games.  Some can be hostile, and others don’t bother you unless provoked or by getting close to nesting sites.  Some are pretty damn tough to deal with as well.  This is another area that I feel they missed out, as they could have had different planet types with various indigenous aliens to really vary up replays, but it’s the same wildlife on the same style of planets, and that was pretty disappointing.
An addition that I really enjoyed was the quest system.  Quests are basically side goals that give you a little to do in turns where you’re waiting.  They are as simple as grab a relic, to story chains that go multiple missions, including victory scenarios.  It’s a really fun distraction that helps fill the void when you’re waiting for a research or unit to finish.  One quest had me find some  escaped slave, take a unit to a randomly spawned “base” ( non sponsor owned camp)  to find out that they are civilians of the camp, and they live their life by modifying themselves, and deciding whether to return the escapees, or destroy the base.  I chose to destroy the base, which then gave me the option to use them as my own research toys or unmodify them .  Each step in the chain gave my different awards such as tech or affinity points.  And it was a fun way to burn off turns.
Closing thoughts
I was really hyped up to play this game.  If you read my preview, I gave it 5/5.  As soon as I booted it up, the disappointment started seeping in.  Less civilizations, no personality, ugly tech web.  I was hoping that I would start to feel better after I got acclimated to the changes, but they all felt like steps back.  I did like the quests they added to help keep you occupied on turns where you don’t have much going on.  It’s still solid Civilization gameplay, and it is a unique twist, there’s just no personality.  I’m more likely to go back to Civ V than Beyond Earth. Matter of fact, you can get Civ V plus the expansions for the same price as Beyond Earth and I would recommend that until hopefully there’s an expansion that adds some more personality to the game.

Continuing a recent trend of rebooting major franchises, Thief comes full circle and starts from the top. The studio behind this particular reboot was also behind Deus Ex : Human revolution, so expectations were extremely high for this outing. Did they deliver?
The answer is... Hum. Yes, sort of.
Here's the skinny. They delivered Thief, but they delivered pretty much Thief as it was in the 90's, with 90's gameplay and AI, the problem being of course that AI -has- evolved in the time since then and well, the AI here hasn't. It's still rather dense, and the gameplay too has that slightly clunky 90's feeling where you rummage through drawers and cupboards for bric-a-brac and slowly accrue gold as you buy an upgrade here, a few arrows there, and improve your general thiefery, as well as avoid the ever present watch.
What has been updated is the graphics and the atmosphere, on my gaming rig, this is gorgeous, I've placed some example screenshots lifted from the game, and no joke, they -nailed- the feeling of the city, right down to the grim, gritty despair that is felt at ground level. The sound, the visual design, the lighting, they got all of that pitch perfect, as well as the movement and Garret's hands (yes, you see your protagonist's hands as they work!) as he goes about his business. Much like the original, you'll crack open houses, mansions, various locations, and slowly pry apart the layers of security, collecting gold, blackjacking guards, and avoiding combat where possible.
Herein lies the major warning, and major difference from Dishonoured, here there is no leeway. Dishonoured has a lot of flexibility, if things go wrong, you can fight your way out, and there's generally multiple solutions (some messy) to given problems, in Thief, whilst there might be multiple -routes- to solving an issue, they all revolve around stealth, but they're all variations on a theme. The idea is you are a Thief. So if you try playing the game like Dishonoured, you're going to find that the game doesn't cater to you. This is mostly how the game has ended up being savaged in the critical press, it's not a game that deals in flexibility. What it does, it does very well, but it only does one thing, it does Thievery. It doesn't do stylish combat or assassination, it doesn't do bravado or grand improvisation. It does patience, and cunning and guile.
As a direct result, recommending this game is tricky. I do recommend it, but only to people who wanted to see the 90's thief given a fresh coat of paint, and are willing to accept the flaws -of- the 90's thief resurrected in this current iteration. If you want a thief style game with a wider appeal and broader base, then I would recommend Dishonoured in it's stead.

Pro:
-Great graphics on all settings, heavily optimized
-Arcade-like driving so it's very fun
-Lots of rims to choose, applicable to every car
-Fun game modes like, Overtake, Eliminator and Checkpoint
Cons:
-Besides some class 4 race cars and the Indy cars, every car drifts in corners unless you go slowly
-Drifting a corner is faster then normal driving
-No driving options like, TC, ABS and so on...
-No cockpit view, both chase camera close and far shake when speeding, hurts your eyes after a while
-Although damage is realistic on the visual side, it's imperfect on the performance side. You can hit a wall and either bounce of to continue driving or destroy your car. Only Demolition cars can have their tires blown
-Only the Online mode has performance tuning, with the car changing into a higher class gets a body kit lift. No options for having body kits in Singleplayer mode
-Even if ingame music is off, there is still music played on example: final laps, last two drivers, 30 seconds left, and so on
-Demolition races have a bug, both Online and Offline, where your position will be changed from any place on the board to last, because the game thinks you cutted the track. No evidence to confirm why it happens, most of them happen if a player is first and made a big gap between others behind him
-The game is 3 years old, and already gathering cheaters. In one session of Online playing i encounter at least 1 or 2 players that are driving two times faster or don't get a penalty for cutting corners
-Drift races are not fun offline. In order to enjoy them, you need to get the Drift Pack DLC
-Replay camera is awfull, made to look like a movie or commercial. So some great momments during a race can't be seen from the track side replay angle. You can view only your car in replay
Conclusion:
Fun game, worth playing. You can get frustrated Online easily.
Not for the Racedriver Grid 2008 hardcore fans.

Yet another example of how "video game reviews" drag down a good game where many hours of blood and sweat went into.
The tendency of reviewers to go mad as soon as a game does not reflect the reviewers expectation a 100%, is tiresome.
This unprofessional babbling has nothing to do with reviewing objectively any longer. Every one can do it. It is mostly just the expression of a very biased opinion but disguised as a review.
One article even rated Thief as alow as 40%....  come on, really? 40%??  This is a highly polished game, with a lot of atmosphere. Even the view of the scenes alone makes it worthwhile to play. How can one seriously rate it as low as a broken game (which 40% would imply - Yet the game is all but broken.)
If you expect the freedom of previous Thief games, you will be disappointed.
However, if you take the game for what it is, it is still a lot of fun. The tone it sets, and the mood it creates is very dark, distopian and gritty. Its first person movement immerse you well into the actions, and there are a ton of options to customize your difficulty. You can even switch off entire UI elements to immerse yourself even deeper.
At times you struggle with the controls, but it is nothing game breaking and I got used to handle it as time passed.
Thief's only big mistake is it's rather linear gameplay in the main missions, which is really the only downside of an otherwise great game.

OK. If you get this game there are a few things you need to do before you actually play it.
1. Make sure all drivers are up to date.
2. Turn of mouse acceleration. It doesnt work if you disable it in the options. (Go to Location below)
3. Go to "My Documents\My Games\Far Cry 4\[account id name]\GamerProfile.xml" and Search for “DisableLoadingMip0="0"” and change the second 0 to a 1, so it should read “DisableLoadingMip0="1"”
4. You might also want to disable motion blurr in the same text file.
After you do these things Far Cry 4 should run without massive stuttering.
Although some people are still having problems with black screens and crashing.

For example: I now finally have total control over deck creation. In some of the past versions of these Steam/App Store/Console games you were unable to have control over land counts. Okay, so maybe you're new to the series, or maybe you've played the previous game and haven't taken the hint yet. Fear not! The sequel is here and any remaining sanity will be forfeit.
For those who aren't familiar, here's a game where you run a restaurant, apparently single-handedly, juggling customer orders, kitchen chores, and the occasional urge to flip the table when some mook wanders in five minutes before closing and orders his steak well done (get out of my restaurant). In the second installment, you must now also handle the holding stations, preparing dishes ahead of time to satisfy the inevitable rush hour stampede, and setting out side dishes to distract your patrons from the fact that you're too busy serving someone else.
We've also got new recipes, far more than the original game, spanning a number of different cuisines. If you've ever wanted to run a food stall selling ramen, kebabs and breakfast cereal (because why the hell not), here's your chance. You can also redecorate your restaurant now, if that's your thing. If not, you can take on the campaign-style "Chef for Hire" levels, earning medals based on your performance while earning peanuts in the form of tips from your stingy customers who clearly don't appreciate the amount of love and lard that goes into their burgers.
There's now local co-op mode as well, so you can share your pain with another human and perhaps begin to understand how much communication is required in an actual restaurant, right before one of you sets the place on fire.
Oh yes, and the developer is still actually maintaining and improving this. It's also 100% microtransaction and loot box free, so if you suffer from underhanded-game-publisher-related allergies, I can highly recommend this place.

The difficulty increases as you progress but it doesn’t take long to master the challenges the game throws at you, leaving players waiting for something new.
That being said, the gameplay is very simple and fun. Your goal is to match three or more tiles of the same color to take them off of the board. Each level gives you a goal of how many tiles of certain colors to collect, you are also timed with a bar that pushes the tiles up to the top or bottom of the screen, once it hits the edge it’s game over. The game adds in new twists to try and change things up, such as gravity playing a factor in where tiles end up. Some levels can seem very topsy turvy with things moving side-to-side even. There are also power up titles that pop up on the board, these can flip tiles over or change titles to certain colors along with a host of other things. I personally found only a handful of them useful and the game didn’t offer new power tiles as often as I’d like. You also gain gold in the game which can be used to buy items which can be the most useful things in the game though fifty levels in and I found myself with a surplus of gold taking away any sort of strategy on when to buy an item.
This is a good title to grab on sale, or even at its current normal price but it’s short and simple. The same music plays throughout the game and the graphics are very basic. While there are certainly better match three games to be found,
isn’t a bad addition to your library.

Pleasently surprised by this game. While the survival genre isn't exactly new (and let's face it, survival as a genre is very over-saturated these days) this game brings a rather unique twist with it being based very cold temperatures that make exploration need very careful planning, as one wrong decision can cost you dearly, either from freezing to death or the alien hybrids that have nothing better to do than to make your life a misery.
Interiors of buildings are randomly generated which in turn mean that items are also randomly generated. Your starting gear is also randomly generated to an extent too, which is rather nice as it brings a fair bit of variety. A decent example is that the first time I played I got a nice revolver with plenty of ammo. The second time round I didn't get a revolver and the third time I got a revolver but had the wrong ammo type.
The hybrids hurt, It is advised to try and avoid combat if possible (however you could go in guns/axes ablazing, just don't expect to be in one piece after though :p). You can sneak by crouching or walking to reduce noise you make, as far as I can tell it seems to work well enough.
While the controls can get a bit of getting used to, they work fairly well. Line of Sight is implemented very well in this game where you have a cone of sight that is movable with the mouse.
Really enjoying it so far, although I haven't put in as much time as I would like. Would love to see more crafting options, randomly generated maps (as well as interiors) and more functionality. I will be following the game to see how the devs expand the game.

*Early Alpha Review*
Frozen State - Released in early Alpha today 7/1/14 I believe this game has a lot of potential and I am excited to see where the dev team will take it. My first playthrough I survived roughly 70 minutes. A brief tutorial gets you going with the basics and throughout my playthrough I found myself bringing up the Manual to check things such as crafting and whatnot. GAMEPLAY: In Frozen State's current 'state' do NOT expect a run and gun zombie killing game. I found it to be much more of a survival of the elements and finding safe places to sleep, cook food and stay warm. Most of my time was spent going from house to house looking through cupboards and bedrooms for useful items to either drink, eat or cook with. Building fires is absolutely necessary to stay alive along with finding safe places to sleep. As if surviving the subarctic tempurature isn't difficult enough, there are zombie-like creatures scattered thoughout the game. You start with a Nagant 7.62R pistol and an axe, the enemies (two varients that I have found so far) are not the most difficult to kill but I found myself avoiding them like the plague just because I was dying a slow death trying to stay alive without dealing with them. AUDIO/VIDEO: Both could use a little bit of work. I don't need my games, personally, to be the shiniest thing int he world but the visuals could maybe use some work. Noticed some animations were missing and some, like the flashlight I found, were really impressive adding to the overall atmosphere. Audio was OK, nothing to write home about at this point.
In the end, I was freezing to death, getting hungry and becoming dehydrated. I was out at night during a snowstorm searching for safe shelter where I could build a fire and sleep. I stumbled across a huge building, I think it was a school, went it and went upstairs looking for either a bed or bathtub. I could hear creatures walking around and it was almost pitch black in the building so I had to move by flashlight and focus in on sounds. (You can hold "C" to focus on noises, I thought this was a really cool feature adding to the survival-horror feel) Was killed by a creature that walked on four legs, reminded me of the 'Licker' from a Resident Evil game.
All in all, I really think this is what survival horror is about. Excellent dark, gritty and isolated-survival aspects. Needs a lot of work but so far so good. They have a lot of content planned and I can only see good things for Frozen State. Worth the $10? Yeah, help the dev team out with your feedback and I believe we will all be well rewarded in the end. Enjoy!

The Thief franchize has been a very unique one over the years. The whole purpose of the game was to steal, remain undetected and discover things that should've remain hidden.
Now, 10 years after Deadly Shadows a reboot of the game has been made. It's not a sequel of any kind or does it share all of it's previous characterisitcs. The developers stated once: "we made the game thinking about what Thief would be like in our times and not as a sequel to the previous games".
Leaving the fact that this is indeed not a sequel of the game aside, there are a couple of changes within the game that seem to cause hardcore fans to not like that much and casual players to be more attracted to it. First off, the story has been changed quite a bit; while it still keeps its mysteries and whatnot interesting conversations, the story is now full of action, enemies, allies and sometimes not as stealthy as one might want. Despite that it has stayed strong, while it might seem cliche at some points it still has it's Thief touch in it.
Another aspect that has changed is the gameplay. It's now possible to complete missions in various ways, but don't get me wrong, anything un-stealthy might sound easier than it is. The mechanics of the game work properly and while thingls like opening drawers and closets while crouching might not be possible (as it will utomatically make you stand up), there is no reason to think the game fails at any of it's gamelay aspects. Focus is another great aspect of the game, some, such as myself, dont think of it as a necessary thing to use in-game but it certainly gives the game a new way of going about missions, in fact it's implementation in-game has been more than justified and it's not just a simple over the top ability you'll get out of nowhere.
Finally there are some interesting aspects I have yet to talk about. The various maps/scenarios are a thing that caught my eye, they certainly are quite the thing and all in all I think the whole exploration and just taking your time to look arround your environment really pays off as you'll find yourself with more loot and a personally amazing level design. To follow that up is the audio, one of the strongest aspects of the previous Thief games and that might've not quite gotten there this time, with a couple of bugs and some reapeating conversations, however it still stays strong and manages to immerse you into the game. As a final note there is a bit of a Horror/spooky part to the game I, as a sassy, found pretty scary, to the point where I had to stop myself from playing many times, I think this part of the game was interesting enough and it surely adds a first in  experiences for me, and despite my struggles I think it was nice for the game to have this many sudden changes of pace.
PS: I didnt mention Dishonored because I believe that's a different First Person Stealth game and wouldnt like to compare it to Thief despite them sharing a couple of characteristics.
TL;DR:
- Good solid story
- Good gameplay mechanics and options (including customizable difficulty)
- Amazing level design
- Ok audio and sound effeects
Looking at the game from a objective point of view and forgetting about the rest of games I'd say it's a amazing game that easily stands up to other games with it's story and gameplay. As a Thief fan I can still recommend the game, because it's still as unique as it's predecessors and I for one think the reboot was a success.

Despite some of the missing banter and humour the old theif had with the guards there is still some humour to be had. The combat system could be better but the idea is to avoid direct confrontation so who cares. I miss the pagans and the undead as well but this game is all the old games were with way better graphics. To those who rated this game poorly, leave the industry and never come back cause this game is easily an 8+ out of ten and to say otherwise is ridiculous.

This game is good and bad.  The world created is impeccable.  The gameplay is likewise well crafted and fun, particularly if you turn off all the visual aids and assists.  The original was ground-breaking where stealth gameplay was concerned, this game honors its roots for the most part, while gently bringing the genre forward.  After Splinter Cell and Dishonored took what Thief began and honed it, rebooting Thief required some tweaking.  This is one of the areas the game suceeds in; most the missions and sidequests are fun to play with a fair amount of choice and diversity.  The world is not entirely open, but open enough to allow exploration without moving too far away from the story.  Story, unfortunately is where the game falls on its face.  It is clumsy, leaves numerous loose ends and often pulls you out of the action to rush you through a thrown together cinematic.  Voice acting is mediocre and audio bugs repeat the same line constantly or layer them over other lines.  The City layout can be very confusing, which does not sooth the frustration of the repetitive running back and forth the game puts you through.  The game contains profanity that seems awkwardly out of place for the time period it tries to mimic and falls into the same childish trend of "there must be boobs!  And sex!!" that seems to be gripping so many Developers anymore.  Personally I thought Disnonored handled its "seedy grit" more professionally.  Maybe I'm just tried of cheap thrills replacing creative content.  Don't get me wrong, as a whole the game is enjoyable with several shining moments.  It's no Human Revolution, but it's entertaining enough for a playthrough or two.  A filler until the next Deus Ex comes out.

I wanted this game to be good.  Thief games are smart titles, a welcome breath of fresh air in the din of shooters and roguelikes.  Alas.  It's not just that it fails to meet expectations for a Thief-lover, it's that the game itself is littered with so many problems and poor choices that it fails to even be a great game- Thief entry or no.
This game is, in a word, inconsistant.  There are great things here, but there aren't enough of them to counteract all the terrible, annoying, broken crap.  For every one good thing there's about ten bad ones weighing it down.  If you didn't preorder this game, there's really no reason to pick it up unless you are a diehard stealth gamer, and even then trust me, wait for a sale. As to fellow Thief fans, well, I am sorry this is the game we were all waiting for for so long, because not only is it easily the weakest entry in the series, it wipes away all the canon we came to love, and it ruins a beloved game character that didn't need reinventing.
In short, this is not a Thief game, nor is it a particularly good game.
--absolutely insulting choices made by the dev team to constrict player freedom at nearly every turn.  This studio clearly has control issues if they don't want the players to jump or mantle on just any surface.  This game felt like someone was telling me what to do and limiting my approaches at every turn.
--Levels are nothing to write home about but they work.
--AI can be a challenge on master.
--the audio is a completely broken mess.
--The music goes to some strange places.  I could've done without the dubstep wobbles, but I like that they aren't going with straight orchestral.  The originals had a disctintly odd dark D&B thing going on that I always liked, so at least there's some throwback.
--The NPC's are some of the worst in any game in history.  Forgettable, cookie cutter, constantly raving and yelling, always saying the same phrases over and over in very close bursts.  Super annoying.
--Garrett.  They got Garrett so, so wrong.  I can not put into words how disappointing this is.
--The story is weak and superficial.  None of the characters feel real, and I don't feel for any of them.  They don't seem like people, they seem like fictions in a made up world to serve the story.  It's the most unfortunate thing about the game IMO.  Even when things start to happen in the city it all feels very contrived and forced, I never once felt immersed in the story to the point that I forgot I was playing a video game- with the exception of some moments in Moira, which stands out as the best mission in the game.  Anyone who says the Thief games aren't about narrative haven't played them.  A single mission from the originals has more depth of content than this entire reboot.
--Start a mission with a cutscene, play the mission, watch a cutscene, mission over.  It's not so far from the original thief model, it's just that the cutscenes are poorly done.  they are trying to be hollywood or something, i dunno.  it's not well done.
--There are boss battles.  Someone please tell Eidos Montreal that there do not need to be boss battles in their games if they write them well and design the levels well.  It didn't work in DX:HR and it certainly doesn't work here.
--The main city hub has got to be one of the most irritating things in any game in recent memory.  They should have cut the hub system from the game entirely and just made good missions.  It didn't work in T3.  In fact T3 suffered from a hub system that is fragmented and difficult to navigate.  That was a BAD thing about T3, why they saw fit not only to emulate it but to expand it and make it worse is beyond all reason and logic.
--Some of the side missions show promise, but they are short.
--The stealth system is servicable, but the loot placement is ridiculous and opening drawers gets old real fast.
--I will play through one more time without custom master.  I may have crippled the game with not using the new items and focus.  (Not playing with focus the first time through did get a little frustrating when you can't jump over pressure plate traps, but have to look around for a single brick switch or something.)

I was in love with this game for about 7 levels. Then, on level 8, it all fell apart. The game starts off as a seemingly fun, free-style trick performance version of Trials. Each level has three different difficulties which require you to hit different single trick scores, overall scores, and perform a specific trick. The game allows a lot of creativity in how you accomplish the overall score, which allows for some insanely fun trick combos.
However, the devil is in the details with this game. There's no restart button, so when you fail something, you either have to intentionally crash to get to the menu with a restart button or wait until your character sits still long enough to time-out. This is especially frustrating, because the game is extremely nitpicky about the tricks you land. For instance, if you have to do a 720 Old School -> Table, but accidentally land it with a manual, it doesn't count. To make matters worse, when playing with a controller, all of the tricks are executed by using the right stick in one of 8 directions. It's pretty easy to perform the tricks mapped to one of the four major directions, but tricks mapped to a diagonal can be maddeningly inconsistent. Numerous times, I performed a tailspin (pressing right) while attempting to perform an old school (diagonal up/right) and then chain into an old school while still holding the right stick in the exact same spot.
These issues could be forgiven were it not for the sudden and unforgiving rigidity in level design. The for the first set of levels, the first seven levels require a small amount of momentum management and the occasional jump that requires precision. The eighth and final level of the set then suddenly requires you to hit every jump nearly perfectly to have enough momentum for the next jump. This, combined with the occasional difficulty of performing the correct trick, makes for maddening moments of trial and error.
It would be one thing if you had to chain your jumps perfectly to maintain momentum and that took you a few tries or if you had to occasionally retry because the controller registered the wrong move. But when you've tried four times in a row to finally get through with enough momentum to perform the trick you need to perform, and then you suddenly find yourself performing the wrong trick due to the way the controls are set up, it gets a little ragey. Then, when you've gone through this loop half a dozen times and have finally performed the correct first part of the trick, but then have to press up two or three times to get it to start the next part of the trick only to crash because you no longer have enough air-time, you want to throw your controller across the ♥♥♥♥ing room.
If you love games that are about levels designed in a way to demand insane precision in performance, you'll probably enjoy this. If you just wanted to fresstyle tricks, you might want to steer clear of this one.

Highschool Romance is a visual novel set in a vaguely Japanese highschool where you play as a guy who has to pretend to be a girl. Of course romance messes things up, there are girls with very different characters interested in her/him, who will Shoji go for?
The game has a very pretty art style, much more in line with western animation than with bog standard anime as is usually seen in VNs. Most of the story is simply told through text with static backgrounds and non-animated big character sprites, but there are also several bigger events with full-screen animated scenes that advance the story.
There is no voiced dialogue, everything is done through text. The game has a very relaxing musical score throughout instead.
The story strays away from most of the clichés this scenario brings and while still somewhat implausible over the whole situation, I felt everyone reacted pretty naturally to everything. Definitely no cringeworthy illogic in here.
Playing one route took me about an hour.
Recommended for any VN fan.

I have eagerly and impatiently awaited the arrival of CSD2 and Chubigans, David Galindo, did not disappoint me as a fan of the hopefully long franchise. With an expanded food library, the recipes have gotten bigger and better in CSD2.
The visuals are equally appetizing and the ingredients you either type on the keyboard or key in on a game controller are both frustrating and fun. Players also have the ability to modify the keys that represent a given ingredient. For example, maybe you don't want mayo to be represented by the "Y" key. You can change that too!
I like that there are now restaurants that you can cook in as a "Chef for Hire". This allows you to try your hand at any recipe as you unlock each restaurant and decide if this is something you want to buy for your restaurant too. You can also go back to your restaurant and create 13 different menus to try out on different days without deleting a menu you liked. This means more theme-based dishes can be served together on different days.
What I like best is the most recent update is a noticeable inclusion of CSD fans' opinions and feedback.
I wholeheartedly recommend Cook, Serve, Delicious 2.

You can go around as a stock explorer with maybe a new hairstyle you can have, but this is a highschool where whoever gets the coolest clothes and hairstyles get all the attention. That being said, as simple as the fighting is, it's pretty in depth with all it's playstyles and stats. Lots of characters to try out, each with different quests, different backstories peiceing together, and I'm a sucker for that. This is the kind of game I loved as a kid. Downloading a game off the BBS by some lone developer. Sure it's not the most graphically intense, but there's a certain charm behind indie developers.
Yes, it's a match 3 game. Yet, this is NOT one of those overly polished games like "Candy Crush" made by a giant corporation . Those insidious games designed to tear your money away from you. I'd rather pay for a game up-front rather than play a freemium game designed to torture me until I give them all my money.
Here, you get well designed gameplay. There's a nice gradual ramp up in difficulty. Gameplay features are added before it gets too stale. When you start to get close to the edge of losing, it becomes rather exciting as you rush to clear any tiles.
Looking at the negative reviews:
"It's not color-blind friendly!"  Look, indie developers can be just one guy/girl. Chances are there was just never any thought of color-blind people. I'm sure the developer isn't color blind so they might not know how to fix this. Make a suggestion in the forums. I mean come on, you're a color-blind person playing a match-3 style game based on colors. Doesn't make much sense.
"The sound is awful": No, it's not. Though, I'd prefer less generic music. But, hey! The great thing about these types of games, is I can mute them and play my own music.
Also: It's easy to rip on people's games. Indie devs don't have giant teams. You can dislike a game and not be a♥♥♥♥♥♥about it. These games are still developed by real people. You may think you're funny, but you're not.
Overall: A fun game. Good game design. That's hard to do in with all the Match-3 games. Suprisingly it starts to get a little challenging at later levels. Ok graphics and sound.  It doesn't wear out its welcome by providing a lot of new and interesting gameplay elements.  This is the perfect type of game to kill a few minutes at a time, and have fun.

If you enjoy match 3 games then this is up your alley.  The gameplay is comfortable and easy to grasp from the beginning and takes a bit before it gets challenging, but once it does it offers a good variety of gameplay and level types.  I would like to see the visuals cleaned up a bit, but overall its a solid experience that I recommend, especially for people looking for some quick, casual gaemplay.

Not colour-blind friendly.
This game initially seems like quite an interesting variation on the classic Japanese
formula.  It adds new features to the game and, if you like the genre, may be worth playing.
However, when I reached the eighth level, they introduced green tiles and for me - a person with red/green colour-blindness - it then becomes a 'guess if the tile is green or red' game.  This is not unique to this game - puzzle games for decades (and other genres) have failed to provide an option for those who cannot easily distinguish between two certain colours.  It would be very simple to add such an option, yet many game designers neglect to think of those with colour-blindness (around 8% of men; a smaller percentage of women).
If you have 'normal' colour vision and like puzzle games, you may enjoy this.

Far Cry 4 - is it just Far Cry 3 Version 2.0?
Some may argue that Far Cry 4 might as well have been a DLC to the third entry of the franchise, whilst others complain about the lack of optimization and stuttering issues, and others think it is just not worth the amount of money.
{Quick warning, AMD Graphics cards have been known to have issues with this game (previously with Watch Dogs), so if you have an AMD card I would suggest waiting if this gets patched instead of directly purchasing it!
Just letting you know, I am playing on a GTX 760 Graphics card on High Settings without Motion Blur with V-Sync, without any stuttering or game breaking bugs.}
Altough i disagree with most of these "issues", I do agree that the price of 60$ and the price for the season pass for another 30$ is expensive, and i am not in anyway saying that this game is worth that much money, but let's face it:
Good games nowadays just have a high price. I learned this the hard way by pre-ordering Assassin's Creed Unity.
As far as the pricing goes I would suggest that you wait until the next sale so the price goes down/wait until the DLC's are cheaper in a few months or so.
So, what good has this game to offer?
-Phenomenal graphics (to be honest the best I have ever seen yet)
-A good story line, which is almost as good as the one in Far Cry 3
-A game which unlike ACU is not broken and runs (for me with V-Sync, at High Graphics) pretty damn good
-Interesting characters with interesting goals
What has not changed since Far Cry 3?
-Towers to clime and to claim for your own good
-Camps to eliminate and claim for your people
-Cutting plants in order to craft syringes
-Repairing and driving cars
-Most of the same transport vehicles
-Map size
-A lot of identical animations
So since they are re-using a lot of old features means that it is basically the same right? WRONG!
I do not know about you guys, but personally i loved destroying camps and towers and i still do and even though a lot of animations are identical, it still looks pretty badass.
What has changed since Far Cry 3?
-Grappling Hooks, which can be found nearly everywhere on the map
-Co-OP Missions
-Make decisions on how you want to change Kyrat to the better
-More weapons
-Much better graphics
-Better looking skill menu/different skills
-Killing enemies with baits, which attracts wild animals to the enemy and thus killing them
-A more dense map
-More active NPC's
-More risks of getting attacked/killed
-Riding Elephants! (one of my favourite features), where you get to control an elephant and kill/destroy everything in your path
Personally I am a big fan of the new features, however i can understand people who say that this isn't enough to please them.
Let's quickly jump into the story [Potential Spoiler Warning]
You meet up with your good pal Pagan Ming only to find out that he is a crazy Psychopath so a few rebels who call themselves 'The golden army' basically take you with them to their camp and then you do almost the same as in Far Cry 3, you start gaining their trust by doing missions for them. Act 1 is basically just helping the people out in different ways and exploring the nature. In this Act I was a bit dissapointed, due to the fact that there were not a lot of new features until then and it just felt like playing Far Cry 3 again in a new area.
But as soon as Act II starts you are smacked in the face with decissions that you have to make concering the feature of Kyrat and to help either rebel leader. Since making decissions was not included in Far Cry 3 I was and still am pretty excited about making all those decissions and seeing what i end up with in the end. Also the Co-Op modus unlocks after Act I so that is a good thing as well. After you have completed the first Act you really get to experience the Map even better and now are able to roam more freely around than before, so that is also a big plus.
Shortly Summarized:
Graphics: 10/10
Story: 8.5/10 [so far, will be updated]
Music/Sound: 9.5/10
Characters: 8/10 [also work in progress]
Variety of Gamemodes: 9/10 [wip]
Overal: A strong 9/10.
Also I have not yet found gamebreaking bugs so that is also a big plus.
So, is it worth the money?
I definetely think it was and I am absolutely in love with this game, but i can also understand it being a bit expensive for some people due to it's big similarities to Far Cry 3. {which aren't bad at all}
Thanks for reading this review, and I hope that I helped you a little big with deciding whether to purchase this game now or later! :)

A:Hey guys let's play CoD war is fun.
B:Nah it is just a run and gun game, let's play battlefield way more realistic.
C:What? Are you all serious? ARMA is the real deal, now that shows you what really is.
Me: You have no idea what the hell you are all talking....
What am I trying to say? Well my friend, that this isn't your everyday war game, hell I can't call it a war game, I call it a survival game.
A conflict is going on, you aren't some sort of an elite soldier that regains health in cover, or respawns if you die, no you are just a person, just like all of us mostly, we aren't exo-suit wearing heroes, or using jets for transportation and etc. We are people. And what happens, when war comes, and people have to survive, since they aren't fighters? They struggle.
This game is unforgiving, it shows that war isn't pretty, and it has its consequences , it shows that war is hell, and makes you feel the atleast the minimum sympathy for what happens around the world in real life.
You might never look at food the same way, or at killing in a game, you might never enjoy a war game, like you did before, this game, it just affects you, you know?
In war there is no happy ending, it is a scar for life.
What my point is, you won't run and gun, you will just feel sad, worried, scared, these characters aren't real, but somehow it feels like it would be the same, if they were, in the end, every gamer should try, because this is one hell of a story.

- Have patience for sale, lots of it

Then you might wanna give it a try.

I felt compelled to write a review for Dark mostly because I saw so many bad reviews. From what I can tell, there are primarily two types of people that hate this game: People who paid $50 for it and stealth game enthusiasts who were looking for another stealth game to play. While stealth is the primary combat tactic in Dark, Dark should be described as a vampire game that happens to use some stealth... rather than a stealth game where you happen to be a vampire. So if you are reading this review and you don't play a lot of stealth games, but you like Vampire games, then you will probably like Dark.  Overall, this is a solid game if you can get it for $10. I would say $20, but with a 7 to 9 hour campaign, it is really hard to justify $20. Especially when you can buy Vampire The Masquerade Bloodlines for $20 and it will give you 140+ hours easy. Details:
Sound:
The protagonist is voiced by Doug Cockle, the same guy who did Geralt of The Witcher series. Personally, I think he makes a great vampire: dark and mostly devoid of emotion. However, people looking for an emotional vampire that sparkles are not going to be happy.
Overall Voice audio and acting quality were fine. (English version of the game). The main issue with the voice acting came into play when you had dialogues between the Protagonist and NPCs.
The voice audio was recorded in sentences and when they played back those sentences during the game, they didn't put in any pause between them. Thus most conversations have the NPC responding way too quickly to sound natural. Like 1 gigantic run-on sentence spoken by two different people. This could probably be fixed with a patch.
Graphics:
Texture wise, Dark has a comic book like styling, with a thick black border around every object and NPC.  (Borderlands style). It gives the game a retro feel. Some people like it, some people don't.
The developers put a LOT of detail into the environments. Each map is also relatively unique: High tech sky rises, Gothic Churches, Ancient Crypts, Woods, Modern Museums, Castles... . This helps keep the game from getting old. NPC models and animations are one of the games main weakness. The models feel like they are low quality, though that may be a side effect of the texture styling.
Plot:
The plot, at a cliff notes level, was actually better than most games I have played. I don't know if that means Dark has a good story or if most video games simply have horrible plots. Unfortunately the presentation of the plot was not done as well as it could have been. I already talked about the dialogue issues above. Plot also arrives in the form of intercepted PDAs and Emails during missions (Deus Ex style). But the game has no means of accessing the old messages. And then there are a number of Bink video that summarize  events I would have rather played through than seen in a video.
Game play:
Dark is a linear, mission based game. You start off the game in a night-club called Sanctuary. Sanctuary becomes your "home base", and you return to it between missions throughout the game. Within Sanctuary you find 4 other friendly vampire NPC's who give you your missions. Then you teleport off to a mission map. When the mission is over, you get a Bink video showing you a comic book like rendering of events with the protagonists voice describing what happened and then you re-appear in Sanctuary. Rinse and repeat.
The game takes about 9 hours to complete (12 if you reload a lot).
For people looking for a VTMB type game, know this: While Dark pays homage to VTMB through some of its environments and background music, it is not like VTMB at all. Dark is very linear. There is no city to wonder around in and find side-tasks. The dialogues are sparse and have no impact on the games events or ending.
Combat:
At the end of each map, you get an XP bonus equivalent to killing about 30 NPCs if you manage to complete the map without setting off an alarm. If someone so much as consciously registers your presence, that sets off an alarm. So there is big incentive to play stealth (and reload when you get caught), though technically you don't HAVE to. I played stealth and really enjoyed the combat. Then again, I do not normally play stealth games.
Other:
Game natively supports various 3D rendering modes, many of which don't even require any special hardware. Even has an option for the old school Red/Blue movie glasses.  I suspect the game is much cooler when taking advantage of this feature.

This review is aimed at rhythm-game fans like myself. Please have that in mind while i describe the game as "way too easy" and such.
First off i have to say, that i just skipped through every cutscene in the game. They just feel super cheasy but take a lot of time to sit through. I think the development time spent on them might have better been used for improving the core gameplay.
Speaking of which, what does it offer?
Well, sadly not that much. The game gives you 7 keys to work with, 4 in the lower row and 3 in the upper row (as black notes), which is not enough. 4 keys in the lower row mean, that you can´t simulate chords propperly, which i felt was missing from this game. Having 5 keys instead to play chords wouldn´t make a huge difference tho, as there is no second hand to accompany it.
With only one hand, the game is just way too easy. It took me 3 levels to get used to the pattern and after that, i felt that there really wasn´t anything to improve on.
Thats even more troubling as the game lacks the courage to put notes onto the playfield. Instead of using fewer notes for the easier difficulties and then gradually increasing the notes in the higher ones, all difficulties have the same set of notes.
There were so many times that i felt they could have easily tripled the number of notes to make me keep wanting to play the game and improve, to make meactually feel like really playing the song...
that said, there are some good notes here. The music is really cool and the overall design feels very smooth. Tho what i took from this game was starting on the lowest difficulty to get used to the gameplay, finding it too easy, going into a higher difficulty and then figure out that i´ve basically seen it all. Now i had fun in this game for a few minutes, so if you´re really bored just go for it, but there are better, free games out there with way more content that i to this day didn´t get tired of.
So yeah, even tho i liked the game, i can´t recommend it...

First off, this game isn't straight-up better than the first Cook, Serve, Delicious! game. The first game's foods have more individual character and the game is more polished. This game has more foods but they're all pretty similar, and the game isn't as polished. Imo the first game makes a better first impression.  So if you're thinking of buying this game, you should consider playing the first one and then getting this one.
However, this game is still pretty good, and there are a lot of things I like about it. I like the large variety of foods (and the great food artwork) as well as how many different levels there are. There is definitely more content and playtime in this game compared to the first one. The new gameplay mechanics added are also fun- I enjoy the holding stations, and I'm totally okay with having to change pages to place ingredients. And most importantly to me, the co-op is WAY better in this game since both players can serve and cook food!
Almost everything I don't like about this game is related to the UI and usability. When the game first launched, it was definitely unfinished. It's a little better now, but it still feels like nobody actually tested it (even though I know that people have). Some of the design decisions are just baffling. Why is it so annoying to put foods on your menu compared to the first game? Why is it so hard to move and erase furniture in the restaurant customizer? In multiplayer, why can't both players control the menus (and if you try, why does it sometimes crash the game/result in nobody being able to control it)? And finally, why do so many foods have the same ingredients with confusingly different keybindings that you can't change?
I know that most of those things can and will probably be fixed in a new update, but imo these things are basic enough that they should have been "right" from the beginning. Most of the issues are things you notice after playing the game for an hour or two. If these issues are fixed the game will finally feel complete.
Tl;dr: Game is fun, but feels incomplete. Play the first game first so you're not turned off immediately by the flaws of this one.

When I first heard about Beyond Earth I thought it would be cool, I love Sci-Fi and i thought "Hey. Civilaition in space. Why not?" I can tell you why not,
The Tech tree is know a tech web which I found confusing, The other players/npc civs in the game arnt based off of any historical context, whcih i found a bit strange given Sids track record with the other Civ games.
None of the vanilla Civs have unique units, in stead you get the unique units depending on what "path you follow" Ypu can choose to go with purley human ideals and conquoer the new alien world which will♥♥♥♥♥♥of the natives, who will mop the floor with you if your not prepared for it. You can choose to go with a more technological/robotics path which will♥♥♥♥♥♥off almost all of the other Civs, who will again wipe the floor with you if your not ready, and stop any trading you might have been doping with them. And lastly you can choose to live side by side with the aliens, gaining alien units to command, which will (like the robotics path)♥♥♥♥♥♥off the other civs and they will attack you.
Another comp[laint I have is about the different victories, for each path you choose to go down and how they are acheved. One involves opening a massive stargate like portal letting an invading army through and coquoering the alien world for earth. The second on involves building a super advanced A.I. (or achieve singularity). The last one requiers you to build a massive alien flower like structure to "talk" to the planet. To sum it up you can either be the marines from Avatar, the Na'vi from the same movie, or Skynet from terminator. The victories can be ahcieved way to quickley.
Finally and this is the biggest complaint I have about the game, and that was Sid Meirers: Star Ships, which was supposed to be compatable with Beyond Earth. When I heard about this I was really excited. I love Sins of a Solar Empire. Space combat combined with managing my ground forces could make this game a lot more intresting. But it wasnt so, The compatability hardly worked (meaning It didnt work at all). I couldnt even get Starships to work by itself, let alone with Beyond Earth.
Civilization Beyond Earth, is not a horrible game by any means, the graphics are good, the idea of setting a Civ game on a hostile alien world is an idea that has alot of potential. But Beyond Earth doesnt realize that potential very well. They have the settings and the charecters down. The aliens as enimes as far too powerful, and as your own units theyre far to weak. (Siege worm Im looking at you here)
The traits they reworked from the older Civ games (the tech web, and the new Civs) are like puzzle peices, that fit but have the wrong picutre on them. they work but not very well. The victories can be achieved to quickley. And the fact that any diplomacy you achive wiht a Civ can be negated by simply choosing differetn tech options annoys the hell out of me.
Both Beyond Earth and Starships had so much promise but failed in a massive way. if your looking for a quick Civilization fix, that wont really take to long, then ny all means play this game. But if your looking for a Civilization gam that won't end in a few hous stick with Civ V. Dont even bother with Starships.

I definitely think that if you're a fan of stealth games, you should pick this one up.

I recieved this game for free from a friend who took part in the Indiegogo campaign.
If you're like me, when you're on the fence about a game you read the negative reviews to see where the criticisms are in order to help you decide if they're valid for you. This review is offered in that spirit.
Read this article before deciding to spend your money on this one. You should also probably know that the kickstarter was pulled after one week and the indiegogo raised about half of what it was looking for.
I personally have about 20 hours into this game and feel as though there's so much potential and promise here. It is
early access at this point, but it's my opinion that there already exists the necessary framework for a truly great game. That being said; there's also a daunting amount of work that still needs to be done before it becomes that great game.
As it stands, the mix of procedural world generation, combat, crafting, class progression, and permadeath, are compelling and addictive (also currently frustrating due to balance issues that could, and hopefully will, be easily fixed).
As of this writing there have been no updates for over three weeks. Prior to that, updates were occurring on a weekly (or better) basis. More concerning than this is the lack of communication from anyone on the dev team in the official forums since that last update. My review is a tl;dr set of statements for people who don't want to read a bunch of reviews.
1) Official reviews/ratings are either outdated or inaccurate, and many of the issues they had (especially with mechanics) I haven't ran into. The game isn't bug-free, but I haven't encountered any significant ones. (There was one mildly horrifying one where a citizen was talking about victims of The Gloom pushing in their eyes, and his eyes whipped around in their sockets [the backs initially faced me].)
1a) Some reviews complain about how close combat is basically a death sentence if multiple guards are after you. This is intentional (The whole point is to NOT be caught in the first place!).
1b) Some reviews complain about a disjoined story. I don't know where they're getting this. Everything plays out fine as far as I've seen.
2) The gameplay is solid, although it feels slightly more restricted than most people (read: those not already fans of the Thief series) expect from an "open-world" game.
3) For existing fans of the series: The developers appear to have abandoned a great deal of the humor in previous Thief games in favor of making it more dark/serious. Personally, I'm okay with this.

GRID series are like Dragon Age series of racing games.
GRID was made by company that is famous for amazing racing games (TOCA, CMR) since late 90s.
Dragon Age was made by company that is famous for amazing RPG games (BG, KOTOR) since late 90s.
Both GRID and Dragon Age are pretty much considered as successors of previous games made by these companies.
And, well... both GRID 2 and Dragon Age 2 aren't worthy of being part of their franchises. Would they be received better if they weren't using these famous names? Most definitely. Neither of them is straight up bad, it's just that neither is up to the ultimate benchmark that first games in the series set years before.
The parallel doesn't end there. In both scenarios developers of each game tried to redeem themselves with third title that oddly doesn't have the number in the title. And both of them kinda succeeded. Neither Autosport or Inquisition is considered to be as good as original game, but it's still miles better than first sequel.
There's one important difference though. With Dragon Age it's good to know the story of second game before playing third one, so it still is slightly recommended to play through it anyways. GRID series aren't story based games, so there's my verdict - avoid this if you liked original TOCA series and first GRID. Go buy Autosport instead... it might have some issues, but it's still miles better than this.

Was hoping for something like trials with tricks, but that's not the case. In this game, you do jumps and ride down slopes while doing tricks. The problem is there is no pedaling at all. You need to use momentum during entire level or you fail. If you don't have perfect momentum and can't climb the hill, make the jump, etc, you lose and must restart the level all over again. Confusingly on some parts when you land on a raised platform you can't use the speed up button. Also even if you are moving foward in parts if you aren't going fast enough you suddenly fall and lose. Its poor game design that forces trial and error because you won't know the next part and be able to plan your jump for it, forcing you to fail and restart it all. Something like checkpoints would be helpful, but due to poor design of having to use same momentum throughout level wouldn't work. The other issue is how finnicky the entire game mechanics are. I would do a jump 10 times, and only land it once. This is because the length or heigh is so far that you have to be perfect. And to be perfect you need to use your increased fall speed at the perfect time at the perfect spot of the downward part of the slope, and then let off it at the perfect part at the top of the jump. Its hard to tell where this is, which makes it frustrating. Even if you get it, you have to do the same thing 5 more times, and if you don't you need to do it all again. Then if beating the level isn't enough, you have to fufill a bunch of random objectives to unlock the next world.
It's poor game design to force repetition and failure and increase game length artificially. Playing this game made me see all the problems and realize how much more fun this could have been as a trials type game with tricks.

This game is really good fun.
Controls (especially for keyboard) and lack of Steam workshop/user-made levels.
I haven't tried with a controller, I suppose it's much better. The main flaw with a keyboard is that there are no hints in-game as to what does what. It's simple enough to figure out though: Arrow keys are one stick, WASD are the other stick, shift (either one) is a modifier button and space bar is to take impulse. Once you figure those out, that's it.
With that said, I have the impression that keyboard makes it much harder to do some of the tricks. Instead of using only two or three fingers to different directions, you ought to use at least eight fingers. That gives your brain a knot! haha. Especially since some tricks are stick diagonal, which in keys mean pressing AW or WD at same time, together with an arrow, potentially shift, and space bar at the right time. Good luck with that. XD
They are good fun and well designed. I've seen people complaining that there aren't enough, or that the game is too short. There are 5 groups of levels, each having at least 8 levels or so? Hence not so little. With 1 hour of gameplay I haven't even finished the 1st group yet, so we're talking at least 5 hours to complete them all. I think I'll take longer. But I'm taking my time, and I'm trying to clear all challenges in all levels, in all three easy/medium/hard. If you don't do that you can zoom past all levels in a few minutes I guess.
But the big thing is: After you've done all the challenges in the 3 difficulties, there's not that much to do I guess. Unless you create your own challenges, and come up yourself with new and wicked tricks of increasing difficulty, or try to beat your own high score, that kind of thing. But I can see myself losing interest rather quickly after completing the levels.
The physics are marvelous. I like that the physics and tricks are "realistic" in a way, not too crazy or bogus. The tricks feel smooth and very satisfying when you land just right. The art is pretty cool. I catch myself laughing at the crashes fairly often. It's very amusing and fun, at least for some time.
If you like these kinds of games, just get it. I am a big fan of games like the flash Bike Mania series, and have tried many clones and similar ones, and Pumped BMX is by far the best and the most fun.
I see reviews of people not recommending this because you can't pedal your bike. Wut?
It's just a game mechanic, indeed you can't. Anyone who knows BMXs know that if you're doing tricks at speed you won't pedal anyway because the gear ratios are just wrong. So it's all about getting the right impulses with your body to launch and land, and that's marvelously simulated in the game! It's great, and it works.
Press space bar to give a first impulse down hill. When you release space the dude will throw his body up, so you need to time your release with your jump for maximum air. Once in the air, press space bar to bring your body down again, that adds a lot of impulse downwards. It's very satisfying.
Sure, if you fail and you scrub all your speed you can't pedal and the dude will just come to a stop and jump from the bike. It's weird at first but it's a game mechanic that works. If you'd start pedalling mid-level from a stand-still you wouldn't have enough speed to clear the following jumps anyway. Time your impulses right and keep your momentum, it's a great mechanic and it feels great when done right!
Also, some tricks kill momentum. As they should. A 360 in the air will slow you down for example, much more than a backflip. A bar spin barely slows you down, a table top slows you quite a bit more. So in the more difficult levels it's all about gathering momentum in the first 2 or 3 jumps in order to get massive air in the latter big jumps. If you try to put too many tricks into the first few you'll not have enough speed to nail the last ones. Again, I find it to be very good and intelligent mechanics.

Pro:
- Developers will release this game in six months (Smed's words..)
- Players can chose the difficulity of the land, the size of the map, and type of gods within the world.
- Dungeons and Point of Interests are randomly generated for the world along with creatures
- Multiple classes (13 right now and will expand to 21, a mix variety of trinity classes)
- Group play is possible as long as friends on steam
- Crafting, merchants are in game
- Crafted items are not comparable to epics
- Creature and characters are nicely drawn and detailed
Con:
- The CEO has a track record of very poor decisions involving key game decisions. Will Hero Song redeem himself from the whole Everquest / SWG circus? time will tell.
- There is lack of communication between developers and the early access community
- Permadeath has several issues if playing on a server. There's only one spawn point, so if a player happens to camp that spot, there's short reaction time to protect yourself. If your not prepared, have a slower computer, or lag you'll be restarting your character (all you're gear & gold drops for them). There are other times where if you are diconnected in underworld, upon logging in, your character may find themselves stuck next to a wall and unable to attack or move. There is no unstuck command so there happens to be another player in there, odds are they'll attack and you'll have to restart again. It can be just sheer fustration so best not to die until you are high enough to take out those that attack.
- Players on occassion cannot save their progress. Seems to be related to multiple characters on one server, it's hard to pinpoint the exact cause as it happened with a brand new character as well (best to start a character and exit character screen to verify character saved, if not, make a new one until you get one to save. Once one saves, there's a 95% chance that you'll have progress saved each time).
- Monster AI combat is very bland for a hack and slash game. AI needs to be smarter with attacking players and creatures ( there is not enough variety of creatures nor world bosses)
- No world events or public quests (multiple players joining in) to take part in
- Dungeons are not large enough for group play nor entertaining. There needs to be traps and mechanics to encounters. More than one boss, mutilple phases, risk vs reward, traps, etc. The one thing Lord of the Rings Online did right was their raids, book/general instances, and in game challenges for easy/hard modes; take all of those and add them as dungeon encounters in this game lol. Right now, you run up to the boss or it runs towards you and you hit on ability and it dies. It drops one item per boss.
- Dungeon loot is an afterthought, the same epic daggers drops each time off a vampire lord in the 30+ different dungeons I have been to, one dagger and it has a durability far less than common drops. If 25 players went to the dungeon everyone would be fighting over the one item, there's no autoloot settings, whoever is closest gets the item, but with pvp enabled.. one might think twice.
- Armor doesn't mean much nor combat stats (and there is stats listed for everything but factions), level 1s can still vastly damage a higher level (20+).
- The landscape gets old after awhile, there's not much life to it, no world events, no goblin invasions, no grey aliens invading, no blood moon.. no kithicor forest, just night and day.
- Classes/Races are massively overpowered for some and others are an afterthought on abilities and combat, I'd recommend a class with range and melee combat, or just range, because one can only withstand 3 to 4 high damage close combat hits before dying.
- The story and lore is non-existent, the history on how the world was created is just a few battles taking place (battle with orcs, invading forces, another battle, etc)
- Not really a clear direction of what do in the game other than to wander around and look for dungeons / point of interests. There's no storyline to why the POI or specific dungeons are there. Most POIs I've found have no creatures.. why is it even special?
- Merchants are very few and far between, don't wander too far from town... Merchants also have limited supply of items
- Map UI is horrendous, seeing a dungeon close by and then spending 3 hours to hopefully find it is fustrating
- Underworld levels rise with changes in the landscape and over level increase I believe, on occasion creatures are 5-6 levels higher than a fresh starting character
- Towns are quite different layout but same general concept, a merchant inside and outside the buildings.. there are a few quests to bring them items, but that's it. I'm unsure why there's even a town to be honest, there's no narrative or history.
I'd recommend waiting until a major overhaul takes place and actually community interaction takes place between developers and early access players.
As long as the devs keep pushing out updates with this frequency (3-4days per update) I'll definetely reccomend supporting this game.

Definitely an early-alpha stage as of November 2016. So take these reviews with a grain of salt!
The work done so far has laid a foundation for a very strong game. While there are bugs, a need for more controls and interactivity, the game has great potential.
I have a lot of hope for this game, the developers have shown that they intend to build a deeply story-driven world that brings many sandbox options and RPG elements. To further this experience, they have built the game on a platform that allows for many people to join in on a single world. Or allow a single person to simply enjoy a whole world to themselves. Even at the current stage, it is still a lot of fun to sit down for a couple minutes to a couple hours and play away as a brand new hero in a brand new world.
At this early stage, yes, there are bugs and game breaking mechanics that still can impact your experience. But that's what early-stage releases are for! With a very lively community, a delightfully responsive development team, the skeleton of a fantastic game in the making, Hero's Song is well worth the purchase! Plus, with a game at this stage, your feedback and input can actually make a difference.
