will please players of turn-based RPGs with its historical setting, neat combat & folklore inspired narrative. That is, so long as said players have the patience to deal with wonky translations, roundabout quest design and an imperfect movement system.
I consider the story top notch, which is saying a lot given how hard it is to digest after the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor localization in English. It's the kind of intrigue and adventure I'd think to find in a well crafted fiction novel. There does seem to be inspiration from folklore (hence the "Legends" in the title). I enjoy how player choice is presented and the different endings those choices lead to. The game's rep for solid story is fair. I love the medieval setting. Cool details add flavor to the period feel, such as time being tracked according to the liturgical, Catholic calendar.
A main campaign featuring several maps (chapters) plus two single map scenarios which add several hours to the game's lifespan. 1st scenario is decently sized, has an involved plot, just like the campaign. 2nd scenario is also a large map with more combat & conquest, but a comparatively brief and straightforward narrative. The tutorial does its job and is blessedly brief. There is a game editor, which I didn't get around to. Nor did I seek out player made content or play any DLCs. In game, there are console commands to play around with; things like adding gold or units.
12 unit army (max) composed of what you pick, but typically 5 melee, 4 ranged & 3 support. Each unit levels up into stronger versions, unlocking more abilities & properties. They can be equipped individually with armor, weapons, trinkets, mounts & potions.
3 unit types: followers, mercenaries, recruits. Followers: "free" allies who don't count against Castle Support, have no upkeep and play some part in the story. They come and go (sometimes unexpectedly). Mercenaries: strong combatants who also require no Castle Support, but demand daily payment in gold. Recruits: standard unit; low initial hiring cost, no further upkeep, but they occupy 1 Castle Support. The # of castles you control governs your Castle Support (max # of units you can field).
I love the combat system here. Mechanics account for weapon & armor traits, unit health, initiative, melee & ranged defenses, willpower, stances, statuses, positioning & more. Battle occurs on a grid fielding two forces opposite each other with one row of empty space between. The area shape is hexagonal and each tile is, too. This orientation allows for different options in deploying units over the course of a fight.
Movement and attack occur as the same action. Also, a unit
act at some point during a turn, whether that be taking some action or attacking; you can have them "wait" but they still have to act within every turn. This led to a satisfactory amount of depth that I found myself enjoying.
Assaulting or defending a castle or guard tower adds an automated system at the outset of regular combat that deals initial damage to units, factoring garrisoned archers, strength of gates, etc. Your holdings can be garrisoned, taxed and otherwise interacted with. A non-military asset such as a town may also be captured, but unless it remains occupied, it will shortly revert to control of whoever holds the local castle or tower.
3 character classes: basically a knight, archer or alchemist with extra perks on top of those units normal abilities. Knight is the clear favorite. Plate armor, hits hard with a broad arsenal of weaponry and can mount up with a lance and warhorse for devastating one hit kills and multi kill ramming attacks. Alchemist is heavily ability dependent, very underpowered until you unlock those awesome spells at higher level. Archer occupies the middle ground in combat effectiveness.
Difficulty settings: Easy, Normal, Difficult, Ultra Difficult & Personalized (random, not necessarily custom). Difficulties affect income levels from land, sale prices to merchants, enemy combatant AI & castle support. One or two points late in the campaign are (by design) extremely challenging at higher difficulty levels and remain tricky even on Normal difficulty. Long story short, you'll need precisely the right troops, items & tactics to defeat these encounters (or resort to console commands).
Your army is either strong enough to take on an enemy, or it isn't...until it is. You run around dodging enemy war parties, leveling up your fresh recruits or saving up to hire top tier ones. It's a lengthy and too often tedious process given the limited opportunities you do have at the start of each new chapter to gain experience, gear and gold. I feel it could be a bit better tuned to aid your rise to power.
This really has to be reiterated: It's immediately obvious the game wasn't originally in English and now suffers from flawed localization. Not only does it cheapen the immersion, but it's especially problematic in deciphering dialogue, cutscene descriptions and the quest log, all of which contain essential cues on how to finish quests and progress the campaign. Absent the linearity found in other RPGs (which would otherwise be fine by me, since I don't like too much hand holding in my games), this situation leaves the player at times befuddled.
Even if the translation weren't obscure, I suspect some quests of being unnecessarily convoluted. Leads to a lot of guess work, back and forth travel. Quest design is standard; I might go so far as to say mediocre. I guess one or two quests in particular include downright poorly conceived steps. While you're given options in how to resolve objectives, the choice is sometimes made for you. What I mean is in some cases, it may be due to one or more options simply not being evident or well explained. Or in other cases, it could be that the option you would like to have chosen, you did not, in order to avoid the extra hassle of absurdly demanding, overly particular or troublesome quest requirements. Puts a damper on the fun of role playing your Role Playing Game. I'd give examples, but no; this review will remain spoiler free.
Another gripe is overall of movement and interaction with objects. It feels less than triple A, more of a small budget quality. Serviceable in most cases, but there are a few situations that require either precise movements (e.g. attempting to catch or avoid an enemy force) or travel within rough terrain such as mountains or dense forest; these are troublesome to get through. Overland map and movement are strongly reminiscent of
, but that game isn't hampered by this issue.
Sadly not all's well on the technical front, either. I had two quest breaking or progress halting bugs that I circumvented only by reloading previous saves and utilizing event triggers via console commands. It's a double whammy, considering how obscure the bad translation makes things!
Nice to see devs addressing issues in Steam forums. To them I'd say, please add a full transcript of encountered dialogue & quest text, maybe in the Notes section. Also rework the notices that pop up when a holding is taken by an enemy. I'd love to be able to click to move from the map & minimap, as well.
Am I recommending this game? I guess so, by merit of entertaining story, genuinely fun combat and decent RPG gameplay. But I'd slot this one a bit further down your list of "to be played" titles and first opt for more popular games in the genre. This was plenty fun but also strangely a lot of hassle! I will get to the sequel,
, at some point too.
TIP: There are quest walkthroughs in the Steam Guides (of some help, but good luck with the translation there, too).
TIP: Units garrisoned in a castle can gain experience over time; a convenient way to level them up for later use.
TIP: When stumped, revisit the tavern and listen to all rumors (just in case).

A nice story-driven strategy game, that has the feel of Mount & Blade map, Heroes of Might and Magic, and Disciples 2.
The main thing that separates this game from the other strategy games is the story. There are no 3D cinematics for this indie company, just old-school texts with the character on the screen. But the story is pretty good.
There are multiple endings for the story depending on which route you chose.
Combat takes place in a small area that is marginally bigger than Disciples 2, but it is good enough to serve its purpose.
You can only have 12 people in your "army", which feels more like a squad, but again it goes back to the old-school ways of Disciples 2 where it's quality over quantity. There are no stacks in this game, a single character is a single character.
Units have upgrade trees where a bowman can become a faster archer or a slower but more powerful crossbowman.
However, you get the feeling that the game could be so much more. There are mythical enemies you have to fight like vampires, werewolves, liches and undead, but you cannot have them in your party.
Overall it is a nice game that is definitely worth trying on a sale.

Yes, it's an early access game. We all get that, and yes buying the game is showing the developer support, etc, etc, but I honestly can not in the right mind give this game a positive review. Regardless of whether or not the games in early access or closed beta.
For starters, it scares me a bit when companies releases something in this state with the concepts running now. Did they actually play or test the game themselves before they decided to put it on early access? I don't even know because with how Hero's Song is built right now...it's not even worth $5 let alone the $20 they're asking.
Firstly, the world. Yes, it's massive and unique based on the size and prominence of the gods you choose. Every world is different. That's great, but doesn't make a difference in fact, because the worlds are ALL EMPTY. You're playing a walking simulator 95% of the time. Mobs are few and in between, not to mention the lack of variety in encounters and things to do.
Don't get me started on the point and click to move and attack. Hard to do vs running mobs most of the time, especially when they're under a tree. They're not outlined/highlighted, so they literally become a blind click click fiasco. Back on point with the world.
The map is a joke, you can walk for 20-30 minutes on a "dungeon" or "town" tile and never find the damn thing because well...the map scale is ridiculous. Coordinates just got patched...but the cords dont update, and you can't click and check the cords of the location tiles either, so...yeah, uselss atm. Nice attempt, but no good.
Speaking of the mobs, the ones you encounter are easily 1-2 shot=dead. That or they kill you easily (if they're not chickens and rabbits). There seems to be no formula for balance in terms of the scaling of monsters. One minute you're fighting e.z.p.z mobs level one, then you walk into a levl 28 mob and boom! You're dead. Upgrades are few and in between in terms of gear, and armor upgrades seem to do nothing in mitigation. You'd die just as easily in cloth armor or plate armor vs the same mob.
They made the world builder great, but the characters have no customization either. Only bare bones like name, race, class, and sex. That's it. Most classes aren't in yet, that's fine, and the ones in are missing passives and skills seem very limited as well. Did I mention you can't delete characters or worlds? Yeah....who thought that wasn't something to put in?
Crafting is e.z as well, but again..walking around for 2 hours to gather mats on the floor or off of mobs, in a 95% empty world, is no fun. Did I mention it's a walking simulator? Ok, I did? Good. Then you go log off, and come back tomorrow to realize none of your progress or chacter was saved...which is fine. No big deal, it's early access, bugs are to be expected. That I know, but terrible design and gameplay choices shouldn't be excusable because its' "EARLY ACCESS".
Take a lesson from Rimworld, who's in early access, which is basically 10x more thought out than what Hero's Song is right now. I think I could write a novel on what's wrong with the game...so lets quit while I'm ahead.

Where to start.
The label shows Early Access, but I don't think they do a particularly good job of getting across exactly how early it actually is.
Its mostly just a "wander around and click to kill things" shell right now. And, not a particularly good one at that. The user interface for combat is brutal in an old school (but not good) way. You are assaulted by fast moving, small sprited creatures that are a pain in the butt to click on.
That irritation will cause you to die, a lot. So much that you'll wonder why you bother.
And you should wonder, because there isn't anything to do anyway except for wander around and die. The map is horrific and though you'll see things like "points of interest" and "dungeons" indicated, good luck actually finding them. You'll wander around endlessly looking for a dungeon entrance as you are assaulted by bees and bats. Because they are so hard to click on, you'll eventually die to them - over and over again.
The world is also sprinkled by NPCs that spout inanities to each other but that you can't interact with - at all. Well, that's not true, if you run into them, you can kind of push them.
The entire experience feels like one giant placeholder.
I love the concept of the game and I hope it develops into something excellent, but right now they are charging money for access to something that doesn't actually need external "testers." Surely everyone working on the game can see that there's no game there yet. A few friends and family alpha testers could tell them the same thing.
I love the work that these guys did with EQ back in the day, but this level of early release is a huge disappointment.
You can do better guys.

The main bulk of the content is killing monsters and crafting in potentially larges sections of barren landscape. The game looks okay with some passable model animation, but there isn't much in the way of purpose or motivation. There is very little to do and the issues with frame rate and failed character saves doesn't help. $20 for a proof of concept.
The game is structured into three main parts: creation, exploration and redemption. Each world is generated using the selection of gods and a slider table that can allow up to seven gods depending on the world size. Each God has certain traits that could determine the geographical layout of the world, the population sizes of settlements and the number of enemies. Using the sliders, the strength of the god's influence can be manipulated for fine tuning any preferred trait. While these traits are far from being balanced, the actual process for creating the world is solid and can lead to some incredibly difficult experiences. It will take some time to figure out the best combination, which ranges between an island devoid of life and a enemy infested forest between a giant settlement and an ocean.
Exploration consist of the main adventure, which requires the player to create a character and basically survive. The creation process requires the selection of a race (determines starting gear and stats), class (almost half of which are available) and gender. Each character spawns at a random location in the world and starts off with some basic skills. A couple of skills are available for purchase using points, which are gained from leveling up. Crafting is also a feature with numerous ingredients to collect, either by scavenging (if you are lucky to find them), monster drops or mining. Health does not regenerate in this game and makes crafting campfires and health potions essential. If the player happens to die, the character is sent to the Underworld (which is changed depending on the god assigned to the slot during the creation phase).
The Underworld offers a second chance for the player to redeem their character from the ill-fated permanent death that awaits if the character dies again. Monsters populate the region and getting through them can be extraordinarily difficult. There is an exit that must be reached to preserve the character, scattered amidst numerous dead ends. Should the character die a second time, the player will be forced to create a new one while their old character is chronicled on the character list. It is a viscous cycle that will either prove fruitful or leave the player with ten dead characters before reaching level four.
I played on a small map during the video, tried a medium map following the recording and attempted several times to get into two different large maps. Whenever I would attempt to join a large map, the game would not load and instead left me stranded on the loading screen. A key binding list is absent from the current version to make matters worse. Options are limited to the resolution and detail levels selected before launching the game (Unity engine) and two sound sliders while in the game. They were both set to 0 by default for some reason.
Bottom line: it would be best to wait for this product to establish itself more before considering the purchase.

Dark, what can I say about Dark? Possibly the most annoying and enticing stealth gamplay I've played since Deus Ex. Make of that what you will. Dark is not polished, Dark is not deep, Dark aspires to one day have the writing quality of a b-grade 80's action movie, But Dark does actually manage to do stealth halfway decent in its own way. But that way is definitely not for everyone. . .
I bought Dark on Steam because it was on sale, and THEN I heard what people were saying about it, oh WHY do I bother to listen? But the interesting thing about the reviews were the comparisons to Thief and Deus Ex, and how Dark falls short, being frustrating, boring and repetitive. I'm sorry? frustrating, boring and repetitive? That pretty much describes my experience of those two games, yet I somehow managed to finish them despite spending hours trying and failing to stay stealthy. Still, the comparisons are apt, I was five minutes into the game, and I found myself thinking: 'okay the story and voice acting are predictable as heck, but why do I feel like I'm playing Deus-Ex?' Granted, Dark will never be either of those shining jewels of adolescent nostalgia that many of us remember as 'Deus Ex' or 'Thief', but saying it falls short merely because it is difficult just reads like nostalgia bias to me.
Let me digress for a moment by leaping sideways into a comparison... When Rise of the Triad recently got a reboot, what emerged from the rebooting process was a graphical update with all the misshapen heart, and twisted soul of the original: lame jokes, drug references and all. Yet what I was left with, was the sense that a perfect recreation of my schoolday afternoons in a modern graphical engine laid bare just how small and easily entertained my 10-year-old mind was. In much the same way, Dark's gameplay calls to mind the stealth FPS games of the late 90's and early 00's: Thief, Deus Ex, Hit Man, etc. but this time in a good way. Clearly I've lost 80% of the audience right off the bat with that one, but nostalgia is a funny thing...
You see. I've save scummed my way through the first two missions, carefully rationing out my two saves per area, stealth-killing my way through enemies, and resetting time and time again. I have rage quit at least two dozen times and taken seven hours of real time to get through four hours of gameplay. But at no point in all my failed attempts at silently taking down a couple-hundred armed mooks have I been able to honestly say: 'that one was the game's fault.' and that's what keeps me coming back, that's the thing that reminds me of Deus Ex (at least, how I played it). I'm not being coddled, in fact I'm being threatened with deadly weapons, but Dark neither blames me for failure nor rubs my face in it when it beats me again and again and again. Success in Dark is its own reward, and failure is a learning experience.
In this day and age of short attention spans and shorter patience, Dark IS frustrating and repetitive, because you will be frustrated at how often you're repeating the same sequence over and over and over. But that is the lot with any true Stealth game: if you screw up prepeare to reload. This is a major reason why any game that involves stealth as a mechanic these days refers to itself as having 'stealth elements' because it will give you a way to fight your way out of the pickles you'll get yourself into. But as soon as you give a stealth game a 'violence parachute' then stealth immediately takes a second seat to the alternative. Why? because it's easier.
I honestly haven't had a problem racking up XP, nor have I had an issue with the controlls, but I think that Dark is made for a particular style of play, and a certain kind of player. That player is definitely me and the play style is 'creeping death': Slowly and painstakingly working your way from room to room picking off all the enemies one at a time. As a stealth action game Dark is also a puzzle room game probably MORE of a puzzle room game than a Stealth action game. Only all the puzzle elements are also ambulatory and packing automatic weapons and supernatural powers. When taken in this context and played in this manner, Dark is actually FUN. The goal of each little segment of level is not to simply get to the next one, the goal is to cut a hole into the web of mutual surveillence the guards are wrapped up in. Isolating and neutralising as you go until you can sneak on through, and it IS possible.
I think however, that there is a better comparison to be made for Dark, the game I am reminded of is even older than Deus Ex, Older than Thief. That game is Robot Rooms. I don't know if obscure shareware games for win 3.1 needed rebooting, but there it is.
If you don't like puzzle games, or if your idea of stealth is more in the vein of Assassin's Creed or Dishonored, Dark is not for you. If you expect AAA voice acting and a complex, deep storyline, Dark is not for you. If however you're something of a completionist, if you're a patient and methodical hunter in FPS games, leaving nothing but corpses with surprised looks on their faces behind you, and if you enjoy a challenge, then you might just like Dark.

The combat is not fluid, in any sense of the word. With the limit of four blood - after you've dumped 3 levels of points into a passive - you can't use the super powers that you see the trailers spamming. The hostility meter takes three minutes to disappate AS LONG AS they don't find a corpse - that can be 10 minutes cold - or get a peek at you. There are 8 skills you can put points into, but only one action slot (besides Jump and Vision), and they don't make HOW TO INTERCHANGE THEM readily obvious. I dug around for a couple minutes, with no luck, before giving up on it. The time it takes to feed off someone is horrendously long, and the inability to even backpeddle to pull your victim into a corner is incredibly annoying. For ten seconds, you're just sitting there hoping that one guard doesn't look around the corner - which he always does - and then you have a damned hostility meter going for 10 seconds while he walks forward, then is immediately refreshed when he sends out an alarm on the corpse. The reviews I read, fawning over "hours of playtime to be had" neglected to mention that 90% of it was spent sitting in a corner waiting for a patrol to break up, so you could pick one off only to wait again. The least of this games sins was the horrendous targeting for non-stealth melee attacks (really? 6 ft guy needs to be on top of someone to land a punch?) and the fact that I had to target predetermined "hidey-holes" that didn't even give me cover for my shadow jump. And God forbid I get shot, or my wrist move AT ALL, because I'd probably end up targeting the wrong spot right as I clicked. Only thing I found fun in this game was the Shadow Kill - when I had the blood to use it - specifically in the situation of effectively poofing past a gaggle of guards, onto the second floor of a building and getting a kill.

As a stealth genre aficionado and connoisseur, I am deeply saddened of what I observed in this title. First off, I'm in no position to judge the game right now, since I'm only 3 hours in, so take this review with a grain of salt. Right off of the beginning, Thief makes you feel more like a common thug, rather than a "Master Thief". The environment is drab and uninspired, linear as well - a cardinal sin in stealth games! Missions also seem disjointed and at certain times, the AI will just glitch out, not moving away from key choke points. There are optional objectives and houses to break into, but since they are unpopulated, you just loot your way through all ashtrays and cutlery your grotesquely oversized pockets can fit. All and all, the voice acting quality is questionable at best, the characters are forgettable, and Garrett is one of the most unlikable characters in a video game to date. Not to mention that the game plays, looks and feels EXACTLY as one of the top notch, all-star masterpiece gems of stealth games - Dishonored. Here are some mechanics that both games "share" - Swoop in Thief = Blink in Dishonored / Steampunk in Thief = Steampunk in Dishonored / Villain, overcome by greed in both titles - check / A loved one you lose right in the beginning - check / Queen of Beggars = Granny Rags - gigantic CHECK.  And this list barely even scratches the lid of what both games share...
As of now, Thief has monumentally failed to impress me wtih what it has to offer - story and gameplaywise. At least it runs smooth and the game movement mechanics feel strong.

Disclamer - I've only played some of Thief 1&2 and was never a big follower. Played more of The Deadly Shadows.
Okay, don't trust reviewers. If you're not a jaded guy that's constantly clinging to his nostalgia, and in dire need to bash something for no good reason, ignore most of whining you can find on the web.
In my opinion, the game is very good. The stealth mechanics are very solid, without any major hiccups or bugs. The city is wonderfully crafted and saturated with atmosphere. New Garret's voice is great and it can only be a bother if you really grown attached to previous voice actor for Garret. The music is very nice, I'm loving the quasi electronic heavy sounds that play when guards are actively seeking you. Graphics are impressive, wonderful animations, very moody exteriors, very detailed interiors with much personality. Crouching in a corner was never so satisfying artistically-wise.
Many people scoffed heavily at the story-line and characters - I'd agree that the story is nothing special, but it has it's charm, and isn't nearly as bad as people would like you to believe. Plot and character wise this game is an enjoyable B movie. Also, I genuinely like how Garret and the people he encounters turn up. Most of them aren't that well constructed, and are a bit one dimensional following easy tropes (rogue with golden heart, corrupt and violent military leader, etc.), but they're OK, for me at least.
Gameplay wise - I'm in heaven. The sneaking feels very good, seeing Garret's hands may be kinda silly when you think about it, but it adds to the feel and atmosphere. Amount of loot is sometimes silly, and I understand how for some gathering pens and letter openers might become repetitive and boring; for me - after 20hrs of gameplay - I'm still having a blast lifting each and every cup I encounter. Sure, it's kinda silly that by the end of the level you will have like 10 cups, 2 plates, ton of cutlery, 2 paintings, 50 gold coins and ♥♥♥♥♥on of other stuff in your pockets, but it's all about suspension of disbelief - if you feel that this breaks immersion for you, well I've gotta say your immersion is easily broken. Also, none of the mechanics or the equipment is sillier than in earlier Thief games - it got less ridiculous. You no longer carry a friggin' sword ('cause, you know, thieving with a meter long piece of iron strapped to your belt is the smart thing to do), moss arrows are gone (some probably will miss them and say that it shallows the gameplay, to which I'll reply: really? Moss arrows? You shoot arrow and moss come out? C'mon), and rope arrows are contextual, meaning they're both more limiting to your exploration, and more believable (for me, at least).
Contextual jumping is present, I'd be indifferent to it, but with it being present you very rarely fell to stupid death, which is a plus in my book; playing as a master thief and falling to your death 'cause of reasons does not feel very good for me. Still, if you wanted to hop around like a bunny when running on rooftops, or glitch-jump through the walls of level - sorry, nothing like that here.
The guards are, as someone else put it somewhere on the internet, paranoid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s on the highest difficulty level. Don't think that being in shadows renders you invisible, don't think that they'll go alone after you. Sure, they're still limited by being AI so they're not very creative, but I've gotta say - there is a world of difference between Thief guardsmen and Dishonored guardsmen. Ones in the latter were blind and deaf in comparison.
Oh, and there's melee combat. I've seen reviews when it was described as clunky and such, and I can't disagree more - it's perfect for this game. When you strike from the shadows, the guards are no match for you; when you go against them one-on-one, with proper concentration when it comes to dodging (which is fairly easy to pull off) you can beat down any guard - you can't take damage, but you will handle yourself, and you feel like Garret was trained for that kind of emergency situation. When two guards are at you? Well, without any combat upgrades, you have some serious problems, and it's very logical in my opinion - Garret must have been trained in one-v-one combat, but why would he fight multiple opponents when it's more favorable to escape? Anyways, I'm lovin' it.
The city is pretty big, it takes reasonable time to move around it, and it's nicely thought out - at first you have NO IDEA where you are and how to get to places, but after few hours you start to feel like you're at home, darting through the streets and rooftops. Loading screens are pretty common, but they were never very annoying for me, so I don't really pay much attention to them. Actual chapter levels, size-wise, are hit and miss - some are pretty spacious with lots of exploring, some are more limited; then again I've never felt like I'm on a theme-park ride and there were always at least some side rooms or vents to explore. Also, when you get into a big house, it actually feels like house - the kitchens are there, the toilets are there, the bedrooms are there - basically, it feels like someone could live there. And, once again, the interiors are masterfully crafted, oozing details and character.
About the hand holding - there can be a lot, there can be none. It's up to you. You can actually get through the game (well, at least the 75% of the game I played) without any quest markers or the focus vision. But, especially without Focus, you will have to be very good at spotting.
Music is, as I've mentioned, very nice - it hit my tastes perfectly. Moody, sparse tones during exploring, and aggressive, quasi-electronic dynamic stuff when the guards notice you. Sure, the game won't get praises for it, but I really liked it.
Oh, and Forsaken chapter was awesome. I' not really a horror guy, so for me at was pretty intense. I'd guess if you played stuff like Amnesia or something this won't be anything special to you, but I had a great thrill playing it.
Now, of course, the game is not perfect, and there are flaws that I can clearly see despite being in love with it. There are bugs here and there - few dialogues cut off mid-sentence, music not playing in certain parts of the level (only met that particular bug twice), NPCs rarely getting stuck (blunt arrow to the head unstucks them, though). I don't really like that NPC's respawn a little too quickly in the City, meaning you have to deal with them again when running from job to job. And there were some more things that irked me but I don't really remember them, so they were pretty minor. Much of what you like and don't like is decided by your taste, though - it's a shame that they didn't put the chapter I as a demo.
All in all, the game, for me at least, was great. I'd recommend it to anyone without a preset mindset of "this game gunna suck". But if you're able to check it out beforehand, do so - I've fallen in love in less than 30 minutes :)
PS. This is first review on Steam I've done - I desperatly want for this game to be sucesfull 'cause I want more content (even though getting through most of the sidemissions and halfway through Chapter VII took me 21 hrs :P)

I love Magic the Gathering. I'm frustrated with Magic Duels. Play the Story Mode, and don't touch the multiplayer unless you want to sink money into coins. There's the TL;DR version for you.
What makes Magic Duels so frustrated is its asinine progression system in building your collection with coins. Not only is the rate of cards gained significantly decreased from the previous game (From fifteen per pack down to six per pack) you only get coins in two ways. Winning duels, or buying them. As you can imagine, the rate of wins is so damn ridiculous early on.
The game's rating system of players determines who you'll duel against, but that doesn't matter when the ranking is knocked back down to zero every season. This wouldn't be so bad iof there was a more permanent, and more casual side system that determined the overall skill of the player. But it doesn't. The game acts like someone who has all the cards in the collection of the previous card sets is on the same even playing field as some poor noob who has the ♥♥♥♥♥iest starter cards to work with, every time a new season starts.
As of the date of this review, DO NOT START PLAYING THIS GAME. Wait if you really want to do the grinding it will take to get all the cards in the game. Because right now, you'll get paired up with people with ridiculously powerful decks against whatever dinky thing you'll be able to scrap together with what you're forced to start with. This wouldn't be so bad if the cards were halfway decent and made your deckbuilding skill determine their effectiveness, but it really doesn't. Just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ commons with loose synergies against far more powerful, far more refined decks. It won't be fun.
If you're a dedicated magic player like I am, it's probably better to just stick with paper magic. Unless you have no friends to play it with, and no access to a local gamestore for FNM. Then you might as well consider it.
If you're a casual, new player, I highly recommend the SINGLE PLAYER aspect of this game, since it is free and it's very thorough in its tutorial. Then, go out to a local gamestore and just play the real game with other people. Hell, go do a draft, even, or just buy a couple of intro packs to play together with a friend.
Trust me, both of those are far more fun than getting killed on turn five by an aggro prowess deck. A little more expensive, sure, but if you're going to pay any cash, it might as well be on the cards that you'll actually get to keep forever as physical copies than on the random, temporary, virtual cards on this awful game.
Wizards. Fire the developers of this game and get better ones. Because this system is broken and bent against newer players. This is the exact opposite thing you want your game to associated with. I don't care if you ask for thirty or forty dollars upfront, as long as I get a game that isn't bent against me just for the cardinal sin of just starting.

Bunny Hop League is a game focusing on bhop, ramping and sliding. All 3 game modes are challenging, fun and there are a handful of maps to choose from. If you have played bhop in games like Counter Strike, you should know how it works.
The controls are fluid and feels responsive enough to let you feel that you have the control you need to success. Bunny Hop League runs great on my PC and the FPS is always high. Remember to have "raw mouse input" off to get more frames.  Overall it's a fun game but it can be annoying sometimes. That's because when you bhop you feel very light instead of heavy as in Counter Strike bhop. You miss a lot of tiles since the lightness of your body makes it harder to calculate where you should land. The maps are well crafted where some are easy, some are hard and some are longer than other maps. The map design feels simple where it's easy to navigate the layout when you are jumping at full speed.
NB this feels nothing like Counter Strike bhop, so don't expect that when you play the game. Sometimes you lose all momentum if you make a sudden strafe. It's hard to explain the movement, but you should practice how this game bhop before making a final thought. The game is cheap and the devs listens to the community where they for example fixes bugs and adds new free maps, as well as launches dlc's once in a while (they are also cheap).
I have not played the multiplayer, but I've tried the sliding and ramping. These game modes works better than the bhop in my opinion. Both game modes are fast paced and the map layouts are hard to master. The devs should focus more on these game modes than the bhop since it is the weakest game mode for me. While the controls feels good, it's something with the movement that makes it unforgivable when you miss a tile you 100 % thought you were going to hit.
I recommend the game because it's cheap, fun and gives you another view on bhop. The game gives the genre a fresh breath, but it is not as good as the bhop in Counter Strike.

It pains me to see that such a great game only has ‘mostly positive’ reviews, whereas, in my opinion, it should have actually been ‘very/overwhelmingly’ instead of ‘mostly’. It is definitely one of my favorite games; in fact, it made my summer last year. I’ve played through it three times (including all the DLCs), twice here on Steam and once elsewhere, and I’m sure I’ll replay it at least for the fourth time.
This game is by the way the first modern RPG I’ve played, and it has also – apart from being a gorgeous experience itself – managed to draw me to the genre (I’ve always preferred playing pure adventure games and eventually strategies) and discover several other awesome games. But this one is going to remain my incomparable first love forever. :) At first I was a bit hesitant about playing it, as some reviews claimed it be too hard/confusing etc., but I cannot agree here. Once I got used to the mechanics, it was a sheer joy to play. At times, ‘Legends of Eisenwald’ can indeed be hard, especially considering your finances at the very beginning and certain fights, but I – almost utterly inexperienced in playing RPGs as I was back then – didn’t find it frustratingly tough. I think it was hard to a very reasonable degree, and I kept on feeling rewarded by the narrative through the whole game.
The title fits the game perfectly. Legends are the shimmering subtle fabric the imaginary world of Eisenwald is made of. They can be heard literally everywhere and in great numbers; most of them are connected to some major or minor quest, but there are also those that just add to the whole Romantic atmosphere. I’m using the word ‘Romantic’ in the terminological rather than in the trivial sense, as ‘Legends of Eisenwald’ give the impression of having been influenced, whether directly or indirectly, by the literary fairytale of the German Romanticism and the general Romantic fascination with the Middle Ages and national mythopoetic tradition. The game writer(s)’(s) imagination is endlessly rich and inventive, and the way individual legends are woven into the larger narrative is just fascinating. I felt as delighted as a child reading a thick book of old fairytales. It was like reading E. T. A. Hoffmann as a 6-year-old for the first time. (I’m not comparing the respective literary skills here of course, just trying to express my own impressions.)
Curiously enough, I found the quests dealing with some supernatural power (taken from the German folklore or stylized as such) to be the most interesting, – although the game in many regards tries to be ‘realistic’. Well, the Erl-King, lost spirits and so on aren’t precisely realistic, but they are very authentic instead, which is much more important I think. It is not history but poetry.
The storyline – both the main one and the multiple side ones – is thus definitely the best what ‘Legends of Eisenwald’ have to offer. Its structure and the pace at which it unfolds are outstanding.  It gives you the feel of a real adventure which in fact would do credit to any adventure game as well. I would therefore absolutely recommend the game to anyone who enjoys a good story, adventures, fairytales and medieval themes.
As for the combat, I found it quite entertaining and challenging enough. Some players have complained about it being ‘unrealistic’, but I don’t think it actually has to be realistic. I am strongly convinced that a certain degree of conventionality (apart from the technically inevitable of course) cannot harm a good game; moreover, sometimes it’s even desirable. It doesn’t ruin the immersion, often quite on the contrary: I think a game is truly immersive when it follows its own deliberate logic and rules, which is precisely the case with ‘Legends of Eisenwald’. I think I read an interview with one of the developers last year, where he described the combat in the game as a kind of medieval chess – an excellent comparison indeed.
I liked it very much that you sometimes have to think carefully before each fight, as positioning your fighters can be crucial for the outcome of the battle.
Towards the end of the game, however, the combat becomes somewhat repetitive, boring and eventually even annoying (especially fighting common enemies like bandits, who tend to respawn), so during my 2nd and 3rd playthroughs I appreciated the possibility to hit the automatic combat button.
I would also like to mention the excellent soundtrack. It contains only a few tunes, but each of them is very pleasant to hear to – even repeatedly – and fits in the game irreproachably. I can still hear them in my head when thinking about this game or writing this review.
To sum up, I’d say ‘beauty’ would be perhaps the most accurate word to describe ‘Legends of Eisenwald’ – not the beauty of some stunning super-modern visuals (although I think the graphics look nice, and I liked the character models) but the aesthetic experience the game gives you in general.
From the objective standpoint, ‘Legends of Eisenwald’ might have certain flaws (albeit for me none of them ever turned out to be game-breaking) and thus be not perfect. But my personal experience with this game says it is.

This long-in-the-tooth HO game will take you on a jumbled semi-coherent ramble through the later life and works of Edgar Allan Poe, blending Poe's actual circumstances with the events of his stories.  The low-res graphics aren't quite up to contemporary par, but they're adequate.  What the game lacks in minigames, collectibles or unity of plot, it makes up for in HO scenes.  The scenes aren't very difficult, so they go quickly, but the game has a
of them waiting for you.  You spend little time puttering about in the overworld, too; you're hustled directly from one HO scene to the next with just a quick dollop of exposition tossed in.
If your main concern is the HO scenes, and ask of the plot only that it be romantic and vaguely historical,
is still worth playing, particularly if you're the sort that chews through HO games voraciously and thus can't be too choosy.

My Story, thus far...
I woke up in the woods surrounded by brethren of my kind. I am a Beastmaster, master of the beasts! I decided to explore the nearby woods and discovered a log and feathers on the ground. After collecting many items, I found my first fight. A band of gnolls were battling a pack of wild bees when I happened upon them. They did not notice me as I carefully took aim with my bow.
Two-three arrows later, I discovered that ranged bow is cool.
I looted the dead and made my way back to the town. There are four shops in town. I was able to buy health potions with my feathers and such. The weapons looted from the enemy yielded a whooping one coin. It did not make sense, but an economy is an economy.
I went back out and dispatched a few more enemies (gnolls, spiders, wolves, orcs) then found myself with the skill points to tame a wild beast. This is where my smile turned into confusion and later to a frown.
The only tamable beast happened to be a Dire Wolf (any variety). A level 1 pet that simply did not reach any level of credible expectation -considering I am a BEASTMASTER!!!
Well...yeah...the wolf died over and over. After finding and taming my fifth Dire Wolf, the icon tray suddenly appeared on the GUI...alas, it did not work. In the end, mobs simply mauled my level one Dire to the point that I did not want to play the class any longer, opting to wait until it is better polished.
(Did I mention shooting my Dire Wolf in the knee? ...instant death.)
After skilling 8 points, I purposely went to the underworld to grab me some Gargoyle crafting parts. Success! I traversed the small dungeon and come out with enough items to craft armor...Oh Sheets! I just learned that the Gargoyle armor is Plate and...well...we all know archers do not wear plate ordinarily.
The ruleset here in Hero's Song seems to follow traditional WOTC DnD (Wizards of The Coast Dungeons and Dragons). The game is nostalgic and brings to mind some find memories of a simplier time. Even with all the Alpha issues, I find myself chosing this first to spend time with.

As of now, there are very few 'creature comforts' of adventure gaming [maps, context based clues, etc].  It is playable and bugs I have seen are limited to:
1.  On joining world, sometimes my charaters are not available, so I have to restart application to fix.
2.  Hover over menus sometimes do not go away when you move mouse.
3.  Backpack item disapeared [not item within, but the bags you attach to give you more room]
No crashes on my system, and I consider this a playable alpha.
Combat control has been fairly good, but in a crowd with trees, you cannot see what you are doing.  Not sure if this is intentional- meaning it is player's job to avoid treeline during fight.   The pace of combat is not frantic, and I have seen monsters chase the character and then retreat when they are in danger.  Bats seem to hang out in the tree line and not directly confront an armed player.  Gnolls have been keeping distance and then 2 or 3 at a time leap towards player.  This is good in my opinion.
Generally, you cannot tell where you are and if you encounter a long thin obstacle, you cannot know which side is inside until you walk the length.  This must be fixed because  it is annoying to back-track around.
There is crafting, of which I am not a big fan.  The upside for me is that you do not have to go to a forge or vendor to create items.  If you have the stuff just utilize on the road.  That is a good decision for me.  The only restriction is that you need campfire to cook stuff, but you can deploy that on the fly as well.
World creation is a stroke of genius, because you select a crew of dominant demi-gods to seed the creation and you must pick an antithesis which will challenge you if you die.  I had the chaos demi-god in my 'Hades' and had to fight through a maze to return to life.  I tested whether a character in one world is available in another and the answer is no.
The key to whether you like this game  is how you respond to games where the narrative is generalized.

I loved the first CSD, and this sequel was made with an interesting approach.
For me, the best part of the game is the Chef for Hire mode, forcing you to try new foods and combinations, with a steady sense of progression accomplishment as you complete challenges. It's satisfying, and holding stations add a new layer of complexity that keeps you on your toes while simply letting you gawk at the beautiful food art.
However, this game is definitely flawed. If anything, I'd say that the game's biggest weakness is its reliance on the first one, Systems where you manage your own restaurant, upgrade your equipment, buy food, and even the emails are all derivative and confused versions of the original game, and simply muddle the experience. Often, playing in your OWN restaurant feels like a complete waste of time without a clear drive. And what's more, is the unsatisfying nature of the rewards in this game, and the fact that the cosmetics all end up feeding back into this mode that is honestly the least fun part of the game. The only reason I've decorated my restaurant at all is because I get to see it during the menus.
This game has really satisfying gameplay, and if you were a fan of the first game, there's bound to be at least one mode of this game you will enjoy, or something you can get out of it.

I loved Farcry 1, 2, 3, and to a degree, 4. I want to give this a "neutral" rating. For $90, which is what I paid for the season pass and this game though? Negative. Here's why:
1) The story falls very short of the first three games, especially when compared to 1 and 3. I feel like a child caught between mommy and daddy arguing. No decision is correct, someone is always♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, and while there are "consequences" to every action, I have to listen to an NPC chew me out at the end of every mission because I chose the lesser-loser situation. Not a fun factor.
2) The much flaunted CO-OP is pretty terrible. Your CO-OP buddy can only join to help you with outposts, herb gathering, and hunting missions. Your buddy is also limited to 150 meters before they disappear off the face of the earth. It's like walking in a world where only the first player can see anything, and the second player is stuck to stare into oblivion only to support you with a few extra bullets towards a goal which is already foolishly easy. Even on hard mode, the game struggles to challenge.
3) UBI: WHAT DID YOU DO TO MULTIPLAYER? One of the great aspects of Farcry 3 was the DM, TDM, and CTF modes. You had a great thing going there. It was a very nice tribute to old school competitive gaming. With this, you do NOT have DM, TDM, nor CTF. You have a messed up version of cowboys and indians where one side gets bows, one gets guns. Sure you can argue there are abilities, but as with every other game that has attempted asymetric combat, in the end, it leads to premade groups and utter frustration. Not to mention... the "indians" are severely underpowered. The average player who doesn't want to gather 5 of his buddies at the same time every night is underpowered because he's stuck in the hunter-gatherer stage of life.
The good though?
-graphics are nice
-story is decent (though not as strong as 3)
-decent characters.
-runs like absolute BUTTER (maxed). Great optimizations.
-Plenty to do.
-nice entry into the seamless coop arena, but it fell short. see above.
-lots of weapons to play with and variations to explore.
Overall, I give it a 6 of 10. Playing Farcry 3 spoiled me, and this is a rehash with a story line borderline dull, a multiplayer that made me want to shelve the game immediately, and $90 less in my pocket which I wish I would have researched more carefully. I would NOT have bought season pass knowing the COOP and the MP was so terrible (in terms of flexibility. Some people like cowboys and indians I guess), and would have heavily debated paying full price for the game. Likely would have waited until it was on sale.
It hurts to say this, because I love this franchise. Once again, UBI fails at multiplayer.

1) The gameplay is actually really nice even tho it's not really easy to understand the first time you play :P There are plenty combos, and EVERY character you can choose have its own gameplay.
2) The game is , for most things , pretty much well balanced, there are no real character who can just 1v5 you and get out alive . If you are doing good, you'll usually make good games, whoever you play against :)
3) This actually surprised me, but for a free 2 play game, the community is almost always nice to us. It's pretty rare in a lot of f2p and deserves to be said :)
4) There are about 5 games modes, and all of them are fun to play, and not repetitive at all , if we add that to the fact that it takes a lot of time to master the "main gameplay" and the "character's gameplay" , the game can make you play for 600 or even 800 hours !! ( I know friends who rlly played so much :X )
-Bad points :
1) The dev's abandonned the game, I dun't rlly know why , but no one is working on it anymore, so you can find some people who hack the game, and they'll never get punished :/ So it breaks a little bit the "fun"
2) The game is REALLY hard when you first start, and even after 20 hours you may have some difficulties ( or I just suck xD ) so you may think some characters are SO UNBALANCED ! I think you must be patient to enjoi 100% of the game
3) The servers ... it's not really a bad point but .. there are a lot of servers that aren't used, and that you CAN'T use, so that gives you only 10 or maybe 15 playable servers , knowing that some of them have around 200-300 ping, it's not rlly playable. That means you don't really have the possibility to choose the server you want, you are really restricted ^^ ( And you can't create servers to play with your friends ^^ At least I didn't find out any way to do it, except if you hack the console maybe ) Anyway there are still at least ONE playable server for each map and it's barely never full, so you can almost always play whenever you want, at any map or gamemode you want ^^ I just wanted to warn you about that.
Anywayyyyyy I think I said everything I wanted to say, I recommend the game to you , especially that it is a F2P !! A rlly nice and balanced pvp F2P game is kinda rare , so you should try it out if it's your kind of game :)
So I wish you good luck if you start playing, and I  wish to see you in a game :3

GRID 2 is a half-simulator, half arcade style racer that is a genuine balance between both styles of racing genre and can be categorised in a league of its own in terms of car handling and circuit design. Interior view has been removed from the original GRID which is disappointing as I feel that this camera view adds authenticity to a racing game, even if it is rarely used, I would’ve liked to switch views mid-race to know that my driver was steering the car.  The music being added at climatic points in each event adds immersion in the racing experience, unlike games such as Forza or Gran Turismo which have static tracks played all race. This game is a minor step down in drifting compared to GRID 1, however city circuit tracks for regular racing seem to have a realistic transition between brick, asphalt and kerbs unlike the games predecessor.
Codemasters has created World Racing League ‘WCR’ were your job is to race a variety of racing clubs from the US, Middle-East, Europe and Asia to attract ‘fans’. The inclusion of ESPN a well-known sport commentating channel in the US adds a layer of mirrored fame found in real life and adds depth in the single player experience, which helps new players to the genre engage in this racing game. The addition of displaying short story clips of your racing fame across YouTube, the WSR in game website and SMS messages motivates you to aim for a greater number of fans. While story typically lacking in racing games, Codemasters has pulled of a story mode that doesn’t ruin the experience of racing or feel that there is any difficulty in progressing to the next race as skipping events is optional. As you near completion of a race, overtaking a threat (another popular driver), complete a race or experience damage issues your crew chief will annoy you which adds to the enjoyment of the game but gets repetitive as you progress through the game. Throughout the game the same tracks, modes and simular challenges were reused however the difficulty of driving a faster vehicle in the later stages of the game compensates for this. Codemasters could pull some of the officially licenced world class circuits from the F1 series into Grid 2.
In short the singleplayer provides a decent range of content despite the large amount of additional content and will give at least 24 hours of gameplay in the base game*, additional tracks including the extravagant demolition derby has been brought from GRID 1 in a free DLC which is brilliant for local multiplayer fun with friends and family. The demolition derby features only one car to choose from that is kitted out just for demolition events which you can select in the quick race menu for single or multiplayer modes. It was disappointing that Grid 2 features the same tracks as its predecessor, which feels like Codemasters reworked the handling of the vehicle in this mode to be significantly easier to control, making it harder to slide out.
*Please do note that I have played this game for console on release week. *
In GRID 2 online unlike the ‘WRS’ singleplayer mode you can purchase and upgrade vehicles performance. The new rivalry mode allows users to set up randomly assigned online players which compete for XP to crown the ‘better racer’, this mode I feel is underused at the time of writing this review but is a great feature that I believe GRID should integrate with the main multiplayer mode of future titles. There is also a global challenge that ranks your account on various tracks against world times and a full featured online mode which has typical lobby matchmaking as you would expect. With some interesting indicators for racers which prefer to drive aggressively indicated by traffic light colour exclamation marks next to their profiles. Also by purchasing the DLC you get no advantage over users who have not purchased the DLC other than the specific vehicle, and all tiers are able to be used from the start in multiplayer however if you want more cars they need to be purchased unlike the singleplayer. Grid 2 is a graphically enhanced GRID 1 with several race types such as checkpoint, time attack, endurance, face off, drift, touge, races that change each lap and regular races found in the single payer as well as the multiplayer.
GRID 2 is a well-priced game to buy standalone during a sale event, do not be pressured to purchase the DLC’s on offer for this title as the content is not worth what you pay for. The free DLC of demolition derby is to be expected as it features the same tracks and cars from the previous title, but I found that the gameplay was more enjoyable for the demolition derby races than in the original GRID. The lack of cockpit view is a major letdown and detracts the simulation aspect found in the previous title. Both GRID 1 and 2 are great games and if you prefer a more Arcady family and friend gaming experience than GRID 2 is the game of choice out of the two which is an easy game to get into for beginners. Overall GRID 2 is a brilliant game that can be set apart from the previous title in ways, however there has been key gameplay features removed and missed from the original game.
*Please do note that I have received this game for the purpose of reviewing it*

I highly recommend this game for any gamer who is into excellent, top notch, stealth games. Where many people state that Thief doesnt provides ways through to an objectives as advertized and that it is only a point A to point B game; yes, thats what it is however, there are MULTIPLE ways to get through to something and it is how you get from point A to point B that matters. You are armed with a bow, and the environment around you, you have the ability to buy upgrades for your gear and obtain Focus points (Perk points to enhance your skills and make the game slightly easier) So it is a stealth game with limits, but you can still play how you see fit.
I will note to anyone wanting to buy this game though, the setting is very similar to that of Dishonored in terms of, there is a plauge ravaging the city but where in Dishonored that was the primary reason for doing things. In Thief a plauge is there as a reason to why there are limitations in the city, it holds little to no focus. The story (plot) is about people fighting for power, how it affects the lower classes, and that greed for power is ultimatley what plauges the city. So for story wise, I also reccomend it, if you keep in mind the irony that you are a Thief and what everyone else does around you. Also, it is a FIRST PERSON game, but one of the best I have played.
If you liked Dishonored, you will like Thief, if you enjoyed the original Thief games, you will greatly enjoy this. Take my advice,  in purchasing this game though; wait until it goes on sale. Square Enix will undoubtedly create more DLC so save money where you can!
Also note, this is a Reboot, people complain that it is not like the original Thief, and it isn't. But don't let that knock you out of giving this Reboot of a series a good shot. This game was released in a different generation and is very good for what it is. Do not let the metacritic scores trick you into not buying this game.

If I had to pick one word to describe Thief, I'd choose "shallow."
Everything it tries to do it does it with such little vigor and lack of polish, and so little depth and care. It's not broken (except for the audio), but it still feels like so much of it was left untouched once a feature was deemed to be in working order. The audio is the only part that feels sloppily done. Poorly synced, horribly queued, and when it works it still sounds bad. Music overtaking conversations, conversations repeating themselves and even overlapping each other. So terribad.
So does the art of thievery actually satisfy in a game titled Thief? You would hope so, but you would be more disappointed in this failure than any other part of this bleak affair. Garret makes his living by taking the paltry possessions of everyday citizens; in a city where people are heavily taxed and can barely make due, where stealing a loaf of bread is punishable by hanging. But hey, Garret's the good guy because he doesn't like killing. And those paltry possessions? Well you're looking at filling your coffers with scissors, magnifying glasses, the occasional bracelet and so many cups, all for several coins each. That is not fun! Digging through drawer after drawer after drawer is in no way preferable to stealing rare jewels and ancient artifacts (oh, and any rare items you do steal go right into a chest, earning you no coin, because Garret likes to look at pretty things and sell common items). Oh, and if you're worried that while you're breaking into a home you'll alert some guard dog or be caught by the resident while they are grabbing a late night snack, dont' worry - not one house is occupied. Not one. This is a world that has an established strict curfew, and no one is home. In a game called Thief, thieving should not be a chore.
In fact, if I had to choose a second word to describe Thief it'd be "chore." The gameplay never evolves, it never starts simple and begins to take shape into something unique and engaging. From the second you start to the moment you finish you are doing the same thing over and over and over.
One of the joys of stealth games is the kill/knockout. Taking down a foe with an instant of an attack after doing your best to elude them or setting yourself up to pounce or trigger a devious trap. There's no feeling of accomplishment here when the AI can be so easily fooled and predicted. Any given guard has one path, and moves from point A to point B, usually lingering at either for about 15 seconds - more than enough time to slip past, steal all their valuables, or put them out of their misery. And yes, I know that it's supposed to be hard for them to see you in the shadows, lurking about, and I accept that. But why is it I could more than easily walk right past a guard, who is brandishing a lit torch, and only get a fraction of a glance from him before he figures it was nothing worth note and continues on to point B.
The story is just abysmal. It's cobbled together from different ideas the "writers" had that never were fleshed out but all told made for enough chapters that they could call it an early week and get started on a six-day weekend. I can't even bother to go into more detail because just thinking about the narrative bores me to the point of suicidal thoughts and I wont let this game have any more negative impact on my life.

Once again Metascore is misleading.  The game is by no means a 69.  True, if you loved the old Thief games you'll be dissapointed by the fact they took out shooting rope arrows anywhere you want.  Big deal.  The biggest thing that happened here is they added atmosphere.  It's very well done and has you immersed as a Thief while making it so you won't be able to pop and fight everyone at the same time and win.  You're supposed to be a ghost, someone who is in and out and no one even knew you were there.  The game makes sure that you know that you're supposed to be a ghost with unforgiving combat.  You're a thief, not a warrior, and the guards and freaks will always have the upper hand on you.  The game is very long as well.  It took me 19 hours to finish it playing the ghost playstyle, and the story plays out the way a dramatic story between thieves should.  It ends the way it starts, and leaves you in the cycle again.  The game does have a semi open world aspect.  When not in missions theres a decent sized series of city segments you're free to explore and break in to.  The stealth in the game is perfectly done, and everything is animated.  The new focus ability is pretty cool, although only useful if you're stuck on something.  Only when you upgrade a few things about it in the late game does it get to be kind of a tool.  You can still jump from ledge to ledge and down things but no longer randomly.  I at first thought that to be a bad idea however they replaced it with swooping.  Swooping quickly became my best friend.  If I didn't want to walk out in to the light for too long for fear of being spotted, I can quickly swoop across the lit up area to the next shadow.  This has to be one of the most useful features in this game along with your lock picks.  Every aspect of stealth is put in to this game, whether it be light, noise, the surface you walk on, distraction, dogs, birds even, or timing, everything is in this game.
So yes, it is true they changed a few things from the original Thief games.  The real question is is it a bad thing?  The answer is a definant no, it is not a bad thing at all.  Adding atmosphere to the game is something that made it very enjoyable for me.  Does it deserve 69 out of 100?  Hell no!  My rating?  95/100.  The Thief series was always the best stealth game series and this game keeps the edge that kept it on top.

A year and a half later its still boring.  I have literally fallen asleep playing it many times. I keep trying to find something to like about it but it just doesn't do it.  Lets start with the map. Even on the largest sized map it insists on plopping the other players only a few hexes away. There will be huge unoccupied areas, and most of the players still end up tossed together on one small continent. I have tried mixing it up with the map settings available but somehow some other, or many civs ends up nose to nose with you with a mainly empty map elsewhere.
The AI leaders are extremely predictable. If you don't agree with their choice of purity / supremacy / harmony they will hate you by the time you hit level 7. The diplomacy is limited and has never been fixed.
The tech web is a mess and makes it difficult to get anywhere.  You have to try to remember where thing X falls in this mess every time you play it. The wonders are mostly meaningless and underpowered for the amount of time and energy you need to put into building them. There are way too many normal buildings which do the same thing in most cases. The cost / benefit ratio is just so wrong that I don't really bother trying to build most of the wonders. Its better if an enemy builds one because they're wasting time and resources.
The aliens... Passive agressive jerks. They make a big deal about how the aliens are supposed to be more intelligent than barbarians in civ. The only intelligent thing about them is if you keep killing them eventually they get agressive planet wide. Which pretty much guarantees that the purity factions will eventually tick them off to the point that if you defend yourself they will swarm. If you play the harmony affinity they are supposed to bother you less, but they don't. They still randomly swipe at workers or anything that wanders by so the best way to play is complete genocide, no matter which affinity you pick. If you blast them from orbit with lasers or planet carvers somehow they still know you did it. I guess thats the intelligent part? LOL
A huge chunk of every map is wasted with arctic ice so you can't navigate through it. Its like a brick wall. Please, they're trying to say a civilization with tech to colonize another planet can't build an ice breaker or submarine? Really?
Alliances are for the birds with AI's. Just don't bother, you're better off without friends.
The game is seriously a mess and all they're interested in doing is attaching even worse DLC's to it, instead of fixing the mess they made with this. Skip all of it until 2k sells the franchise to some other developer with brains.

A hardcore Action RPG for hardcore gamers, with hardcore gods that mold procedually generated hardcore worlds, filled with hardcore enemies. There's lots of different races and classes (they're all hardcore. Trust me, I checked).
I shouldn't have to say this, but the game is not finished so expect bugs, some unbalance and instability, specially if you're planning on playing online (which is not very user friendly at the time), not everything is going to be there yet, or it's not going to be polished, if you can't get over that fact i would recommend you don't buy the game yet until it reaches a stage you're happy with.
When you jump into a game you have enough things to keep you busy for a while, there's a lot of gods you can pick from when you create your world, lots of classes and races to try, you can explore the world, find mobs of different kinds of enemies, craft (food, potions, armor, jewelry, weapons), there's dungeons, which at the moment are hard to find, but i guess that's part of the fun, it makes the experience seem more valuable since you busted your @zz to find it.
The core concepts of the game are there, it takes a couple of runs to figure out how things work, but when you do you start seeing the game's potential... don't get attached to your characters, permadeath is a real thing, it's gonna happen often.

If you want to support the dev team, enjoy hunting bugs and testing systems. This is definitely worth it.
If you want a finished and polished game I would wait untill full release.

The challenge mode is a nice extra, but considerably difficult for even experienced stealth players.  Widescreen, controller steam overlay and achievements are natively supported.  DARK is a worthwhile game for fans of the genre, but probably not worth full price.

To everyone concerned about any "mixed" reviews - understand this:
The only reasons to buy Early Access games are -
CONCEPT/POTENTIAL, and
DEVELOPER ACTIVITY
On those two things, it is unquestionably a thumbs-up.  Please take a grain of salt/actually read the negative reviews.  They predominantly like the game, they are just trying to warn anyone that doesn't understand the concept of "Alpha" builds.
Again, remember that you are purchasing this game because you BELIEVE it will be good, not because it is CURRENTLY perfect.
That being said, there are SO many cool things about the game, even now.  It really is trying to shift to a new way of doing rpgs, and it's a great idea.  No more just spamming clicks on screen and paying zero attention to townsfolk.  There is truly a thinking/planning undercurrent that modern rpgs have been straying away from.
Know this - this game is not a hark back to old things.  It adopts a lot of new, innovative, and super fun ideas.  The fact that zombies walk a little too fast for 12 hours before being patched should not give this game a bad name.
Give these guys your $20, you will not be sorry!

Video review:
Text review -
Legends of Eisenwald is a turn based strategy adventure RPG type thing. It’s really a very interesting concept. The battles are all turn based strategy, navigating the map takes place in real time, and the story is advanced with very RPG-esque mechanics involving branching dialogues and choices in the storyline that can affect how things go for you in the future. The most important thing to note off the bat is that this is a game where if you want to be a completionist with quests you’re going to be looking at a guide a lot since the game doesn’t mark all of your objectives for you and isn’t always the clearest on what your objectives are. A lot of quests for example tell you to go somewhere, but refrain from letting you know that the trigger for the quest only occurs between eleven at night and five in the morning.

The story of this game however is absolutely its biggest strength. The world you are thrust into is bitter and gruesome. And the thing that got to me the most was just how horrific it is. There are little to no positive or well-moraled characters in this game, and the ones that seem to be are either killed off quickly by someone else, or you are forced to kill them. This game will constantly play with your emotions assuming your heart isn’t a frozen cinder block as it forces you to choose between lesser evils, do horrible things to survive, and to continue on as even your closest allies turn against you and your even slightly immoral actions come to bite you harder than you could ever have imagined. Whoever’s world this is? Whoever’s characters these are? Congratulations. You made an amazing gritty masterpiece of a struggle with this game. Doing the right thing around the wrong persons comes with dire consequences as the world tries to bend you into becoming an immoral heartless survivalist. It’s a horrible feeling but it’s absolutely amazing that this game was able to deliver it. However not all is bright with the story. This game features many quests that intertwine with each other so I don’t think “Side quest” can be properly assigned to many of the quests. Except maybe the type that come out of taverns. You see this game communicates a lot of legends and rumors and etc by listening to rumors in taverns. But you can’t actually listen because there’s no voice acting. So instead you have to read text walls of lore and a ton of extra information that, while good for immersion, can become tedious considering that out of all this text you only need a few sentences of it for your quest. You HAVE to read it though if you’re trying to complete all the quests, because the game rarely ever marks the useful information anywhere for you to see. And there’s an entire area late in the game that is filled with quests like this and barely any main plotline to compare. You might find yourself giving up on this rumor-based quests by then. I know I did. Oh and there’s also one series of main missions that you can fail due to a time limit. They don’t tell you there’s a time limit though which really pisses me off to extremes, but luckily the game auto saves enough that you can try to just barely defeat the time limit. Occasionally there’s repeating dialogue as well which is odd for a game with no voice acting.

The gameplay works well in that the turn based strategy combat is for the most part solid. The biggest issue it has mechanics wise is by design. By design you have no movement points. Melee units must move to one of the nearest enemies and attack no matter what to simplify it. Placing yourself in the proper square for an attack isn’t always easy as the detection seems off. And this mechanic can come to haunt you when you’re fighting undead. Ghosts can blaze past your troops and lock your melee units into combat with their spectral form which they can’t even harm unless you give them blessed weapons which are usually rare or ineffective. The gameplay suffers due to the way this mechanic works in combat involving ghosts, but is for the most part fine in every other regard. In terms of other types of gameplay there really isn’t much. Traversing the world map can be a little annoying as you find yourself double clicking a lot since the movement is entirely point and click and doesn’t support updating your movements unless you cancel your previous movement. You get castles and towns that give you gold income and towers that you can store troops in. Castles generate gold and defense units which train over time which makes them entirely useful while towns only generate gold and cannot be defended. Towers generate nothing and only serve to store your own troops which makes them useless assuming you have a castle.

The graphics are obviously nothing special, but what’s so surprising to me is that neither is the performance. You’d think with these visuals it would be easy to maintain a high framerate on a 1070 and an intel 6700k. Nope. This game has a glitch that doesn’t apply to everyone, but is basically unfixable if it applies to you, where the framerate gets locked between 12 and 22 FPS. Occasionally the game will give you more reasonable ones, but for the most part you’re going to have to get used to slideshow framerates to enjoy this game. There’s a plethora of miscellaneous bugs here too from units looking like they’re riding horses around but the horses are missing so it’s more like watching them float around like an idiot. Occasionally you try to move your character on the main map but the camera gets stuck for no apparently reason and suddenly your camera just pivots around every time you click until you buttonspam to fix it.

Sound effects work, but aren’t always synced with animations. This is most noticeable when you kill a unit and you hear his body hit the ground long before it actually does. I feel like this ties in with the reduced framerate though as that seems to slow animations down. The soundtrack is a glorious repetition of tracks that I’d usually bash for lacking any form of variety, but during my days playing Eisenwald I found myself humming the theme everywhere I went. It’s catchy. It works. No complaints here.

Overall Legends of Eisenwald WAS fun and is certainly something I’ll remember for a while. It was very unique. I just wish the team behind it had the budget to fix the optimization and that they had chosen to make the game easier to play as a fair chunk of my playtime was actually staring at a guide trying to read the horribly translated English to understand what was preventing me from completing quest A or quest B.
