Pros:
Writing: The writing is extensive, engaging and makes the world fun to explore, you get to see all these different rather flawed people and then once you learn about them you’ll usually have to decide of who is the lesser of two evils and ally yourself with them.
Setting: The game takes place in Central and Eastern Europe during the renaissance and because of that it has a lot of great stories and legends from that time period that shows off the culture of the area, which usually isn’t explored in video games.
Cons:
Combat: The combat is very simple, if you’ve ever played Heroes of Might and Magic it’s just a simpler copy of that grid based combat system, and honestly after around dozen matches I just auto skipped them.
The Grind: Each time you start a new map you start with peasants, which are the weakest troops and have little to no money to your name. So for the next two or so hours you will be hunting bandits and similar ilk in order to level up your troops just enough that they can stand a chance against the story enemies. After each battle you pray that the bandits had enough money to heal your troops and be able to fight again. And once you’re done with the map all those hard trained soldiers are gone, and in the new map you start again with peasants.
General Thoughts:
I wanted to play this game more and I will remember the story fondly however I am not willing to grind for two to four hours on each map to be able to further the story. It’s a greatly written game, but the game mechanics makes progress time consuming and tedious, especially since after grinding for few hours your army’s progress is undone and you’ll have to start the grinding process all over again. If you want a similar but better experience try Heroes of Might and Magic, it has good writing and solid combat mechanics.

I've played just under 2 hours and I think I'm on floor 2.  My only slight concern is that everything keeps looking the same in the further levels, as in the drab green and brown pain job.  This isn't even that big of a concern though, since the exploring's done pretty well and just the sheer fact of pressing on so you can find a save state is a pretty strong drive.  I just hope there's some other even cooler environments later on!

I have played various trickjumping games and mofidications since 2003, and so far this game has to be one of the worst of them. I encountered so many bugs in the game within the first 5 minutes already, that any sort of early access or beta in the name wouldn't justify for the amount of bugs.
First, I went through the tutorial which is not even worth being called a tutorial, as it only tells you to press jump and has horrible "jokes" by the narrator. After that, I tried to play the first actual map, only to respawn inside the floor and not being able to press any button in game any longer, had to ctrl+ald+del and close the game.
Once I restarted the game, it was in windowed mode and no matter what I tried, I couldn't get it back to fullscreen. I went through the options several times, restarted and minimized in between, but no change. Windowed forever.
I proceeded then to continue playing, only to notice that if you change any settings and go into playing a map, and come back to menu, the settings are unsaved. I didn't notice any "apply changes" button anywhere, so I assume it takes changes in use right away, as it seemed to do ...sometimes. I tried to mess around for a few minutes to get my desired settings, only to lose my nerves after some of the settings reset magically and some not.
Settings aside, I finally went to play the maps and test the gameplay functions, only to be disappointed yet again. The gameplay didn't offer anything new, in fact it's like playing bhop in CS:GO, except worse. The jump is higher, game didn't seem to register mouse movement as sharply as I moved the mouse, and the maps are just plain bad and boring.
Now for the part that has fooled most people into buying this game; Graphics. I didn't play through all the maps, but from the ones I did play, I noticed the game relies heavily in the use of reflecting surfaces. The actual structural work in the maps is extremely plain and empty, making the graphics very cheap. Also there are shootable targets that open doors, but once you shoot there's no sound or anything visual showing that you actually shot, which makes it very confusing to know did you actually hit your target or not. They could've at least made level-wise sounds for the doors or some beep noise for the targets when hit, but I guess they were just too lazy.
Soundtrack choice is also kinda mediocre FL Studio crap, mostly very annoying. Oh, and beware when you start the game, all the sounds are to the max and your ears will explode.
CONCLUSION: I wouldn't play this game even if it was free. Refunding right after I'm done writing this review. There are multiple better choices of games, even free ones, to go for. 0/5.

This game's stealth is INCREDIBLY difficult! And enjoyable. DARK is a challenging stealth game, putting you into the role of a vampire (you do not sparkle) trying to find his creator so he doesn't end up a mindless ghoul. The AI is well done; they follow good pathways and block exits normally, and during hostile moments they wander, and work well together. They cover each other. THEY GIVE COVER!

Frederic: Evil Strikes Back is the sequel to one of my favorite rhythm games of all time, Resurrection of Music. If you haven't yet read my review on that game, take a minute to do that now.
RoM was a fantastic game for many reasons, the most important of which is the music. Carefully remixing select compositions from Chopin's work was a stroke of genius, and was the heart and soul of an amazing experience that should not be missed. If you haven't yet played it, you are missing out on something really special. So the sequel should be another masterpiece, right?
It is with a heavy heart that I have to condemn this game for what it is. What made the first game special, the music, is why the sequel falls flat on its face. Take the heart and soul from a work of art, and you're left with an unrecognizable shell, feeding off of the success of its predecessor. That is what has occurred here, and I couldn't be any more disappointed with the results.
When I try to imagine what they could do to make a fantastic sequel, I see many possibilities. Something as simple as more of the same, remixing more of Chopin's compositions into more tracks, would have been perfectly acceptable. Teaming up with other well known musicians like Beethoven or Bach and remixing their music would have been great as well. If the premise isn't broken, then you shouldn't try to fix it. Forever Entertainment has already proven that they are more than capable of doing any of those things, so my expectations were high for the next game in this franchise.
Unfortunately, that is not the direction the developers took with this sequel. All of the tracks in this game are completely original, and instead of matching the style of a particular country, they match the style of famous musician. For example, a couple of the characters you come across are parody versions of Michael Jackson and Lady Gaga. Not a terrible idea, but the original music fails to be catchy, fun to play, and in some cases, even tolerable to listen to. As I have stated in the past, rhythm games are only as good as the music they include, which makes this game absolutely terrible.
Taking Chopin's work out of the franchise entirely just doesn't make sense to me. Remixing his compositions to fit the style of these particular musicians would have been easy enough, and it would have been interesting to hear Lady Gaga's rendition of Raindrops. Without his music, this game just feels uninspired, and it becomes a chore to even finish it.
To be fair, the rest of this game hasn't changed a bit. The gameplay is exactly the same, the art style hasn't changed, the story is just as nonsensical, and the voice acting is just as stroke inducing as in Resurrection of Music. There are no surprises here.
It's a shame that the developers forgot what made the first game so special. Maybe the third game in the franchise will return it to its roots, but I will be researching it first before wasting money on another sequel.

Even if you remove their items and put them in your inventory, you are assigned a new inventory at the start of the next chapter. With this game mechanic there is no reason to level up people other than yourself since they won't be with you in the long run.
Second, the quest log can be very vague at times. I understand that in order to fully understand a quest you need to read dialogue, but to include important information in dialogue and not the quest log is very frustrating when you are trying to complete quests. As you forge your destiny you will have to decide which path to choose...to live by your conscience, power or might? Or will you live by justice...and what is your justice really? Gather your troops and take off for adventure through the mysterious lands of old Germany...The Iron Forest awaits!
This title features an very interesting non-linear story that unfolds in various quests that you accept as the narrative plays out. The main campaign consists of eight chapters plus two additional scenarios with hours upon hours of total gameplay. As far as conflict goes, Eisenwald's tactical combat is very challenging, unique, dynamic and leaves you with a true sense of satisfaction each time you win a battle. I often find myself clapping my hands together and yelling out "Yes!" after a victory. The fighting takes place on a hexagonal battlefield in turn-based format where you can rotate and zoom the view, ala Dragon Age: Origins, to get the best possible vantage point in order to decide how and where to attack your enemies. In the past, one thing that really bothered me with many strategy games is that simply moving a character cost you an opportunity to attack but this is simply not so with Legends Of Eisenwald. Your troops are still able to move across the battlefield and initiate an attack without recieving a penalty which is fantastic. As your legends win battles and complete quests you will, of course, earn experience points that allow you to level up your units via a very diversfied skill tree that also manages to provide cosmetic changes to your army. Building a powerful army is essential to your success in this game and there is a large selection of weapons, armor, spells, trinkets and abilities including the option to use mounted units at your disposal. If you are an obsessive compulsive R.P.G. gamer like me then you could literally spend hours of your playtime just trying to equip your people with the best and most appropriate gear as you carefully read each description and statistic to determine who should have what. One has to be careful though as this title has a heavy dose of inventory management thrown in for good measure. Just like in real life, finance is important so one can't go all willy-nilly and spend every coin on gear without having to maintain a balance of resources for other vital things or face disasterous results as a consequence. The developers even go so far as to state this on the game page...
IMPORTANT NOTICE:
Similar to games like Disciples 2 and HOMM, there may be points farther into the game where you lose it all, troops, gold, inventory. All those things you worked so hard for. This is part of the game, not a bug. And you wont know when....BE WARNED.
WOW!!! That's truly scary but the risk is also part of the excellent gameplay of Legends Of Eisenwald.
Graphically, I think this game is gorgeous a true feast for the eyes. The entire presentation of the title is executed quite nicely and looks very professional. I always love the isometric look of the strategy based R.P.G. titles and Legends Of Eisenwald is no exception. It successfully captures the spirit and atmosphere of the medieval ages esthetically and runs ever so smoothly doing it. The campaigns cutscenes consists of a combination of beautiful hand painted art and detailed character models which are crisp and well animated. However, I simply cannot go any further without mentioning the superb symphonic soundtrack that this game features. The brilliant orchestral tracks manage to create a charm that truly immerses you within the medieval ambiance of the story. This is definitely a title that has an O.S.T. that I listen to out of game on a regular basis because it is just that good. The sound effects are also quite effective as well. For example, when you're in a tavern listening to idle gossip or some merchants outrageous story, the sounds of people chattering and dishes clanging in the background are so immersive and crisp. The game is also laden with extras in the form of D.L.C., the aformentioned O.S.T., a Scenario Editor with the full set of developer tools for the modding community, Steam trading cards and Steam achievements. It's a great package for the price especially if one manages to catch the title on sale.
I found myself enthralled with this game within the first few hours of playing it and I plan to spend many many more doing so. In a genre that is laden with lackluster titles, Legends Of Eisenwald stands out as a unique take on a tried and true formula. Strangely enough, this game fell under my radar but I was lucky enough to have a friend point it out to me. It's always great when you come across a title that you had no idea existed the day before and that game ends up becoming a true favorite. The battles are extremely fun, the story is intriguing and the soundtrack is fabulous. Legends Of Eisenwald is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED to both, fans of the genre and casual gamers also.
Even though the story gets confusing sometimes, it is a truly good RPG. Only problems are that the graphics look outdated and some objectives are hard to figure out. Other than that, it is quite fun.

Want to click on the map in the corner to set a destination......sorry no. Want to move around the map to look for something......sorry no. Want to drudge around drearily to your next possible destination only to figure out that it was on the other side of the map......yes you can do that a lot.
In combat for example you cannot move tactically; you can only move towards the nearest enemy. If your archer is engaged in melee with someone with a shield they cant hit them unless they have a skill to overmatch. Your healers/priests/rear line do not even have a weapon to attack with in melee. The story driven narative was interesting at first but eventually just turned into click click click what fetch and carry quest dear peasant would you have your mighty lord carry out for you today type of thing. Also the quests themselves can be quite baffling and the log is no help; vague is putting it midly. You simply only have to google the undead graveyard quest to see a litany of baffled seekers; one of which even trolls, and rightly so, one of the developers who decides to post in the thread.
I will admit there is something about the game that keeps you playing but after the first chapter i just couldn't face the thought of levelling every sinlge character in my party again, despite figuring out how to use potions out of combat by this stage......there is no tutorial as such; wait there is it just doesnt cover things like potions. Oh yes they game on every new chapter strips you of items.......gold.......party members but you do get to keep your carry over on the final chapter from what im told. Can i skip ahead to that last chapter then so my hours of play don't feel like such a dissapointment every time i complete a chapter......sadly no you can't
There are older and better games out there that do this better than this title; it had a lot of promise in pre release but sadly it never lived up to that promise.

Despite the initial release feeling like a content-lacking beta, the developer has continued to support the game to reach its potential. It is definitely an improvement over the first game with some considerable caveats.
Positives:
(+) Amazing art work.
(+) Exquisite soundtrack.
(+) New gameplay mechanics. Holding Stations to offer more convenience & sides to offer more patience
(+) Being able to customise the design of your restaurant
(+) Significantly increased number of foods to choose from. 180+ in CSD compared to 30+ in CSD1
(+) New modes offer more variety. Classic CSD, Zen mode, Chef for Hire, Stress Kitchen
Negatives:
(-) No “real” progression. Every recipe card for the food is unlocked when you buy it, meaning there is no gradual increase in difficulty.
(-) The game is inherently grindy and repetitive. You only unlock new foods after 10 experience levels and number of medals earned. What good is 180+ foods and 100+ Chef For Hire levels if more than half of them are locked behind level caps? This ties in with the lack of progression, making the game feel less rewarding and more of a chore.
(-) Less satisfying and immersive controls. E.g. In CSD1, soup used to require chopping vegetables; in CSD2, everything is done by the press of a button and is very repetitive.
(-) Still has fewer modes, game mechanics and immersiveness than the original game: catering, Iron Chef, health inspection, level up prerequisites, Online functionality & challenges are all missing. All of these added a refreshing take on the game, but are not present.

This game is ancient by hidden object game standards, but if someone can appreciate the dated mechanics, obsolete items placement, and low-res graphics, they can find a surprisingly good title under all the virtual dust.
Midnight Mysteries: The Edgar Allen Poe Conspiracy was released in mid-2009, just before hidden object games switched to the modern lightweight adventure game format. The result is an old-school game of hidden object scenes, but one with a hefty amount of plot going with it.
Said plot is about the spirit of Edgar Allen Poe contacting a struggling writer to unravel the mysteries of his murder, which coincidentally requires the solving of two other ancient crimes, both based on a short story by Poe himself: ‘The Mystery of Marie Rogêt’ and ‘The Gold-Bug’. (Both were significantly altered for the sake of gameplay, naturally.)
Storytelling is quite simplistic– cut-out characters and text balloons– but its fits Poe: it is dark, mysterious, and engaging. I imagine many would expect a lot more in terms of gameplay nowadays, but this story is still good enough to make this old HOG enjoyable for today’s audience.

This game is amazing. If you're a fan of the series, then like me you've probably been worrying. New studio, new continuity, new Garrett's voice... Would it be true to the thief spirit, or would it be a shoddy knockoff?
Thief spirit all the way. This game understands what makes the series great, and improves on it. You can loot your way across the city as you please, deal with guards as you see fit, and loot every valuable that you can get your mitts on. There's multiple routes to get to your goal, and each level is liberally sprinkled with secrets and other goodies to keep you entertained. And of course, there's no shortage of NPC dialogue to listen in on.
I've heard some people don't like Garrett's new voice. Honestly, it's... fine. Not amazing, certainly not the old voice (but who could ever compare to that?) but it does the job. The script is top notch, and always entertaining.
There are some bugs running around (I've run into an invisible table, and the dialogue is always out of sync in my cutscenes) but it's pretty minor stuff and I expect it'll be patched sooner or later. I've not run into anything game breaking.
So what are you waiting for? Get thiefing already.

It's still a relatively fun game, I suppose.  The map is large, there are plenty of missions and map elements to explore (assuming you interract with it like a motion picture rather than an actual game), and the upgrades are somewhat interesting.

A good honest stealth game. There are some decent criticisms you can level at Thief but the whole package is a game thatis really god darn fun where even some annoyances won't really ruin the experience. To get them out of the way: some of my biggest complaints are mostly technical issues such as traveling through the main city hub being interupted by having too many loading screens when crossing zones disrupting the immersive experience, there are some visual glitches and hard cuts on audio  that seem like a glitch as well as some looping audio that I think is unintentional, nothing gamebreaking though. Some of the mediocre things, but not terrible, are a few of the maps on earlier chapters feel a little linear this is made up somewhat by some of later maps in later game chapters being pretty great and cleverly designed especially the asylumn and the Baron's mansion levels. There is a tendancty to use cutscenes to deliver exposition which is something I don't really care for out of personal preference but I can easily overlook it if I find the other aspects enjoyable. Another potentially dissapointing aspect is that the story is nothing to write home about, but that isn't to say it is terrible. It is serviceable enough to the gameplay and sets a great tone for some fantastic world building. And while the main story arc is a bland some of the writing for the npc diologues are actually really great and often funny. Now some of the things I really liked are: the visuals are stellar, great textures, particle effects, reflections, lighting, etc. some of the best I've seen. This is probably one of the reasons that there are too many loading screens in the city hub, this thing does have to run off grandpa Unreal Engine 3, I never even noticed any texture popping a staple problem with unreal 3. This is paired with some really excellent animations, sound design and voice acting, for the most part. The stealth is really good, as you would expect from a stealth game, it gives you a lot of tools to play around with and I really admire the fact that this game actually pushes you to not kill people by making combat tough as nails, if you fight more than 2 people you are pretty much screwed. Plus, if you are one of those hardcore types you can customize the diffuculty and make the AI smarter, while taking away some of garett's exploitable abilities in the normal game. One really nice touch are some of the games sequences, including one of the best horror levels I've played in a game and one of the best "escape from a burning building" sequences I've seen in a game. Lastly, big props for the pc port on this. Gotta respect a developer/publisher that cares about pc gamers and does a great job optimizing it for pcs, which seems like is becoming rarer sadly.
So yeah, just a good fun game, not amazing, maybe not great, but really enjoyable to play. It's kind of a shame it is scoring so low on reviews because I think it deserves more praise but I think many people can't help compare this to the original thief games which I haven't played, so I guess this skews my perception of this game or maybe even makes my opinion unbaised, but I hear they are amazing. I suppose it is fair to judge it against those games but I find it a bit unfair since the games people are comparing this to are beloved masterpieces. So yeah, if you can enjoy a thing for what it is then you will probably like this game, maybe wait for a price drop or something? but it is worth playing.

I'm first gen of gamers, and played all Thief games on release, and bought them all again on Steam recently while waiting for this to be available, just to get back into it.
Yes it has some minor issues, such as guards repeating phrases (same happened in the first 3 games by the way now and again) Yes it is more linear than the originals, but still quite open, depending on how far your in to the game and what mission you are doing, and it is a different background and story to the originals. The story isn't as good as the first 3 games, in my opinion, but it isn't bad at all, it's just average for a story/plot in games these days. I quite enjoyed it. As usual these days…crap ending to an enjoyable game.
The voice acting is good, I laugh at people freaking out just because they changed the voice actor from the originals. This new guy is good and does a good job. The quality of voices throughout the entire game is of high standard.
The hub is a pain to navigate, but no more so than in Thief 3.
The mature themes are ok for me but they are definitely mature with lots of bad language used throughout the game and some graphical sexual images and scenes. For me it was a little bit over the top and not really needed, but it does kind of fit into the setting so I can say it was ok in context of the setting and game. 18+ for sure.
The AI is just as good as in all previous Thief games, and on Master/Custom settings, better, and harder. Those who think otherwise are recalling with nostalgia, not fact. Go play the first 3 games which are very cheap to get on Steam and you will see what I mean. The guards and their patrols in all 3 previous games were just as dumb as in this game, probably more so.
Thief 4 guards actually react harsher and help each other better than the originals in most circumstances, and unlike the original 3 games, you can't really fight your way out of things and take them on at harder difficulties you will be dead pretty fast. You’re a Thief, not Chuck Norris, throw a flashbang and run is the idea, or kill them with arrows, silently, from a safe and hidden distance.

Solid Thief title. Overall extremely fun and enjoyable for those who like stealth games. Played game with the expensive rescources (not recommended because of boss fight at end of game), no focus, and no targeting reticle.

-Sound is occasionally messed up. Sometimes it would seem that you were making a lot of noise but really weren't. Sometimes the oppisite would happen. Not enough to mess up the game but is noticiable.

-The Forsaken was an excellent level that reminded me a lot of Shalebridge Craddle from Thief 3. Excellent horror level that really kept the tension high.

As with its predecessor, this game is loaded with cheese, bad acting, and a horrible story; but it makes up for it with some really great music. If you are a classical music fan and was hoping for more Chopin interpretations, you'll be disappointed. Unlike the first "Frederic" that used modern takes on Chopin classics, this version uses close approximations to more modern music. The music is still really good, though. (As a Queen fan, I particularly enjoyed their take on "Radio Ga Ga".)
And also like original, I recommend this more for those who have laptops with touchscreens or a Windows Surface. Trying to play this game on a PC keyboard is a source of great frustration for people who play musical keyboards because it's very difficult to get keyboard keys in a position that accurately approximates a musical keyboard. But playing on a touchscreen feels amazingly natural. Even more difficult levels still feel good to play with a touchscreen.
So, if you have a touchscreen laptop or a Surface, I *highly* recommend this game as  well as its predecessor. If you're on a PC keyboard, remap the keys until they feel just right for you or else you're going to be in for a lot of frustration.

First of all this game is somewhat fun, hence recommending it. I also recommend you play with a MIDI keyboard (if you own one), although game does not support anything other then keyboard inputs you can just map midi signals to keystrokes with Bome's MIDI translator (free). It's a lot more enjoyable and I'm sure most keyboard/piano players will appreciate it as well as feeling slightly authentic.
It's a shame it doesn't have MIDI instrument support, not sure how easy it'll be to integrate but otherwise the way I do it is somewhat fiddly process. Nevertheless as a pianist I found this rather enjoyable.
The story follows a 'badass' chopin around as he travels round the world defeating various famous figures/musicians on a search for his harp... Yeah.
The story and writing is bizarre, it's like so bad it's good, only to be beaten by the voice acting which just adds to the bad-good thing. It's fun and I beat the normal mode in about an hour (watching all the cutscenes etc.) so it's not a long game but still was worth playing and now I'm going back to finish achievements and complete it in chopin mode!

An interesting game, quite enjoyable. I recommend getting both in the bundle, don't bother with this game alone considering the similar price. The gameplay is good, with a few new note types in this game. However, the entire style of the game shifted awkwardly. Visually it seems better, but Chopin is less charming and less developed as a character. He's no longer a stranger in a new world, but more of a 80's popstar working to save himself. More of the jokes go from awkwardly hilarious to groaningly memetic. Meanwhile, the voiceovers that could've started their own memes are notably toned down. It's harder to tell that there are only a few voice actors in this version, but it's less charming and natural.
Probably the most important thing is the music. This time it is far-less inspired by Chopin, but the tracks are enjoyable to play. Nothing stuck with me the same way as the first game, but it's still fun. Fans of the story may be underwhelmed, it's not quite a classic. There is fair replayability if you are aiming to improve and complete higher difficulties, but it's easy enough to complete on the lower difficulties in 90 minutes. I can recommend the bundle at full price if you like the idea and plan to beat all the difficulties. If you are just wanting to play once or twice, I'd recommend a 50% off weeklong deal.

I really wish I could give a "Wait for it" review option but overall I like it so far.
First and foremost, this game is very early access. Some basic concepts like combat and world generation are in but the game is quite barebones at the moment. So if you're not willing to buy an incomplete game, then simply don't. If you're willing to bet on them improving the game, the go for it.
+ The combat is generally fun. There are a number of classes each with a set of 4-8 abilites that you access as you level up. The combat is a pretty basic barebones ARP style. The threat of permadeath is what I think makes the combat exciting more than anything. When you die, you go to the underworld which you can escape. If you die in the underworld your character is toast.
++ World Generation is pretty cool. You pick a number of gods ranging from 3-7 depending on the world size. Each god has 3 influences on the world like more desert, a certain race being more dominant, more peace or magic being more common. You can set how influential each god is to determine how strong its effects are. This could be really cool since each server would have a different world with different influences. Apparently the underworld will also be different for each god later in development. The world is a little bland though as is.
- Content is rather lacking at the moment. There are only a handful of items to craft or loot. There aren't any quests and the towns are rather lackluster. I take this with a grain of salt since it is early into development but for those of you looking for a heavy content game, maybe just let this one slide for the moment. There are also only a handful of monster types.
+ The developers are active and have put out three updates in a week. They seem competent and have a reasonably sized team for this. A lot of the devs are already veteran game designers. This isn't the same old story of 2 guys who have never made a game before bite off way more than they can chew!
TL;DR It's a pretty good game for how early it is into development, but don't buy it if you are looking for a completed or nearly completed game.

An arena fighter with plenty of downsides but much more upsides.  The hardest thing to get used to is the game's inflexibility with ping.  As it uses the unreal engine, you'll have to aim, block, attack, where you estimate your opponent is going to be.  If you fail to do this, the game will feel lagged and unintuitive.  However, if you can imagine yourself and your enemy 100-200ms into the future (depending on the server you choose).  You'll find your attacks, dodges, blocks, and taunts to be reliably on time.  Every character has a unique feel and takes learning making it that much more rewarding to explore.  You are practically guaranteed to find at least one character that fits your style whether it's to chip away, heal the team, life switch, etc.
A super fun arena battler with a decent community.  Shame the developers couldn't afford to develop it further.

This is a good pick for people who like HO games that focus almost exclusively on the HO scenes. If you're the person who skips over the HO parts of Artifex Mundi games because you can't stand them, you'll hate this.
As such, the plot is imperfect and is just a chain to link one hidden object scene to the next.  There are some mini-game style puzzles but very few.  There is some very simple inventory management but really nothing requiring much thought (it will be very obvious what needs to be used where and when).
HO scene objects are sometimes hard to distinguish due to the resolution but overall they aren't terribly bad.

All in all, I would recommend this ON SALE to people who like the HO aspect of these casual games. The documents and those stolen collections will take you while to see them through, but they are well designed and you won't feel boring when reading them or admiring them.

Then, the game moves to its pain in the @ss part: map switching and envirnment design. In a standard of open world game, thief doesn't have many elements: smooth map switching, day/night changing, fast travel and the judging system of being caught or being chased by police (watch, so called in game).

First, the judging mechanism "kill on sight" is a element that kill this game. Whenever I want to go somewhere or trying to do a mission/side deal, those watch will slow down my step and could will killed me during the process. The developers could add another mechanism that the more enermy you killed the more likely you are gonna be chase by watch or by pealing off your "wanted" posts on wall in certain area, the watch will be less aweared of your actions; nevertheless, they could add a option that players can wear civilian clothes that would not alart the watch when passing-by but carry much less items to use when exploring the city. From the stand of developer and the stand of publisher, there are so many ways they could do but they didn't to let more common public play/buy their game and I think that's why the game didn't get a high score from the general media or public.
Second, map switching. I don't have much to say about this since almost everyone are complaining about this mechanism; for a long period of time I thought I were playing on a mobile device like PSV or iphone instead of PC only because of the freaking switch (and you cannot cancel the action once you do). I have to say this design is a real threat that kill the game and spoiled all the goods the game bring us.
In the end, I understand that the game developers want to maintain the hardcore of a theif game, but when compare to other game like Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light which does have a successful adjustment to general public that gave them a wilder sale while winning a welcome in its hardcore players, thief failed.

For a game that promises to be bigger and better than its predecessor in every way, Evil Strikes Back falls flat in almost every area except for (arguably the most important) the music. Whereas the previous installment was equal parts satire of the recording industry and love letter to the late, great Frederic Chopin, this one has more nods to musicians that were deceased far more recently, with amazing tributes to the likes of Falco, Freddie Mercury, and Michael Jackson. You won't hear Chopin's influence here, but you'll still hear some amazing tracks that duplicate the folk and contemporary music of the regions that you visit. It's not only deceased musicians who get their due, either, with characters lampooning the likes of KISS and Lady Gaga.
The part that was disappointing to me, however, was the story. The first game was quirky and charming, with clever satire mixed with other jokes and jabs at pop culture or random silly bits strewn about. Frederic himself was a somewhat smug, if charming, fish out of water, what you would expect of a composer who had been dead for a century and a half being brought back to life in today's world, trying to adjust to modern musical trends while keeping his own legacy alive and learning the reason for his return.
This time around, Frederic is almost insufferably full of himself, not to mention extremely modernized. This could have worked if some amount of time had passed, but the story is supposedly set immediately after the ending of the last game. He frequently trades substance for style, which seems to be running theme of this game this time around. It's still entertaining, it's just sad to see the hero, who was so lovable the first time around, turn into something rather obnoxious with little reasoning for it.
SPOILERS:
At the beginning of the game, Frederic loses his heart (I assume in a metaphorical sense, considering the imagery), which could explain the way he's behaving, if it weren't for a few things: 1.) he still manages to be kind and charitable when it suits him, 2.) he was acting this way both before and after it was returned and 3.) the first game already dealt with him trying to find his heart, in a more literal fashion (a nod to the controversy surrounding the fact that while Chopin was interrered in Pere Laichez cemetary in Paris, his heart is enshrined in an urn filled with alcohol in Warsaw). Basically, he's already gone around without a heart, and managed to be a good character regardless of it, if an unwitting pawn in a grander scheme.
That's not to say this game isn't without its  own degree of charm and humor. Most of the references are nods to internet memes this time around, sometimes subtly, sometimes more obviously but to hilarious effect (especially the ending). But as a music game, if you're not in it for the story, then it's still more than solid. The soundtrack is easily equal to, if it doesn't surpass, the first game's, and the gameplay hasn't been radically changed, but mixed up just enough to keep it fresh.
It's sad that the storytelling isn't as strong as it was the first time around, but like the previous game, the fact that it includes a free copy of its stellar soundtrack makes it worth the price of admission alone. That you get a fun and quirky music game in the deal is all gravy.
Not many songs to be played, but it is a fun game. I have stupid fingers, so it is frustrating at times. If you can grab it on sale, it is a good buy.

I've finally started playing this game, although it's been waiting in my library for a while now. I kind of forgot about it, but I recently noticed there was a DLC out, right about the time I was looking for something new to play, so I figured I'd get the DLC and give this game its rightful chance.
I can't give you a thorough review yet, but I can tell you that at least so far (10 hours in), this game feels just like the previous games in the series, or at least like Civilization 2-5. I've never played the first, so I don't really know what it was like. I'll get to the specifics after spending some more time playing, but generally, it's pretty much what I was expecting, and what I suppose anyone who's ever played a Civilization game before should expect.
Anyway, I know this game wasn't received as well as the last couple of Civilization games, and honestly, if there's a good reason for that, I haven't found it yet. I'm writing these very lines after forcing myself to stop playing, so I could get some sleep before a long day tomorrow. I could have otherwise easily kept on playing for a few more hours at least.
More info to come as soon as I feel I have a good enough grasp of the specifics, especially in comparison to the previous games in the series.
Update (14h+):
While my general opinion of the game hasn't changed much since I started playing, I figured I'd share what I now consider to be its biggest flaw, which was also mentioned and discussed by many other reviewers. While the formula hasn't changed much since Civilization 5, the game's main backstory theme has, and in my opinion, it has changed for the worse. Up until Civilization 5, the series, at least for me, was about history, culture and progress. While Beyond Earth is also about progress, it lacks the other elements. Sure, each faction has its own history and culture, but those are totally alien and meaningless to me, as they're not an important part of the game, and I feel no urge to learn about them. If Civilization 5 was based, loosely as it was, on some true historical background, Beyond Earth is pure fiction in that regard. Some people may find this futuristic theme curious and refreshing, but I, for one, would rather have it the way it was before.
Having all that said, as of now, there's no other strategy game I'd rather play. Not even Civilization 5, which has my highest playing time count (500h+) on record ever since I installed Steam.

I recently received Legends of Eisenwald as part of the latest Humble Bundle. I was unfamiliar with it going in, but as a fan of classic turn based strategy games like Heroes of Might and Magic, Disciples, Warlords, and so on, I thought it would be worth giving this game a go.
I'm now 10 hours into the game and on the third chapter of the campaign. There are definitely some rough edges here but I'm enjoying my time overall. On the negative side, the interface is a little buggy and obtuse. There is no easy way to compare the stats of two different items and considering the game is asking you to fully equip up to a dozen soldiers, that can make inventory management a bit frustrating. There are also a number of item abilities, but to my knowledge there is nowhere to go to see what effect an ability has. Some are obvious, such as one called something like Vampiric Touch. I can get a solid idea of what that does, but others are not as clear. More problematic, is that I also have been unable to find a way to look at the upgrade trees for various soldiers, making my choices pretty much random. And even when I have made a choice there is often little explanation of what has changed or improved with the upgrade.
So poor inventory and stat management combined with a decent but not excellent translation (I assume from German) makes the game a bit hard to get into, but as someone who has been playing games for 25+ years, I can easily remember a time when every foreign game required a bit of guesswork, so that didn't bother me too much. That said, I can easily see how a less patient gamer might just end up giving up on this before they figured it out.
Once you do get a hang of things most of the rest of the game is a big positive. You have a fair number of upgrade paths for your soldiers without things being overwhelming. You need to outfit your entire force but there doesn't seem to be an inventory limit so you are free to keep things for future use, and combat is tough, fun, and quick while not being too complex. There are also a ton of hidden secret areas in each level you can find that would earn you high quality gear if you go exploring.
As a final note, numerous reviews here and on professional sites have said that the quest log is poor, but I have not found that to be the case. You can hit the magnifying glass on most any quest where you need to go to a specific location and have it mark it for you on your map. Others have said rumors aren't saved in your quest log, but that is also not true, they are just located under notes.
Lastly, there is the debate about losing your soldiers and inventory at the end of each level. While standard practice in this type of game, traditionally you are allowed to choose a couple soldiers or items to keep and take with you to the next level. Here you just get your main character and whatever equipment he has on him at the time, which is fine but I would have liked to select one or two additional units to progress with me. As it is, you have to start your army from scratch each level, which can be a bit deflating.
All told I would recommend this game to fans of classic TBS titles from the 90's, as well as any younger gamer who enjoys slower paced titles and is willing to put up with some rough edges they might not be accustomed to.

Hero’s Song is a game where you shape your own world.  It’s a rougelike game, and in each world you create you’ll never know how much time you’ll be spending in it because of the game’s unique death mechanics.  Unlike other permadeath games, in Heros Song you get to die twice before your character is erased from time.
You begin by crafting this world by influencing parameters to the games geography, environments, enemies and cities by selecting gods to represent your world.  From among this pantheon are gods of both good and evil, some allowing for more rivers, oceans and lakes to be generated, some populating the world with more enemies, others giving the building blocks for more neutral cities, towns or species of specific races such as dwarves and elves, and etc.  Each god has a slider that you move up and down to indicate the degree at which the impact occurs.  Move them up for greater frequency, and down for the opposite.
Your next step is to select a god of the underworld, which is the hell that you are sent to once your character perishes for the first time.  Each god will have a different underworld and you’ll be charged with fighting your way out of it lest you want to live to see another day on the surface.  If you DO end up eating the canvas, it’s hasta lavista to your dear old character and you’ll have to start anew.
Of course designating your class is something you’ll have to do before generating the world, and there are a ton of them to choose from.
After one of the creators of the original Everquest, influences to MMO’s are pretty clear to spot in its combat.  It’s a slow paced action game, suprisingly slow at first.  It’s got kind of a strange perspective at first, it feels isometric but looks more top-down than anything.
The combat reminds me of a mix of an ability based MMO, diablo, and Dark Souls, more than anything the ladder because of how cutthroat the damage outputs are.  You can die quickly in this game, as will your enemies.  Approaching environmental combat in a game like this is for the most part exciting because each world you create is unique, so the procedural generation helps to keep things interesting with not only varying enemies and enemy placement, but how the geography, dungeons, cities and other game assets either upon themselves up to you, or require you to travese the practically endless frontiers of the game if you selected god traits that crafted the world in a more barren fashion.
Each of the classes has an assortment of auto attacks, spells and items that are usable in combat.  It’s pretty snappy, and eventually you’ll be able to buy items from merchants, talk to npcs, journey into dungeons and allocate ability points to tailer your class to your liking.
Choosing the wrong combination and mix of gods can result in you wandering for hours wondering if there is really anything to this game.  So you could say the god and world history system is the games strongest and weakest asset until proper balance comes into play, and until players start to discover the best combinations for themselves.  It’s not a binary system - exploration type players will best serve themselves right by designing large worlds with more cities than enemy camps and dungeons, and more action oriented players might want to condense the game world to make sure they don’t lose interest.
Also, i’d like to see the animations tidied up a bit and the combat and traversel speeds increased to a more modern pace.  It just feels too  slow for me, but perhaps thats subjective.
I wouldn’t say Hero’s Quest is ready to slap a price tag on.  You’re buying this game in trust for the future of it as with most early access tiltes.  I’m not into early access games too much, as its basically a glorified bug test, but if your going to put it up for sale and ask people to fork over those  dollars for it than as far as I’m concerned its upon to critique and the game has to stand up on its own.  Hold off until it’s full release if your interested.

The Midnight Mysteries series contains some of my favorite hidden object games.  These are the more typical hybrid type games, that have some adventure elements (puzzles, moving between locations, talking to people) as opposed to the find-objects-only style.
Midnight Mysteries are interesting in that they are based on real historical events, then add some fictional what-ifs to fill in blanks or give alternate explanations for known events.  As a result, not only are the fun as a game but they spark some interest in reading about the real events on Wikipedia.
They also tend to have a slightly creepy vibe.  MM1, about Edgar Allen Poe, is one of the creepier ones with a bit of mystery to it.

I didn't like this one as much as the Mark Twain one (which is the only other Midnight Mysteries game I've played so far).
I think this one was the first in the Midnight Mysteries series, and I can see how the series has improved over time.
It's not a long game, I've completed it and logged 4 hours and at least an hour of that time was spent afk.
It's definitely not as well balanced or visually attractive or as in depth as the Mark Twain installment of Midnight Mysteries.

Stunlock going all out on their newest attempt to nail eggs to a wall. A very lack luster yet heavily hyped up and marketed battle arena that gained attention through streamers comparing it to WoW Arenas and League Of Legends. That in itself sparked a lot of tired veterans from both respected genres to meander over and give it a shot for a while.
Now that the hype has died down, the only people who stayed were the sunken eyed, uninspired, trash talking toxic losers who claim "There's no turrets or minions just straight to the action" basically as an attempt to bash League Of Legends and all other moba concepts for having depth because they're probably 600 games deep in low gold at best and feel like this is a more simplified approach to being a dead inside loser.
The first few days of launch were pretty fun because it was all new for everyone and we were all trying to figure out what every champion did (basically taking a break from our main game we've been playing for years) but now that were familiar with everything it's time to inflict our cognitive bias on each other and spew elitist rhetoric like most online communities do and try too hard at try-harding and google searching the "pro" meta and now everyone is lashing out over losing rounds. I'm seeing constant insecure remarks, disconnecting, and basically people who would rather be right than be teammates because they think theyve have it all figured out and everyone else is garbage. The report system will slowly diminish their numbers further as time goes on in order to keep a PC-friendly competitive environment.
But honestly, all of that is fine and accepted as the new normal for online competitive communities. The main reason I cannot recconmend this game is because of how unbalanced it is and how meta strangles things. You'll either be matched in a clear win or loss, very few games will feel contested based upon mistakes. That doesn't change the higher you climb however and you will have to start deciding on conforming to the small pool of "top meta" champions or inching along slowly on a less competitive champion. I made it to platinum with Rook, it was starting to get challenging as most meta champions could outsustain my heal over time or could simply out zone me over time. He's not the best or the worst he's just considered good. I'm confident I could've improved my own gameplay and squeezed out more divisions but theres clear limitations that can't be dismissed by a simple "git-gud" and all of it has a hand in turning their profit.
The same old sleazy marketing attempts I've seen in so many other games where they release a new champion that is overpowered in order to push their "champion specific" lootbox incentives which honestly gives a subtle undertone of pay to win. Games like this are 100% meta and when you have a champion that is clearly better they will be exploited. A good example is how they released Thorn with a lot of particle bugs and overall OP ratios and they did not care to address it until right before they released Destiny as if to say "Bye Thorn, hello Destiny $".  I'm just calling it as I see it and it comes off as a marketing 101 tactic. It's all just my opinion and what i've witnessed in my experience of playing it. It seems designed for the typical lazy gamer who only knows winning through conforming to a guideline or meta and grinding the match making until the ladder pushes you up (the travel rate is dependent upon who you play, how solid you play them, and the rate you spam matches).
The only plus side is having a /Disablechat command which cuts a lot of problems in half (out of sight out of mind). That only gets you so far as you need communication in the few contested scenarios that land you in game 5. But it's a damned if you do/dont scenario as communicating with overly competitive, jittery kids who are always on edge will most often time land the wrong way and you must constantly be gentle with these little snowflakes and do exactly what they want you to do. Even by playing the exact way they specify, sometimes you will still be outmatched and lose and they will blame you and rage. If you win, they will remind you of how they carried you and you're just a peon that took orders and adapted to their superior intellect, because teamwork and communication doesn't exist anymore. It's just an art of grinding meta matchmaking.

At release the game was a step down from the sequel as you were essentially thrust into the role of a mercenary chef working for dozens of different restaurants. You own a restaurant as well, though, it does not have nearly as many progression hooks as the first game did. The variety of food upgrades in the first game have been replaced with an extensive range of unlockable decorations to customise your restaurant. Because of this the game got boring much sooner than I thought it would.
After a couple of months the developer has added emails and different modes that make the game more fun, such as zen mode where customers can have infinite patience, and stress mode where the orders just keep coming in. While the emails in this game are amusing and work well to break up the gameplay, they do not live up to the 'Cook4luv' dating-system of the first game. You can also upgrade chores now, but since you have to buy pretty much all the foods for your restaurant with money that you earn working for other restaurants (or your own restaurant which early on has very limited foods and decorations), your role as a mercenary chef specialising in cooking all types of food is undeniably the main focus.
Fans of the first game will enjoy a familiar gameplay experience. New comers should be directed to the first game to understand the hype behind the sequel.
Playing this game is still fun even if it also makes it easier to acknowledge the first game as a restaurant simulator that really got it right. Kind of like an Arkham City to Arkham Asylum scenario.
I nominated this game for "The world is grim enough lets just all get along" steam award since the gameplay hook facilitates feeding people nice food.

It really is a great game... But it does have it's pros and cons. Please read the following. (Both pros and cons)
PREPARE YOURSELF FOR A VERY LONG REVIEW... but highly infromative.
Pros:
-Fun overall gaming experience. (A good introduction to MMORPG's)
-Very fun gameplay (Completely my opinion)
-Lots of classes and skills.
-Tons of leveling to go through. (Max level is 255 for most classes, if not all)
-Big community. (In terms of the amount of people playing)
-(Going w/ the above statement) Many online forums that are involved.
-Great music.
-Nice Scenery/Textures.
-One of the better Free-to-Play RPGs out there. (It's not a Pay-To-Win)
-Leveling doesnt take forever. (Unlike before, where it truly felt like forever leveling up)
-Many quests.
-Huge world/Many areas to explore.
-Simple, costumizable control setup.
Cons:
-Abuse of the cash shop and in game perks. (i.e the "Cube" items)
-Pretentious, boring, and childish dialogue. (Although some lines are funny)
-The community, although big, is all about "Merching" and are far less social and involved than before. (Excluding forums)
-TEMPORARY removal of certain areas (They will be added back eventually, but it's an inconvienience)
-Annoying filters. (Not the worse thing but still some people do have problems with it)
-Dumbed-down mechanics in-general. (Earlier versions had more emphasis on how you use your SP/Skill Points, Avoidability, and AP/Ability Points)
-Not very fulfilling. (i.e when you maxed out a character, nothing feels very special about it)
-Quite a few dumb quests primarily fetch quests. (Although not as tedious as before)
-Too many new, worthless features. (Mainly to expand audience, but they feel like they take away the originality and fantasy feel from Maplestory)
-Too much emphasis on Item stats (A terrible addition to the game) which will want you to spend a ridiculous amount of money just to have "the best" of that item. (Don't waste your money, it's not worth it)
-Next to no plot. (I mean, they have one, but it's oh so weak)
-Terrible costumer support. I mean, It's REALLY bad. I hope you're ready to wait up to a month before someone responds.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

I don't care that it is too similar to CivV, my problem is the lack of diversity within the game. The game added good concepts and it is good but not good enough for a standalone game. I played Civ V since its release and all the other before it, perhaps I had just set my expectations a bit high for this game.

Direct comparison to Civ 5:
Pros -
1) I am a very big fan of the new tech tree. The web allows for diverse tactics and technology disparities across a game. For example, fighting against a friend he dove early for a heavy armor purity offensive, while I pushed for economic and strategic resources.
2) I enjoy the new upgrade system. Most buildings and almost every unit have a fairly interesting upgrade system associated with them. Upgrades are a essential part of economic and military progress.
3) Affinities. This is a pro and con actually for one I love the idea of affinities, on the other hand how they are implemented is terrible. Lategame, you essentially have everything. That being said, would like to see a system where you choose your affinities based on your actions, similar to how the upgrades work. For example, exterminate a alien nest and get a stack towards your next affinity level - but only towards purity and supremacy.
Cons -
1) Lategame. Its fairly bad. Not really a lot else to say there, everyone get basically everything and it becomes a rush to finish whatever win condition your gunning for.
2) Diplomacy. Hahahahahahahaha no. Being diplomatic in this game is taking your tanks and driving them into your enemies capital. Thats about it.
3) AI is dumb as bricks.
4) Espionage is basically a micromanagement game with a ton of waiting. And the success rates and counterplay are so terrible your better off just giving up on it then actually wasting effort trying to shield yourself.
5) Larger empires are proportionally stronger. Single city or 3 city empires get absolutely crushed. Expansion and city crowding is heavily rewarded. Cities are incredibly easy to take and can be siezed with minimal fire support.

A friend once remarked to me that everything he knew about human history, he learned from Sid Meier’s Civilization games. Well, at least the stuff that he fondly remembers—not the Indian history lessons hammered into his brain thanks to the fear of an impending exam the following day. With Firaxis’s Civilization: Beyond Earth, however, there’s a different kind of learning to be had—you learn more about yourself as a person, or more particularly, whether you will turn into a megalomaniacal dictator with a thirst for blood, a defender of humanity in its current state of technological and social evolution, or a future-ecologist who has a curious love for all things alien.
If anything, Civilization: Beyond Earth made me realise that it was never too late to go back; back from the ocean of triple-a blockbusters with obscene production values and downloadable content to a game that’s mostly about building stuff, indulging in a spot of faux diplomacy and spending several hours to get a minor Tile productivity bonus. This is interesting because Beyond Earth is doing the opposite as far as the series is concerned; it’s going forward. No longer constrained by our miserable little blue planet (which Firaxis foresee becoming uninhabitable in the future), Beyond Earth takes you on a journey to the stars—the story begins with a moving cut scene in which we see a father bidding farewell to his daughter so that she can find hope for us all somewhere else in the universe—a theme that carries through across the game.
There isn’t much of a departure from the way in which Civilization fundamentally works in Beyond Earth—fans will be greeted with familiar visuals (which could use a sprucing up after all these years) and scenarios that require decisions to be made. While the game does allow for players to choose their own path by picking an ‘Affinity’, of which there are three: Supremacy, Harmony and Purity. Suffice to say, they’re both akin to ideologies from Civ 5, but offering military and other bonuses.
With Beyond Earth’s considerably hostile planets, armies are of utmost importance. Alien life-forms can be quite aggressive, while planets are laden with Miasma, a harmful gas that damages units over time (at the beginning, at least). Over the course of several hundred turns, I noticed that pretty much all non-military activity plays second fiddle to the might of your armies and their quest for blood. Yes, you can still achieve endgame objectives without annihilating all other human factions, but having already built up considerable forces to repel alien threats, it feels like a no-brainer to achieve your goals through might. Besides, diplomacy doesn’t always produce good results given that the AI is pretty dodgy for the most part.
Civilization: Beyond Earth is the absolute perfect follow up to Civilization V, with strange new worlds to explore and advanced societies to establish. What’s more, Beyond Earth’s sandbox allows you to really play the way you want—made possible by the flexible research tree/leaf system. The quest system gives the game much needed context while easing players into the kind of choices they will need to be making on a macro level, while the endgame is greatly affected by the path you take in terms of Affinity. On the downside, I found the emphasis on combat to be excessive—more so than previous games in the series, while the UI (despite streamlining) can still feel overwhelming to new players.

Omg, finally! This is Magic: The Gathering for PC the way it should be. I'm not sure why they didn't bring this up some 15 years ago, but it's ok--it's here now.
It's like Hearthstone: free to play and you can buy card-boosters with Gold acquired from defeating opponents, finishing the Story Mode and/or doing daily quests--or for real money, of course. But it's much, much better than Hearthstone--because it's Magic.
Unlike Magic 2015, in this one you can acquire all cards just by playing (with Gold), make your own deck however you want, and fight AI or real opponents whenever you like. Everything is finally how it's supposed to be.
If you're not familiar with Magic: The Gathering, put simply, it's by FAR the most complex card game out there, the grandfather and master of all the others. If you are, just grab it--it's what you've been waiting for.
It has 854 different cards available at the time I'm writing this review, divided into 5 separate collections and more of them seem to be released once in a while. Also, as usual, each collection comes with its own new type of "card skill" (now we have Ally, Emergence, Devoid, . . .) The deck-strategy possibilities are huge, and even the AI is kind of amazing--sometimes I get the feeling it's smarter than me (and yes, I do know this doesn't mean much.)
Paying for boosters with real money is rather expensive here in my country (about 3-4 times USA/Europe's price) but at least for those who live in first world countries the price seems to be fair. If you can't afford to pay $15 for 5 boosters like me, you can go for Gold. It will take a while, of course, but this system is also fair, and actually better than Hearthstone's--30 gold per win against a real player, 60-80 for daily quests, and a booster with 6 cards costs 150 gold.
So, there's really nothing to complain about the core stuff in Magic Duels. It has been done right this time. Just go ahead and download it--and don't be frightened by the amount of information thrown at you if you're not familiar with the game, just stick to it--you'll get it eventually, and the game is awesome.
There are some minor issues which I'm gonna throw in here hoping the devs will see it, since the "in-game feedback" takes you to writing a Steam Review:
- Matchmaking's connectivity could be improved. Fiding players takes a fraction of a second, but connecting to them sometimes takes quite a while--not rarely, long enough for you to close the game and reopen it to try again.
- Although there are indicators in the deck-building screen to help you manage how many/which cards you put in your deck, it's still a bit complicated and hard to manage it. A search-field to locate specific cards/card-abilities and indicators of how many creatures/sorceries/enchantments/etc. (each) you have of each color in your deck would be helpful.
- Sometimes you have to start over targetting cards with "multiple-target actions", i.e. red damage spells, because you are not sure how many times you clicked on each target to distribute the damage (or because you fu**ing Razer mouse double-clicks/holds the click/doesn't click 2 weeks after you bought it.) Adding some sort of marker to the targets, or at least a "X damage remaining" to the tab at the bottom of the screen would solve that.
- Also, the "Give us your feedback!" and the "Complete the Story Mode to get gold and boosters!" pop-ups should cease after you have writen a review and completed the Story Mode-- at least.
For those who weren't willing to read everything: if you even remotely like card games, GET MAGIC DUELS NOW.

When it comes to a retro feel, something that reminds you of Diablo 2 or even Realm of The Mad Gods, Hammerwatch does exactly that. I followed this game from the Steam Greenlight forums and even tested the beta. From the beginning I knew that this was something I wanted to get my hands on once it came out.
The game takes place inside of Castle Hammerwatch, where your goal will be to travel from down the prison up to the royal chambers in the top and kill the evil dragon. You play as either a Paladin, Wizard, Warlock or Knight and each character has its own weapon and special ability.
Don’t be fooled, this is a serious game; and even on medium difficulty you will still have a hard time fighting through the numerous levels in each Act. The game is better played in multiplayer mode, but to be honest, good luck joining a game. For some reason I find it impossible to host a game, but I am able to join others, and this is when the game is best played.
Hammerwatch also offers a few perks, what they call “crutches” in the game if you choose to host your own single or multiplayer game. Different options allow you to make the game easier or a little harder. I suggest playing with the HP Regen and Infinite Lives crutch on when first playing, that way you can get a feel for what you’re about to be in for.
A game that is still in beta and continuously going through changes is sometimes hard to review, taking everything into consideration the game is awesome. Aside from the bunk multiplayer Hammerwatch is worth every penny. Constant battle action laced with power ups, secret passages and hidden doors makes Hammerwatch a soon to be classic and a necessity in any gamers library.

Holy smokes this game is long. And I didn't even unlock the "secret", deeper endings. It has a polished lore, complex story and quite unique taste - I've never encountered a game with so many interesting legends, fables and stories - not only that, but majority of them is also connected to the core plot of the game!
The game succeeds in making some interesting gameplay experiments which allow you to feel something very special. Just imagine: it’s a dark night. You, a betrayed knight/sorcerer/crossbow-female-knight, together with your servants and companions pass a lonely bench under a tree and get to a tavern. But there are no generic black-cloaked quest-givers inside, not at all. But there are common folks all around you and you start listening to what they have to say. Some peasant and mercenary talk about a knight who lives nearby – the peasant heard the knight keeps some weird barrels in his basement and the mercenary claims he knows what’s inside them. A peasant girl tells the innkeeper that apparently some other knight sleeps with his own sister, while the innkeeper claims he saw the same knight entering a brothel in nearby town. A monk tells the gathered people a legend about the saint man who is the patron of the local monastery while a drunk beggar talks to himself about a ghost which he believes he saw next to the ruined tower...
The variety of side quests, main quests and level structures is impressive and often you have to figure out on your own if a legend has some truth in it or is just a silly gossip. The story is very complex and it tries to show every side of each story as grey and conflicting as possible. Even though the core story is mostly straight-forward and very tightly holds your hand, sometimes you have to make decisions and choices which most of the time feel as “judging what is the lesser evil”. Very rarely the game offers you an easy choice such as “do you prefer some amount of gold for doing something evil or more XP/an item for taking an extra mile to do the right thing?”. Most of the things you are going to do are neither right nor just, and sometimes not even that honorable. I like it a lot and it’s hard to not compare it to Game of Thrones and it’s mean-spirited portrayal of royal families as normal, weak people who always see themselves as heroes and find excuses for their bad deeds.
However.
The game has many flaws, some of them - major. UI is absolutely terrible and could be improved in so many obvious ways it gives me a headache. Multiple performance bugs can annoy and break the immersion, although not as much as the fact that through the entire game we control only 5-12 (rarely) people and with their help we destroy huge noble families, conquer castles, lands and so on (I don’t mind “unrealistic” approach, but it sometimes get rather silly). Some graphics are amazing, some are terrible. Sometimes music makes a fantastic atmosphere, yet sometimes it gets glitchy – a couple of songs play at the same time, volume spikes up and down and so on…
It is very clear the developers had to make some budget cuts and had many interesting ideas which they couldn’t bring to their full potential because of lacking resources. A good example may be the watchtowers and outposts. These structures, once conquered, may become a defense posts for our army – we can keep in them our spare soldiers and try to stop some of the roaming A.I. (which has tendency to conquer our villages while we are on the opposite side of the map). However, transporting soldiers is an absolute pain in the♥♥♥♥♥since you have absolutely no extra space or tool to do that – if you want to have a filled watchtower, you have to go to a castle, leave there your soldiers, take spare soldiers, take them to the watchtower, go for new soldiers and also bring them to the watchtower, then you can take your own army back... It’s ridiculous and it feels like the developers just couldn’t create the entire balanced system of army management so they decided to leave it just like it is, even though it’s completely useless.
The battle system is also far from perfect and it lacks “depth”. Once I got bored in managing my units I started to use the “automatic battle” option 95% of the time and thankfully the game handles it pretty well. Very rarely you face an enemy which you can defeat by strategy and not just by probability count introduced by the game. Many reviewers find the combat system the most important flaw of this game, so if you want to play this game mostly to lead your knights and soldiers to battle, you may be disappointed and I would suggest looking for a different title.
The English translation sucks a lot. I’m not a native speaker myself but even I was often distracted by unnatural phrasing and generic mistakes. And there is A LOT of dialogue to read so a good editor is definitely not a part of the game where you should save a buck.
-----
TL;DR 7/10 is a fair rating, however there is lot in this game to love. I think it can satisfy most fans of medieval-fantasy RPG games (especially if they like games like “King's Bounty” or “HoM&M”), but there surely are some people who are going to be absolutely enchanted by everything this game has to offer - especially because of the clever writing. Judge yourself if you can forgive some bad gameplay decisions, poor UI and other mistakes.

The game punishes you when stealing or killing by lower morale of your whole team, but as long as you can balance it with some good acts (gives meds, food to neighbor...) you will be fine. After 1-2 tries, gradually you realize that stealing and killing are the easiest way to survive the game. The more you play, the more of a psychopath you become. Common tactic is:
- Day 1-2: Gather materials to build bed and stove.
- Day 3-4: Steal everything from an elder couple, especially food to feed your characters in 5th day (the couple will die from starvation when you come back later).
- Day 5: There is always a location which grant a shotgun + ~15 ammo if you kill an armed civ.
- Day 6: Raid the Military Outpost, kill around 8 soldiers. That area alone gives you enough food and weapon to survive tull endgame.
Usually one scenario lasts around 43-45 days. The first 20 days are quite fun gathering resources from various places, but the remaning 20 days become boring fast when you have enough material and food to just let people sleep and eat without further exploring, until cease fire date. Gathering resources becomes a chore, and you will find more fun bringing weapon to kill bandits and soldiers alike. Hell, I even  massacre every single one in the Central Square area because I was too bored.

I played this through in one sitting, so can confidently state that it is about three hours worth of playing time from beginning to end, give or take a little depending how good you are at hidden object games, if you use hints, and so on. I would not consider it to be worth the price with the short playing time, unless you really love the genre, but having gotten it in a bundle myself I definitely paid less than it was worth, so I can't complain about my cost. In any case, keep an eye out for a sale if you're interested.
As to the gameplay itself, it really is rather straightforward and not terribly challenging. There were only a handful of times when I had trouble finding something or solving a puzzle, only to find that the answer was basically right in front of my face, of course. Fortunately, if you do get stuck there is a hint system you can use to show you where an item is or the next step in a puzzle, so there's no reason for a relaxing game to become at all frustrating. Unfortunately, the ravens that you collect in order to add to your hint total are a little bit too plentiful, so that even using the hints whenever I was getting at all annoyed with the time spent searching, I still finished with ten or so remaining. Also, I would end up using a hint for kind of lame reasons, like not lining the next item in the puzzle up exactly right. In other words, it's a little bit touchy at times. Just remember, what you think is the solution probably is. You just may need to adjust your positioning slightly.
All of this being said, it is rather fun as far as hidden object games go, and that has never been a preferred genre of mine. As an Edgar Allan Poe fan, I found the concept of building the game around the mystery of his death to be intriguing, the overall story quite well done, and the gane performance flawless. I run Windows 8 and had absolutely no issues. So, this is definitely a nice way to have a few relaxing hours of casual gameplay with no time limits or losing or anything, when you're in the mood for that kind of thing.
4/5 It's a fun game with a nice story line. However it relys heavily on hidden object scenes and not so much puzzles. Worth 5 dollars.

Hero's Song has potential. As other reviews are saying, if you like the look of the game and want to support the developers -- buy it. I can tell that this is going to be a good game, but right now there isn't that much to do and what is there isn't polished.
However, the 3 hours I've played at the time of writing this review have been fun (although I spent at least half of that time exploring one single tile of the map that was supposed to have a dungeon in it until I eventually gave up...those tiles are BIG). The world generation system (gods) and the variety of classes are the best things about it at this stage, and there's plenty more planned. Everything the developers say they'll implement between now and final realase sounds awesome.
I guess the main negative for me is that you've got no direction when you start the game up -- and even though exploring allows you to discover towns, dungeons and events on the map, the map tiles cover such a wide area it's difficult to find the point of interest. But hey, maybe that's just my bad navigation skills.
It's also worth noting that I haven't tried this in multiplayer yet, but I reckon it'll be a lot more fun with friends even in its current state and I'm especially looking forward to playing on big servers when the cap is raised to 200.
