The game feels like a very very very early alpha build. I understand it's EA, but it definitely shouldn't have been released yet. After twenty minutes you will be bored due to lack of content.
Also some of the "features" are just poorly executed. The world map is grid based, but each "square" in the grid has no map of its own and is rather large because of how zoomed in the camera is in the game. It would take probably 20-25 minutes to FULLY explore one square on the grid. The map shows icons where dungeons and events are, but once you get to that "square" there is no indication of where that dungeon or event was. I spent 20 minutes looking for an event, pretty sure I scoured the entire square, and found nothing.
I see the potential, but right now it's just not fun. There's nothing to do and most of the "features" are poorly implemented. Don't give into the hype like I did.

This review is designed for people who have played Cook Serve Delicious 1. If you havn't, I would recommend you play it first, it's more polished and easier to pick up, not to mention a great game. Come back here if you've enjoyed it.
If CSD1 was a perfectly cooked beef Wellington, then CSD2 would be a big burrito pizza with everything on it. There is so much more content and ingredients that it's crazy. That said, at the same time, it's messy and it doesn't really know what it wants to taste like.
There are 100s of unique foods in this iteration. The variety is just astounding, and graphically it's a banquet for the eyes. The sacrifice is that they lose a bit of the unique gameplay mechanics from CSD1, for example the kebab building where you can't place ingredients next to each other. In CSD2 the foods are more simple overall.
The variety also brings a few quirks like the same ingredients working differently accross recipes, making for easy mistakes.
Whilst CSD1 was a pleasure on both KB and Controller, CSD2 is very poorly optimized for controllers, due to requiring the triggers to be held down at all times.
The music is still great, with some classy bossa nova tracks that always keep me as happy as the foods on display.
From the start you have the choice to play in classic mode (build your own restaurant), or  "Chef for Hire" mode where you work for different restaurants with a set menu that increases in difficulty.
Whilst this choice is great, there is no going back, as the current progression doesn't really make transitioning between one and the other mode very smooth. Campaign progression was a lot more polished and balanced in CSD1, but again, in CSD2 there is a lot more to do, just more messy.
All in all I still recommend CSD2 to those of you who have completed and mastered CSD1. It's an evolution of the concept, not a rehash of the same thing. CSD2 really tries to break more boundaries and give the player a lot more options. It's just still a bit undercooked, but the dev is addressing most issues with patches and future content updates, and given how polished CSD1 ended up, I can only look forward to this one finally coming out of the oven.

This game had a lot of potential at the time. It's fun, but the thing that everyone seemed to have complained about Pay to Win (P2W). I started to think this is true. When they had the old starter kit you started with all this armory that gave you an upper edge. I understand it's something that gives the player something for being supportive, but it didn't need to give the player so much to start with. There were two ways to pay for armor real money so you can buy tokens, and in-game money that you get for each match depending how well you did. Tokens had the potential to get you the item sooner that the in-game money. That was something I thought was pretty good.
The servers were possibly the worse of this game. For me living in the western part of the US I can still get pings in most games under 60, but when it comes to this game. I'm lucky enough to get one that is remotely close to 70. The servers had the worst ping reading and made it almost impossible to play.
The gameplay is really simple. Move click click dodge dodge. Just a regular beatem up style game, but there's one flaw to this. The range attacks. I can see that they wanted to touch on all aspects and classes as much as possible, but when it came to players using just one button it made the game completely boring. I don't remember that Ice girl's name I used, but her and very very few characters were actually somewhat balanced. The characters that can go strictly range made the game boring since you move as fast going backwards as you do going forward.  The characters that had a roundhouse attack which I think only one did at the time I played players abused it alot. Abilities like that needed to have a strict cooldown so players didn't resort to just that.
The game has a lot of unique characters and some I never thought I would see. The game kept you wanting to play, but due to it's lack of support from the developers after seeing how things were getting abused and how servers didn't meet up to par with ping. I'm not kidding, more than 90% of the servers they had weren't even populated so there was no need for them. Certain Characters overpowered the other characters. Players relied on one move to win them the game with no mix ups. I spent a lot of time in the training sessions for every character before picking my first one and let me tell you Archeblade players:
Every character has combos if you can't land them then try to approach them differently.
My Ice character was a short melee player which can dish out a lot of damage. I spent time on her the most and won a lot of matches against players who were supposedly title "Pay 2 Win players" It's a challenge but it's not impossible.
Gearing up wasn't really too bad. Obtaining gear required 2 steps.
1) Get to the level required to unlock it
2) Have enough money to purchase it (Tokens or In-game)
Step one didn't have a problem to it. It was just the money part. Matches didn't give you a lot even if you win the match. This was a flaw mistake made by developers which I think was something they thought of to get players to buy the starter kit rather than waste the time getting beat up from other players who were higher skilled than them. That's not how you draw a crowd to play your game. It's like putting a band-aid on the player for them giving you $20 and holding their hand through everything. That doesn't teach the player only gives them the thought that if they just cough up the money they can have whatever they want.
Gaming isn't like that. Call of Duty, Halo, Super Smash Bros. All these games have something unique and every player new or veteran have to learn new things bring up new tactics against other players. Archeblade had that going for it, but the way you obtain gear from not getting enough money and players just having enough and buy the kit gives them the wrong mind set. As a developer you should listen to your community, but not to a point where you give them everything they want.
This brings up another argument. As developers you guys refused to listen to your community. Even when there was video evidence over unbalanced content. That's what disappointed me the most getting shut out by the people who brought a great game and watching it fall with the team. I may not be a developer, but I know that if you screw up on a game and not listen to your community you are going to start losing them one after another.
The team has then separated and they are under a new team. Whether they still have license to Archeblade is beyond me. I recommend this game to give it a chance, but I don't recommend to those who believe in Pay to Win parts of games.
Developers if you read this I want you to understand I played this game for 5 months even though my time playing it over all is 10 hours that was because I was trying to find matches to play in each day and server pings were really bad, and the reason Archeblade failed wasn't because of financial reasons it was because you guys didn't want to listen to us. As an Archeblade player I say this.
You guys still have the potential to bring this game back. I pointed out 3 flaws in your game that I think caused this game to fail. What you guys do from this point on is up to you. I have put my review in and I'm not one of those high end groups like IGN that put a review only a day after a game's release. I give it a chance to show it's true colors over time. I gave you a fair chance just like the other developers.

I've played about maybe 40% of Thief when I write this. I've been having fun playing, but there are still a lot of things that buggers me. Thus I will recommend it, but for a lower price.
My playstyle
===========
This is sort of relevant for this game: I've been playing on Master, with Focus and that modern stuff on, but I've avoided combat. I've not played the previous games, so I can't compare to them.
Plus
===========
+ When you break into someplace and sneek around steeling stuff and picking locks - you really feel like a thief. I love the feeling of robbing someone blind :)
+ Pick pocketing people is endless fun. "Oh, those ear rings, you don't need them do you?"
+ There are some interesting puzzles
+ The feeling of being in the dark vs light is well done, when you enter light the border of the screen becomes slightly white, and dark in shadows.
Negative
=============
This will be a long list...
- The sounds and dialogs of the NPCs: There seem to be no real positional audio, and a guard that's two rooms away sounds as if he's just next to you. A critical miss in a stealth game. On top of this all the guards repeat basicly the same 5 phrases over and over, and they say something every 10 seconds, so it get's repetetive - fast. There are some "events" thrown for variation (some poor guy getting bothered by the guards for example), but even those repeat every time you enter the area...
- Only "scripted" jumping: You can only jump on designated places, otherwise nothing happens (or you "swoop" which is the same button), in some places where there are jumping puzzles, this is extremly annoying.
- Small areas with cutscenes, loading-screens and QTE's (hold E, press E repeatetly) to get between them, this really makes it hard to get a feeling of direction and navigating anywhere without getting really frustrated. It kills the joy of exploration.
- Garrett seems to be suffering from the "cutscenes - my only weakness!"-syndrom. After not beeing detected through a whole level, he often get detected in the end cutscene...
- Speaking of cutscenes: The sound mix in them seems bad, and it is at time hard to hear what they say (increasing volume sort of works, but there's music too)
- Music: In sensitive times (like when you are close to being detected) they though it to be a good idea to mix in loud music to drouwn all the sounds you need to hear.
- Performance: It leaks memory like there's no tomorrow. When I start playing it uses ~2GB of ram, and after a couple of hours it's up to 5GB and the game starts to lag (this resets if you restart it).
- Bug: Since I reload when I get into fights, I still 40% into the game get the tutorial dialog "Press V to dodge" when entering fight with a enemy...
So in summary: Lot's of issues, but still overall fun.
Thief is not a bad game. Actually, it's a great game, as long as you regard it as standalone. It's definetly not a sequel to Deadly Shadows.

Quick review: Did you like Far Cry 3?  You will definitely like Far Cry 4 and then some.  Didn't play FC3? You should go buy it when it's on sale for cheap.  If you like it, get FC4.  Did you play FC3 but didn't like it?  FC4 won't change your mind.
Long review: I really enjoyed FC3 so when it started looking like FC4 was going to be that but more and more polished, I was stoked.  It really is FC3 + More.  There's more variety to the environment, for starters.  FC3 was gorgeous, but if you've seen one jungle next to a beach you've seen pretty much all of them.  Kyrat offers snowy mountain peaks, lush valleys, sweeping rivers, and more.  There's more variety to the missions too!  Sure you've got the standard tower climbing, outpost raiding, hunting missions, but now there's also rescue ops, phtography missions, and others too.  There's more weapons, more vehicles (getting in the buzzer and dropping grenades on guys below like the world's biggest seagull with the worst case of explosive diarrhea is great fun), and more collectibles.  There's also the concept of verticality, which FC3 sort of lacked.  Using your grapple and the buzzer to get around and go up and down really makes the world seem bigger and opens up some interesting new routes.
On the story front, while I haven't finished it yet, the story is also shaping up as an improvement.  I was never a huge fan of Jason Brody, generic Bro-Dude de jour, and how he saved all the magic brown people.  It felt awkward and clunky and forced and...y'know...racist.  Ajay Ghale, being from Kyrat and having personal ties to the villain automatically makes me feel much more invested in whats going on.  Characters remind you of what your father wanted, why your mother fled, and Pagan Min (voiced by Troy Baker to perfection) is so wonderfully creepy because he can get at you on that personal level.  The dual-path choices for the major story missions are a nice touch as well, and inject some replayability into the game as well as making it feel like you're making a difference in Kyrat, good or bad.  Also, unlike Vaas, it looks like Pagan Min is in it until the end, something FC3 stumbled on, showing you their strongest villain up front and then ditching him halfway through the game in exchange for Hoyt, who was about as forgettable as they come.
If I had to point out some faults, I'd say that FC4 feels more like an elaborate, well-crafted expansion than a true sequel.   Going to an outpost, marking the badguys, then sniping them or letting a tiger loose feels exactly the same as it did in FC3.  There's no real big game-changer or anything like that.  Also, it seems to be repeating some of the missions from FC3 verbatim, like setting fire to drug fields.  Which is fine.  FC3 was great.  But I'd like to see the series stretch its legs more and spread out if it's going to continue.

I can't say enough good things about Legends of Eisenwald.
Aterdux has managed to create, for me, the ultimate medieval atmosphere.  It's what the Middle Ages feels like to you when you're a kid and all you know are the stories about knights and castles, before you learn about all the bad things that happened in history.  Eisenwald is a journey across an idealized medieval landscape, to the sounds of a beautiful score, with the sun lighting your way as it wanders across the sky.  Your quests will take you across a green countryside and into castles, towns, churches, and taverns.  You will listen to rumors, hire men-at-arms and healers, and battle brigands in turn-based tactical combat reminiscent of Heroes of Might and Magic.  I've made it sound overly simplistic, but the truth is that it's not a complicated game.  It's a vacation, a trip into a simpler time and place, and there is a beauty and innocence to the atmosphere that few games could hope to capture.
Aterdux themselves are a wonderful team, and Alex is the friendliest project lead I've ever met.  He's always taken time out to answer any question I've had and to indulge my curiosity, both as a journalist and an Eisenwald fan.  This is a developer worth supporting, and a pleasant journey you owe it to yourself to experience.

So, it's been quite some time since Magic: Duels released to us back in 2015. In that time, they've made some really grear progress in trying to create a compelling experience for players, thanks to the addition of new cards from current sets and campaigns that serve as nostalgia moments for the more experienced players. However, I would be remiss if I didn't inform you of some of the larger issues with this game.
The first, is a criminal lack of variance in deckbuilding options. While, technically, you can build any pile of common tripe you so desire, this doesn't mean that you will be successful. The amount of money (or, even worse, time) you have to spend to build one of the very few competitive lists is insane, for all the variance this game offers players at the onset.
Truly, though, the larger issue with this game is the rather large difficulty spike. You can't be matchmade with players of equivalent skill level (and deck power) so often you'll try to go into a game, only to get crushed by white's domineering presence or sheer card advantage and quality.
In short, if you feel like spending some money, Duels is a compelling Magic experience for someone who is more used to casual play -- but don't expect it to serve as a replacement for actual magic.

The game engine is very dated. You will crash on occasion and lose your buffs. Lag spikes will take your hard-earned EXP. There are still some small exploits running around.
To my knowledge nothing game-breaking, but I've presented GMs in this game evidence of game-breaking bugs and they chose not to do anything. Hopefully times have changed for the better.
Gameplay is where Ares excelled, to a point. There is true open world PVP, a handfull of Boss mobs, Warfare, and several dungeons. This is where the combination of Pay 2 Win and script bugs/exploits come in.
Leveling in this game is tedious. The grind is rather real and requires a monthly premium to both adjust the rate you earn experience as well as your defensive stats in game. The plus shop is mandatory at higher levels of game play.
This is inescapable.
Once players have established themselves and a hierarchy of power has developed the game begins to devolve into a player vs environment vs GMs. A lot of he-said, she-said quibbles. Let me break it down like this:
Bosses are killed by Mages in this game.
The highest level mages gravitate toward the most powerful guilds, securing them kills and putting them further ahead of the rest of the player base.
Enough janky/random players send in CS to GMs targeting said mage(s) accusing them of cheats/exploits/really anything.
Mage(s) or high profile characters get banned, and their options include: quit, make a new character, or buy another from someone.
Legend of Ares is a world I hope I never forget, but like all worlds it has it's problems.

Recommended, with an asterisk.
The game is clearly intended for CSD1 vets. If you haven't played CSD1, you will find yourself dumped into the deep end with little to no guidance here.
It's been improved in many ways while keeping the fast-paced core of the gameplay. The recipes are now very standardized and all the silly gimmicks that made several recipes in the original a pain in the neck are gone - kebabs are no longer the Worst Thing Ever, wine doesn't take forever to serve, soup no longer makes you despise its presence on the menu, etc. YMMV on whether or not this is a good thing as all recipes are now "hit the right buttons in the right order" with no timing mechanisms or context switches.
They've implmented fast-food style holding stations, which let you make several batches of a food at once. You are no longer cooking an entire pot of soup for 1 person; it makes 6 servings that can be instantly served. Some recipes still require a little bit of prep afterward but many go straight out the door. Side Orders share space with these, and they give you an extra 15 seconds of customer patience (before orders start to slide off the screen). If you are having trouble, you can add more side orders to buy more time.
The problem with CSD2 is that they haven't really fixed the issue of the game eventually becoming a chore to play; it just takes longer (66 hours vs. 30 for CSD1, for me). The restaraunt management simulator is gone (but is promised to be added Soon(tm)) so now it's just a series of challenge stages with a pre-set menu. Sure, there's a free-play option, but there's no real point to bothering with it. The speed at which you unlock new stages, and thus, new food is quite quick until you hit the Level 50 mark, which is where both level gain and food variety slow down massively. Why have an extended endgame if there's little new content in it?
Axing the management aspect also means the mini-games are gone too, which helped break up CSD1's experience. No more catering parties, iron chef challenges, or other things to help you get specific, complicated foods down (since the range of complexity is vastly decreased).
Another problem is that most recipes beyond the starting ones have key-bindings that make the recipes Fake Difficult to fill in. It's wildly inconsistent; it feels like multiple different people did the keybinds, where one guy went "I'll keep ingredients the same across as many recipes as possible" and another went "I'll make them as convenient as possible for this recipe only". It eventually got so bad (particularly with the eastern foods) that I switched to Mouse+Keyboard controls.
It's still fun, it's better than the original, but it still has problems. It's also still in development, so these problems may go away in time.

CSD2 is enjoyable as a fast-paced cooking sim game, but it lacks the focus, charm and elegance of the original.
I'm left with the impression that too much focus was put into the restaurant customization and the breadth of food options available, at the expense of honing the experience and flow of the game.
The Good:
The gameplay core of fast-tapping gameplay is altered a bit with a new page system for ingredient management, and somewhat more emphasis on putting things together in stages. It also adds Holding Stations, a new element of play which has become a core focus of the sequel and offers a new dimension of time management which is mandatory for some foods, optional for others, and unavailable for the rest. Drinks become maintenance chores rather than serving orders, and drink+side+perfect gets you a bonus.
All of these changes take a little bit of getting used to. The array of chores and the way some of them are executed has also been changed. It's different, and it works.
Chef for Hire mode offers a good way to get exposure with different groups of food types on a theme, with what might be considered a curated difficulty curve. They serve as examples that might offer you inspiration for what to do with your own restaurant, and give you an alternative if you don't care for the management choices.
The game also has a quite enjoyable soundtrack, although for some reason I don't understand, sometimes the rush hour music leaves a long gap of silence in the latter half of rush hour, failing to support the hectic mood well.
The Bad:
These menus are so bad that I am convinced some of the issues must be glitches. For instance, sometimes if you move the mouse at all, the game stops letting you use the keyboard to navigate the menus. No-one would design this on purpose. The fonts are made ugly and distorted on some resolutions, but that's just an aesthetic matter. The huge number of options of foods, and of some design elements, have horribly overgrown the available means for navigating them.
The pages of long lists of options are desperately in need of scrollbars or drop-down menus. Many menus require needless extra clicks or keypresses, and are confusingly laid out. I'm looking at the save file selector here, which made the process of starting a new game confusing.
Having so vastly many foods in the game is impressive, don't get me wrong. However, the lack of CSD's upgrade mechanic to create progression with those foods or the tags that enable you to plan synergistic menus with them makes the breadth of options disappointingly shallow. Also each one comes with a silly fictional description about where it comes from. This would have been a fabulous opportunity to offer the player a chance to learn something new, or give them hints about how that food fits into the gameplay, the way the original did. Instead, there's several paragraphs per food that offer a joke based on false history. Some of these might have been funny, but trying to do it for every one makes it horribly stale, and I'm annoyed that the information is both useless within the game, and since it's made up, also useless outside of it.
Being stuck having to wait for sometimes over half a dozen loot boxes to open upon unlocking some new piece of loot can be annoying. The design mode itself has many obnoxious limitations, like not being able to move or delete multiple items without going back and selecting move/delete again for each one. The Undo button is really, really easy to mistake for a Back button to returning to the previous menu, and that's a really aggravating mistake to make.
One last point. It took me a while to figure out this was one of the reasons I was having so much less fun, but it's important:
Since completion is tied to the medals and the medals are tied to days, you can get stuck. Instead of fluid progress, if your finger slips once and you hand off the wrong order or add one wrong ingredient for a bad/average order (as it has always been so easy to do), you'll be missing something. In the original game, if you made just one mistake, you shrug it off and you move on. A little less buzz, but no big deal. You're still steadily progressing toward your next goal. In CSD2... Perfect isn't an awesome cash bonus anymore, something great and special to be celebrated when it comes. It's an expectation, and anything short of it an irritating promise that as far as your trophy collection is concerned, you're not done.

Day One Review
Gameplay: It's definitley Farcry, it's loyal to past gameplays while attempting to build on it. However there is a terrible lack of new innovation in the gameplay mechanics, the only major ones being the flight suit, and the grappling hook. Being able to climb in certain areas is interesting, but it feels more like the traditional concept of ledges instead of Wow I Just Climbed a Cliff. So while gameplay remains loyal to Farcry, it remains almost to loyal, and lacks any major changes. They also recycled Radio towers and Outposts from farcry 3, which add familar mechanics, but offer little in the realm of new challenges and modes.
7/10
Graphics: It's very well done graphically, not stunning photo realism or anything, but it isn't horribly glitchy or poorly optimized (LOOKING AT YOU ASSASSIN'S CREED UNITY). The game does a fairly good job of seemlessly rendering in additional detail as you get nearer to an object and slowly becoming less detailed and distinct when you back away which is a refreshing relief from the concerns I had after the Unity rendering made it seem like an seemless distance rendering was just gone from Ubisoft games. But Unity is a different review... The graphics aren't anything to write home about, but they are well done, remain very Far Cryish in their style, and are nice enough to just look at.
9/10
Enviroment: This is where the game really set itself apart. The enviroment is shockingly unique, from mountain paths, to long forgotten statues deep in the mountains. From bears fighting each other, to eagles swooping down out of the sky and picking up small goats (Which I just saw, it was quite amazing, very realistic.) The enviroment is incredibly fun to be in. You can be driving on a road which has had ground along side it for miles, then take a left and suddenly drive off a cliff. The enviroment has beautiful changes, snow, waterfalls, rivers, small temples nestled in mountains, wild animals (all but a few which seem to want to kill you). It's gorgeous. No better way of putting it.
10/10
Story: This is by far the weakest part of the game. The story is sort of recycled, much like the gameplay, from the previous Farcry. Instead of being on vacation, SPOILERS, you have traveled there to spread your mother's ashes, her last wish. Naturally you are kidnapped by an insane dictator, and thrust into a civil war, between rebel groups fighting for "Freedom" and the insane government of sociopaths. I haven't gotten far into the story yet, simply because it has interested me. Your character, unlike the previous main character in Far Cry 3, doesn't go through any sort of struggle becoming who he is, a warrior, a killer, a soldier, whatever you want to call him. He simply picks up a gun and becomes a super soldier for the Rebel group. There is no plot behind this, no explantion, no training. You just grab that gun and start going bonkers. Soo yeah. The character lacks development, especially early on, and so do a few of the side characters. The most interesting two characters are a priest who deals weapons (Awesome guy) and a woman who you will see quite often. Well the "president" is interesting too, in a psychopath sort of way.
5/10
Summary:
The game has its' ups and its' downs. Like every game...Good graphics and a beautiful unique enviroment are hampered by recycled game mechanics and stories. Overall I would reccomend this game, but only if you are in it for wandering around, discovering things and chausing a general ruckus in a foreign land FarCry style.

This RPG reminds me of the days when games made had real lore and not just fancy hack and slash.  When you actually had to think things through to figure out how to make the best of a quest. I've played them all and many of the first person slashers just for the fun of it.  But there isn't much like this GEM on the market today.
If you like to read and puzzle out the meaning of the lore than you will love this game.
Regarding the battles they are a lot of fun and very interesting in the classic Rock, Paper, Scissors mode.  I've seen a few people complaining that they know who is going to win when the battle starts...  Wow, really?  In a good RPG the goal is to keep the damage down on your team to the least possible amounts and gain the most experience.  Truly, If you  expected to lose the fight you should have never entered it in the first place.  That said if you have played through the game and not had only one or two seriously wounded team members survive... well you are a better man than I.
Folks, this is an RPG the way is was meant to be made.  Test your mind versus how fast you can press a key... And when all else fails... there is always that all knowing god that can help with any question... google!

I want to say that I truly am perplexed by the mixed reviews. I've been a strategy, simulation and tactical combat guy for 25 years. I honestly am not sure if some of these other reviewers know the difference between rpg elements and tactical squad based combat and so on and so forth.

What i think best for a review here is to give you refernces within the genre and let you decide if that is what you are in the mode for...so here goes.
This is a fresh take on an old school popular genre where it has elements of adventure, rpg, squad based tactical combat and a little resource management in relation to income, outgo, spending on troops and equipment and potential maintence of those troops.
You will like this game if you enjoyed:
Heros of might and magic ( mixes adventure and story into the map like this title with combat similiair but a lil diff)
Battle brothers (like in this title manage your money and expenses or go broke and into ruin)
Expeditions Conquistador ( EC does have much deeper characters but the storyline of LoE just does it differently focusing on the main character vs the party)
So in conclusion if you want to enjoy a fresh story from a setting very few other games touch that combines elements of adventure, tactical combat and some minor income/outgo finanicial management this is the game for you.
I do recommend the game as fans of the genre or of any of the above mentioned games will enjoy it. I really do not think the mixed reviews are fair as the reviews are focused to much on what the game isn't ( no game is anyones ideal) vs what it actually is and what it does correctly that it set out to do. So, it's been quite some time since Magic: Duels released to us back in 2015. In that time, they've made some really grear progress in trying to create a compelling experience for players, thanks to the addition of new cards from current sets and campaigns that serve as nostalgia moments for the more experienced players. However, I would be remiss if I didn't inform you of some of the larger issues with this game.
The first, is a criminal lack of variance in deckbuilding options. While, technically, you can build any pile of common tripe you so desire, this doesn't mean that you will be successful. The amount of money (or, even worse, time) you have to spend to build one of the very few competitive lists is insane, for all the variance this game offers players at the onset.
Truly, though, the larger issue with this game is the rather large difficulty spike. You can't be matchmade with players of equivalent skill level (and deck power) so often you'll try to go into a game, only to get crushed by white's domineering presence or sheer card advantage and quality.
In short, if you feel like spending some money, Duels is a compelling Magic experience for someone who is more used to casual play -- but don't expect it to serve as a replacement for actual magic.

Thief (Or Thief 4, as it should be named) is the newest incarnation of the Thief-games, agian starring Garret, the Master Thief.
TL;DR at the bottom. Lazy butts!
Since Thief 3: Deadly Shadows, quite a bit has changed. Namely that Garret now has an apprentice. And that he seems to have lost all the tools he acquired in Thief 3.
Now, let's skip the blabber and get to the core:
Thief 4 is not like any of the other Thief titles. It draws a lot of it's atmosphere from its graphics. Which means that you will miss quite a bit of its awesomeness if you are not able to play the game of medium or higher. Preferably higher. If you can not play this game on medium settings, you should probably only buy this if you are a fan of Thief.
Without a powerful machine, the city loses a bit of its flair. It looks less dark and threatening, and just kind of cold and sterile.
And the glitches ... whooo boy. I'm running my game on a fairly old nVidia GTX9800, and so far I've had two encounters in Chapter 6 where the game didn't evne LOAD the next section. I fell right out of the level, and after 1-3 reloads, the level was FINALLY there. In addition to that, lightsources are not displayed properly. I get affected by the candlelight alright, and I see that the candle itself is lit, but the floor, the wall, everything of the environment looks like the candle has already been blown out.
Which makes it INCREDIBLY awful and difficult to gauge where there light ends and the shadow begins.
Which is crucial for a Thief-game, but whatever.
Might be because the developers got sucked into the whole ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t of "We run best on ATI, but our game sucks on nVidia for that".
The Story itself is ... dark and quite Thief-y. There's a good amount of betrayal and deception, lots of occultism and snarky comments about The City. However, doing the side-missions (or "jobs" as they're called) gets REALLY tedious somewhat fast. In addition to that, despite it being a very competent game, you have LOTS of loading screens. It's not that noticeable in the main quests, but the sidequests have you run across the city, and that is when you notice the unncessary amount of loading screens.
The other thing you'll notice quickly is that a lot of the chatter of the guards is done at importnat crossings of YOUR way. That means you can most of the time NOT sneak by, but instead you HAVE to listen to them until they are finished and then start their patrolling.
While it is a Thief game, I don't think the fans of Thief will really enjoy it that much. It has the typical Story, it has Garret, but aside from that, it has very little of the Thiefs of old I feel. The main missions drag on and on, and while they're generally entertaining, there are points in the game later on, where one might think "I get it ... could we skip forward a little? I like getting loot, but just making the building large to stuff more loot away is dumb". It's also very easy, for someone whom played Thief, to find out where the QTEs have been that they decided to kick after the backlash. And while they might have a certain degree of action, they don't really feel like they belong in the game.
Overall ... it's a AAA alright, but one definetly notices that it has been in development so long. And under so many hands.
TL;DR
Don't buy it for the full price unless you have a high-end machine and can play this game with all settings on top end. And even then you should think twice.
I'd recommend waiting for it to drop by 10-25%. Then it's definetly worth it!

This is one of many cases when I regret that Steam reviews can only be positive or negative, and not neutral.
There are aspects of this game I like: The graphics are nice, so is the music until it is repeated once too often, and a lot of thought went into the quest plots.
On the other hand, there is a lot I do not like: Quests require you to read lots of long dialogues, without voice acting (should be standard in a modern RPG!). Quest objectives are often described vaguely, which makes you wonder what to do, wandering around the land until you enter a village you visited before and encounter a merchant who just recently appeared (because he was artificially unlocked by the quest progression) who can sell you an item that solves your problem... that is irritating, especially as in this game, lost time costs you a lot of money, because you have to pay your companions regularly.
I do not like that your tactical choices in combat are so limited. There is an arbitrary rule that you HAVE to attack if you can, and as a melee fighter you can only attack the enemies standing closest to you - more than once I was forced to attack a heavily armoured opponent with an almost dead peasant, which was a kind of a suicide attack; meanwhile, my healthy and well-equipped main character stood two tiles away, but could not intervene because a mediocre henchman stood next to him and was the only valid target. This example should make it clear that the strict limitation of tactical decisions makes it impossible to develope actual strategies, and as enemy groups often display the same battle formation over and over, the fights become repetitive quite quickly.
I do not like that you cannot see equipped items on your character or the NPCs, only in their respective inventories. This takes a lot away from the immersion, as your choices for armour and amulets do not have a visible impact on the world, just on the stats. My character in particular kept his looks identical through the whole process of levelling up, even though I changed his armour three times.
I admit that I did not play the whole game. But up to now, everytime I entered a new chapter, my whole army was disbanded and their special weapons and trinkets lost, as I had to begin the new chapter alone and only with what I carried on my body. This felt very frustrating, as I invested a lot of care into the hiring, levelling and equipping of my soldiers. When the game made them simply disappear with all their gear, those efforts and every imaginary bond I could have had with my named NPCs who fought beside me through heated battles - just became pointless in a second.
For me personally, the negative aspects outweigh the positive ones slightly, and I give this game a 4/10.

This is my review of "A Dream For Aaron" after approximately 2 hours of gameplay.
I have been a fan of this developer since the Timore series which was played by Youtuber Markiplier. It was my first introduction to this developer and I really enjoyed watching the series, but never purchased any of the games personally.
Today I decided to finally purchase this new release before watching Youtubers, as I wanted a fresh and personal experience without spoilers and boy it was worth the purchase.
This game took me back to the arcade shooters of the late 90's and early 2000's. A game where you attack waves of different enemies and then attempt to survive long enough to face the level's final boss. I really had a lot more fun than I expected, and I can see myself trying new levels and challenges in the future.
I noticed a large variety of creatures with varying attacks, that relentlessly hunt the player down through a very creative map. The maps also seems to include day/night cycles and weather effects.
The difficulty level can seem quite high at first, but not to the point of raging. Once you come to terms with the map design and the little quirks the game presents to the player it becomes easier to defeat the level.  It may take some trial and error to find out the best way to defeat enemies and it's smart to avoid running into dead ends, which can easily lead to your demise.
The game is also great for casuals and those who want a "pick up and play" experience.
The music was pretty cool as well, and I felt it helped set the mood and pace of the game quite well.
I would love to see a co-op mode for this game or even a VR style version as it would be a lot of fun. I also look forward to more levels and even crazier level design and maps.
On a final note, some scarier maps would be appreciated as well!
The game has a lot of potential and for the price tag you can't really go wrong.

Beyond Earth vanilla feels like an unfinished game. It's basically Civ 5 but with a futuristic make over with a few changes. I feel like it's gonna be like Civ 5, when it got released it was bland and boring and it took a few great DLC's that were developed over the course of a few months and years to make it a great game. CIVBE has a lot of potential and even with the new DLC which makes the game much more enjoyable it still has it's issues.
Aliens/Barbarians: The aliens in this game is much more intelligent then the barbarians in previous games, they don't go on blatant suicidal attemps to ♥♥♥♥ with you and waste your time. For the most part they leave you alone unless you get close to their nest or if you have killed a bunch of them. They also play more of a crucial part depending on what path you go down.
Affinities: Is a really awesome system. Basically the tech you research gives you EXP towards a certain affinity which is like an ideology. Once you level up in a certain affinity you can level up your units which will give them a cool design and stats based off of what affinity you went down. Like if you main in Supremacy you get to build giant siege robots and have robotic looking boats it's pretty cool. It's better then everyone having the same unit just with different colour pants.
Tech Web: It takes a bit to understand, but it lets for more personalization towards what kind of game you are looking for. In old civ games you would pretty much research everything but in CIVBE you have a giant web to choose tech from which is really cool, you aren't forced down a certain path.
Ways to win: There are much more ways to win now. Each affinity has it's own way of winning if you either want to take over Old Earth, or save the people of Old Earth or have sex with a bunch of aliens. There are also much other ways of winning like making contact with intelligent aliens or domination stuff like that.
Spies: Are really much better then previous games, you can send them on certain tasks. So instead of sending them to steal tech, you can send them to steal gold, research points, and recruit deserters. So depending on the situation you can send spies out to help you.
Leaders: have no charisma and aren't interesting in the slightest, whenever you talk to them they all have the same blank expression. In other Civ games when you talked to leaders you would be warped to their environment, it being a castle, boat, sacrifice chamber, or deep in the forrest it was really cool, with the new leaders the background is just transparent and bit fuzzy which helps strips the leaders of any charisma.
All the resources, buildings and wonders: In other civ games when you build a libary you know what a libary is going to do, but in CIVBE when you're researching something you don't always know what a certain building can do just by looking at it so when you have an entire tech web staring you in the face it can be hard to figure out what you want by just looking at it. Same things go for wonders and resources, in other Civ games you know what iron does and what you can build with it, but in CIVBE when you have Xenomass you are probably gonna be confused for what it's utility will be until you need it to build a unit.
Affinities: Even though affinities are pretty awesome they still can get annoying because you need to focus in on one affinity and if you don't you will be left in the dust.
Just the game in general: Is pretty bland and can get boring very fast.
Diplomacy: They COMPELTELY revamped diplomacy. Now you get diplomacy points which you can get from doing certain tasks and you can spend them on getting leadership traits that give your civ abilitys, you can also spend the points on other peoples traits, if they accept the deal which is pretty cool. It is much easier to become friends with Civ's now. CIVs have a respect and fear counter which basically means the more they respect you and like you the "respect" points will go up for that CIV and they are more likely to make deals with you and accept to be allies, instead of completely sucking a CIV's♥♥♥♥♥to be their ally you can spend diplomatic points on becoming their ally or trade partners if they accept of course. Fear is basically like it sounds like the more they are scared of your tech and military and the more conflicts you have with them the more "fear" will go up, the higher it is the more likely a civ will declare war on you.
Building Civ's on ocean tiles: Is pretty awesome, no longer are you confined to a tiny continent or island you can build small cities on ocean tiles and if you want move the city to a better spot. They are completely op tho, they don't generate culture and they don't expand much unless you but the tiles.
Hybrid Affinities: Are what affinities needed to make them more fun to use. It's what it sounds like you can make a hybrid of two affinities with their own special units, make for more fun customizable units.
Declaring War: Now instead of having civs being completely anal and not giving you anything even though it's clear you whopped their♥♥♥♥♥now depending on how much a civ kicked an other civs♥♥♥♥♥they will be forced to give you stuff.
Diplomacy: Because of the "Respect" and "Fear" points taking stage you no longer can actually make choices and talk to a civ or call them out you can only change your relationship with them. Also "Fear" needs some more work done with it. If you've gone to war with a civ and completely decimated them their "Fear" for you will be pretty large, this will compel them to goto war with you at random times even though they are not prepared in the slightest to attack you. I've had civ's just randomly declare war on me three times with only one or two units to attack.
Trading: You can no longer directly trade rescources with other leaders which is absurd, the only way to gain or get rid of rescources is to set up a black market with your spy, but it costs 50 diplomacy points per turn WHICH IS A ♥♥♥♥ING CRAZY AMOUNT. So far I'm lucky to get around 40 late game. I think they should just bring back trading normally.
Declaring War: I feel like this system is so close to being awesome but it falls short. See, you don't get a choice in what you want a civ will just give you what they calculated to be fair which is good sometimes and annoying other times. Because sometimes they will give you a trash city they just made which is a half the planet away and you have no choice but to take it because you probably don't want to continue the war.
Alliances: Can get VERY annoying VERY quickly. Because if you are allied with someone they will pull you into a war that you have no interest in, even if they started it. One day you will be making nice, nice with everyone then you ally warmongering mc♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ will declare war and will ♥♥♥♥ everything you worked towards over.
All in all, even though this game has it's failures I feel like it has a lot of potential and most of my problems with this game will be fixed with updates and DLC's, for example the rising tide dlc fixed a lot of my gremacies with the vanilla version. With Rising Tide I have a lot of fun with it but I feel like it will lose it's magic soon.  I would recommend buying this game and it's DLC on a good sale if you are looking to play a new interesting game.

As of writing this, I currently only have 1 hour of the game. That said, I'm enjoying this game a lot so far. I'm bad at writing in-depth, good reviews, so I'm just going to list the additions/features that I like.
I haven't really ran into anything I dislike as of yet. I guess the only con I have is that they removed the upgrading foods feature, because I liked that feature in CSD1.

I loved the first game and this sequel has a few issues but overall I disagree with the negative reviews. To get the negative out of the way first, I would agree however that I think this game should have been released as an Early Access title as there are indeed some features which are currently missing/being added by the developer in big patches. For instance, features such as upgrading your equipment so that chores are reduced/easier, the YUM feature is currently underdeveloped, and also the restaurant decorating tool is quite frustrating currently. I would also say there's a lot less rainy days which I loved in CSD1 as they feel so cosy. In my experience the rush hour beginning and ending animations across the screen is quite bright and can affect how well you can view your orders. I have not experienced any crashing in this game however I do get a fair amount of flickering/artifacting in the background at times in the restaurants, and also some outlines around people/objects are strange (I have an r9 290/4690k/16GB RAM for reference). A positive is that the developer is listening to feedback and there are large patches in the works. Also, I don't think it is just me but I do think there are some levels, that currently without any way to improve chores, are actually not even possible to get gold medals in! Very frustrating if you are a perfectionist like me! Though again this is something the developer is currently addressing in patches (and CSD is addictive so I end up coming back soon enough after ragequitting, ha).
There are substantial improvements to this sequel; the holding stations are a big mechanic which freshens up gameplay and makes levels feel different. There are several pages of ingredients for many foods which makes some foods more complex to learn but in a satisfying way. There are a lot of levels to play due to the chef-for-hire levels and also your own restaurant (this aspect is as aforementioned currently awaiting patches for development, but there are enough chef-for-hire levels to keep anyone occupied). Gone also are some of the very irritating foods to cook in CSD1 such as popping the cork in wine, slicing vegetables in soup and holding down buttons to fry foods, you can also now see how many times you have tenderized chicken incase you mess up your counting. There are many new foods which are fun to make. The soundtrack is good also. Ultimately CSD2 is just as satisfyingly addictive and at times painful for perfectionists as its predecessor but with a lot more content coming.

I have to admit, I am one of those very weird people that just love casual time management gaming. I have played nearly 200 hours of CSD1 and therefore have been looking forward to see the second game being released probably more than I was excited about the new Witcher coming out (and that itself says enough about how much I love this game).
The new one is missing some of the features of the old CSD but who the hell cares - the mechanics are different, it's something new to try, so much more content and I absolutely love the Chef for Hire feature! Literally have been just playing through these for last few hours and it doesn't get tiring at all.
Would recommend  to anyone, if you liked the first one I cannot see a reason why you wouldn't absolutely love this one. And if you never tried playing this before - just don't start. It's too addictive :)

So why did I stop playing halfway throught the campaign and couldn't bring myself to complete the game? Grind. Save your main protaganist, all other members of your party are typically not carried forward from one scenario/map to the next. The trouble is that party mebmers can level up just like your protaganist and upgrade into elite troops. It goes without saying the scenario's end battle requires a full complement of elite troops. But all my efforts in training party members is lost every change of map. It feels horrible.
I probably should have just used the cheat codes to auto-level the fresh recruits I get at the start of every new map. But this is not without its drawbacks since the early encounters in new maps are balanced for fresh recruits. Ugh. Anyway, I couldn't bring myself to keep playing in spite of the positive values of ths game. tl;dr- no.
Maplestory has changed a lot over its ten year career, but at its core it is still a complete and utter grindfest. Though the time it takes to get to an acceptable level to really explore the content that the game offers has been shortened, it still feels extremely long and drawn out. And even if you end up actually making it to this level you reach a point where getting gear overtakes leveling in priority, the cost of acquring entry level gear for fighting some mid difficulty bosses becomes pretty high. At this point is where the game really blossoms. There is a rather decentvariety of bosses and encounters, and are often rewarding and create a cool sense of progression and challenge. But, after this point is where the fatal flaw of the game lies. You reach a point where the only way to  progress is invest a major amount of money into gear, larger than many other f2p games. Aside from that, still a fun game, but lacks the same charm and community it had when it came out.

This is written from someone who has only had four hours put into the game so far, as well as full experience (including the bonus star stuff) of the first game. So if you're expecting a review based on knowledge of the whole game, look elsewhere. That being said I will update this if I feel any of my opinions have changed. I also write a lot so i'll probably put a simplified list at the bottom if you don't want to read all of this.
Cook, Serve, Delicious 2 is definitley an improvement on the first, in many ways. The most obvious way is the art style, which in my opinion looks great, but that's completely subjective etc. The game still follows the basic core, with some changes and improvements.
The first change being that there are now multiple pages of instructions possible for singular food items, somtimes requiring you to change page to insert certain commands. While a little overwhelming at first, this does add more challenge but as you play the game it does get a lot easier to manage. I can say that sometimes if a food is particularly complicated on top of having multiple pages it has made me shy away from using that food.
The second change is that now there is, along with the serving stations for preparing things, holding stations. These holding stations can be used to prepare certain foods ahead of time to cut out some of the wait on your serving stations. Sometimes certain foods NEED to be made from holding stations, and there are optional foods that, if prepared, give your orders little bonuses as your customers take those side dishes out the door with them. The mechanic adds a sort of material management element. You need to prepare certain foods with them, taking up some slots, while you can also use those slots to prepare other foods and save time, but you also want those bounuses from having side dishes. It gives you something else to think about, and I personally enjoy it.
This time around, not only are you working for the main restaurant, but also hiring yourself out to many other lands of dining. This mechanic gives you new environments to work in, as well as allowing a way to practice with many foods to see what you like and dislike, while still making cash and progressing, unlike the practice mode in the first game. The practice mode is still in this game, just the chef for hire lets you practice while still making a profit.
Speaking of new environments, you are now also able to customize your restaurant with decorations that you collect as you complete days and chef for hire shtuff. These items range from floors, walls, paintings, booths, tables, chairs, lights, etc etc. It lets you really make your main restaurant how you feel looks best and makes the overall experience of working at the main restaurant more enjoyable.
Also there's a lot more food, drinks, and side dishes if you're into that, thought i'd mention it.
oh, I almost forgot, the humor in the game is just as grand (at least to me) as it was in the first game, and considering EVERYTHING, from the foods to the chef for hire diners, have flavor text, there's a lot of humorous dialogue to go through.
And for the cons, The only real issue i've had, and it's a small one, is that sometimes learning new things is really overwhelming since there's so much you could have to do for some foods. The chef for hire helps and you never really HAVE to do those foods you dislike unless you do the chef for hire missions with them or put them on your menu, it's never forced on you so if you don't like how a food feels then you can either practice with it or never use it again.
And the sountrack is as good as ever, it's honestly fantastic. Fits the game so well and still has the same charm it did in the first game.
-------So, for summary, the pros:
-Improvements on base game
-More complexity while more ways to learn said complexity
-Fantastic soundtrack
-Material management elements
-Chef for hire
-Restaurant customization
-------And the singular con:
-Sometimes a bit too overwhelming, but never to where it's off-putting
-I did see someone mention how there are foods that are basically repeats of other foods, and I can agree that's kind of annoying. Yeah maybe cooking times are different or prices but they don't feel unique at all. But, as previously said, there are a lot of good foods still and you never have to use those ones. Not saying that's an excuse for duplicate foods but it could be a lot worse.
------------------------------------

I will never say that if you disagree then you're wrong (unless it's a factual thing then that's different) so please don't bug me about my opinions, 'tis just how I feel. Thank.

A decent game, but weird game design decisions, feels unfinished.
Loved CSD 1, and was looking forward to this game all year, so I picked it up right after it was released. But I feel mixed on CSD 2 and it pains me to give a negative review. Here's what I think:
What the game does right:
+ Good art design, good music
+ Decent challenge (at times)
+ Generally fun
Needs improvement:
- Some foods are impossible to mess up. In CSD 1, you had to use your brain to make sure things got put together right. While that's still true to a certain extent in CSD 2, the game won't let you put some foods together wrong, so there's no way to mess up (like the Pig Blood recipe - you have to do step 1, before step 2, before step 3, etc). While this is beginner-friendly, it doesn't make it much of a challenge. Same with the burglary/robber that shows up occasionally. Just look over at the right and it shows you exactly what sequence of keys to press (you CAN'T press the wrong keys). This turns CSD into a typing game, and if I wanted a typing game, I'd play Epistory or something like that.
- Advertised as a "fast-paced" restaurant sim, but that's highly variable. The problem is there's a HUGE difference between regular time and Rush Hours. It's often so quiet during regular hours that I'm literally tabbing out or checking my phone until the next order comes in. Rush Hour is usually pretty good, but all too often the foods take too long to cook, so I'd have all 8 order stations cooking, and it takes like 10 seconds until the next one is ready, so I'm just twiddling my thumbs during that time? Maybe I am too used to CSD 1 NG+ mode, but the down time is no good.
- Weird time scale - in the morning, time seems to pass quickly, but I swear the clock goes slower at other times. Then songs will finish, and not start up again for another 20-30 seconds. So at some point during each day there is no music playing...it's weird. Maybe it's my computer that is slow...? Not sure.
- No mini-games, no email, no Chef Risotto, little of the small things that made CSD 1 so quirky
- No use for the money you earn in the game
- No upgrading of foods
- No purchasing of new machines
- Too many chores. Once I literally had 7 chores at once on a 10 slot restaurant. And 3 of those were trash chores. It's too much. Where are the orders? Not to mention, pausing the middle of a day to wait for the dishwasher is lame.
- Resturant designer has no influence on the gameplay
- No way to skip the unlocked "prizes" at the end of each round. I don't care about these items. I just want to make orders. Once I had like 10 items unlocked at once, it was painstaking to sit through the award music for each one. A list would have been fine.
- Bizarre interface decision to use SPACE bar instead of ENTER to select options in the menu
- The oddest choice was to either use the keyboard or mouse EXCLUSIVELY in the menus. Usually I'll use the keyboard but sometimes I'll thoughtlessly select something with the mouse. Then I'll go back to keyboard. Unfortunately the game goes into mouse-mode and doesn't respond to keyboard commands. Several times I thought the game was frozen because it wasn't responding to keyboard.
So, IDK, I like the game, and I think the game has a lot of potential, but in it's current state, it's hard to recommend whole-heartedly.

I have been a massive fan of Thief since the very first release. I would have never though that 10 years later there would have been Thief (Rebooted). I must say that when I seen some of the screenshots for the game I was absolutely taken aback. The levels are stunningly well developed, and the attention to detail is overwhelming. I doubt if there will be many complaints, but rest assured… there will be the ones who just about complain about every f****** thing. They’ve spoilt the game, they have ruined it. It’s nothing like the original.
And Like I said the complaints... Well they have been flooding in. I have read some dreadful reviews about this game. To be honest I actually don't know what all the fuss is about. I have a very high spec rig and I am one of the fortunate ones who can upgrade my Rig with new technology. And I appreciate that not all of us are have the money nor the ability to upgrade as often as I do. Some people will not be able to run this game, so I would urge you check your spec before purchasing. It is a stunning game.
This is a re-release, with a new story based on the original characters and that is just about it. What you can do within this game compared to a decade ago with Thief 2… there is no comparison. The shadow detail and gameplay of the game is awesome. Although, the controls compared with the original game are completely different. And I am afraid this might cause further complaints about the complexity of the controls. My recommendation, use a gamepad it will be a lot easier than using a keyboard and mouse. If you are lucky to have a gaming keyboard like myself then you can program an assortment of different keys to your liking.
The only thing that I do not understand with Thief (Rebooted) why the developers decided on using UE3 and not UE4 (Unreal Engine 3) which is more advanced than the predecessor. The development of the game was rocky and nearly didn’t get developed. Although Eidos Montreal came through with what might be the best release of Thief (Rebooted) since the initial release nearly 2 decades ago?
Will the PC version play up against the PC4 edition. I don’t know, I have seen the PS4 edition and I must say the attention to details is just mind blowing. I was absolutely stunned at the attention to detail. Although, we shall have to wait and see on the 28th February. The spec for the PC version I thought was very reasonable… If you’re lucky like myself to have a very high spec PC then this game should run flawlessly. Although, with the troubled development at Eidos Montreal I would expect to see and wouldn’t be surprised in the slightest if there wasn’t some issues. It’s to be expected, with all games that are developed. Hardware configuration and drivers have a huge impact on games, especially when they are new. Spy Chameleon - RGB Agent is a top-down stealth puzzle game. You play as chameleon secret agent who needs to make his way through 75 levels without being detected.
Overall the game looks decent enough but the levels are bit boring visually and get quite repetitive after a while. The way the game displays vision cones can be problematic too and telling multiple overlapping vision cones apart is quite hard.
Sound effects and music are passable enough but nothing particularly memorable.
The game is structured like a typical casual puzzle game. You play through 75 levels split in 5 sets. Each level has three challenges: collect all 10 flies, beat the time limit and collect all the ladybugs (which only appear once you have completed the level once). In practice this means that you need to play through each level two or three times if you want to complete all the challenges.
The levels themselves contain various enemies and other hazards and every time you are detected you are returned to the previous checkpoint. Unfortunately the stealth mechanics in the game just are not very good. Your main tool as a chameleon is your ability to change color to blend in the background. Unfortunately the game does not do a very good job with this mechanic and it's useful only in specific areas.
The level and puzzle design are quite weak, too. The puzzles are extremely simple and the levels themselves don't have enough variety. The game is passably fun early on but starts feeling repetitive way too soon.
Overall the game isn't particularly difficult even on hard, although to be fair I only completed the Get All Flies challenge in most levels. Pretty much all the puzzles have obvious solutions and the only difficulty comes from levels that require precise timing.
The default keyboard controls are pretty bad and there does not seem to be a way to rebind keys. You can play with a mouse too, but this felt rather imprecise to me.
There's no real story and very little writing.
The game suffers from some annoying bugs and glitches. For starters, every time you launch the game it will reset to normal difficulty. This can be pretty annoying, especially if you going for the hard-only achievements.
The hit detection is pretty bad too, and the hit box for your character doesn't quite match the 3D model.
Spy Chameleon - RGB Agent is a fairly bad puzzle game. The level and puzzle design are rather weak and the stealth mechanics are poorly implemented. I wouldn't recommend the game, you are much better off playing something like Stealth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Deluxe or Mark of the Ninja for your 2D stealth puzzle fix.

Legends of Eisenwald is a solid turn-based combat game at heart framed by a weak RPG element, which becomes more and more irritating as the game progresses.
It's a pretty standard set-up from the off; pick a fighter, archer or mage and off you go trying to right some terrible wrong to your kingdom.
The objective of most chapters is to take over the whole map, largely done by levelling up your hero and his companions through a series of fights.
The hex-based combat works nicely, with troop composition, formation and tactics vital to success - reminisent of the turn-based
(1996!).
However, you find yourself horribly mismatched at the start of nearly all chapters, forcing you to spend long times dodging larger armies for a fight with an easier army, then waiting for that army to spawn again.
It becomes a tiresome and tedious grind until you can take on enemies which you think you can beat.
This is exacerbated by the fact the only outcomes are victory, bringing loot and experience, or defeat, which is game over.
There's no chance to retreat/be taken prisoner like Mount & Blade, forcing you to pick your battles carefully. You'll find yourself constantly reloading saves to beat a difficult battle, instead of being able to a take a mauling and then licking your wounds after.
After a while the novelty of the combat system wears off; your army rarely changes and you find yourself doing the same opening moves again and again, watching characters amble across the screen to attack.
You know before you attack exactly how much damage it will do, which inevtiably reduces most battles to a predictable affair, necessary only because you fare badly auto resolving battles.
There's also a stage in every chapter when the balance of power shifts dramatically. You go from running from most battles to completely dominating every encounter without breaking a sweat.
The RPG element leaves a lot to be desired and feels completely superfical to the combat. There's castle, fortifications, different terrains and a day/night cycle, but it feels like very few events impact your battles.
The quests are rlike an afterthought after developing the great combat, there's no depth to most of the characters you encounter. The main character might have some dialogue with some of the chaps wandering around, but you rarely get an input into the conversation.
They're just something to improve your army with rather than to get emotionally involved in for the most part.
I know the developer intentionally didn't want to handhold players through missions, but I had no interest in them because they felt so incredibly shallow.
With that in mind, the game felt like it went on too long with too many drawn-out chapters, rather than fewer that were well polished.
A fun little indie medieval fantasty combat strategy game let down by a lacklustre RPG element.

This second title of the CAFE 0 series from roseVeRte feature a different female protagonist Corliss Green who took up employment as a servant maid for the Ashford villa while searching for her lost aunt Sophie Evans ends up at Cafe 0. With the Cafe 0 waiter Noir, Corliss is sent back to the living to uncover pieces of her past, discover more about herself and the mystery surrounding the Ashford family and eventually find peace in her journey after death which is unavoidable and will always occur within 7 days at the time of returning back to the living world. At the Ashford villa, Corliss is introduced to two members of the Ashford family Ethan Ashford and Nathan Ashford and the family butler Barclay. As Corliss attempts to find out more about her past through each character, she will return to Cafe 0 and back to the living again, reliving the same 7 days prior to her death with additional hints and past memories before eventually choosing an ending without returning to Cafe 0 in a tale of mystery, intrigue, subterfuge, fertility, love, honour, jealousy, duty, loyalty, superstition, witch-hunting, betrayal and vengeance.
The game has plenty of save slots to allow different gameplay and dialogue choices to be made during the game, with a different coloured heart(black, blue, green or red) or gold gear popup icon to reach a different storyline branch and the option to skip and fast-forward any part of the game. Soundtracks and overall game presentation are good after factoring in theme song with vocals. Recommended when game with theme song and soundtrack DLC are at discount or in bundle offer as it takes less than 10 hours to unlock all past memories, reach all endings and unlock all CGs and achievements.

is RoseVeRte's latest visual novel and the second game in CAFE 0 series so far. Comparing this newest installation to the previous one, it should be an obvious conclusion that RoseVeRte came a long way in five years and acquired a significant achievement in producing
. Following the same concept in a different story, this sequel presents a similar supernatural mystery with astonishing depth this time.
Our protagonist and the one to find her way to the strange CAFE 0 after her death is Corliss Green now. She is a young girl who has been working as a maid in the Ashford Mansion, residing on countryside near a village, for a week before her death. Apparently, Corliss came to the village to find her aunt Sophie Evans to fulfill her mother’s dying wish, who was missing for 15 years now and was offered a position as a maid by the household butler of Ashfords, Mr. Barclay. Being the stoic, apathetic woman she was, Corliss accepted the position without a thought since she had nothing else to do around. Apparently, she was always better at following someone else’s orders rather than deciding for her own. When she ends up at the cafe, she is greeted by Noir - another waiter equal in rudeness to Sui, yet less creepier, much scarier I'd say - and informed that she is to relive the last 7 days of her life before choosing a new destination for her afterlife. Oblivious and somewhat insentient to the events of her past and the true story of her aunt's disappearance at first, Corliss is forcefully sent back by Noir. Now she is expected to make choices, relive the week and discover her true self by learning certain emotions. While doing so she will also collect various information concerning the past and the current inhabitant of the mansion to shed some light to the case of the Sleeping Beast.
The narrative quality and the event flow in the game are spectacularly good. All characters are fleshed out, with layered personalities, traumas, expectations, personal needs and distinct attitudes. It has been a delight to watch different characters in different probabilities and interactions. I'll state this directly: there are no stereotypes in this game. Every single one of the characters involved are presented with depth, nature and demeanor worthy of a Victorian novel. The whole idea of living through the same time interval affected by different choices and results is a beautifully used narrative tool here. This way, developer also manages to gather all different playthroughs into a single story, establishing a neat narrative consistency, which is a rarely achieved feat in this genre. Watching Corliss to discover about different emotions and grow as a character was a sorrowful delight. The mystery itself and the whole setting is a deeply melancholic one, so if you'd prefer cheerier stories, this might not be your cup of tea. Be warned about probable heartbreak and disturbing insight into human nature. But I know that I appreciated it all.
Did someone said artwork? Well, CGs are not various, but the ones that we are presented with are top-notch. I know I'd love to see Ethan, Nathan and Corliss in more CG artworks but hey, I'm not complaining. Compared to the previous installation,
displays a magnificent growth in artwork department. Also, the game soundtrack prepared by Yuang Chen and performed by The Seycara Orchestra is a complete delight, fitting for a glorious anime OVA even.
Gameplay itself is somewhere between a choice option VN and a kinetic VN since the choices that we have here around are not various, yet their results reinvent the storyline so massively, you don't get to be bored of reading it. For the first three days, you'll have some choice options, which will effectively make you end up in one of the 4 paths. After that point, you'll just sit back and watch the path itself unfold. In each of these paths, you'll be collecting "hints" through your conversations with the inhabitants of the house. At the end of the day, Noir will use that hint to show you a fragment of the events concerning your aunt 15 years ago. After completing all 4 playthroughs and starting a new game, you'll get the opportunity to play the "true path" to solve the mystery of your death and the mystery of the Sleeping Beast once and for all.
Would I recommend it? That is a definite "YES" coming from me. What we have here is a visual novel well-done with all its mechanics, artwork, narrative functions and setting development. Go ahead. This will be a impressive journey!
