This is definitely Roseverte's best game so far, and I will tell you why.
First of all, I'd like to say this visual novel isn't really an otome game; rather, it's a mystery game heavily focused on love. But what is love? Love is not only romantic, there are different types of love (such as family love, frienship love, etc) and THIS is what I'm talking about. Cafe 0 ~The Sleeping Beast~ is a game about love.
You play as Corliss, a maid hired to work for the Ashfords, a noble family living in a modest village. Unfortunately, Corliss is dead by the start of the game and arrives at Cafe 0, a place where "lost souls" gather when they don't know where to go after death (it reminded me of a sort of limbo). Here, she meets the grouchy waiter Noir, who tells her he'll send her 7 days prior to her death so that she can find out why she died...or could there also be something more? Of course there is, it's a mystery game after all ;D
The game has a total of 5 routes; 4 of them are for the Ashford twins (2 for Nathan and 2 for Ethan) and the remaining one is the true route, which is unlocked after you finish the other 4. Personally, I recommend this order of playthrough:
1) Nathan Family route
2) Nathan Friendship route
3) Ethan Couple route
4) Ethan Partner route
5) True route
Wait, what? Couple? Is this an otome? Well, although there is a route focused on romantic love, remember what I mentioned at the beginning of this review: Cafe 0 is a game about different types of love. Corliss is, how should we put it? A doll-like person, she's not what some people would describe as a 'kuudere'; rather, she's empty and only does as she's told. It's thanks to her interactions with the twins that she'll discover different feelings along the way (or along the routes haha) and, therefore, grow as a person and find herself.
Some may think Corliss could be boring because she "doesn't feel anything" but NO, ladies and gentlemen, Corliss is a GREAT heroine who will also make you laugh several times due to her bluntness and, as she starts developing different types of feelings, she'll warm your heart. Then, of course, how can we forget the twins? Nathan, the tsundere yet kind boy and Ethan, the cheerful yet mysterious boy. I don't want to spoil anything because it's really a much better experience if you found out for yourself just how charming and loveable these 2 are.
There are also other characters which will make an appearance in the past; this is due to Noir's power, but only when you find a HINT. Another reason why I recommend to play Nathan's routes first is not only because they have the least spoilers,  but also because the game gradually gets darker and darker...and I'll leave it at that.
So, to conclude, what are this game's pros and cons?
Pros:
-Beautiful art and GUI
-Excellent OST (the developer is thinking of selling it, yay!)
-Great story with lots of mystery and twists, but also heartwarming and funny moments
-Great dialogue
-There are very little repeated conversations, and they actually function as a sort of bookmark to the story
-Amazing characters (especially Corliss and the twins)
-Incredible japanese voice acting
-If you leave the default name 'Corliss', the characters will call her by her name <3 (like in certain otome games)
-You can easily go to the menu with just a right click on the mouse
Cons:
-The descriptions are not as good as the dialogue; many words such as "suddenly" are repeated plus there are certain phrases which are too commonplace (for example, the typical 'tears rolled down my cheeks')
-This is not really a con but the birthday scene only changes on the true route, which is ok but I would have liked to see a little more variation of this scene on the other routes as well
-This is just personal preference so you can ignore it if you don't agree but, having played a wide variety of visual novels, I've really grown accustomed to skip buttons being on the textbox. It's true that some of them are quite big and, therefore, cover a bit of the screen, but I've seen many visual novels (particularly otome games) where the skip button was small and convenient
So, in the end, do I recommend this game? Of course I recommend it! It's a must play!

This is a graphic-lite resource management sim where you walk the tightrope of bare subsistence over the pit of starvation. The protagonists (that you control) consume resources, while you task them with building enough of a surplus that one raid won't leave you all dead.
Some games suffer from obtuse rules or too much RNG. In This War of Mine, the rules are upfront, the RNG is only as crippling as you are impatient, while the randomly-generated locations allow for replayability and starting over without mindless grinding and memorization. Further, you get to control the actions of the people you send scavenging, giving you a sense of ownership superior to a roll of the dice.
Overall the game has great atmosphere, artwork, and gameplay elements. This War of Mine could be improved by voice-acting for all the characters to compliment the speach-bubbles. Further, the game will be a smoother ride if you the player are a fast/comprehensive reader, becuase there are helpful gameplay clues and cues that all come in the form of text. My last gripe is about how slow characters move. It does give a sense of gravity and immersion, but during the day-cycle where you are fortifying and working within your stronghold, it can also be cumbersome if you placed two related items far apart from one another.
Despite the caveats above, I am very much enjoying this game for doing an excellent job of everything it means for itself to be: an oppressive resource-management story-telling war-time sim selling itself on visual and audio atmosphere.

It has been a while since I cooked up some food in a virtual restaurant. When I first came to play Cook Serve Delicious! I have to admit, I did not see the appeal to it. But after restarting and picking some other food to start out with, I quickly got addicted. Building up my restaurant with hard work and even dating on the way. Let’s just say...I never made it to 5 stars due to a busy schedule and could not bring myself back to it. The shame of forgetting the buttons and bringing my restaurant down was too much to bare!
I do believe that by the time I got into Cook Serve Delicious! it was when the second installment was being developed. And now, it has released! With the obvious improvements with the graphics, let’s see how Cook Serve Delicious! 2!! handles and how it learned from it’s predecessor.
Right off the bat, the food has gotten a huge upgrade in graphics. Now looking as realistic as ever. Of course, there are some aspects that does break the realism, but overall everything looks like you can just reach into the computer and pull it out. Ready to eat and undoubtedly delicious without having to cook in real life! Due to this, I do recommend not playing this on an empty stomach. The game's smallest dishes or dishes I personally do not like makes my mouth water. With customer designs, there is a lot more variety, though they all do look like they need to go shopping for new clothes and get more sleep.
Once you get into cooking, the execution is simple but hard. As soon as a customer walks through the door, they will have their order how up on the left. At the same time, the amount of customers you have at a time will depend on the amount of spots you have to cook. Once the order comes in, you need to do the corresponding requirements before you can serve it. Say they ordered a hotdog. First, obviously, you need to cook it till perfection. Then, once you go into putting toppings, you will see a menu to the side of which buttons to press to add what the customer requested. If you undercook the food, or put/forget ingredients the customer will not be pleased. As the customer will not wait hours for their order to be served, if you let the time run out or let the food be severely overcooked, the customer will be furious. There are also some specific items that need to be perfect, as it is a pass/fail type of dish.
There is no story, or nothing to go on, in this installment. In Cook Serve Delicious! the whole premise is to work your way up from a zero star, dingy restaurant barely getting customers, to a glorious, five star restaurant. In Cook Serve Delicious! 2!!, you are kind of thrown in, with no explanation to why you are working in other restaurants, or Chef for Hire. You still have your own restaurant, but the main focus is Chef for Hire as more restaurants and shifts are unlocked with your level. Coming from the first game, I did feel conflicted over whether or not you were supposed to work with your restaurant before I figured out that Chef for Hire was more important. I did not personally go into this game looking for the same thing as the original, but I do think that there could of been something there for the player to know why we are a Chef for Hire. Perhaps repurposing emails to be ways to know which restaurant opened up to you and if you got a new shift available.  Nonetheless, there is an update coming soon that will bring the original campaign and emails.
Watching gameplay or reading about the gameplay is very different than playing it. A lot of factors play into menus you have, creating layers and layers of decisions to make. First, it is the type of food you personally like, the ones you are most comfortable with and know most of the keys for. Not so complicated dishes are obviously easier than other complicated dishes. Then how is it prepared? Do you cook it? If so how long does it take? Do you need to prep it before it goes in? After it fully cooks, how is prepared afterwards or is it ready right off the bat? At this point, it all depends on what the customer wants that dictates what you put on or in the food.
At this point, the original games deviates from this one. While the first installment worked more with you building your own menu and how that affects how many people will like your restaurant; Cook Serve Delicious! 2!! does not deal with this as you will most likely not work in your own restaurant. Progression is mostly with leveling and stars, which every ten levels equals one star, as new shifts open up based on your level. The food is automatically fully upgraded and as this can be overwhelming at first, it does get easier as time goes on. And with shifts being integral, it does make it easier as you do not have to worry about a whole block of new ingredients showing up suddenly. As each restaurant and shift already has their own menu, which revolves around what they specialize in, you do not have to worry about which item will work best in your menu. However, holding stations add in a new level of strategy. There are some food items that require you to use a holding station, some that are optional, some that can not be cooked in a holding station, and side dishes. Making you take some time out to start the required holding station items, and the optional food makes it easier on yourself. With side dishes increasing wait times and making your dishes oh so more delicious.
Despite how different this is, that does not mean this installment is any less fun or addicting. Both installments have their own aspects that draws people in, and that is good. With a shift lasting about seven minutes real time, this can easily turn into a "just one more" situation especially since the game is fast paced. It is hard at the beginning, but once you get in the groove, it becomes easier. Though I do recommend not trying out the last shift without doing the others. It can suddenly become overwhelming compared to doing them in order.
A new feature is the ability to decorate your own restaurant. With seeing the different designs of the restaurants you work at constantly, you can also decorate your own the way you like. Though, decorations are unlocked by your level and medal milestones by boxes opening up at the end of shifts. This can be annoying, especially when you are unlocking multiple items. This also serves as a way to show you dishes you unlock, which can unlock when you obtain a perfect day or gain a star.
Though the one feature I do wish that was added was the ability to restart a dish. Accidents happen, even if you accidently took funnel cake out too early or accidently put relish on a hotdog you are not able to cook it more or risk having the customer become impatient as you recook their dish. You are forced to have your mistakes served, even if you were so close to having a perfect day.
+ Addicting
+ New addition of holding stations
+ Updated food graphics (Delicious!)
+ Decorate your own restaurant feature
+ Developer quick on fixing bugs and considering fan suggestions
+ All control options (controller, keyboard, mouse) comfortable so preference up to you
+/- Not able to restart a dish
+/- Differing ingredient listing from order to ingredient list (Honey Glaze -> Hon. Glaze)
- No direction story-wise (why are we a chef for hire?)
- No reason to work at your own restaurant
Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! is fun and addicting. If you played Cook, Serve, Delicious! before, you will most likely love this installment as well or if you were interested in this type of game. Though if you rather build up your own restaurant overtime, I do recommend the first installment as this mostly deals with Chef for Hire. Both games have their own pros that will draw people in, and at this point I can not decide which one I prefer more.
More content in this one, and a bit more complicated than the first, but the challenge makes it more fun to be honest.

I'm very half and half about this game.
On one hand, the game at it's core is more of the same of the first, but expanded and continued. It's great in that aspect and certainly fun. You'll get many hours out of the hundreds of food combinations you can get up. Expanded customization of your establishment is great. The music is still fantastic. The gameplay is still fast paced and it really challenges you the more complicated you go. The addition of preset levels also adds in a lot more longevity to the game as you definitely feel the need to ace them all.
That said, there's so much missing. Running your own restaurant is practically nonexistant besides buying the food, setting up the menu, and decorating the place. There's also a problem that, while yes the menu is larger, many of the foods are prepared in the same exact way, making them just skins of the others instead of their own unique items. The prep stations are useful, but don't feel like they add anything truly meaningful to gameplay. Instead of cooking the customer's hamburger, you just have it ready to go instead. A few require the prep station instead of it being optional, but I still can't shake the feeling like it was thrown in not to add anything to the game, but as another check mark onto a list of features, if that makes sense to you.
I can't give it a downvote with good conscious because the game deserves to be played, but it's a very hard. I love the first game and believe that you're not missing much if you have to choose between this or the first.

This is an excellent game.
Pros;
-It finds the perfect balance of staying faithful to the original while adding enough new content to make it woth it. It adds holding stations, which changes how you play the game completely.
-There are a ton of foods, sides, and drinks, which makes the game very interesting.
-The game keeps the hectic and rushed feel of the original.
-You can work shifts in different restaurants, which is very interesting and fun.
Cons:
-Upgrading foods is no longer a feature, which makes it definitely feel like something is missing, as you do not unlock new ingredients, and the foods do not become more expensive as you progress.
-You cannot buy equipment that changes chores, tips, etc.
-Progression does not really feel the same, and is lacking.
Basically, all of the cons are just comparing it to the original game. Looking at it by itself, CSD 2 is an absolutely excellent game, and no matter what way you look at it, if you liked the first one, it is worth buying.

I'm hooked on this game, thoroughly. The AAA titles I picked up during the summer sale have all taken a backseat to this Indie gig.
Every map is its own intriguing story, packed with tons of lore and legends. Exploring is fun and compelling. The story is so well written that reading dialogue boxes never becomes tedious, and the occasional bug is easily forgiven. All this, combined with a period soundtrack make this a seriously immersive late medieval experience. Anyone interested in this period in German history will be hooked by the atmosphere alone.
At first, the tactical battles seem restrictive and underwhelming. If you stick with it, however, you will soon realize that the most strategic elements of the combat occur before you ever arrive on the battlefield. How you outfit your troops is an important aspect of combat, making the rpg aspect that much more meaningful. Money is hard to come by early on in each map, which leads to some agonizing decisions when it comes to hiring, healing, and purchasing gear for your men. Café 0 ~The Sleeping Beast~ is a melancholic, mystery otome game with a playtime of approx. 10 hours (I betatested this game outside of Steam, so that's why my playtime is just 4 hours). It is very intriguing and has an overall mystery that's hinted at in every single route, which is finally unveiled in the True Route.
The characters are interesting and the music is to die for, not to mention the past is dragged directly into the story, thanks to a clever hint system which I'm personally very fond of. The Japanese voice acting is great as well (go, Eva!) and makes the characters come alive.
It deals with loneliness, identity, love, death, loss, and many other themes, so it's very melancholic in spirit and left me affected for quite a while afterwards. While many would consider the playtime low for the price, the production quality is high, and the game is miles ahead of its predecessor, The Drowned Mermaid.
If you dig mystery and melancholy, you should definitely consider buying it!

Maplestory has went through some major changes in the last 10 years. While some are negative (accuracy being a completely useless stat), most are positive. Easier leveling means less time doing the exact same thing. The revamps to item enhancement means Pay2Win is not as prevalent as people say. New areas encourage play together for the most part.
While the game is "simplified", it's a good time and you should play it.

I've been playing Maplestory since 2005 and it's not the game it used to be. When I first started playing it was a grindfest, but it was fun. It was challenging. And there was a mostly friendly community. But as the years went on, the updates continued to dumb the game down. Nexon wants more players, so they made the game easier. Then they wanted more money, so they made the game pay-to-win. That said, I still play on occasion. Or, more accurately, my 7 year old plays on occasion. It's a perfect kids game with its simple mechanics, easy progression, and cartoony art

Pros:
-Easy to follow tutorial system for new players. Low pressure learning curve.
-Simple layout of both menus and game HUD.
-Cards translate directly to the paper game. What you learn here can be transfered.
Cons:
-Slow and tedious for advanced players.
-Heavily insentivised micro transactions
-Earning coins early on is slow, so building a deck on your own will take a great deal of effort.
-MTGO exists, where you can redeem most cards and play other formats (Modern, EDH/Commander, Etc)
-(Nitpick) In game cutscenes resemble N64 graphics. Awful, but kind of charming.
Conclusion:
If you or someone you would like to play wants to learn the game and steadily gain an understanding of more complex gameplay or deck building, this is a risk free tutorial game. Though advanced players will likely get nothing new but some headaches form the speed of the game and an emptier wallet if one chooses to invest. All of the essentials are at play and can be a good few hours of fun for your would-be Planeswalker. A reccomendation is a tepid yes.

I know a lot of people have been dissapointed with the change to the progression system, and some would say there is none. But I personally really enjoy the way that each "level" has a set menu. There's always the option to make your own menu instead of doing catering style jobs as well if you don't fancy it. There are 30 different themed restaurants, each with plenty of different set menu levels, and each one you have the potential to earn bronze, silver or gold on. So in terms of level content in the sequel it's been thought out incredibly well, especially since each menu has varying levels of difficulty. And even when you've finished each level once (which will take tens of hours in itself) completionist's like myself will want to earn a gold medal on each level by getting a perfect day with that particular menu.
Another differences in CSD 2 is that foods can't be levelled up, they are what they are. But considering the huge range of different recipes that are included instead this makes sense and gives a huge variety and replay value in my opinion. Each food has many differnet recipes and possible ingredients, a lot of thought has been put into the creation of each one, and whilst some are purposely more simple (due to the new mechanics of the game which puts more of a focus on strategy), others have a large number of ingredients that need to be included. Overall each food is fun to learn the hotkeys for.
The final and I think most loving detail of CDS 2 is the restaurant designer! Each time you earn a medal or level up you unlock multiple new items to include in your personalised restaurant. Although it sounds limiting it's actually incredibly fun and designing interface is simple and easy to use. With such a variety of different decor to use once you've levelled up enough you can create multiple themed restaurant backgrounds to match your pre-set menus.
In conclusion, CSD 2 is different from the original in quite a few ways, trying to improve upon the grindy progression system and small selection of foods. In order to do this the developer has changed certain mechanics but has done so incredibly well. They all fit together in their own way to make CSD 2 a true sequel but a game in it's own right. So much time and effort has been put into the development of this game as the graphics are art, masterpieces even! Each food is vibrant and ever so realistic. I've been following it's development since Chubbigans announced it, CSD 2 is truly a game that has been created with love and passion which is clear to see in every aspect. I really recommend you give it a go without being too tied to the way the last game was made.

I almost hate to write this.  I can see Trace Vector being appealing to certain people.  I am not one of those people.
Gameplay is a combination of memorization and reflex.  As you are shown levels in advance, you can memorize the direction changes necessary during the preview.  Or you can rely on reflex, picking your course as you play.  You can also perform a combination of the two.
For a game based around fast decision making, the game feels artificially slow.  While the section previews allow you to plan your path in advance, they are unskippable and can become annoying.  When you add in the other filler of a section title display and the line exploding into particles, it can feel like you are spending as much time not playing the game as playing it.
Direction switching is not instantaneous.  If you wait until right before a junction to switch direction, you won't switch direction in time.  This can be annoying, particularly if you are relying on reflex.
Levels consist of several sections played back to back.  If you fail, or just get bored and quit, you have to start over from the first section no matter how easy it is.  Again, this makes the game feel artificially slow.  The game is seemingly forgiving in that running into a dead end isn't itself a failure; you simply restart the section with your current fuel.  You can force a manual restart as well, again losing spent fuel.  But running out of fuel is failure.  The whole fuel mechanic feels like more artificial slowness, both in dragging out a run that has crossed into failure and in forcing the game to restart at the first section upon failure.
The game simply feels like a game that wants to be fast, but has a design that repeatedly conflicts with that desire.
As for the music, while other reviewers like it, it does absolutely nothing for me.

Trace Vector begins with a soundtrack. Well, to be exact it begins with a line. Lines upon lines purposefully arranged into perfectly angular designs, burning neon star charts and spacecraft into an empty galaxy. It’s the soundtrack though which sets the tone, one which the game then eagerly joins in a chorus of 80’s sci-fi nostalgia.
Thumping, reverberating drums and swelling synth mesh into retro adrenaline, drawing you into a minimalist time vortex while keeping its archaic roots at arm’s length. A lot of games draw from classic 80’s sci-fi movies and themes; Terminator, Aliens, Star Wars. But almost always they do so in ways which are more reminiscent of the decade than part of it, possibly as the most common films drawn from are franchises which have yet to disappear themselves and thus things inspired by them inherently feel less dated. It allows for recognizable settings and characters, but often misses the beauty of something clearly antique but loved for that very reason.
Trace Vector feels like a game ripped from an outmoded computer and remastered with a modern sheen. Sparse geometrical collections of stars and the lines collecting them create a distance between you and the game in such a way as to give you room to fill in the missing details yourself. Every line and dot is precise and plain until your radiant ship draws a path through them, leaving a blaze of shifting color in its wake. Small embellishments create a sense of atmosphere and movement among the stars, and give the sense that Trace Vector is acutely conscious of its style. Its design is minimal because it wants and needs to be, not because it was all the artist could manage.
Limiting you to selecting whether to travel up or down on a branching path gives Trace Vector an omnipresent sense of urgency. There’s little room for error or a capacity to slow down, requiring you think several steps ahead and careful observe the map less you send yourself down a dead end and waste what little fuel you have. The contrasting priorities between collecting fuel cells, often taking you into the most dangerous areas of levels, and getting through as quickly as possible provides a constantly evolving feeling of engagement. I was constantly having to weigh the odds between picking up extra fuel and playing it safe and having to decide in a split second or miss the opportunity.
Trace Vector isn’t an easy game, but it’s not so hard as to become overly frustrating. The intensity with which you direct your ship has a habit of making the game feel more impossible than it actually is, heightening my senses to the point they began to overwhelm my ability to plan effectively. Trace Vector counters this with moments of calm, inserting levels where it’s impossible or extremely difficult to lose between those that require a higher level of reflex.
Positioned in the midst of all this is the unassuming narrative developing between your ship’s pilot and the AI controlling it. In keeping with the game’s design, it’s minimal but focused, asking questions of the value of artificial life and its right to free will. In another context this could have unravelled into overly philosophical monologues far beyond the game’s scope, but Trace Vector never extends itself further than the task at hand. It’s story is entirely between two characters, but without excluding the audience drawing more from it.
I didn’t expect much, maybe not anything from Trace Vector. It seemed rudimentary and unrefined, but within itself there’s a world of nuance that’s difficult to grasp from screen shots. The more I let it take control the more I grew to love its unified design and simplicity. It’s a really special game that is likely going to have trouble bringing in an audience, but once they’re here I can’t imagine them wanting to leave.

This game is a 1980s arcade classic that never was.
Incredibly simple gameplay, all you basically do is make sure your 'ship' follows the correct line by moving it using the up or down arrow at the correct time. As you progress through the levels the speed increases so you will need machine-like reflexes to keep up... or just use the handy space bar to termporarily slow down time.
Every time you die it's because you made a mistake, nothing cheap about it.
Graphics are minimal but provide the perfect feel. You can even toggle a CRT mode along with different levels of glow in the options, to make it look even more authentic.
And the music... oh man. Pefect 80s synth sound that is 100% matched to the game's levels and keeps you pumped. It's almost worth a recommendation just for that.
The game is split up in smaller level segments so you can play in somewhat brief burts, but also has an endless mode that is just that: you keep playing as long as your reflexes allow you to.
If you like old-style arcade games, or, more to the point, modern recreations of these like the excellent Bit.Trip series, you will also love Trace Vector.

If these terrible features ever get patched out of the game, I'd highly recommend it. As it is now, you're just punished way too heavily for actually trying to play the game.

Spy Chameleon is a puzzle game where you are a chameleon who has five missions to conduct "spy-like" actions: take some pictures of a famous person, steal secrets, hack a computer system. Each mission has 14 levels leading up to that end of mission level. In each level you must stealthily make your way to the end collecting flies along the way. Once you reach the end, another play through will show some ladybugs, usually in hard to reach locations, that you can grab as a snack.
As a chameleon, you have the ability to change color to blend into your surroundings. Early on this isn't required, but later in the game, you will need to move from colored location to colored location avoiding the light cones of the guards.
While the game is technically a puzzle game, if I had to classify it I would call it a top down platformer - if there is such a thing. In order to do more than burn through the level, i.e. speed run or grab the ladybugs, timing and color switching (by pressing buttons like you would jump with a platformer) with precision. I only played through the normal levels. The developers had to add a normal setting because too many people were complaining about the difficulty of the original (now called hard) default setting.
Don't let the cartoony graphics fool you - this isn't a child's game. It may appeal to puzzle players (there is no penalty for getting caught other than the timer keeps going) and to platform players.

If you played the previous 2004 game "Thief: Deadly Shadows" and enjoyed it, you won't regret buying this one. The new Thief carefully recreates the same atmosphere and game pace with modern graphics/sounds, a whole new plot, and a modern-ish unneeded tutorial mission. The gameplay is practically the same - you will do a lot of searching, puzzle-solving, walking, hiding, stalking the guards, planning and stealing. Some people could find it boring. The game has really dark atmosphere and quite a slow pace, which isn't for everyone.
Despite the trailer definitely reminds me the Dishonored one, the game itself is very different. There are no magic abilities neither fencing/shooting your enemies in the face. You will do much more stealthy, hidden actions. It's basically Hitman:Blood money without killing (well, almost without).
The game is REALLY atmospheric and involving. You shouldn't rush it. Treat it as a horror game, play it slow and careful, to get the full experience.
The stealth system is very good, in my opinion. You have your old good "shadow gem" indicating the light level. Guards have a range of aggro levels, from a little suspicions to a real manhunt. Your changings to the environment matter. Sound matters a lot. You can move with four different speed modes (rush, run, walk or slow pace). You have a bunch of gadgets, from old good bow with a range of arrows, blackjack and flash bombs to new context-sensitive tools such a crowbar, a scalpel or a wrench.
If you play on easy difficulty you could find the guards a kind of buggy - dumb, slow-reacting and having their field of view too narrow. If so, swich your difficulty level or try custom difficulty.

Okay.. phwoa!!... long game. Just finished it - in at around 100 hours - Final Fantasy eat your heart out. A few late nights let me tell you. I bought this game on sale for a few pennies (I can't remember now but I think it was for under $5) and didn't really have too high hopes for it considering its price and look but was then completely overturned in my opinion by what is essentially a really great game that in no wise is properly represented by its appearance. DON'T judge a book by its cover! Boy, don't judge this book by its cover, it is a great game for what its worth.  I think this game goes for around $20 more or less on steam and that is about the right price for this game. You won't regret parting with that hard earned cash. If you see this game for anything less than $10 buy it straight away, don't hesitate, you won't regret it. You might ask if it is such a great game why is it only worth $20 dollars? Well that is what I will attempt to explain.
Although I did derive a lot of joy and pleasure from this game, it still very much feels like an Indie production, which is exactly what it is. A beautiful and well done Indie production but an Indie production none the less. There are a host of issues which will remind you of that time and again but they are heavily outweighed by the things that the game gets SO right. Like the loot, merchant and trade system which I guarantee will be the end of you. These guys have got it so spot on that its just scary how much time you'll be spending tweaking your characters inventories and travelling the four corners of the globe in search for new places of trading. Certain hero's you defeat will drop unique items that you will be on the verge of crying over whether you want to sell them for their insane item values or keep them and derive the benefit from them that few items will be able to match or you will need an assortment of items to do what a single unique or rare item can do freeing up those super valuable item slots. yep... thats the one.
You'll be doing a lot of fighting and some can be pretty intense and take up quite a bit of time so you won't be missing out on anything there. The battle system is a little different from what you may be expecting but just accept things for as they are and get on with it. Sure I felt as if some of the things in the combat area are a little counter intuitive, such as not being able to move your guys where you want and not being able to attack whoever you want but don't let that stop you from enjoying the game as a whole. This game is an experience but the game isn't designed around just combat. It is designed around a story, and it is the story that is the main hero of this game. The combat is just there to spice things up... and provide you with loot to sell to buy stuff at the merchants and traders... WARNING, get those sick day excuses ready cos you are going to need a few with some of the late nights you are going to be putting in.
The leveling up system feels right but is severly let down by the fact that you have to retrain your troops at the beginning of every chapter - 8 chapters I think - so all of that hard work to level up your characters (barring your main character) and tweaking their equipment and shopping around to get the best stuff will all be in vain by the end of the chapter as you will be stripped of all of your sellable equipment and all your troops. You will be forced to start from scratch all over again (very small but significant exeptions) at the beginning of the next chapter and collect all of your equipment - AGAIN - and level up all of your guys - AGAIN - but as dissapointing as that sounds, it is actually worse. You will continuously be at a compounding disadvantage as you will have to start with raw recruits each time and although that might not be too much of a problem in the first, second or third chapters, buy the time you are well progressed into the game you will need to start with raw recruits going up against enemies that are more matched to your main character who has advanced significantly by this stage.
The sounds, music and graphics are all very beautful. There is no voice acting, all dialogue is written so get used to doing a bit of reading. The story is generally pretty good with very few 'cringe' moments that you might expect from japanese rpg's but the underlying theme of the storyline is quite mature and developed and centres around choice, consequence, belief and ego. The character models are not redrawn for each character in the game but are simply taken from a dozen or so stock character models, given different outfits and then regurgitated as different characters in the game so don't be surprised when Joe Blogs from the smithy looks a lot like the Duke from the castle with just a different hat. Thats because that's all it is, just a different hat, different name and different stats. See... told you I'd explain why its only a $20 game and not a $40+ game. One particularly annoying trait is the lack of sideward camera scrolling. The view is centred on your character and although you can rotate the angle and direction you cannot move the camera off of your character which means you are forced to constantly give them move orders to the edge of the screen, wait till they get there, give them the order again and keep repeating this untill they arrive at their destination which could be a world away. Fun I know. Then there are the bugs which unfortunately can become very frustrating.
Do these things really make the game bad? No, they don't. The GAME is great despite these flaws but they are a reminder that you are not playing a big publishing house A+++ title. Thats what I was saying before about it being on the mark for its price. If I had payed top dollar for this game then these issues would have surely offended me but I can overlook them considering the value I believe I am getting for the game and the enjoyment and play length that it offers.
In conclusion the game is great. Great story, great graphics, great sense of character progression and most importantly, great fun. It offers countless reminders of its indie roots but these should be kept in perspective of the price you are paying and the quality and quantity of enjoyment you derive from the game. There are always gonna be people who can't keep the reality in focus and are going to dwell on the negative despite ALL of the positive that the game offers. But thats the story of the world really. Final verdict... 7.5 out of 10. Excellent score all things considered.

A member of the Steamified community was so enamored with Legends of Eisenwald that they firmly requested that we run a feature of the game on our site. They had completed the game numerous times and couldn’t get enough of it. It had been a game that I had personally considered prior to the request but as a title that was released prior to our launch but not meeting our 2014 or earlier Steamified Revisits period was a game that I had personally placed on the backburner. However, I can honestly tell you that I am thankful for their recommendation.
One of the first things that I want to say about games such as this one is that it is one that I can leave playing in the background and can dedicate short periods of play to it at a time. There are a lot of games that you really have to be dedicated to playing rather than having paused for periods of time. As a lone hand at Steamified I don’t often get to play games through to completion before having to make their feature. In some ways my nutshells are a first impressions plus (several hours of gameplay rather than completion) and so I feel a bit like a full time employee who would like to get through a massive list of games when its not a reality unlike say someone who works for a publisher and is paid full time to play new release games through to completion – sometimes multiple times – before writing on games. Titles such as Legends of Eisenwald are perfect for me. I can write and work around playing them. Games that constantly need attention (e.g. multiplayer games) are at a disadvantage in my life right now.
But that means that the content that I need to play needs to be engaging. I need something that I can feel a part of albeit for a brief period. This game was perfect in that regard. I found myself involved in its world immediately. This is a game that immediately pulls you in and grabs you. The manner in which the story is told, the narrative, the characters backgrounds and the status of the world are all conveyed in a thorough manner. I had no trouble in jumping in and out of the game at any point throughout the first six hours of the game.
This isn’t necessarily a game that you’re going to be expecting great graphics and sound from yet everything is at a level that I can appreciate. It’s more so the gameplay and the turn-based combat that needs to be top notch and it is. I thoroughly enjoyed the various strategies that I employed and tinkered with throughout the early game. The story telling was also exceptional. Obviously people are going to make comparisons to the Might and Magic franchise and the King’s Bounty games and I believe that the story is stronger than both. The setting being the Middle Ages and European history is a strong point of differentiation for this game and one that it conveys to the player extremely well.
Legends of Eisenwald deserves your attention if you have yet to play it and are a fan of the genre. It represents solid value for money given the amount of work that has gone into every aspect of the game.

I'm not as much of a reviewer that is going to dislike the game just because I have nostalgia goggles on, I'm going to give you a view of the game while including my own experiences to show you how the game is.
This game as it is, in 2015, is an extremely pay-to-win driven game. Over the past 6 years (for me) they've consistently been dumbing down the game to where it practically plays itself with things like 100 level tomes which just make your character level 100 no questions asked, no effort produced. The sidequests are generally repetitive and unrewarding (and unrewarding isn't necessarily a bad thing if the quest was fun). They have special global quests (which when were created happened once a month or couple of months) every single day which reward you with gear for your level and experience automatically, you do not have to go out and kill mobs/bosses to get rare drops or complete a questline anymore.
When I began playing Maplestory in 2009 it was a simple game that allowed you to do practically whatever you wanted, you had no guidance (or very little) and were encouraged to explore the entire world which made the game very fun, it was absolutely great at making you feel accomplished and as if you discovered something new. Now you have something called a Hyper Teleport Rock at almost all times (from the global quests mentioned prior) that can take you literally anywhere in the game, no long trekking, boss battles, or sense of adventure. You can avoid all of that.
The game was more challenging which made it more enjoyable when you leveled up. Back then (pre Big Bang), to put how easy they've made the game into perspective, to get to level 30 generally took around a month and level 70 took maybe 4-6 months. Now, with no exaggeration, you can get to level 30 in an hour and level 70 in about 4 hours. You can hit level 200 (which pre Big Bang would have taken a year or more) in a week, maybe less.
This game also never had a story, just quests. There was no "ultimate evil" or dedicated storyline, but they made that with the Cygnus Knights. I joined the game again just to play the Black Heaven storyline which was extremely boring. The character dialogue just droned on and on with no meaningful interactions, it was almost entirely just characters making cheesy jokes to eachother and other useless non sequiturs which completely dilutes the idea of an overbearing being, so I found myself just holding down my spacebar to fly through the dialogue a lot and I never felt like I missed any information. Then there were things you had to do, and you could tell it was just all filler content. You had to kill 30 of these robots, then go through the portal and kill 40 of them, then go through the portal and kill 60 of them and I wish I was kidding, you ACTUALLY do that up to 100 robots. And you do that a couple more times. You also do the same thing with collecting things from monsters you kill. They're forcing a story that has no weight and is so clearly thrown together that it hurts.
This game is great if you're looking for just a straight casual MMORPG to just♥♥♥♥♥♥around in and waste time, if you want an experience and a challenge I would go find another game.

Cons:
- AI Civs have no personality and quotes are exactly the same as Civ V

Really liking that this game is similar to Cook Serve Delicious 1 without being an exact replica. Some of it could be improved upon as well, though. Ultimately, my recommendation is that if you enjoyed CSD and want some of the same, but somewhat different, give CSD 2 a try.

Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2 is manic, twitchy, and extremely good. When you first play, you'll be lost, flailing and fumbling over keys or shoulder buttons while you attempt to throw together a hot dog. Just when you think you're getting good, you unlock new restaurants with new foods that come with increasingly bizarre timing and button-combo challenges. All the while, you're using your cash to buy new meals and put together your dream kitchen. The central loop of learning how the various foods and service items work, and trying to juggle nine different things at the same time, remains incredibly satisfying. The writing is extremely funny to boot. If you can't handle stressful, high-energy games, this won't be for you. But if you can stand the heat, the adrenaline rush Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2 delivers makes it all worthwhile.

I loved CSD and was hesitant about 2 because of the negative reviews I was reading, saying that there was much less of a 'story,' with little progression for your own restaurant, no upgrades to foods, no catering events, and little reason to get interested in all those new meals. I think it's actually a very successful sequel, but it tells a different 'story.' While you can still focus on your own resto whenever you want (and using extra $ you've earned elsewhere), the challenge here is to work at tons of different kinds of themed restaurants. This forces you to learn other people's set menus (like a real journeyman chef has to), rather than just building your own favorite menu every day, where it gets easier and easier as you master each item completely. I've done shifts at about 6 of these restaurants so far and I like the challenge and variety of each one. Then, I can use my know-how to decide which recipes I most want for my own restaurant. I actually don't miss upgrading my food or equipment at all - it feels totally unnecessary given how much new content there is.
The food looks amazing, and there is still humor - the descriptions of the restaurants' histories are hilarious. The streamlining is great - no more using both the arrows as well as letters, so you can move faster. The soda machine was a huge annoyance; now refilling the soda machine is easy. The holding and prep stations are a great success and offer 2 new levels of juggling timing and planning. I'd recommend this for fans of CSD (as long as they read up a bit and realize it's a slightly different game, not just more of the same) as well as new folks; I also plan on recommending it to a couple kids - it's so family-friendly.
I haven't gotten to the point where it's challenging yet - maybe I'm not playing my own restaurant enough. I'm looking forward to my days not having large gaps of quiet - that NEVER happened in #1.
I'm impressed with how the dev is responding to things so quickly. Few notes for him:
-I'm running out of music during the Rush Hour for some reason, so it just becomes completely quiet except food noises
-Deleting things in the Designer mode is still really clunkly. Having to go back 2 menus and then toggle through items before hitting the garbage can - it's just bad. You should be able to point to an object and right-click a menu to move it/delete it/exchange it, etc.
-I understand not having the option to change key bindings for each individual food item, but for the meatloaf, why would sauce be "A"?
Enjoy, all you keyboard-clickers!

The addition of a few strong mechanics such as being able to pre-make cumbersome orders that take a long time and the ability to fully customize the resturant make CSD2 a nice sequel and I even enjoy the campaign of working for pre-set restaurants... in theory.
However, the sheer lack of any kind of progression really does hurt the game. When I read the reviews that said this, I initially thought "So I wont be able to build the restaurant from the ground up, big deal." but it actually is, as the biggest deal with the way the first game was structured was that it slowly built up understanding of both the games mechanics and the orders you were filling as you slowly earnt them and upgraded them.
In the sequel, especially with the pre-made restaurants the campaign is made up of, you are thrust right away into the deep end, with no understanding on how exactly you're suppose to do the order and on orders with huge amounts of selection such as Ice Cream or a Burger, you're left with no build up of knowledge of what every single button does. The worst candidate for this I have seen so far is the Cannoli, which has several ingredients beginning with C, so remembering which one is which without that buildup of upgrading the order is a nightmare.
What initially seems like a minor problem fans of the first are complaining about is actually a huge hinderance to this game, as things are extremely poorly explained and you are placed in the deep end from day one. Making CSD2 more of a frustrating experience overall.
I still recommend the game as it is fun and the improvements added are nice. But the ugly issues from the first game still remain, such as confusing keyboard shortcuts for ingredients and the overbaring amount of chores (which, actually has gotten worse with more chores added and no upgrates to slow them down or make them more infrequent). And on top of the lack of progression to ease you into the game, I can only really recommend it to people who have utterly mastered the first game. If you have not played the first one to completion, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.

I had my qualms about Dishonored when I first played it, because of the plot (that ping-ponged you on the outskirts of a real story, leaving you no real choices) and and its decorative, linear world. But compared to Thief remake, Dishonored is a masterpiece. And the sad thing is, Thief is totally playable, solid game - but slightly annoying in all possible ways, and also completely ridiculous. Slightly amusing TL;DR next.
Thief is not a horrible game - rather, it's quite mediocre, despite all of the evident labor that went into its making. The source of the most excrutiating pain is the game's plot: it's all incredibly half-baked, illogical twists and baffling characters who are all over the place. Yes, including Garrett, who is part action-star jock (delivering one-liners in the most inappropriate situations), and part piece of wood, that chooses all the worst moments to insert a meaningful silence (so they all look like bug-eyed weirdness). All in all, Garrett reminded me of Shia LaBoeuf, which is Eldritch enough in itself. I won't even get into the game's half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt at political commentary, because it's clearly pulled straight from other movies and games without any thought. Dialogue is simply very bad (though overheard "flavor" conversations are perfectly OK). For me, the highlight of writer's craft  was when chief of criminal police explained to a notorious thief the meaning of the ubiqitous in-game word meaning "thief" (along the lines of "You see, when they catch thieves, they scald their hand in tar, so thieves are often called blackhands. Did you know that?") The ending is so muddled and confounding, it's almost high-art surreal.
OK, let's disregard the plot (and we can, literally, since there are several nice little, interesting side missions to play). Game mechanics (like the plot) is a smorgasbord of Dishonored, Hitman: Absolution, Assassin's Creed and others. Each one contributes a lovely bit of gameplay - and almost all of these bits don't work. Including the bits from original Thief. For example, Absolution-style closets for hiding are so completely useless, developers made them double as save points. I beat the game on Master using stealth, and I used the cabinet for hiding once. And I could do without it that time. And you can save anytime anyway.
Stealth is not very good: on one hand, enemies are deaf and dumb, on the other, there are only two lighting situations for the player: brightly lit and totally obscured by darkness. The end result looks rather ridiculous, player prancing around people, snatching earrings out of their earlobes and cups before their eyes, hiding behind a coffee table in a lit room, hiding in plain sight in the middle of the stairs and so on. Another example of (Dishonored-)pulled mechanic is the Swoop - a cool accelerated stealth motion that is almost silent for some reason. Again, it's sometimes cool, but it undermines the tension and calculations of stealth: if there is a danger of detection, you just swoop around enemies like a terrified jetbike caught in hostile waters.
Close combat leaves you feeling like an idiot: to make Garrett more thievy, they denied him the use of any edged weapons, so even if you make a tough moral decision to murder the guy who discovered you, you will have to hit him repeatedly with a small club until he is too tired to block. Yes, I'm not joking, it's the only kung fu in Garrett's arsenal.
Open-world navigation is incredibly infuriating. In attempt to make the (very small) town into kind of a puzzle, developers closed off 90% of the roofs and plotted extremely arbitrary and convoluted paths, without any consideration for how the hell could anyone live in this city at all. And where is everybody. The "overheard conversations" mechanic always works as disembodied voices from inaccessible Nowhere, SOMETIMES EVEN IF THE CONVERSATION IS INSIDE THE APARTMENT YOU'RE IN. And it glitches sometimes, so you hear the same chat about a nice-smelling sex-worker all over the level, like it's a ghost that haunts your undersexed thieving self. Apartments that you rob, meanwhile, are always ominously empty. The nail in the coffin is arbitrary window-portals and "narrow-passage-portals" between maps, that never tell you where are you going. They're slow, annoying, and for all of their lengthy animations, they still end up showing you a loading screen.
And several hours into the game, you realize that you're stealing everything from everyone, from lowly vagrants to artistic types to dead people to nobility. That's because neither Garrett or the game itself do not differentiate. For them, it's like collecting rings in Sonic.
Oh, and Garrett can't jump. It's OK as a design choice, there are a lots of designated climbing points... but Garrett also can't jump over small and deadly pressure plates. He just expires, raising his hands in despair (that's his dying animation, for some reason).
Anyway, it all comes down to the plot. You could gladly trod though not-so-perfect-but-totally-OK gameplay if you didn't roll your eyes every half an hour, or if any of the NPC's caused f***-giving counter to show of the myriad readings not amounting to zero. I certainly trodded through Thief all the same, and went away with something to tell - like the SUDDEN Silent Hill revival in the mental institution, or the need to set up precise soft flesh headshots, or cool side missions, or the HONESTLY COOL peripheral/central vision stealth mechanic (when enemies' reaction time depends on how peripheral you are to their vision cone). I have the utmost respect to its developers who churned out this enormous amount of content and threw in a couple of good ideas.
There is a lot of things in Thief, and many of them are righteous. But the demonic side won.
***I should clarify, after reading other reviews, that there are many smart bits about new Thief's stealth. Detection of open containers, peripheral vision, multi-level alert, cumulative alert and so on. At the same time I should add that the game world (which is part of the plot, so it's covered in the review) is not very convincing. It's 1920's (or later) technology, household items, fashion and overall aesthetics in a sorta medieval world. Rachmaninov playing on voxophones but lighting with torches. Wirecutters that cut rope. Rope that controls electrical machinery. Ratchet wrenches, metal ductwork and compound bows, and no firearms.

The original Thief (The Dark Project/Gold) is without question one of my five favorite games of all time, possibly my favorite. So it was that when I first heard they were working on a new Thief, I was very excited. I've been waiting for this game for a very long time. But I'd also heard the criticisms of the game during development, and was nervous. Having played through a few chapters and side missions now, I can say I'm pleasantly surprised with this reboot.
While in some ways it is lacking in the original Thief mythos (no Hammers/Mechanists/Pagans/Keepers that I've run across yet), it still feels like home, playing on Master difficulty and having the Focus powers turned off. Eidos is to be commended for the customization they have allowed the player to make the experience as much like the original as possible (personally, I'd prefer that that original experience was the only experience, but as long as I can experience the real game myself, I guess I don't really care if other people choose to cheat themselves out of it). That was one of my biggest fears as development progressed, and I'm happy to say that for the most part Eidos has done a good job in making the true Thief shine through (again, at least optionally.  On easier difficulties, and with other option settings, I can't say. But then I only ever played the original Thief games on the hardest difficulties so that's the only point of comparison I can make anyway).
Some of the other complaints I'd heard, and I'll lump several somewhat related things together here a little, was a lack of freedom - that the game had an "on rails" feeling, that the levels were small, etc. These criticisms do have some merit; however, I don't think its quite so bad as that. The levels do have a little bit of a linear feel and they might be a bit shorter than those in the original game on average, but I don't think too much so, and the open world of The City helps compensate for that a bit. The side missions are definitely much smaller, and it doesn't seem that there are as many main story missions as the average 15 or so from the previous games (going by the Steam achievements, it looks like there may only be 8), so there is that. The one area where I do really feel the lack of freedom rearing its ugly head is the inability to jump whenever you want and to lean forward or to the sides unless you're right at a specified corner (and even then, the actual lean doesn't seem to add much to your field of view at all from just the basic "peek", and its a little - though not too much, so this is a very minor complaint - harder to duck back around a corner compared to the old games where you could just let go of the lean button and be moving at the same time). There were a lot of places in the old games that jumping wouldn't help you reach any further anyway, so I don't know that the real effect of this change is that monumental, but it still does create a definite constrained or chafing feeling. One instance where I've found the lack of jumping to be a great hindrance is not being able to jump over pressure plates.
One other thing to say is that the game is gorgeous. Its absolutely every bit as beautiful as playing through a dark, gloomy, plague-infested, crime-ridden city could possibly be. Overall, though I'm still fairly early into the game, from someone who loves and cherishes the old games, this new Thief gets my stamp of approval.

Spy Chameleon is an incredibly fun action puzzle game wherein you must reach the exit of a level by avoiding vision cones of enemies. It utilises interesting mechanics that I haven't seen in other games, such as the ability to blend into the environment to avoid detection, as a chameleon would do in real life.
- A unique concept that really makes for an enjoyable game that you will keep coming back to.
- Beautiful graphics.
- In-game collectibles. Perhaps you've already beaten a level, but you can always go back and try to collect all of the hard-to-reach ladybugs!
- Trading cards and achievements. The achievements are well-paced, varying in difficulty. Unlike most games, there's no stupid achievements like playing for 40 hours or beating the time of 10 others on your friend list.
- An emphasis on speed. Each level has a challenge time to beat, and there's also an achievement for beating every level in under 18 minutes. That's no easy feat, and adds a real challenge to the game once you've already beaten every level.
- Cloud saving and controller support. You can stop playing on one computer, then start playing on another, with no loss of progress. You can plug a controller in mid-game and the game will automatically update to show you controller controls rather than keyboard controls.
- Global leaderboards for times. So you think you have a fast time? Check how you stack up globally!
- Some of the levels have ridiculously narrow margins of error regarding precise movement. For example, the final level has a vision cone that must be blocked by a filing cabinet to pass, though the cabinet is mere pixels wider than is required. Pushing the cabinet even slightly too far will mean you have to go back to the last checkpoint, essentially ruining a speedrun of that level.
- There's a few minor 'detection' glitches; you will occasionally get detected when you shouldn't, and occasionally fail to get detected when you should. This doesn't have any real impact on the game, as the difference either side is only a fraction of a second.
- In addition to beating the challenge time on each level, the gamer is also prompted to beat a much faster time shown when starting Speedrun mode. I can only assume these are developer suggestion times for the 'Sprinter' achievement. While it's nice that they gave suggestions, many of the times are literally impossible -- no-one in the world has beaten them.
Spy Chameleon is an incredibly fun game, and one that should definitely be picked up. While I typically advocate going for games when they're on special, the price for Spy Chameleon is already cheap as chips for the content delivered. I'd actually recommend paying full price for it so that the developers are able to work on a sequel sooner! :)

I have played this game since 2007-2008 and I can tell you the game has not only declined, it's plummeted. Hackers and botters were always an issue so I won't touch on that, as well as the P2W nature. We all know P2W is bad and I've sunk easily far too much money into this while I was still on my parents' alllowance. Still, many MMOs follow that route and I've become inured to it.
No, what gets me is how far the game likes to think it's come when in reality it hasn't moved at all. On the one hand, I like the multiple character classes, as even though they feel just like all the others of their niche(Tank, glass cannon, rogue, etc.) there's little perks that make the classes interesting for a time(My favorite so far being Mechanic, though since I haven't played in ages they've likely been nerfed). That leads me to one of my main gripes: The lack of balancing for the numerous new classes. Not only that, but the game itself doesn't change to suit each new class and their newfound overpowered strengths or crippling weaknesses. This leads to many classes being pointless or obsolete(Who even plays as the classic four/five character classes anymore?) which clutters up the game.
The game itself is very cluttered, as well. I get that traveling is a big part of any MMO or any game with a large world for that matter, but if your game is a 2D, linear style, the back and forth of traveling is a lot more tedious than choosing the shortest route in a 3D game. Not only that, many parts of the maps are just lines with no connecting rooms or hubs, leading to a lot of needless backtracking. However, this is another feature of the game that I got used to(Though pre big bang the map was a circle, which was very nice).
Those are my two biggest qualms right now, though for the most part I don't feel comfortable completely bashing this game since I've had so much fun with it since when my brother introduced me to it as a young teen. I wouldn't recommend it in the state it's in, though. I'm going to try Mabinogi and other Nexon MMOs, though, because I've heard they're better now than Maplestory has been in a long time.

I had my settings for the bloom and luminosity effect high to the point where I felt I was enjoying the most of what this game had to offer me. Not too high though, just high enough. (Your eyes will bleed if you max out settings.)
Personally, I think getting the right brightness and the right bloom will really help you have a great time with this game.
So that said, two thumbs up on my end.
But as for the price?

It is very much a "jack of all trades" kind of game. There might be games that do open wheel, tuner, or street racing better, but autosport combines them all into one fun package with relatively realistic sim-cade physics. Each discipline in Autosport is fun, and together they make for a winning package.
Grid Autosport might not be enough of a simulation for hardcore racing sim fans, but it's not supposed to be a racing sim. What it does do is package a wide variety of racing disciplines into an accessible yet realistic-feeling game.

I'm really torn on this game. On one hand, I really appreciate that Codemasters went back and tried to fix the wrongs they made with GRID 2 in just one year. The in-car view is back, there's no "story," it's >10 hours long, etc., but in the end the game is... boring.
Two things that made the original GRID one of my favorite games was its level of personal detail (creating your own personal racing team) and the cinematic & chaotic closed-circuit racing (
). In Autosport, both of these these are completely absent; you simply bounce from preselected teams between seasons, and the racing itself is just stale compared to GRID and even GRID 2.
Another issue I've seen other reviewers point out is the game's experience system; due to how XP is distributed, you're going to spend a lot more time playing disciplines you're not a fan of vs. playing ones you are a fan of. Over-emphasizing the not-fun parts of games is an Ubisoft stategy, not Codemasters!
Overall though, I still happily anticipate a GRID 3 (4?). One great thing I can say about this series is with only 3 games Codemasters has made 3 very different racing experiences. If you're looking for a solid racer that you can zone out and listen to podcasts with, etc., this game may be perfect for you. For me, it missed the mark.

I'm rather up in the air at this moment in some regards to CSD 2 yet also delighted by it in other ways, I'll start by giving a rough overview of the first game for clarity's sake to highlight differences:
Cook Serve Delicious, for those not familiar w/ the "Series" if you will is essentially a practice in mnemonics (memorizing acronyms for example PEMDAS *Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally* for mathematic equations for instance). It's bright and colorful graphics suggested in the first game a deceptively casual title. In truth the first game ramped it's difficulty quite respectably as new recipes were revealed in the 'story mode' by unlocking various dishes.
The game also had a certain story to it wherein you were a startup in an office building seeking to become a 5-star restaurant. It offered random challenges (One example may be say, nailing 30 perfect orders in a row later on, meaning you had no errors at all) It also had fixed goals you had to complete to move from a 1 to 2 story restaurant and so on, ensuring that you could handle the stress the next tier of challenges may bring.
What made the game so fun was that it allowed you to more or less set the challenge for yourself. You could choose dishes easier to prepare, but often they were far less profitable than other; complex dishes.
Now, getting onto CSD 2:
I find this game has thusfar proved far less daunting thusfar. While I haven't tried Soups nor Pastas (often considered one of the hardest dishes to memorize in the original, w/ 26 different combinations to memorize for pastas alone.), the dishes all thusfar are incredibly easy to memorize.
There is also the matter of "Appetizers".
Where there was an upgrade in the original game that gave you more time before a customer got impatient and left, here, you're given a "Side bar" to prep certain foods in advance (such as fries; burgers and the like) so that you could not only quickly get customers dealt with, having sides made actually increases the time customers will wait, certain foods will even increase the amount you're paid getting a 'delicious' score for that customer where it might've been "perfect" otherwise.
While there are FAR more dishes to memorize in CSD2, they have thusfar been fairly straightforward and far less stress-inducing to memorize.
Overall: I'd give this game a solid 7/10, As the developer (whom: btw, is still patching this game and answering player's questions) continues to improve this game I forsee that score raising.

Cook, Serve, Delicious 2! was the game we were all waiting for.  This game does a lot of things well, not least of all giving us so many food cravings we never knew we had.  I've been playing through the game with my fiancee casually for about two weeks now and while the game is just as much fun as the first one was, there are a few things I'd like to highlight as things that are particularly great about the game and things that are particularly underwhelming as well.  We'll start with all the things I really liked about this game - things that make it even bigger, better, and more delicious than the first one.  Keep in mind that this is simply my humble opinion, and I encourage you to have your own whether you agree with my points or not.
1. Graphical Improvements
This point goes without saying - the graphics and detail in everything in this game are really well-done.  The level of detail the developer went in definitely shows.  No doubt about it, this game is beautiful.
2. Variety
Not only the incredibly diverse selection of different foods - noticably much bigger than the selection in the first game - but also the seemingly endless choices of restaurants, menus, sides, and drinks make this game much more emersive and expansive than its predecessor.  Certainly this game lacks no amount of gameplay.  As a gamer with ADD, this is exactly what I want in a game - tons of options and the ability to get bored with one restaurant and simply jump to a different one for an entirely different challenge.
3. Detail
The incredible amount of detail that was gone into the development of this game is one of the strong points that I feel many people might unfortunately overlook.  Did you know that some people like eggs on their burgers?  Have you read the backstories behind the numerous different restaurants in the game?  So much work was put into the little things in this game that it really feels polished and well-done, sunny-side up and grilled to perfection.
4. Customization
YES!!  I am a very big fan of games that allow for customization of players, levels, and everything!  The ability to customize your restaurant's menu was a given even in the first game, but the amount of customization you can have with drinks and side options is incredible!  You want a Burger and Oatmeal with a side of Bacon and pineapple juice to drink?  No problem!  But beyond that, customizing even your entire restaurant is an experience of its own.  Sure, there are a few nitpicky things, but overall they don't detract from a great additional feature in the game.  I'll be sure to post screenshots when my fiancee and I have completely finished our "most sexy" restaurant theme.
5. Multiplayer
Seriously, if you haven't tried the multiplayer yet, you need to grab your boyfriend/girlfriend/casual fling/random guy off the street and just go for it.  My fiancee and I used to have two separate keyboards plugged in to my PC to play multiplayer in the first game by making food together; now it's much more sophisticated and much more realistic.  The multiplayer allows you and your player 2 to run everything about the restaurant together.  I get this order, you get that one.  I'll do these chores, you prep the holding stations.  Everything feels so natural and flushed out that I honestly can't even play single player anymore.  It's also just not as fun for me to do everything by myself either.  That's a sign that a game has a good multiplayer.
And now that I've spent far too long bragging on all the things about this game I like, there are a few things that I want to highlight that I feel could've been done better.
1. The Level System
The level system is a neat addon that I really like - however, the biggest criticism I have of it is that it just doesn't feel like it really means anything.  Sure, you get customization rewards for levelling up, but you also get them for completing days at almost any restaurant in the game and for earning milestones.  Sure, you get new stars for your restaurant, but that really doesn't have any significant effect outside of earning new holding areas and prep stations to make your own restaurant a worthwhile challenge.  At the end of the day, the level system just feels like more of a tracker for how much you've played the game and doesn't really warrant any of the things we crave for earning higher levels (most namely bragging rights).
2. Your Own Restaurant
Most of the people I've seen play this game (and myself included) almost exclusively tend to focus more on the alternative restaurants in the game than on their own.  Customization aside, there isn't really any benefit to playing in your own restaurant.  I keep thinking that its weird how levelling up increases your Star Rating for your restaurant.  How does doing a week's worth of cooking in Max Weiners make my restaurant look good? (#ROASTED!  Sorry Max Weiners I still love you and your hilarious name)  Then again, if you're the most renound chef at XLR Purple then people may hold your own restaurant to a minimum standard.  At the end of the day, having your own restaurant is basically just a glorified sandbox - which is nice, don't get me wrong - but a bit underwhelming considering that the first game made it such a big deal.
3. Food Upgrades
Wait, what food upgrades?  Oh, right.  It kinda bothers me that this game completely got rid of one of the biggest mechanics from the original - all the foods are as is from day 1.  Understandably it would make a TON of extra work to include 3-5 upgrades for each of the 186 food items currently in the game.  Still, I can't help but miss my favorite foods getting progressively more stressful to make as the game gets harder and harder with no remorse.  It's part of the Cook, Serve, Delicious charm.
4. Realism / Lack of Gameplay Variety
While this isn't necessarily something that's wrong with the game, it does feel like a really big missed opportunity.  These two headers are coupled together because they're both raised by a single point.  Being able to play in a bunch of different restaurants is awesome and enjoyable, but at the end of the day, they're all too similar.  Sure, different menus and different food styles vary up all the different locations enough for them to pull their own weight, but they're all more or less the same challenge with slightly different button combinations.  To expand on this, as you would expect you'll always see a rush hour at noon and another one at dinnertime.  For most restaurants this is expected.  But why are so many people in Breakfast & Breakloose ordering cereal and pancakes at 12:30pm?  I mean, I like to sleep in as much as the next food patron, but you'd think a breakfast joint would have a rush hour much earlier in the day, right?  And this is the missed opportunity I brought up.  Instead of the same day with a different menu, each restaurant could have different rush hour times and operating hours.  Sure a breakfast restaurant may be easier to work at than a bar with literally All The Sports, but are you prepared to handle a Rush Hour at 8am?  I feel like this kind of realism can add a new prospect for the game's challenges - that just like in real life, all restaurants have different rushes and slow periods.  They also have different hours, too.  This dessert place has an adorable mascot, but it doesn't really feel like most people would be swarming to get a bowl of ice cream at 9am in the morning.  Then again, who am I kidding?  I'd eat a bowl of ice cream any time of day.
Because of Review length limits, I'm going to have to stop here.  Overall I would certainly recommend this game if you enjoyed the first one.  Feel free to leave your own opinions about things that were done well and/or things that could've been better.  Please be respectful and polite, and if you offer criticism please make sure it's constructive.
Overall, I rate Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! as 7.5/10.  Thanks for reading!
