I would really like to recommend this game but I can't it just has to many problems that tend to pile up after a while. I was very excited for this game I love the Thief series it has always had a certain charm to it that made it one of a my favorites. Yet this new game just feels like it was designed by people that just did not know what they were doing, or just did not care about the series. I know that sounds harsh but I cannot think of any other reason a game like this would be considered good. It feels old (let me explain) It feels like it was designed for tech from around 5-7 years ago not taking advantage of the huge amount of processing power that newer machines can produce. Now that is not to say that it is not a pretty game it is absolutely beautiful in some cases such as when you first emerge from the clock tower and see the gothic/victorian/steampunk landscape of The City. It makes you want to go exploring....and that is where the first of the many problems begins you are very limited to where you can go and how you can get there. This would be fine for games pre Assassins Creed and Arkham City which have shown what an open world in a city can be like. You cannot jump nor climb without it being in an exactly correct (scripted) spot, this just makes you feel like you are being guided along which just kills the last shred of "free movement" you might have had. Also to add to the small feeling of the open world the city is sectioned off by loading screens which adds to the frustration of trying to go anywhere. Even going into some small closet sized buildings require you to go through a loading screen (which they disguise as jimmying open a window) I could forgive that if you did not have to do the same thing to go back out. Seriously you take out your small crowbar and jimmy the window open from the inside. Also whenever you go from one area to the next all the guards and all the torches, fires, or lights you have put out they are lit again as well as grates, vent covers, and doors you have unlocked are now all locked back. This means that unless you memorize everywhere you have been and what you have done you will find yourself going back into places you have already been to multiple times. Anyway there is still more wrong with this game this is just the tip of the iceberg.
The story is a mess and I could not care less about the characters if I tried I mean it try to remember anything about the story such as the rakes name or your partners name. It just feels like a story that has been through way to many writers hands. In the end you have to take a second and figure out exactly what just happened and why. It is incredibly underwhelming.
The AI is passable at best and down right moronic at worst. I can't count how many times I was able to avoid a guard simply by staying slightly to the left or right of him. If you get killed in this game by a guard even at the highest difficulty you are doing something very wrong. Also whoever did the sound mixing needs to be fired immediately I swear at some points you cannot even hear the dialogue yet you can hear the same inconsequential line you have heard from a guard a thousand times before three streets over perfectly. (I DON'T KNOW WHAT HAPPENED TO THE SLOOP SELLERS I WOULD HOPE AS A CITY WATCHMAN YOU WOULD KNOW!).
I wanted to like this game I really did and in some places it is absolutely amazing, it feels like a Thief game. Like when you are making your way through a crooked jewelers shop stealing his wares and avoiding guards It makes you feel like you are being clever and stealthy. Sadly those moments are to few and spread out to really compensate for all the missteps the devs took. The tragic thing is under all the problems there is a really great game here. Hopefully when the next game comes out it will fix all the problems of this one and if it does we will have a truly amazing Thief game.
Final Score 6/10

Here we go, my favourite franchise of all time got rebooted in this new game, simply called Thief.
I will not review this game based on nostalgia, since its a reinvention after all.

PROS:
-Immersion is fantasctic, I never felt more of a Thief is those next gen mechanics. You can see Garrett hands interact with everything you can, his feet walking in realistic ways. The way they designed this made me buy and like this game. That moocap thing really proved itself.
-Darkness is very appealing, feels like a warm touch while avoiding any source of light. Light effects are very good, and they react very realistically with the enviorment. The overall design got a lot of love, and feels like a true improvement over the old games.
-The gameplay is very solid, respecting the old tradition with special arrows and how you can react with the enviorment. Even though you can't jump anymore (only in contextual mode), the new mechanic "swoop" is very addicting and I welcome it with love. What swoop does, it let's you dash fast in the wanted direction almost invisibly and with precise agility (you can stop at any time during the maximum range). After 4-5 swoops you get tired and can't do it efficiently so it's balanced. Even if you sprint (makes alot of noise) will tire you very fast, leaving you in spots where you can swoop only once or twice before needing rest.
-Game offers very complex hud costumizations and overall gameplay experience to make it a hardcore experience like the old games, and even beyond that. You can turn off all interface tips, tools etc. for a pure immersion, you can turn off the markers for objectives, highlights for possible interaction.

You can costumize your difficulty also to make your game even harder like turning off focus mode, no upgrades, no takedowns, more expensive arrows (rope arrow will be 600 gold), and maaaaaany more like Ironmode (no saves, you die, you restart from prologue). Each new mod you check adds extra points upon compling the game based on how difficult the add is, with which you enter a world leaderboard.

I myself played with full hud turned off and on Master with many mods added and I am currently in Top 100 Leaderboard, making me excited in trying a new playthrough with even harder mods to keep up in with the other thieves.

CONS:
-Voice actor comes close to real deal in terms of voice depth, however he lacks charm and for first half he didn't convince me of the old-new Garrett transsition. After some hours nostalgia kicked in and I embraced him as the old Garrett.
-The city is bigger and more complex than ever, sadly it has no life on it's own. Not so many people lurking around, just the normal guards and some citizens here and there. You can hear alot of conversations from inside houses but in the end they felt like scripted events only because they have very generic accents and conversations.
-Old Thief games were based around a world that had it's unique charm, people had a certain way of talking with words common like "taffer". This new one is exactly like a solid american product, nothing memorable.
-Level design is a very simple get from point A to B layout with a few different ways of approaching it. First 2 Thief games had very large maps, they just threw you in, and you decide how to approach things. You had complete freedom while this game forces you to play like how the producers want you to. There is no more jumping unless the game wants you, it's more focused on contextual interaction.
-Story had strong potential, combining good elements from all games in a single bowl, bassicaly you will see alot of copy/paste of all the good stuff from previous ones in a more modern setting. However I am very sure that due to last minute changes and that theyr time was out, many elements were cut out from it to finish the game in a "playable" state by realease time.
The story is told to you in cutscenes which take away all the intended epicness that tried to deliver. Overall picture felt very bland and now you can see Garrett's face from any angle cutting away all the mistery the character had. All previous games had a movie on the end of the level, presented to you in a dark setting that just wanted you to crave for more, and Garrett was also vigilant and always tried to keep his face in the dark.
Overall the story had potential and as a fanboy I saw what they tried to do here (new players won't get it) was good. Sadly the cutscenes that really don't connect the story, poor voice acting and obvious missing pieces that are visible cut out from the game made me not care at all in the end, it felt very forced down my throat.
This games has alot of potential, trying to combine many cool elements resulting in a product with only half baked ideas and no personality of it's own. Where this game finds itself bland, the gameplay and immersion makes up for it, balancing satisfaction with contempt giving overall, a worth playing product if you are a stealth purist. The game is focused on pure challenge, and it has a lot of replay value.
It's not the Thief I hoped for in terms of world presentation and story, but the gameplay will make up for it. I could write many more things about this game, but the whole point of it, is for each individual to experience and judge it for himself/herself.

I initially gave this game a great review, but now having played a good deal through the game, I have to reverse my initial review.  This game still has some glitches that need to be ironed out, for instance, upon stealing a mechanicle hand for a side quest and turning it in to the NPC, the game gave me an additional quest, to steal a mechanicle hand.... again....  the exact same quest that I just completed.
The game gets really repetitive, lock pick this, watch out for the noisy glass or papers on the floor, etc etc, it's so linear that it practically removes any decisions about how to go about stealing something, which just kills the replay value, and even get's boring going through the game the first time through because it's the same stuff over and over again.  This game tries really hard to capture the magic of Dishonored, but ultimately, it just doens't... not even close.
The story is so generic and even follows a little to closely to dishonored, plague?  check.  Corrupt city leaders, check.  Garrett is so serious and monotone all the time, it's hard to really get into his character.  Is he truly upset about Erin's fall?  It's hard to tell because he doesn't show much emotion at all.  Even the silent protagonist Corvo some how, seemingly displayed more emotion than Garrett.  I haven't beaten the game yet, so maybe things pick up and Garrett faces some tough decisions that flesh out his character a little more, but right now, it's just disappointing.
I would still recommend this game, just not at a price point of 50 bucks.  It's not a horrible game, it just has the lofty expectations of the previous Thief titles (open world, non linear) and followed up an excellent steath title in Dishonored, maybe our expectations were just too high?  I'd pick this up on the summer sale if your on the fence, it's worth a play through at a discounted rate, just don't go into it expecting a title similar to the older thief titles, or gameplay/story that is as engaging as  Dishonored.

The legendary Thief series is back, and while the game take a few precarious mis-steps, the essence of Thief's predecessors is still intact. If you've never taken the opportunity to try out possibly the most immersive, well-designed stealth games of the late 90s, the latest incarnation is a great place to start. It's not going to please some of the purists, but as somebody who was enraptured by the earlier games, I found it a decent enough return for Garrett the master thief.
However, the mis-steps are hard to ignore, and if you are the kind of person who demands absolute perfection in audio and graphic fidelity, then you won't be pleased. Cutscenes in particular are a little embarrassing, while audio bugs are rife throughout the city, causing voices to repeat over the top of themselves like some kind of demonic reverb.
If you can look past these two issues and the overall sloppy storytelling, what exists as the game itself is quite pleasant to engage in. Move between the shadows, douse torches with your water arrows, and either eliminate guards or completely outmaneuver them: the choice is up to you. Most sections have multiple entry points, and while it has been done before and better, the Asylum level is one of the best examples of psychological horror available in current gen games. It doesn't hold a candle to Deadly Shadows' Shalebridge Cradle but it's far ahead of the rest of the pack in trying to emulate it.
On a final note, the game does suffer from a case of console-itis. One issue in particular is that there is no actual jump button. Instead, you must rely on the game to contextually detect the situation where you might want to jump; a system which is far from perfect and can lead to frustrating outcomes. It's definitely an annoyance, but in the grand scheme of things its not worth skipping over some of the best stealth gameplay to appear from the shadows in years.
+ Exquisite stealth gameplay
+ Incredibly immersive...
- ...Until an audio bug ruins it
- Cutscenes and storytelling in general are sub par

I now hope that they learn from this and actually make a good Thief V game. Going back to the original story and the (fat) Garrett roots: The real steampunk City, The Keepers, Hammerites, Mechanist, Burricks, Ghosts, Zombies, Graves, Catacombs, and the Mansions.

This has a slightly different style to the first game, but I think it's a good iteration. The first game was more in depth with the foods, but the 2nd is more in depth with the menu, restaurant, etc. I still play both regularly.
For those who have never played the first game: Cook, Serve, Delicious 2 is a game where you are a chef at your own restaurant. You determine how your restaurant looks, and determine what foods, side dishes, and drinks are on your menu. With over 180 foods, that's not an easy task. Your menu must have a balance between items that require lots of preperation, and items that are easy to make, because customers don't wait around forever.
To elaborate, this game is mostly about the food, and you, as the chef, making the food. If you want to make pancakes, you have to put them on the griddle, wait until they cook, and then add toppings once they're ready. Generally, you need to do other things while you are waiting for other dishes to cook, because again, customers don't stick around forever. This is accomplished through a series of minigames, which vary between each food, but the buttons for each tend to be relatively straightforward, with some exceptions. For example to make a burger, you cook the meat, then add whatever toppings the customer wants, like tomatoes (T), Mushrooms (M), Onions(N), cheese (C), Swiss Cheese(S), etc.
If I had some criticisms of this game, the first would be that the ability to rebind keys per food is gone. With over 180 food items, I can understand why that would be a hassle, but that was part of what made the first game great, and I still miss it. The second thing is that the buzz system has no real limit, which means that your customers will eventually start expecting impossible things from your restaurant, and eventually you will lose buzz because you just can't serve them all in time.
Lastly, I feel like there's no real reason to serve certain (maybe 20ish out of 180) foods as entrees (they're usually OK as side dishes), because they are either too complex to make and not worth the money you would get for them for the time you took to make them. Or the foods are simple to make but too cheap. For example, Gumbo, Chili, and Soup sell for $4-$8 as an entree and has lots of complex ingredients to make, but also sells for $2-$4 as a side dish? That makes no sense. Meanwhile, Spaghetti is much easier to make and serve, but sells for $12. Steak, similiarly only requires choosing the cut of meat and cooking, (2 buttons) and sells for $18.

As an enthusiast of the original Cook, Serve, Delicious! game it was practically a 'no brainer' for me to grab this. I hadn't read any reviews or feedback beforehand and was surprised by what this game had to offer. This review will be covering the game for new players as well as those that played the original.
Cook, Serve Delicious! 2!! is a game all about running your own restraunt. That goes from creating your own menu to serving up exotic dishes to disarming armed robbers and all whilst keeping the toilets clean. The premise of the game is to build your restraunt the way you want it as well as getting hired by other restraunts to unlock more decorations, recipes and more difficult menus for the restraunts that are hiring you.
The majority of the game is to simply select the correct inputs to build exactly what the customer ordered. Sounds simple, right? Wrong! All it takes is one incorrect button press to accidentally add the wrong topping and ruin your customers fine dining experience. So surely you would take your time to process the order correctly, right? WRONG!!! As you're serving the customer and preparing their dish you will have other customers come and place orders but if you take too long they will leave in a huff and leave you negative feedback. As the day goes on you will have chores to complete like setting rat traps, washing the dishes and stomping the rubbish in to your filled up skip at the back of the restraunt. If you fail to complete these then you will score sickness points which sounds cool but actually does damage to your restraunt. Just when you think you've got the hang of it... rush hour hits you like a tonne of bricks and really gets your blood pumping and sweat glands working! Lots of customers appear at once and you must appease them all! After the hussle and bussle of the days happenings you close your doors and examine your profits and whether you did your restraunt proud or drove it into the ground.
The gameplay is extremely addictive as it only takes about five minutes to complete a day of work and you can use that day to simply see how your restraunt works with the menu you have created and whether it creates too many dishes to be washed up or puts you under pressure if you've chosen too many complicated dishes. You can also choose to work in a different restraunt to gain medals and unlock different items and recipes for your own restraunt. One messed up order does frustrate you but it keeps driving you to replay the day to get the coveted gold medals. There are so many levels and medals to unlock that it does get daunting but it won't put you off the game at all. Again, it just motivates you to play 'just one more day'.
The controls can seem a little overwhelming at first, even for the veteran Cook, Serve, Delicious! players as cooking styles, toppings and meat selection can span over three pages which you cycle through with a key or button press. The game does try to help you by colour coding ingriedients which match the page you are browsing. What can buy you time is preparing simple side dishes which gets your customers waiting longer to be served. You do have to keep an eye on these side dishes though as you will run out of stock or even have it go rotten if you're not keeping an eye on them.
The only relaxing part of the game is decorating your restraunt. It can be confusing at first as it doesn't look so simple to reverse mistakes but you soon get used to the slightly clunky way it works.
Speaking of relaxing, the music also makes the game. there are different themes for decorating, rush hour and how you did for the day. The music is extremely friendly to the ears in each given situation too.
Now before I give my personal recommendation for the game I will talk a little about the differences between this game and the previous one. The second outing is not a simple brush up of the original. To a degree, I would even almost say this was a completely different game! Sure, the overall mechanics are the same where you can't keep customers waiting and you can't mess up their orders but the controls are different when creating recipes. It almost seems like there are no 'easy' recipes compared to the original. My personal favourite was the lasagna. As I use a controller, all you had to do was rotate the joystick a couple of times and you were done! Anywho, this can seem a little frustrating for veterans but you do get used to the new layout. Also, their isn't a story based goal anymore. No longer can you try to romance your partner, put bets on yourself or aim to become the iron cook. That focus has now changed to collecting medals and becoming the best you can be. One dissappointing element is that at the time of this review there are no weekly challenges where you can compare yourself to your friends or the world. Although cookery doesn't neccessarily need multiplayer it does seem like a fun feature was taken out of the game. What you do get as an extra in the game though is a vast array of customisation. This is a huge plus compared to the original. It really does leave you a feeling of pride looking at the restraunt you created and developing the menu.
All in all for both new players and veterans I heavily recommend this game. For those thinking this is like a Simon Says game you couldn't be further from the truth. Although fans of the original will miss a few elements it doesn't take away the brilliant gameplay from this version. Dare I say it, you could quite happily play both games still and appreciate the unique qualities of them while still feeling a sense of accomplishment after each shift you work.

TL;DR: This game does not handle exactly like bhopping in CSS/CSGO/TF2/Gmod, but once you get used to it you may find it feels a lot smoother and nicer.
Full Review:
I'm a bhop fan and have been for a while now, I've played at least 150 hours of bhop on TF2 and made over a dozen maps.
In the very beginning I didn't really care much for this game, I only stayed because the graphics were neat. Then I started playing more, then more updates came.
Now that 1.0 is out, this game is very, very fun in my eyes. I can't even bhop in TF2 anymore because I've gotten so used to how bhopping feels in this game, and it feels great if you ask me. Sure, occasionally you'll miss a platform you'd swear you'd hit in Source, and occasionally you'll narrowly make it to a platform that you'd never make in a million years in Source, but if you look through that and learn to work with it, then it makes for a very impressive display of what a few developers passionate about a movement mod can create.
There are currently 30 maps as of the writing of this review. Overall, the maps are what I'd call "Pretty good", with a lot of very excellent, good looking, good flowing maps, and a handful of awful maps. However, I don't feel any one map is too awful to simply not play, even maps that I find extremely frustrating and poorly built such as Generic are still worth running from time to time in my eyes, if anything they'll only teach you more. But when you focus on the best maps, such as Cobble and Zen, you'll start to see that this game has a lot of excellent maps to offer that you just can't get anywhere else in the Bhopping community.
Physics-wise, I'd say that the devs have made this game mimic the Source engine about 80%, there are a couple of exceptions such as the fact that surfing doesn't really work very well unless you're constantly moving downwards along ramps, and bhopping on upwards-facing slopes will gain you a lot of height but not in the same way that it does in Source games. Regardless of these physics differences, after a few hours of play I can confidently say that I am now used to the physics and can run maps fast and without failing due to anything but my own mistakes.
With more maps to come, further improvements, and developers that actively listen to the community, this game is currently a shining Gem in Steam's under $10 game pool and with just a little more work and help from the community, it could grow into something phenomenal and likely find a huge following in the future.

I'll get this out of the way now: I have not played any of the previous games in the series. My opinion on Thief comes from Thief and Thief alone.
While having potential, Thief lacks what most stealth games do: an element of stealth.
The stealth aspect is virtually non-existant. Enemies will not notice you so long as you are crouched, swooping, walking, or otherwise in the shadows. Nevermind the fact that they're mere inches from your face in an ominous alleyway. When their guard is down, they are completely oblivious. When their guard should otherwise be up, they are still completely oblivious. It is entirely possible to crouch by a group of guards in plain sight with little to no reaction beyond a "What was that?"
Too often are there instances where the game provides little to no ingenuity. While each map supposedly has "multiple paths" for the player to take, the paths are few and far between, with little to no deviation from a linear trajectory. The maps are set up to allow you to find your own way to get from point A to point B, but after starting your path, it's simply a matter of holding down a few keys until you arrive at your destination.
On top of all else, the controls are needlessly bizzare. Let us assume you wish to hop down from a rope you're climbing. One would expect the jump key while looking downward would do so, or perhaps the crouch key. One would be wrong. Instead it's required to bind seperate keys to all of these commands. Instead of grouping together contextual keys in a sensible fashion, Thief takes the approach of "4 keys for 1 action", leaving you scrambling for the correct key when another should do the same thing. Each additional bind is purely contextual, rendering the alternative bindings useless save for specific situations, and indicating that Thief missed the simple concept of one key being able to do multiple actions in order to allow the player to respond more quickly. To top off the controls, Thief's handling of input commands is lackluster. It often requires multiple key presses before any one action is actually completed. So expect to fall to your death a couple dozen times before Garrett finally decides to hop that 2-foot gap in front of him.
All in all, while Thief seems appealing, it utterly lacks in any and all expected components.

If you are somehow finished with the Challenge mode then comes the really most grinding part: The Versus mode. Naturally you play against yourself if you don't have your friends at home all the time. I watched Legends of Eisenwald (LoE) as it made its way through early access. I liked the graphics and I loved the Middle Ages feudal setting. I put it on my Wishlist and when it went on sale I bought it.
My first play, however, didn't quite go as expected. It wasn't that I disliked it. It was just that I had a bit of trouble understanding some of the game concepts. I stopped play after an hour or two and moved on to other things. About a month later I decided to try LoE again, but not before I watched some gameplays on YouTube. There I learned about right-clicking and stopping time. Right clicking on my troops allowed me to study their specific attributes, blessings, curses, etc. Stopping time limited the characters on the world map to move only when my army moved. Those two simple things completely turned the game around for me.
I'm sure glad I gave it a second chance. I believe that I've invested 60+ hours in it so far and I know that this game is one of my all-time favorites. (For the record, Number 1 on my list is the Heroes of Might & Magic series 1-7, and number 2 is the Spellforce series 1-2.) This game is unique, but has a number of elements, especially combat, which reminds me of the Disciples series (another favorite).
Some might complain about the amount of text, but I really believe that the developers went out of their way to make an interesting story. My only small complaints are the vague information provided for a number of quests and the re-use of the same face for multiple characters.
Anyway, a long review, but I HIGHLY recommend this game. If you enjoy turn-based strategy, the Middle Ages, and think that you might like taking a castle by force, collecting money from your serfs, and building up a strong army to take out your enemies, pick-up LoE.

**MINOR SPOILERS***
This game really grew on me after I reached the third act. At first I found the game charming but flawed, I loved the setting, the writing and the aesthetics but found gameplay lacking, particularly the combat. This all changes as the game progesses to the third act, the combat turns from an imbalanced grindable seemingly simplistic system to a beautiful puzzle with a satisfying level of strategic depth and challenge.
Do not allow yourself to be put off by the first two acts, the fist one is a tutorial obviously so it's expectedly simple, the second is a showcase for the unit types and item customization which make up your strategic avenues in the game, and thus it allows grinding.
You will lose everything except what your main hero has equipped on progression to the third act except for at least one possible artifact, this includes companions. This has caused controversy because some people invest a lot into building up in the second act. Of course this is by design, the second act like I said is a showcase where you can test drive different unit and weapon comps, unfortunately this is not adequetly communicated leading to a somewhat rude awakening for some people. Don't get too invested, the game truly starts in act three.

I can only rate this game a 2 out of 5.
I like the concept and generally how the game works, but there are inconsistencies with the urgency of quests as well as the relative difficulty of encounters vs when you're expected to fight them.
In "Way Home" there is no urgency whatsoever to any of the quests.  You can complete them in any order you wish and take as much time as you need.  In "Run Away" you can't dally/explore at all as is normal in isometric RPGs or Berthold catches you.
The difficulty is also quite unforgiving, even on "Normal", for a few of the encounters that are expected to be fought early on new screens before you have a chance to build up your squad.

This is a fun RPG game with an engaging story and satisfying quests. Well done for an independant developer.
The primary difference between LoE and other turn-based-combat games is that you do not get to attack whoever you want in battle. You must attack the closest emeny to you. This allows for less strategy in battle and makes battles more difficult. Thus, it is important that you arrange your ground troops correctly according to their initiative, front row to back row, otherwise an infantry man will get stuck behind another troop and not be able to act until that troop is able to move. In the case of archers, you can attack anyone but the further away they are from the enemy the less damage they inflict.
All in all, worth the money.

Seldom has a game captivated me like Legends of Eisenwald has over the past few weeks. It's a unique blend of role-playing and strategy, in a historical medieval setting with supernatural elements.
I particularly like the amount of customization and choices you can make. I made three playthroughs, one with each of the characters (Knight, Baroness and Mystic), and each with a different driving force (honor, profit, revenge) and despite following the same general storyline over the same 5 or 6 maps, so many of the details differed that they felt distinctly different. It also made me realize how much I missed on my first playthrough, by not exploring enough, or not paying enough attention to rumors in taverns, etc...
Some people seem to think the combat is simplistic and lacks strategy, but I beg to differ. There are so many variables that you can play with that affect the outcome of the battles. Party size, positioning, items, weapons, terrain, whether it's day or night, whether you're inside or outside. Getting good at using all this to your advantage will save you a lot of money on healing. ;)
Another issue that people have with this game is the fact that your party and/or money get reduced between the maps. Personally I liked the challenge of each map, figuring out when to do what and how to get strong enough to take on the hardest opponents (or lure them into a forest at night so they couldn't fight on horseback). It also invites you to do side-quests which will yield useful rewards like powerful items, cash or people joining your party.
Aside from perhaps the last map, where you return to part of a previously visited map, every map has it's own distinctive feel, which ensures that the game never feels repetitive.
In short, I whole-heartedly recommend this game. I have to confess that I was originally put-off by the (in my opinion) relatively high price tag and waited until it was on sale. I now regret this, I would have gladly paid the full price. Especially if you see the amount of effort the devs put in this game and the way they respond to every, even minor, question. To make up for that I bought the Knight's Edition and Season pass despite already owning the first DLC, because I feel such dedication should be supported!
I wouldn't really recommend this sort of game to anyone who isn't really into it, but for those who are, it's really good. My only disappointment is its rather short length.

This game is truly excellent.  As to be expected of a choose-your-adventure game, there's a multitude of options:  but they're gripping, well played out, and genuinely change the course of the story.  Your skills and relationships influence the plot as well; they're not superfluous percentages that have no bearing on your gameplay.
As should be the case, what I loved most was the /story/.  The excitement of battle, the attention to detail, the complicated politics -- all very well done.  The writing is very good.
What initially tipped the scales for me to buy the game was the fact that it offered not just an option for the MC to be queer, but ALSO gave you the chance to be poly, AND gave you the chance to be trans or nonbinary (or trans nonbinary).  Like, damn.  What game does that?  Those features were crucial to my engagement wit the game, though I do wish my gender identity had been mentioned/acknowledged a bit more.
Overall, yeah, strongly recommend Choice of the Pirate.  You can be a poly gay trans pirate queen and honestly isn't that what all of us want?

There are a lot of pros and cons that go along with this review, but the majority of cons will boil down to content that made the first CSD great that has not made its way in yet.
Should this have been more of an early access release? Yes. Am I mad it wasn't? Absolutely not. Does it miss that story charm from the first one? Of course (but it will eventually be implemented).
As far as I'm concerned, I would've purchased this either way, and it's kind of fun in a frustrating way when you encounter a bug, and then the developer actually LISTENS and REPLIES and FIXES it within a reasonable timeframe! It's absolutely impressive how fast he has pumped out fixes, and had he just waited the extra time to release the game, there would have been a group of angry individuals anyways. I cannot reasonably tear down a single developer for not having his timing on point.
When it comes down to the gameplay itself, like I said, crazy and challenging. Sure things get 'easier' once you've memorized the keybinds, but that doesn't necessarily make those final levels of each restaurant any less challenging. I've seen a few reviews trash the side items for adding time to dishes, but it's really not that easy if you have to prepare 4 items around the clock (e.g. Lasagna, Spaghetti & Meatballs, Chili, Soup), some of which you will want to have multiple prepped due to the TWELVE order tabs that spit out like crazy during Rush Hour, and then having the challenge of one, two if you're lucky, extra side tabs for side dishes.
I can't wait for what the future patches add to the experience!

The Game is great! deffinetly the best civ game i have played so far! Its a beautiful blend of the classic Civ games, with influences from other games like Alpha Centari and Fallen enchauntress. This games best features in my opinion are the Unit Customization, and wide varieties of wild life in the form of aliens to kill or be killed by (instead of those stupid barbarians that never change...)
In this game you choose between 3 affinities, and between those three, there are drastic changes to units, bonuses, victory conditions, and it even effects how you are treated by the alien life. Making them either be horribly aggressive to you, or even helpfull to you to the point where you can start to train them for your armies.
This game has also completly redone the diplomicy aspect of the game, and while there is no longer a diplomatic victory type it is arguably more important now, and will be very important no matter how you choose to win. Instead of letting you choose some helpfull or harmfull game disissions, Diplomacy now grants you permanent bonuses to your troops, economy, and relations with other civs.
In short, this game is nothing shot of amazing, with a very well thought out gameplay system that makes every game different and challenging. its everything I have wanted in a civ game since I first descovered the franchise. Spy Chameleon - RGB Agent is stealthy in much the same way taking a sack full of hammers to the face is stealthy; while the perpetrator announces his assault beforehand with a vuvuzela blast.  That is to say, it's not stealthy at all.
Wow, that's a pretty rough opener for a supposed stealth game, eh?  But you'll notice I still gave this one a thumbs up.
To continue my metaphor, the stitching on the bag was just exquisite, the sound of the hammers crashing together was a tour de force, and the bits of my skull moved in ways that frankly astounded medical experts.  Fortunately, I am the kind of guy who can appreciate these things.  Though I'd have appreciated them more if they'd happened to somebody else.
You see, as the living, breathing reason banks feel compelled to keep their pens attached to chains, I think of myself as something of an expert on stealth games.  There's nothing I love more than stealth done right in video games.  But what is a stealth game and why doesn't Spy Chameleon qualify?
Well, a stealth game has you move through an area, usually attempting to accomplish some objective (say, take everything not nailed down) and leave without being seen.  There's a danger of being caught and that requires some intelligence on the part of the challenges standing between you and your objectives.  For a game to be a stealth game, it needs reactive enemies, otherwise it's just an obstacle course.  And that's what Spy Chameleon is: a time trial, obstacle course, collect-a-thon game.
Yes, it has the trappings of stealth.  You play as the titular chameleon spy, you are told briefly that your goal is to steal a thing and shown a picture of the thing at the end of several levels, and the obstacles take the form of "enemies" with vision cones.  But everything moves in perfect clockwork without reaction to your presence.  Changing your color to "hide" is just another form of dodging a static obstacle.
You'll notice stealth is even a Steam user tag.  The devs themselves describe Spy Chameleon as: "a challenging arcade-puzzle game where the player needs to avoid being spotted thanks to the color-changing mechanisms of the main character."
So, yeah, Spy Chameleon fails as a stealth game.  But, now that that bone has been picked, if we judge it as an "arcade-puzzle game" or by my own moniker, "run-aroundy, collecty, obstacle torture time," then Spy Chameleon is an excellent example of its kind.  Personally, I couldn't stand playing it, since I don't much care for time trial obstacle courses that play to my OCD desires to collect all the bits.  But I have to admit, there's a Rube-Goldberg machine-like complexity to the levels and the timing required to solve them that makes them satisfying to complete.
Like the sack of hammers, it's fundamentally solid in its design and its presentation is surprisingly nice.  Spy Chameleon's soundtrack makes up for the game's lack of true infiltration by seeping it's bassy post-modern jazz into that part of your brain designed for looping catchy tunes.  And thanks to the artists, my favorite part of the game was failing the levels (which is good because I failed a lot).
Each failure shows you an image of the hazard that caught you: giant staring gold fish, trash-can robots spewing bold japanese writing, and the spy chameleon with a look of soul-wrenching embarassment for being caught about his naughty voyeuristic business.  The art assets manage to convey a ton of character, and - as you'd expect for a game called RGB Agent - it's all in bright eye-catching primaries.  Even the rather thematically dull environments: lab, office, storage rooms; are bright and good looking.
It's just a shame the art designer's theory seems to stop at the visuals.  The game looks like it has a ton of character.  Even the very premise that we're specifically playing a chameleon who is a spy is appealing.  But it never really goes anywhere with it.  There's no narrative to speak of.
Oh, you're told that you're trying to get a photo of some celebrity with their paramour or steal a work of art, but you just run 15 levels of obstacles and then see a picture of the thing you got.  I'm not necessarily asking for War and Peace, or even any dialogue or text, but it feels like an opportunity was missed to tie all the whimsical characters together into some sort of cohesive story.  That might have gotten me to love the game despite not enjoying the gameplay.
And to better explain the gameplay:  You control the chameleon from a top down view and you navigate a room full of hazards: field-of-view cones attached to enemies that move in a set pattern.  If you touch a cone, you lose.  In addition to just dodging the cones as they move, you can stand against colored objects in the background and not be "seen."  Naturally, you've got the primary colors and the chameleon's natural green (i.e. 360 controller colors).  Along the way you collect flies and ladybugs strewn about the level for points and to unlock more levels.  You are, of course, challenged to beat a certain time.  There are a few variations to these basic mechanics: switches to open doors, movable obstacles to block vision cones, etc.  It is best to think about the levels as a puzzle, where the solution is where you move and finding the proper timing.
The game has a sort of phone-game sensibility to it.  You play a series of very short levels and get ranked at the end of them.  It's clearly not a mobile port.  It just has that arrangement.
It's mostly flawless in its implementation.  The only mechanical problem is that the chameleon's model obscures the parts of his body that are vulnerable to being seen.  Only the trunk of his body seems to trigger a failure and his bulbous head and tail make it hard to see the exact point you can safely stand.
That might seem a fussy complaint, but Spy Chameleon is a harsh time-trial collection hell.  The difference between you getting your lovely leaderboard/completionist cheese and a big fat shock for losers in this particular rat maze is literally measured in thousandths of a second. Well, okay, it is measured in that, but just getting through will probably require you to operate on the scale of hundredths of a second.
No big deal for you speed-run, obstacle course aficionados, I'm sure.
That does lead to my other complaint.  I found there's not really a good balance for the difficulty.  It's a minor complaint since the game includes an easier mode and you can even skip levels that are giving you trouble, but it still stands.  On the "normal" difficutly I found the game to be a really boring exercise in just going from point A to point B.  Like connect-the-dots in full, glorious 3D.
On hard, though, (which is the only difficulty that counts according to the game and its lusty achievements) I found the timing to be just outside of human reaction speed at points and my success was basically a matter of luck and treating my controller in a manner that would no doubt have it taken away from me by the authorities if they only knew.
And that's Spy Chameleon:  terrible stealth game.  Good speed-run, puzzle, collection thing.
I suppose it's been mislabeled since there aren't a lot of games that marry stealth and speed well and somebody's gonna want that.  The only one I can think of is The Marvelous Miss Take (which looks a bit like Spy Chameleon, actually).  If you want stealth and speed, play that.  But don't overlook Spy Chameleon because it doesn't do stealth.  Just be sure you're the kind of person that enjoys a sack of hammers to the face.

What's a Dragon Quest?  Where are the Dragons?
If you're not familiar with Square Enix's Dragon Quest, I'm not surprised.  The original RPG was titled “Dragon Warrior” and was released on the the Famicom and NES in the 80s.  After that most titles were lucky to have made it out of Japan.  DQH seems to be the first of recent attempts to re-enter the Western market and the first Dragon Quest game to make it to Steam (a port from the PS4).  In DQH you'll take control of a bunch of main characters from past Dragon Quest Games, to fight hordes of enemies from the series in a third person perspective with weapons and spells.  You'll be able to level up, choose stats to upgrade, morph abilities, and craft accessories.
The GOO-REAT & the Slimey
Any crafting lover can find love in their heart for the crafting system in DQH.  While it's not the most intuitive crafting system, it can feel very rewarding to craft a helpful item, and even more rewarding with the chance that you make a perfect accessory to add a random stat bonus.  Each character can hold three accessories at a time (That’s a lot of bow ties).
At first glance, DQH can seem deceivingly button mashey.  Attacking in succession will usually perform three weapon attacks, and that’s pretty easy to pull off if you know how to push a button three times.  You’ll encounter enemies where certain abilities have distinct advantages over others.  Lightning based moves for example, will disable movement and attack of certain mechanically based enemies momentarily.  Also if you can time it, blocking and dodging will help you a lot.
Lastly DQH does a great job bringing to life the characters that people grew up playing in entertaining cutscenes throughout the game.  Most characters are loveable, but the I’ve found the that relationship the two main characters Luceus and Aurora have to be less likable than the others and shallow.  The main male character is often contemplating over complicated strategies outloud, while the main female character interrupts him and gets straight to the point.  In contrast, two new characters introduced in this game:  King Doric is loveable and warm, and Healix, who can dislike Healix? (*slurp*)  Minus a few crashes I had in one specific dungeon and the alt-tab issue that causes your screen to go all black, this game is almost perfect for Dragon Quest fans, or new fans to the series!

A passable Musou game hamstrung by also being a soulless cash-in.  I suppose I'm lucky the game runs at all instead of crashing like it does for so many people, but I do have the never-fixed error where cutscenes have out of sync audio.  And how the creators have refused to fix that is a pretty good indicator of how little they cared about the game in general.
I don't ask a lot from Dragon Quest.  Since the franchise is wired to my nostalgia, simpy identifying which installment each background jingle is from keeps me pretty happy.  Naturally I enjoy a mindless grind once in a while, so the combat is... mostly okay.  Until you get to certain flying enemies who the game arbitrarily insists you miss any time you swing at them until they descend a milimeter.  Watching attacks you very visibly just landed not count is unimaginably dumb in an action game centered on easily hitting things by the truckload.  It's not like there's any real strategy to fighting them besides some extra waiting and other annoyances.  There are some gimmicks in here that seemed to be thrown in without really thinking about how obnoxious they would be.
And I would count all item management and half the shops as annoying gimmicks.  Gathering drops in the game is a needless pain that wastes your time making your character slowly plod over to identical bags that take a second too long to appear after an enemy dies, blown miles apart to the edges of every room you had a fight in.  It's a slow, badly thought out interruption to the murdering.  When you beat a level in a story mission, all items on the map automatically get teleported into your inventory and you get a satisfyingly long list of spoils... which any sane developer would have noticed should have been the default method of collection.
Unfortunately, these are developers who decided that they also needed to sh*t all over your drudging item-gathering by giving you too little inventory space for no reason.  All your tiresome hunting and gathering goes to waste because you're not even allowed to hold it all.  You must try to use up all excess items in a whole other, needlessly slow, repetitive alchemy gimmick clicking through 10 text screens at a time and watching the same dialogue and animation play out to make one combination... over and over until you have freed up some inventory space.  A problem that never had to exist in the first place when even back in the SNES era, Dragon Quest sensibly threw inventory limits in a ditch.  DQ Heroes resurrects it, adds more reasons to hate it, and rubs it in your face.  You can increase your item limits... by doing several story missions... except that also means inevitably collecting more items you cannot carry.  But it's the only way to make this Dragon Quest game stop punishing you even harder for grinding before jumping into some place under-leveled.  It's a problem that only serves to interrupt both the jRPGing and the Musouing that never had a reason to exist.
Dealing with text in general is painful in this game.  At least, when you're actually given control at all.
There is story dialogue that insists on waiting 30 seconds ebtween messages that are only in there to waste your life, I suspect because the lead director is a sadistic time vampire.  Even when you have control, they gutted the franchise's usual text speed options.  You can only speed it up the scrolling by hitting down or the cancel button... which is guaranteed to screw up your decisiosn in shops, loaded with 10 different pointless, repetitive dialogues with completely unnecessary yes/no questions kept from the NES era, so now you will accidentally choose 'No' or move the cursor at the wrong time.  If you're in a hurry or just sick of seeing th same chain of dialogue for the millionth time, you are in danger of accidentally quiting out of the game without saving.  A lot of the DQ series' interface is charmingly retro, but DQ Heroes' is a devolved, counterintuitive clusterf*ck.
The game has an English dub that is honestly commendable.  Though that might be because I have no idea what a decent non-American accent is like.  So to me, Terry is the only character that sounds like the groan-inducing anime dub.  I feel like there was actual effort, as most actors ham it up as hard as they can to give every cahracter a distinct personality, speech, and presence.  I just wish it had happened to a better original script, as the plot is painfully phoned in, most interactions are trite cliches, and the cutscene pacing is slow and drawn out.  In an industry mired with botched translations and dubs, this is one of those rare cases where the English translators and voice actors tried to spruce up and save something awful and dull.  They deserved better than the crappy text controls and buggy audio sync.

I was pretty disappointed when I saw some of the negative reviews, and almost waited for more patches before I picked up the game-but I'm glad I decided to get it now instead. +Chef for Hire is great and provides some missing direction
+Tons of new foods
+Looks far more polished than the first
+Soundtrack is fantastic
+More frantic feel to rush hours, plus alerts before they begin
+Holding stations add more strategy and difficulty
+Designer lets you customize to your heart's content
-UI can be a pain to navigate (especially in Designer)
-Not a strong feeling of progression in your own restaurant
-Buzz isn't a strong focus this time around*
-No emails*

There is no getting around it: yes, it does suck that there is no feeling of direction as it existed in the first game. However, even with the features that are missing from the original, it is still an absolute blast to play and is, in many ways, an improvement over the first. Added features like the holding stations and the leveling system are what save the game for me, and because you have to earn money and do well to unlock more objects and food, there is still a feeling of moving forward in the game-even if it is different from the progression as it existed in the first.
Overall, Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! is addictive fun, and a game I’m definitely going to spend just as many hours with as the first—if not more.

I've been having soooo much fun playing CSD2. It's different than the 1st (of course), but there's so much to do and I'm looking forward to seeing what else is implemented in later updates.
Clearly I'm a fan of the new format where you're a chef for hire that goes around to different restaurants with pre-set menus. Each restaurant has different "shifts" that you can unlock, and each shift has different conditions (a certain amount of buzz, slightly different menu items, # of holding stations, # of work stations). You can linger at the different restaurant that you enjoy cooking for (the dessert and breakfast places!) and then move on when you want to switch it up. I'll try to make a list of some of the points that I've been enjoying most.
-I love the custom/cosmetic options to add to your own restaurant. It's something that I wanted back in the 1st game. I haven't played with my restaurant a lot yet, but I would love if the original campaign came back from the first game and you could apply it to your restaurant. That way when you change your menu, you could change the look of your restaurant if you really wanted to. It's something that I definitely look forward to seeing in a possible update.  :)
-The art is amazing and everytime I play I get so hungry, but I really love it.
-Music is catchy and fun.
-I'm having no issue with the difficulty in this game. Personally, I disliked the completity of some of the foods back in the first game (soup mostly). I haven't unlocked every food yet, so I don't know how everything is prepared. I'm just finding that the preparations of most foods are much more fluid and more suited for my tastes.
-The food history is a good read on all of the foods available for purchase. A nice detail.
-No food upgrades! There were some foods in the first game that I loved making, but when I updated them, I hated them and then stopped using them for my menu (lasagna).
I think that covers most of my thoughts for now. I can't wait to see what updates are added in the future.

Before I even start, it will be important to a lot of people for me to note that I own CSD1 and have played it to completion and then some.  So I do have experience with it.  I should also note that I received a beta copy for free, but I deliberately waited to review the game until I'd seen some of the changes and fixes I knew would inevitably come shortly after a brand-new release.
I am thus far enjoying my time with CSD2.  Certainly there are naysayers who spout about how they gave it a thumbs-down because it doesn't match up to CSD1, but really, CSD2 is seriously supposed to be a different, more balanced experience than CSD1 was, and I'm enjoying it because my mind is open enough that I can see that the changes are for the better.  CSD2 is a great game already, and is shaping up to be even better.  For those who don't read dev notes but do read reviews, you're missing the fact that the developer is still balancing and adding new features to the game, and that he truly works TIRELESSLY to make this the best experience he can manage.  He essentially works on this game every day, all his waking hours.  If you don't think he does, spend some time on the CSD Discord server.  As for his attention, he listens to fans, and additionally watches Twitch streams of CSD2 to watch player reactions to see if he's done a proper job balancing the game, and to watch for bugs he hasn't spotted in his own personal testing.
But anyway, on to what I love about the game.  Firstly, the food variety.  CSD1 had too little food in general, in my opinion, and CSD2 fixes this by having a greater variety.  People have said things about CSD2 no longer having food upgrades, and that was a deliberate decision on Chub's part, because the more you upgraded a food in CSD1, the more attached you grew to it, and soon you didn't want anything else on your menu because you were so invested in your favorites (and didn't have the money for new foods anyway because you spent it all on your upgrades, thus more or less locking your decisions in).  I would know; I had this issue myself.  The new variety allows you more mental freedom to make the decision to branch out your food choices.
Secondly, I enjoy the leveling system.  Although CSD1's system of "earn your stars by performing tasks" made sense, progress was occasionally rocky and didn't feel like it was going much of anywhere.  With CSD2's Yum Level system, progress feels much smoother, and it feels like you're actually accomplishing something with every day you complete.
Chef For Hire is also interesting; instead of setting the menu yourself, you take on a set menu, with each shift being like a different difficulty level for the restaurant you're working for, and you see how well you can do.
Instead of your restaurant automatically looking prettier only with each star you gain, we've been given a Designer Mode, and as you play, you unlock things you can place in your restaurant.  Sure, the naysayers can complain all they want that this takes away a certain sense of accomplishment, but what said naysayers are missing about this is that it allows you to make your restaurant look how you want!  Got bored with your seating and want to change out your tables for booths for a few days?  You can do it!  Change which pictures you've got hanging on your walls?  Go for it!  Want a tile floor today instead of carpeting?  Absolutely!
Also important, the addition of Holding Stations.  You can prepare certain menu items in bulk to place in your HSs, and serve them from there until they go bad and need replaced.  Each food is either HS Required, HS Optional, or No HS; proper use of your Holding Stations is an important part of CSD2.
And there's more on the way!  At the time of this writing (September 24th), the next major upgrade is being worked on which adds a CSD1-style mode for those who enjoyed the boosting/detracting effects of the menu's food selections, and aside from that, other features will be added as well, such as equipment upgrades, and the return of e-mail!
I'll say it one more time since I don't think it can be stressed enough: The dev will listen to your feedback.  If you think you've found a bug, or something doesn't seem right, *tell him*, and he will address it.
I love this game, and I love the guy who made it, and is still making it better.
If you loved CSD1, just get the game and buy lasagna.  You can spam PSCR PSCR PSCR just as easily in this game as you could in CSD1.
If you've never played CSD at all before, and are wondering "could a restaurant simulator really be [hard/addicting/enticing/rewarding]?," the answer is yes.
Overall I'd say CSD2 is worth your money.

I really hesitate to recommend this game for a single reason--the final boss. But before I go into that, here's my thoughts about the rest of the game.
First off, it's got a cute art style that while pixelated is easy on the eyes and still manages to convey a lot of character detail. Starting off as a newly hatched dragon and learning the ropes through solid tutorials both obvious and subtle was nice as well (for example, the game has "Press Z to jump" printed on the wall but also has lighted crystals in certain parts to show you a glide and jump path). It feels natural to play, and the controls are decently responsive without being twitchy.
There's a definite sense of progression too, as you upgrade your jumping/gliding, health, and fire breath via in-game creatures, many of which are hidden in areas you'd miss just sprinting through the game. Plus, as you progress, you'll grow larger in size, which seems to upgrade your jumping height by extension. While it was disappointing to not ever reach the size of an adult dragon, it didn't really take too much away overall.
The enemies are fair and easy to figure out once you've run into them a few times. Most of the creatures in the game are passive, although later on you'll run into beasts that will aggressively approach you on sight rather than meandering around or only attacking when you're close enough. Discerning what will hurt you on contact (bats, for one) and what won't is trial-and-error, but it comes quickly and easily enough.
Now for some complaints. I felt some aspects of the branching story (which really only branches into "Lonely Ending" and "Hero Ending") were not obvious the first time around, and felt a little too obtuse. The enemies could be frustrating at times, especially during the first 'boss' when a bunch of ranged and melee enemies would swarm you. Luckily it was never too overwhelming; but it never felt challenging in a good way, just annoying.
Which brings me to the boss. Apparently, his difficulty was increased at some point in a quiet update. I only just got the game so I cannot confirm this, but from reading forum posts and guides it seems his attacks are much faster, more responsive, and therefore more difficult. However where it runs from "challenging" to "rage-inducing" is when this difficulty runs into a few before-this minor problems with the controls and gameplay.
For one, the boss cannot be defeated with your fire breath and fireball attacks alone. You need to learn to effectively use the 'ground pound' attack, and dart in and out during certain attacks. The problem here is that the controls can be somewhat clumsy, especially with the jumping and ground pound, making the first phase of the boss a test in praying the controls respond and good ol' luck (hoping he'll stay on the lower level, letting you pound stone blocks onto his head without taking too many hits instead of jumping up to slash you or spamming his AOE attack). Where before the unresponsiveness would mean losing a heart to some skeleton or goblin, now it means forfeiting at least two or three hearts to a rapid-fire assault of sword slashes.
The second phase isn't much better, but in hindsight it's more about taking the shots you can in between dodging around his hyper-fast and jumpy movements. It took me about 20 tries, quitting, taking a break, and then coming back in a single attempt to beat the boss. It's all about keeping yourself alive more than dealing damage.
Then, after you've finally managed to beat his second stage, the boss comes back for one last go, where he chases you at lightning speed slashing away. Basically at that point it's all about jumping and mashing C, and just hoping you've got at least 8-10 hearts to work with as he cuts you to pieces as you attack.
Then, you're done. And unfortunately as much fun as I had with the first 90% of this game, the ending battle really soured the experience for me. But you should pick the game up and experience it for yourself. It's a fun little game that won't take long to beat at a more than reasonable price point.

Dragon's Wake is a charming little indie game that is pretty much exactly what you get for its price - a short little romp around as a hatchling dragon trying to grow up in a harsh world, all with a black knight out to get you.  You're not alone in this harsh world, however, and you soon find yourself with an adoptive family of lizardfolk who worship/adore dragons like you.
PROS:
-Once you get used to the controls, it becomes a joy to fly around the various levels, eating various critters, and seeing if you can find more upgrade critters to eat.
-Minimalist narrative means that the story is told entirely through your experiences - even the background history of the world is told through tattered tapestries.
-It's actually very easy to care about the characters despite the lack of understandable dialogue, and failing to get the Good Ending can actually be a very sad experience for a first time player.
-Music is atmospheric and definitely makes you feel safe, in danger, or in a creepy place
-Achievements are fairly straightforward to get, but becoming a fully upgraded dragon is definitely more complex than anticipated (in fact, I'm still trying to get this one as of this review!)
CONS:
-The controls are floaty to begin with, and you may find yourself shooting past your target when flying when first starting out.  However, the more your flight gets upgraded, the easier jumping around becomes.  The Dragon has a tendency to back up when partially hanging off an edge, which adds a sense of realism but can be distracting for the player.
-The loading screen artwork helps tell the story of the game, but the artwork itself is of a fairly decent DeviantArt level with somewhat jarring anime-esque eyes.  They do their job, but it can be a little distracting.  The artist has potential, but perhaps a more skilled artist should have been commissioned for this particular project.
-Getting the Good ending requires performing a good deed in an event that has no obvious effect with the event in question.
-This game is very short.  It's easy enough to replay, but aside from the gameplay and the achievements, there's very little reason to replay it.  However, if you can get the game on sale, I would say that the price is worth the length.
-The game is also pretty easy, until the final boss, where the game suddenly becomes very difficult.  It's a rather sharp difficulty spike and even when you know what to do, the fight may take several tries.
In short, is the game worth playing?  Absolutely, yes.  It might even be worth buying at full price, if you have that much disposable income.  There is a sequel in the works at the time of this review, so I'm definitely looking forward to that.

Very disappointing; a nice idea with polished presentation, and as such when you first start it seems like there is real potential for a solid game - but it quickly falls to pieces.
Once you pick up the basics it becomes unsatisfyingly rudimentary to blaze through all of the early levels. You will have to repeat each of them if you're inclined towards completing all the challenges, but far from feeling like this adds value to the game, it comes across as padding, and simply makes the gameplay feel old all the sooner.
Then, when you hit the more challenging levels, the real problem arises. The difficulty is never increased by clever use of the game mechanics, but rather without exception is created by the imprecision of the controls and the lack of clarity in the visual style.
It is incredibly frustrating to be forced to restart again and again because you were a few pixels off the precise spot the game determines safe, or because you moved a fraction of a second off when the game wanted you to move. As a result, when you finally beat a challenging level, rarely is there the feeling that your skill has prevailed at last. I wouldn't even say there was a genuine feeling of satisfaction - nothing more than a relief that you don't have to restart the level yet again, having hit the exact sequence of key presses the game demands of you.
It requires such a robotic approach, and such repetition, that despite only having a few hours of content it manages to become crushingly tiresome before it's done. Despite costing little, there's dozens of better games on steam at half the price.

This game is great! I’d compare it a little to Witcher II with the level of depth and detail.
The backstory has been well thought out, and you really feel like you are playing a role in a larger plan.
The rumors, and stories you hear and read about in the game are interesting, and I've read each of them. Usually in a game like Skyrim, I'd read a few, and then just skip the rest. The stories all tie in very well with the game and atmosphere, the writing is really top notch. There are some typos, and some bits that did not translate well to english, but you'll still catch the meaning.
The combat system is easy to grasp and enjoyable. The rules are simple, but you must make use of some strategy to maximize the damage you can deal to the enemy, and prevent yourself from taking too much damage. Injured party members can be healed with spells, potions, and local temples, but those all cost money, and money is sometimes difficult to come by.
If you play the game, read some of the forum post stickies as they offer additional insight into the game mechanics. There are also some YouTube videos that show some easy tips to follow. For instance, it was not until chapter 2 that I realized the map could rotate! The right mouse button is your friend in this game. RMB everything and see what it shows and does.
One of my favorite parts of the game is the inventory system when you go into a market or store. It is just like most games with a buy/sell system, but if you click on a party member, the store items rearrange themselves and turn different colors. It is almost like each party member has a wishlist of the equipment they want. If you have the money, buy the green stuff at the top pf the list! This is so much better than reading and comparing stats between multiple weapons to determine if a certain sword is better than a certain heavy mace.
My least favorite part of the game WAS starting over at each chapter. I say WAS, because now that I know to expect it, I can prepare for it. Sure, you lose your awesome party members that you trained from a lowly peasant to a war steed riding knight of death, but you get to do it all over again, and this time you’ll make even better choices. There are a few times when you get to carry over two party members, so you don't always have to start fresh.

I'm an old hat Taffer. I've been with the series since it started, and I'm not ashamed to admit up front that my review is biased. I have played Thief TDP and Thief TMA to pieces and back and then some. I also enjoyed Thief 3 and while in the end I must admit it was a fairly respectable game in its own regard and I also enjoyed it for what it was. In the origional games you had free reign of the city, go where you please when you please, even if it was something utterly asinine like becoming a member of the rootop climbers guild (some of you may know what I mean, others may not) or seeing if you could jump out of the map or just screwing around looking in every nook and cranny just because you could. This new reboot of Thief, or Thief 4 rather (though I shudder to think of it as part of the series I love) is nothing more to me than a regular run of the mill game that is nothing special or even that good, and a cash grab.
There is no jumping in Thief so far. Yes, you read that correctly. You are GLUED TO THE GROUND. A real throw back to when I played FFXI and FFXIV online. At one point there are a pair of floor traps early in the game that any reasonable human being with half a brain could jump over, and for our acrobatically gifted Garrett should be no problem to jump. As you can't jump, you have to take a predesignated route around the traps instead of just jumping over them. Do you want to go up a wall? You need to hold spacebar and can only climb in designated spots. Do you want to go up or down a ladder? If so, you need to hold spacebar until you have a mini cutscene happen (and it IS a mini cut scene, as your character takes control of himself to turn around and face the ladder then takes a few steps onto the first rungs when going down, or takes the first few steps  by himself to latch on before you can go up) and you actually get on the ladder. There is no more auto latching on ladders (a crime in itself) and it becomes a nuisance and frustrating to have to hold a button to get onto a ladder, and then become glued to said ladder until you either reach the top or bottom. Did you enjoy rope arrows and their magical ability to catch on ANY wooden surface in the past? Guess what kids, designated spots only!
Speaking of mini cutscenes, lets talk about mini games that serve no purpose. If I want to open a window, I hit "e". But wait! We need a mini cutscene where you pull out a crowbar and have to tap "e" a few times to open the window. Or move a beam from inside the gap out of the way. Another tap "e" moment to make me waste time. The character is completely automated in his movements in both going through the window and gap sliding, so why are you making me tap "e" at all. Either let me open the damn window in one smooth fluid motion without having to play a tap "e" minigame, or skip the stupid cutscene and just let me interact to open the window and mantle through as I please. Same with being forced to move objects out of the way.
I can't speak for the story yet. When I (sadly) finish the game - and I know I will I will likely update my review. So far though all I can safely say is they've used a few throwback names older fans recognize to try and appeal to them. To be fair as well, they added back in things we asked for like rope arrows. They added in options to turn all of the new flashy hand holding garbage off. They added options to make the game as difficult as some of us are used to. It's not enough. The game is just flat out bad to me because it feels so much more restrictive than previous games. It does have a very Thief 3-esque feel to it, but it just hasn't jived with me at all even several hours into the game.
On another note, I was more than ticked off at not being able to collect a collectable in a side mission as apparently the game adds a few required tools - in this case a razor and possibly others- to loot specific items -in this case a painting. Unfortunately for me the side quest to do this mission becomes available BEFORE you can even purchase the razor, so if you want to get that collectable then tough luck, you can't go back to that area again later in the game (so far at least) to get it, it seems to be lost to the ages. Not very wise game design there in my opinion. I hope I'm wrong and at some point you can go back because this♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off to no end, and I don't normally fluster easily.
By the way, I was on the fence the entire time about buying this game, especially after seeing it at E3. I decided to try and give it the benefit of the doubt and buy the Master edition of the game. Imagine my complete and utter shock and surprise today to see that there is already DLC for the game, and not only that if you paid the extra money for the game, you don't get all the DLC, just one called "The Opportunist". Really? Seriously, REALLY? The extra mission comes no matter what version you buy, and I couldn't give a damn about digital art or soundtracks or TF2/DOTA items. I paid the extra to have the DLC, and then you put out more that isn't even included.
TLDR: If you only liked the first two games of the series and hated Thief 3 its a definite don't buy. If you enjoyed Thief 3 then you may also enjoy this, though it is far more constrictive than past games (not such much Thief 3 which was also fairly linear in it's own way, but definitely 1 & 2 where you could pull off some fun and amazing things by going where you shouldn't and/or getting out of the map.) on where you can and can't go (notably because every rope arrow and jump is in a predesignated spot). Removing something as small as the ability to jump when and where ever you want really killed this for me, it takes away a freedom you don't know you've lost until its gone.
I really, really wanted to love this game but I just can't. :(

As a fan of both Dragon Quest and the Dynasty Warriors series, this game takes the frenetic action of DW and adds the awesome characters and RPG elements of DQ for a solid action game. While DW has a more mindless combat system with using only attacks and Musuo attacks, this game's combat is a bit more robust. Being able to use skills and magic along with standard attacks makes the battles much more enjoyable. You can even summon monsters to help you out and defend key points and people. Grinding is prevalent but once you unlock the free mode of a stage, the game allows you to stay in the area for as long as you want and leave once you've sated your grinding appetite. Finally, when you die in a stage, you keep the EXP and Gold you collected and get to retry, so losing isn't all that bad.
Some cons: Some cutscenes aren't synced properly with voiceover so they aren't as enjoyable as they could possibly be. Characters are also pretty one-note in their personalities which doesn't add a lot of depth. However, the characters are all pretty endearing and you'll probably find some you like more than others. Story is also very by the numbers but it's a small gripe as something this wacky can only go so many directions without making it too confusing.
30+ hours in, I'm still enjoying this title... if you're a fan of DW combat, I would definitely recommend this game. The game's difficulty is pretty average to high at some points, but finding the right strategy will usually help you prevail.
