Dragon Quest Heroes is a game I were super hyped for when it came to steam, but I didn't get to buy it before the summer sale 2017, mainly because I've been to school and somewhat forgotten that I added it to my wishlist. But enough of smalltalk, lets get to the review.
Dragon Quest Heroes is from my understanding the main characters from the other successful games in the series binding together to fight against Darkness who has been taking over the world and made the monsters turning against their old friends.
I for one really enjoyed this. While I'm not 100% complete with the game at the moment, my 28 hours in the game gives me a solid insight in this game. Because, it's pretty repetative. The quests and story-quests are pretty predictable after a while. There's 2 main quests in the story, either:
1. Kill all the monsters on the map
2. Defend this thing and kill the monsters on the map.
The side-quests are mainly this aswell, but with a new twist: "Kill these monsters who drop these ingredients".
You also get around 11 characters, where you can mix a party of 4, or 3, as you're stuck with your main character no matter what. All the characters have different playstyles and different spells of course, so there's variety there.
Aside from the repetativeness, I actually think it works pretty well for my liking. It's a hack'n'slash combo-monster killing-game. It could, and probably should be more diverse, but I've heard the 2nd one fixed this problem. However, to me it's not a big problem.
The story itself, is to me really good. I absolutely loved following all the cutscenes and reading the story as it grew, and how everyone met and became friends to fight evil. How everyone got together and grew together. All the different personalities. Now, I'm not usually one to follow the story too much, as a couple of the games I've played has been fun playing itself and the story easily got boring and made me skip cutscenes and spam "A" to get to the game asap. Not this, however.
The music is also nice in this game, and the graphic is exactly what I would expect from DQ. Cartoony-animated series. Definitely gives the series a nice charm of its own.
All in all I'll give it a 4/5, though a personal 5/5. If you like the Dragon Quest series then you would probably enjoy this aswell. If you're easily bored by killing tons of enemies, then this game might not be it for you. The story makes up for it in my opinion. I'm glad I got this, and I would recommend it if you need a chill hack'n'slash RPG to kill some time, and millions of monsters.

Your choices boost certain stats, allow for certain events to happen, etc..
So far, you might think it not very different from other choice of games, but this one has its unique features. True, not
single choice has a huge impact, such as the cosmetic ones for your flag and article of clothing... But most do influence things delicately. And the storyline has quite a bit of humor in it.

Aside from generic high fantasy and superheroes, pirates seems to be a popular genre for CYOA works from Choice of Games. Several of their offerings already explore life and on the high seas. Not to disparage the other fine offerings already on hand but I hold the opinion that Choice of the Pirate is the best one of them yet.
For one, it presents a wide scope in the narrative with a meaningful choice between civilization and freedom. Neither side is shown to be an absolute good but rather present different views on what people value in life. It also has a strong Carribean feel with native magic being intrinsically tied to nature. The set pieces are fun, especially as you meet creatures like merfolk, sea monsters and ghost ships.
Overall it is well-written and a fun romp. Each playthrough takes approximately 40 minutes which is decent for a CoG title so no fear of a truncated game either. I won't lie, the previous two offerings from CoG did not impress me much. Heroes: Redemption was basically the author strongarming the reader into listening and playing along with the author's political views while Sea Eternal was kinda meh. Choice of Pirates on the other hand is a strong offering that ranks alongside some of their best works.

This game is lightyears better than civ 5. (yes, without rising tide!)
Why?
Every decision counts! In civ 5, early game doesn't really matter, more or less. Expand, kill some bar-bars, make alliances. By mid to late game the decisions you made in the entire first half don't really matter at all. In BE, every decision counts. You start towards your choosen affinity from turn one. What affinity to choose largerly depends on your surroundings (resources, abundance of aliens, etc...), and from there, you can beeline for specific techonologies. All this means that every turn matters, which I would not say of the first ~1/3 of civ 5.
Research Net: Only go for tech you need. That simple. This means that every civ in game is very different from eachother, which changes up the fighting a lot.
Combat: There are fewer military units, even when you are around halfway through the game you may only have 2-3 good specialized units. Combat is much more fun because you are fighting against units different that your own and how you fight depends a lot on what affinity and units you have. Rather than knowing what side will win from the beginning, based on who has slightly more advanced units (civ 5) its hard to tell what units each side will have and who will win. Combat is interesting every time. Orbital units add a entirely new element to combat as well.
AI: The AI in this game are simply better than the AI in 5. AI in BE will ambush you with a full army that can sweep cities in a turn, as opposed to the AI in 5 which will try throwing a few units at you now and again in pathetic attempts to wear you down.
The only thing that irritates me still about this game is that diplomacy is a little messed up. I hear this is fixed in rising tide. But, it's no worse than the diplomacy in 5.
In short, this review is so long because I felt everyone was really wrong about how awesome this game is.

It was a mess at launch, now after many patches it is a lot more playable. It is still overpriced at 40$, but if you can grab it at 10$ or so it is a pretty good ride for 50-100 hours.

- Civ in space. Do i need to say more? If you are a fan of everything scifi and space related, it is a big plus.
- Brand new tech tree, futuristic and scifi inspired. It is fun to think about how humanity might evolve in space. Even though there are some nonsensical stuff like "physics" tech. I am pretty sure you have long mastered physics if you are exploring space.
- A bunch of new mechanics that feel fresh if you played civ5 to the ground and are tired of it. New affinity system, new virtue system, miasma, alien creatures, etc.
CONS
- AIs lost their flavor. There is nothing as charismatic as montezuma for instance. Also a useless "favor" system where AIs will basicly ask you for free stuff instead of offering money and goods as usual.
- Some short sightness in design. For instance there are no melee boats (for taking cities) and you can't boost embarked move speed, so going for a sea conquest your boats will move 7 tiles at a time while your melee units (necessary to take towns since there are no melee boats) will lag behind at 2 tiles per move.
- The tech tree is a head scratcher. More complex without any streamlining or core axis of development. After 10 games i am still confuzzled everytime i look at it.
- It feels like you need to by the DLC (that is also overpriced) to get the complete experience. Some things are missing from vanilla like melee boats and diplomacy is almost non existant in the base game.
- Color scheme feel weird at first but you get used to it after a couple of games. Still don't understand why grassland looks almost exactly the same as plains etc. Would have been nice to be able to tell the difference without tooltips.
VERDICT
Overall I recommend it, but ONLY on a big sale , and if you can grab its DLC also that would be ideal.

Any problems I've found have been minor, and most of them have already been addressed by the dev.
Check out my detailed review of the game, which also compares it to the first game feature by feature (note that some of the things I was disappointed by have already been improved):

Reviewing with the rising tide expansion.
This game suffers from what a lot of 4x games does, which is to say there are very clear and defined routes of victory that are much stronger than others.
Unfortunately in beyond earth, this goes even further into not just having it so that military victory and surprise attacks are far and away the most effective method of play, but there perks, skills, techs etc that will send you to this victory much faster than others. In short, a game in a genre that is supposed to be about having a thousand paths to victory is really a game with one path to victory and 99 wrong answers.
Basically, you can invest in tech, science, culture, energy (money), and a few other things. But buffing your military skill is far and away the most effective means of victory, for a few very poor reasons. Foremost, there is a very early perk you can get that gives you bonuses to science for killing other units. You can also customize your leader to get basically the -exact- same bonus, and yes they do stack.
What this means is that you can pump up your military to the point that youre earning more science than the guy who just invested in science. That is extremely poor design, in my opinion.
Culture is practically worthless except as a means to gain perks to your military. You will not make any significant game plays based on culture.
4 of 5 of the victory conditions involve getting a certain tech and then waiting. What will make you survive this wait? You guessed it, your military. Except there was no reason to wait. You techrushed, took the biggest guy's capital, and then everyone else left the game.
Another thing they changed between civ 5 and beyond earth, is cities are now hilariously easy to take. I'm not sure why they made cities practically defenseless, but if you have a significant tech advantage over your opponent, you can take a reasonably sized city with a single unit.
This is helped by the fact that units are divided by arbitrary tech tiers more than anything else. And moreover, your basic units can be upgraded the whole game so that they always stay relevant. But what this means is that you never have to invest in any tertiary tech if you don't want to, because your basic warriors will later be top tier shock infantry. Just invest in military. Always.
This game is fun until you realize the trick to winning. When the people you're playing with arn't aware of the mechanics, the game is fun, unique and interesting. Unfortunately after you figure out how to win, it's no longer fun.
It has a lot to offer. The alien interactions are interesting, the affinities are pretty interesting as well, but it's a poorly balanced game that often feels like 6 hours of seeing who got the luckiest with tech. I can't really recommend it. It needs so much changed to be a solid game. But honestly it would be as simple as an overhaul of numeric values. Bonus to defense here, nerf to attack there, this perk gives less, this perk gives more, etc. The framework is all there, it was just handled very poorly.
If they do a year of balancing it might very well be an excellent game. Or maybe some enterprising modder will take up that mantle.

CSD is back with CSD2 and this time they've shedded most of the complexity and nuance of the original game for.....quantity.
Upgrading your restaurant appearance via restaurant level (1, 2, ,3 etc stars) is gone in favor of lootboxes. Depending on performance each day, you unlock new items and sometimes even new menu items. Using a rather ineffective, and frustrating, UI that is not nearly as smooth as you'd expect, you can do some Sims-like visual design on your restaurant using booths, tables, chairs, booth separators, table ornaments, floors, ceilings, windows, walls, lighting, counters, and decorations.
Mechnically, the most significant change is that they added prep stations somewhat similar to Overcooked. You can prepare as many of your menu items as you have prep stations for, and in most cases actualy must do this otherwise the day won't start. Prepping makes rush hours into a joke and kind of removes most of the skill needed to get through them, but at the same time once your prepped food runs out, it's hard to interrupt the rush hour in order to prep more. If you don't prep, many of your menu items will never be ordered - pretzels, macaroni, fries etc. While the depth of the menu items is still there, they've changed the focus from remembering more advanced patterns and key mappings, to basically an interface where you still swap between ingredients with space, but each ingredient tab basically uses the same keys. If normal onions on tab 2 are N, then carmelized onions on tab 3 are still N. That makes good sense, and is easy to remember, but at the same time seems a bit convenient.
Graphically CSD2 is a lot smoother and prettier than the first game. If you acknowledge that it was a bad idea to play CSD when hungry, it's an even worse idea now. There is completely new art work for all of the food (obviously) and as far as 2D cartoony food goes, it looks pretty good. The patrons have more detail in them, too, and more variety this time around.
The campaign again takes place in a tower, but this time, the tower has tons of restaurants - not just yours. Each time you rank up, you unlock a new restaurant and each of those restaurants has a diverse, changing menu. You can choose to work several different "days" - essentially challenge scenarios where the menu and conditions change. Doing so is a great way to get used to new menu items before you can afford to buy them, and it breaks the monotony of otherwise using the same menus over and over in your own restaurant.
The biggest addition I am aware of is co op, but I have not tried it. I'm interested to see how it works versus a game like Overcooked, where it was pretty much mandatory to have a partner unless you're cheating.
Overall, despite the lack of the Iron Chef-like challenge modes and some of the subtle features like romances or the sidestory, and the obvious dumbing down of a lot of the game, it's still worth the price. If nothing else, it will at least help improve your dexterity. I'm still enjoying it, for sure, and rarely ever do I install a game and then immediately play it until 1 AM without stopping.

When I first saw that a CSD 2 was in the makings, I became both extremely happy and worried. I loved CSD 1, but the concept didn't seem broad enough for a sequel. Boy am I glad I am wrong.
Something I really like about CSD 2 is its graphical overhaul. I loved the art style in the first game, and instead of keeping everything the same or go for another art style for this version, instead it's an improved and extended version of the first game. Everything feels better. The menus are much more clear in what they do; navigating through them is a breeze, but more on that later.
The graphics feel right. It really feels like I'm there, owning my restaurant, with a very chill and relaxing mood. Even though the art isn't realistic- it looks warm and cozy and it wants me to actually go to that place and drink some coffee.
I know that CSD 1 & 2 are made with Game Maker (Studio) and I've worked with the engine myself in the past. Granted; it was an older version, but looking through Game Maker's history, not /too/ much has changed when looking at the core of the engine. And I just want to applaud you - developer - for using it right.
From my experience with Game Maker; things like resolutions, cross-compatibility, sound levels and settings in general can be a real pain in the bum. I've rarely see a Game Maker game do them right- Hotline Miami 1 and especially 2 are a great example of this. The resolutions in that game are a damned mess as is the sound.
However, CSD 2 is different. It supports all my resolutions; 720p, 1080p, 2k and everything beyond and in between. You don't have to restart the game to put the new resolution into effect. Even more so- there are graphics details options. Which also don't require a restart. As well as all of this; the game runs very smooth 60FPS and the animations are gorgeous.
But- to top it off: You can change every single volume settings. You can set a different level for menu music, gameplay music and EVEN a different level for the Rush Hour music (part of the gameplay)! You can set different levels for weather, the guests, the preparation and the GUI. This level of detail isn't seen- well, in any other game on the top of my head. I love it.
I have to admit; when I clicked on the "Design" button, I did not expect relaxing build music and a categories menu at the bottom. And I giggled. What can I say? Some might say this is just blatently stolen from the Sims, and they might be right, but I thought it was a funny addition. This game didn't need it, but after a while, it would have felt empty without Design mode.
I, btw, -love- that I can make the entire wall a glass wall. God, it looks so good. In addition, I love that there is so much stuff. I can really style and design my own restaurant how I'd like it to be.
I also like that all items in Design mode have to be earned by levelling up: this is a good way to keep me playing. I don't know what's next, but it'll probably be a nice addition to my design- or I'll just redo the whole damn restaurant again. And that keeps me way more motivated to play than when I just earn stars.
There are a few downsides to the implementation of Design mode however:
And while those "bads" look like major issues, they really aren't. Having no grid sucks yeah, but at least coming close to aligning things is very easy and most of the time, you won't notice it while playing. I love its feature, but hopefully these flaws will be fixed in the near future.
I can't think of an original header for this one. I also can't say a lot about the music.
It's
. The music is awesome. Genuinely awesome. It creates the right mood for a restaurant, making me feel even more like I'm there, but it also calms me down. And the rush hour music is gorgeous as well, really making my adrenaline pump. The music never gets old or boring and is even better than in the first game.
About the sounds- they also sound so satisfying. The sound effects are realistic, and the amount of bass in them when putting tomatoes on a burger really makes me feel like some sort of master chef. I love that some sound effects are the same as in the first game: it's a nice bit of nostalgia, and they are still awesome sound effects.
If I had any critique on the first game, it might have been gameplay. Levelling up was terribly slow, and on the first 3/4 stars it felt boring at times. There was a lot of dead time between customers and the recipes felt a bit generic at times.
CSD 2 basically fixed all of those issues. Levelling up is now no longer based on stars, but on your level. Levelling up grants you extra stuff for Design mode and sometimes little extras. Then you have stars; you now get half stars, and it seems to happen based on your quality and how much you've played. Next to that, you have daily challenges. A lot to do, basically, and I don't think I'll die of boredom any time soon with CSD 2.
Especially not since dead time has been fixed: since the very start of the game, you won't get any rest. It's not a 10 hour rush hour of course, but customers are more frequent. The recipes at the start are better as well, and a lot of new recipes feel better and more thought out than in the first game.
Not only that; but the addition of Holding Stations is a great one. It adds a tactical element to the game. You need to prepare some foods before you can serve them, and you can batch create them in the holding stations. So if you see that pretzels are more popular in the morning than evening, you can batch create them that morning and do less of them that evening. But, they also can be used for Side Dishes to make people wait longer when you're not helping them. It makes you think about what you should do and when, and can make your life either easier or hell. It's the one thing I missed from CSD 1: Tactics.
Co-op also seems like fun, but I haven't tried that one yet.
Now, of course, the gameplay is not perfect. I didn't like the "thief" part in CSD 1, and I'm glad that in CSD 2 he got much less annoying. But he became too frequent; my restaurant is being robbed every day which doesn't seem believable, but is also annoying and breaks the calm restaurant atmosphere. On top of that, you beat him by kicking the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of him in a cartoony way, which also doesn't flow well with the rest of the game.
Other than that, I can't think of any other bad thing. Mail is gone, but I don't miss it personally. I liked it, but it wasn't a must-have.
So, conclusion. I think CSD 2 is a sequel done right. Everything has been improved and everything feels different. It's not more of the same, but it's also not entirely different.
It also feels more like a "professional" game now. The menus, the music- everything feels like it's been made with a serious budget behind it. Not only that, but I know from CSD 1 that the developer is seriously committed to pushing out updates (even completely new features for free) and respects the community and its users, so I can only imagine that the game will get even better and better over time. I definitely recommend buying it.

It’s a finicky thing trying to update a decades old game for a modern audience.
On the one hand you’re presumably trying to preserve the essence of the original, but on the other times have changed and games that were once incredible are often astoundingly simple compared to what developers are now capable of. And so there’s a fine line to ride between recreating outdated mechanics and deviating so heavily that the result bears little resemblance to its forbearer.
Karateka, and complete remake of the Apple II game of the same name, falls on the side of defiantly indulging in a wholesale recreation of its former self. The visuals may be drastically improved by way of a slick (if somewhat washed out) cell shaded look, but the core of the same is still the same rhythm based fighter it always was, and therein lies the problem.
I don’t think Karateka is bad, it’s just entirely as one-note as the now three decade old original, and wears out its welcome just as quickly as you’d expect. Though it resembles a fighting game, Karateka is far closer to a rhythm game. Attacking and blocking relies on proper timing and attention to visual cues, but there’s little player agency beyond reacting to the Simon-says feedback the game is giving you.
The idea is actually one I find pretty neat as a fan of rhythm games, and I was enjoying Karateka for at least the first handful of fights. But nothing ever changes beyond the simple fights your put through to learn how to play, and even at less than an hour long I was ready for Karateka to hurry up and end before it was even halfway through.
The repetition is grating and the game’s refusal to acknowledge and react to it frustrating. It’s not a game without merit, it just doesn’t know what to do with itself. That it’s constructed around a groan worthy damsel-in-distress plot, which culminates in the woman you’re rescuing effectively becoming your own prisoner, is only more bothersome and shows a hesitancy for Karateka to move past its archaic beginning. I’m not exactly sure who this version of Karateka is for, but as someone without any amount of nostalgia for the first it clearly wasn’t me.

After my first playthrough of 2012's Kareteka the thing that struck me the most about the experience was its brevity. My memories of the original version from Broderbund, at a time when the Apple II was the cutting edge of personal computing technology, are hazy at best. I remember it not looking even as sophisticated as some of the beat-'em-ups of the day like Bruce Lee or Kung Fu Master, but I remember virtually nothing about the gameplay. The new Kareteka utilizes a peculiar, rhythm-based combat scheme that is easy to learn and difficult to--well, it's just difficult.
You play as one of three would-be rescuers attempting to save your beloved Mariko from the "evil warlord Akuma." You move through several environments doing battle with Akuma's minions with the ultimate goal of reaching his palace and the final battle. Mind you, you're not choosing which protagonist to play the game with; you start with Mariko's true love. If his health pool drops to zero, he falls to his death, and the monk takes his place. Should the monk perish, the brute takes his place. Finally, if the brute is beaten down, you have the option to continue, losing a certain percentage of your score in the process. Each successive hero has a larger health pool and stronger attacks. When grappling with a new opponent, your objective is to counter each punch or kick in a sequence by pressing the "block" button at just the right time. Even if you miss one or two and get hit, as long as you block the antagonist's last attack in that sequence, you are given the opportunity to launch a flurry of your own blows. After a series of 3-4 attacks, your opponent will become invincible again until you block another sequence of attacks. This dance continues until one of you is defeated. There are also purple flowers that you will encounter along the way that will partially or fully restore your health pool. Opponents gradually increase in difficulty by varying their attack patterns.
It sounds clever and fun on paper but in practice, the controls (even with an XBOX 360 controller) are wonky and your blocks don't always appear to register correctly. Even though you can easily run through the roster of opponents in less than an hour, I suspect even the most gifted Guitar Hero player will find himself unable to succeed in completing the game with Mariko's true love. The artwork looks good and the music is thematically-appropriate, but the gameplay itself leaves something to be desired. Kareteka makes for a brief but rather frustrating distraction from more complex games.

Karateka may seem somewhat familiar if your memory goes as far back as Commodore 64 or even earlier computers and your mind would not be playing tricks on you for a change because it is, in fact, a remake of an old namesake classic. Besides the obvious graphical facelift, remake also sports a different rhythm-centric combat system, actual health to make it more bearable and expanded story where you get to play as three characters in succession after previous one falls in his effort to rescue the princess from the clutches of evil martial arts master Akuma. It's a short game lasting barely 30 minutes or so if you don't skip cutscenes, but some achievements will have you replaying it couple of times if you want to get them all for the sake of completion.
Would I recommend Karateka? If you know what you're getting yourself into and can accept a short game for what you paid for it, sure. Just don't lose your cool if you keep getting hit for that one perfect achievement. I know I did.

Second: In many instances, I get the feeling that some options and possible choices are not yet implemented. Maybe it really is that way but this is just another point where the game's atmosphere lacks some depth.

I really wanted to like this game but now I am just glad I bought it when it was on a -50% offer.
Disappointed to say the least.
The interface is retro and basic but it serves its purpose and is usable. The battles, when you get over the dodgy pathfinding/target selection issues are fine. Nothing revolutionary but how much can you improve a turn-based, hex-grid combat sequence?
This game makes you work. Its not handed to you on plate. Neither does it treat you like an idiot.
And, once I got over my initial pre-conceptions and actually got into the game, I enjoyed wandering around the map, fighting and exploring. So all in all it doesn't sound that bad right? Well, for me, the problem is all the hours I invested in building up a little force, equipping them, choosing upgrades and deciding which partciular career path they were going to take. Then, you complete the current mission and whammo! There you are........alone......... and almost penniless. Your team has gone! All that time and effort you put in was for absolutely nothing!
Now you kinda anticipate that when you get to the next mission the baddies are going to be tougher and better equipped (this is a TBS game after all), so you naturally want to take your team so you can cope with next mission, yes? Wel, no. What happens is you are droppped into the next map with only your characters gear and enough money to buy a bowl of gruel, should you happen upon an establishment that sells bowls of gruel, which you won't.
The very next mission sees me recruiting a base level healer and two pitchfork wielding peasants. Have a guess how long they lasted against the pursuing bandits. Not very long at all., They die. There's nowhere else to recruit anymore peasants from and there are several waves of bandits heading your way that you simply cannot escape. It is totally pointless.
Like I said at the top of this review, I really did want to like this game. I'm long in the tooth as a gamer. I go back to 1993  and The commodore Amiga and TBS games are my thing. But this one, well, my advice is not to bother. And that is all I have to say.

When I first heard there was a Thief 4 in the making a number of years back, I couldn't wait till I got my greedy hands on it!  Well "Thief" is the Thief 4 and the wait was definately worth it.  I recommend turning off all the hand holding things like glistening gems, pointer marker etc and just keep the game like the original thief series.  ie use your map and some brain power and you will have a ball.
Graphics are great, music very moody and it will get your heart pounding if/when cornered.  The AI is pretty good, the soldiers are very smart and will attack you very quickly if you do something dumb.  The citizens just cruise about unless you threaten them.
The gameplay is excellent.  Stealth means stealth this is not a first person shooter.  You need to think out side the box and use your eyes (if you do not use the focus option) and search for doors and windows to open, goodies to collect etc.
Lockpicking has changed slightly, but is fine.  Opening up a window is very "life-like" and I really like how they made it that way, but I am not going to tell you what the devs have done :P.  Not all doors and windows will be able to be opened.
Taking your time is a must.  Rush through the game and you will miss so much.  It is not too linear, and has "areas" where you enter through a door/gate with a sparkling light to do your next "job". Exploring is a lot of fun, as is the pickpocketing steathly - not always easy at times so the blackjack comes in handy sometimes.
So if you enjoy games like the Thief series, "Thief" (minus the hand holding options) will not let you down.  Headphones are a must as is a darkened room, plus a decent chair because you will not want to leave the game.
I forgot to add that although Stephen Russell is not the voice over for Garret in this game, as he was for all the thief games, the new actor does a decent job.  Not quite the "smokey drawl" of Stephens Russell's however :(

Is it perfect?  No.  Is it a SquareEnix/Koei Tecmo masterpiece?  Maybe.  Is it a lot of fun?  Absolutely.
It's basically Dynasty Warriors mixed with Dragon Quest RPG elements.  The combat is very hack n slashy where you'll fight against hordes of monsters over and over and over.  There's lots of XP grinding, side quests, and skill upgrades if you care to go after it all.
You spend a fair amount of time in a central hub where you can shop and accept quests.  From there you can decide when you want to continue the main story questline or just focus on optional content.  You could ignore a lot of the extra content but there is enough here to keep JRPG fans happy.
I beat it with roughly 40 hours into it but I could have kept going with TONS of additional content that I'm ignoring for now because I want to play Dragon Quest Heroes 2.
The story is about what I'd expect for a DQ game.  Light hearted and comical.  They actually managed to get me to laugh quite a few times.  I tend to prefer the more "serious" SquareEnix titles but they did a great job with it.  You don't need to have play any other DQ games to enjoy this.  I've finished a few so I recognized some of the characters and that's about it.
Fun fact:  It does make me want to go back and play some of the old Dragon Quest games.  If SquareEnix was smart, they'd start releasing the Android/IOS versions on Steam/PS4/Switch...  (refusing to play on my phone)
My only real complaint:  Where is my 4k resolution and advanced graphics options in general!?  The game looks nice in 1080 but I play on a giant TV so some simple fixes would have gone a LONG way.  There are mods out there to fix it but I just sucked it up this time around.
GIVE ME MORE RESOLUTION OPTIONS!!!!  (thankfully this is not an issue for DQH2 from what I'm told)

When I first saw that a CSD 2 was in the makings, I became both extremely happy and worried. I loved CSD 1, but the concept didn't seem broad enough for a sequel. Boy am I glad I am wrong.
Something I really like about CSD 2 is its graphical overhaul. I loved the art style in the first game, and instead of keeping everything the same or go for another art style for this version, instead it's an improved and extended version of the first game. Everything feels better. The menus are much more clear in what they do; navigating through them is a breeze, but more on that later.
The graphics feel right. It really feels like I'm there, owning my restaurant, with a very chill and relaxing mood. Even though the art isn't realistic- it looks warm and cozy and it wants me to actually go to that place and drink some coffee.
I know that CSD 1 & 2 are made with Game Maker (Studio) and I've worked with the engine myself in the past. Granted; it was an older version, but looking through Game Maker's history, not /too/ much has changed when looking at the core of the engine. And I just want to applaud you - developer - for using it right.
From my experience with Game Maker; things like resolutions, cross-compatibility, sound levels and settings in general can be a real pain in the bum. I've rarely see a Game Maker game do them right- Hotline Miami 1 and especially 2 are a great example of this. The resolutions in that game are a damned mess as is the sound.
However, CSD 2 is different. It supports all my resolutions; 720p, 1080p, 2k and everything beyond and in between. You don't have to restart the game to put the new resolution into effect. Even more so- there are graphics details options. Which also don't require a restart. As well as all of this; the game runs very smooth 60FPS and the animations are gorgeous.
But- to top it off: You can change every single volume settings. You can set a different level for menu music, gameplay music and EVEN a different level for the Rush Hour music (part of the gameplay)! You can set different levels for weather, the guests, the preparation and the GUI. This level of detail isn't seen- well, in any other game on the top of my head. I love it.
I have to admit; when I clicked on the "Design" button, I did not expect relaxing build music and a categories menu at the bottom. And I giggled. What can I say? Some might say this is just blatently stolen from the Sims, and they might be right, but I thought it was a funny addition. This game didn't need it, but after a while, it would have felt empty without Design mode.
I, btw, -love- that I can make the entire wall a glass wall. God, it looks so good. In addition, I love that there is so much stuff. I can really style and design my own restaurant how I'd like it to be.
I also like that all items in Design mode have to be earned by levelling up: this is a good way to keep me playing. I don't know what's next, but it'll probably be a nice addition to my design- or I'll just redo the whole damn restaurant again. And that keeps me way more motivated to play than when I just earn stars.
There are a few downsides to the implementation of Design mode however:
And while those "bads" look like major issues, they really aren't. Having no grid sucks yeah, but at least coming close to aligning things is very easy and most of the time, you won't notice it while playing. I love its feature, but hopefully these flaws will be fixed in the near future.
I can't think of an original header for this one. I also can't say a lot about the music.
It's
. The music is awesome. Genuinely awesome. It creates the right mood for a restaurant, making me feel even more like I'm there, but it also calms me down. And the rush hour music is gorgeous as well, really making my adrenaline pump. The music never gets old or boring and is even better than in the first game.
About the sounds- they also sound so satisfying. The sound effects are realistic, and the amount of bass in them when putting tomatoes on a burger really makes me feel like some sort of master chef. I love that some sound effects are the same as in the first game: it's a nice bit of nostalgia, and they are still awesome sound effects.
If I had any critique on the first game, it might have been gameplay. Levelling up was terribly slow, and on the first 3/4 stars it felt boring at times. There was a lot of dead time between customers and the recipes felt a bit generic at times.
CSD 2 basically fixed all of those issues. Levelling up is now no longer based on stars, but on your level. Levelling up grants you extra stuff for Design mode and sometimes little extras. Then you have stars; you now get half stars, and it seems to happen based on your quality and how much you've played. Next to that, you have daily challenges. A lot to do, basically, and I don't think I'll die of boredom any time soon with CSD 2.
Especially not since dead time has been fixed: since the very start of the game, you won't get any rest. It's not a 10 hour rush hour of course, but customers are more frequent. The recipes at the start are better as well, and a lot of new recipes feel better and more thought out than in the first game.
Not only that; but the addition of Holding Stations is a great one. It adds a tactical element to the game. You need to prepare some foods before you can serve them, and you can batch create them in the holding stations. So if you see that pretzels are more popular in the morning than evening, you can batch create them that morning and do less of them that evening. But, they also can be used for Side Dishes to make people wait longer when you're not helping them. It makes you think about what you should do and when, and can make your life either easier or hell. It's the one thing I missed from CSD 1: Tactics.
Co-op also seems like fun, but I haven't tried that one yet.
Now, of course, the gameplay is not perfect. I didn't like the "thief" part in CSD 1, and I'm glad that in CSD 2 he got much less annoying. But he became too frequent; my restaurant is being robbed every day which doesn't seem believable, but is also annoying and breaks the calm restaurant atmosphere. On top of that, you beat him by kicking the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of him in a cartoony way, which also doesn't flow well with the rest of the game.
Other than that, I can't think of any other bad thing. Mail is gone, but I don't miss it personally. I liked it, but it wasn't a must-have.
So, conclusion. I think CSD 2 is a sequel done right. Everything has been improved and everything feels different. It's not more of the same, but it's also not entirely different.
It also feels more like a "professional" game now. The menus, the music- everything feels like it's been made with a serious budget behind it. Not only that, but I know from CSD 1 that the developer is seriously committed to pushing out updates (even completely new features for free) and respects the community and its users, so I can only imagine that the game will get even better and better over time. I definitely recommend buying it.

Was a big fan of the original CSD. Very pleased with the sequel so far. It didn't blow my mind, but shows improvemet without losing what made the first so much fun. Some things were removed - food/equipment upgrades, random challenges - but the new features that replaced them make up for it.
My favorite addition are the holding stations, and with them the whole side dish+drink concept. It adds an extra layer of strategy without radically changing the core gameplay, and also makes the whole thing a little more realistic - after all, no one goes to a restaurant to order a pot of soup and nothing else.
I also like the Chef for Hire mode. In addition to running your own restaurant, you can also work shifts for other restaurants, unlocking more as you gain reputation. It adds a bit of variety and showcases some of the new foods the game has.
Speaking of which, there are a LOT of new unlockable foods this time. I was a little iffy about this at first, since even with only ~30 or so dishes in the original, a lot of them felt kinda same-y to cook. That's still true to a degree, but the Chef for Hire mode hints at what they're really about, which is customizing your restaurant. With so many options, you can tailor your menu to be like a fast food join, or a bakery, or a pub, or an Italian bistro, or any number of other things. It's a fun bit of roleplay that ties in well with the gameplay. Especially when combined with the ability to customize your restaurant's interior. That part's not really my thing, but it seems to be well implemented.
So I'd call this a successful sequel. I expect I'll be enjoying it just as much as the first.

Spy Chameleon - RGB Agent is a fun, unique and charming indie game for fans of stealth and puzzle games.
It a fairly short, but challenging game. I completed the game with 29/30 achievements in a little over 11 hours. It can be difficult and will have you raging at times, but it's very enjoyable. There are some indie games that are so challenging, you feel like the developers hate you and just want you to suffer. However, this game is difficult enough to make you feel challenged without making you feel like completing it is an impossible task.
There is no story. It's just 75 levels of pure gameplay. In addition to the 75 levels, each one has 3 corresponding challenges to complete. There's collect all flies, collect all ladybugs and beat the time. This gives each level replayability. I was surprised at how innovative the game felt. As you progressed through the game, the levels not only became harder and more complex, but they added things into the environment that added advantages and disadvantages. There's colored surfaces to help you blend in, button-triggered moving walls to hide behind, boxes to hide in, etc.
This game is worth checking out if you're a fan of stealth games or puzzle games and is definitely worth the $5 it's priced at. There is no story. So if you need a plot to enjoy a game, this game doesn't have it. But if you just want a moderately challenging puzzle game, this is a good one.
Actually a really fun title. If you like puzzles and thinking fast, as well as being stealthy, this is a game for you. I am enjoying it quite a bit.

brings a nice and innovative idea that will keep you entertained for a while.
Unfortunately, as with many other indie games, RGB Agent suffers from the developer's inability to balance the game's difficulty.
There is a "normal" and a "hard" mode, but the normal difficulty is already turned up to eleven.
To name the major annoyances:
- Security cameras are able to see you
in the level, whether it makes sense or not.
- The security robots are moving way too fast for your chameleon. There is a "turbo" button, but it doesn't make much of a difference.
- The default controls don't make a whole bunch of sense and
be changed. How is this acceptable by today's standards is beyond me O.o
- You don't have to have a controller to play this game, but if you do have one, it's going to make your life much easier.
The keyboard controls are out of question and the mouse tends to get "stuck" when it leaves the boundaries of the level, which is a serious problem.
Now I'm not saying that RGB Agent is a terrible game. It's not.
What I'm saying is, if you prefer forgiving games with well balanced difficulty, RGB Agent might not be your cup of tea ;)

I went into Thief 2014 with high expectations. Having been a fan of the series since the first game, I essentially spent a portion of my life playing the first three games over and over again. I've always been a fan of the Thief series, so I was so happy when I saw a reboot was in production.
Immediately upon starting, I was sucked in. Garrett's new voice actor did a very good job of making him sound familiar enough to old fans, but also engaging enough to make new fans listen. The City has been given a facelift, but you can still see the old nods to the arcitecture from previous games, and it still feels very much like you're in a Thief game. The new thieving tools (and returning ones) help you explore every nook and cranny, and it's fun to see what you can find if you keep your eyes open.
The attention to detail for Garrett's actions is exquisite. Previous games had the loot merely vanish with a jingle, and while that was satisfying, seeing Garrett's hands physically pick up the loot and every item you come across in the game just makes it complete.
The Custom difficulty setting will definitely make for replay value, and unless you're using a guide, you may not get everything in one try. Thief 2014 has high replay value for me, and I will be playing it over and over again.
About the only thing most people won't like is the ending. While it does tie up some loose ends, they left an obvious hole for another game. While some may be angry about this, I welcome it. I've been without a new Thief game for so long, so I look forward to the next chapter in Garrett's adventures.

SHORT VERSION: The free-roam, Mount&Blade-style RPG part of the game is decent (although simplistic... there are way too few stats and skills, for instance), but the combat system of this combat-centred game is irredeemably flawed. With too few tactical options and somewhat unclear rules, it fails to impress and STRONGLY encourages save-scumming. All in all, the game’s neither good nor bad - an okay-ish, relaxing experience that I (unfortunately) cannot wholeheartedly recommend, not for the full price. 5+/10 or 6/10 at best.
LONG VERSION: The combat lacks depth. Let’s define depth as “the number of meaningful choices a player can make at any given moment”. If you consider that a.) you can’t freely move the units, b.) you can only attack the nearest enemy unit and c.) there are hardly any special attacks, abilities etc., the player often feels like there’s very little he can change (it feels almost like auto-resolve at times, you just do the clicking, not the decision-making). For example, if you have a warrior (a young noble, let’s say) and it’s his turn, you can only do 3 things (apart from drinking a potion): attack the nearest foe, postpone the attack on said foe or skip his turn entirely in exchange for a defence bonus in the next turn. There should be more tactical options like:
- special attacks (e.g. a shield bash that does little to no damage, but lowers the defence of the target so that you could have a specialized character with high initiative that would make the enemy vulnerable to your slower (low initiative), but hard-hitting characters),
- will points (limited points that you can use up to make the attacks stronger or more accurate or whatever; it worked great in The Banner Saga, why not here?),
- flanking mechanics, defence penalties for being attacked by several enemies and, generally speaking, the ability to move your troops more freely (even if there’s a penalty for that); seriously, why do I have mounted troops if I can’t go behind the enemy line and kill that pesky healer in turn 1? That’s what cavalry does, flank and charge,
- more “spells” (or at least alternative, stronger versions of the same “spells” which you have to “charge up” for a turn and which can fail if the caster takes damage in the meantime),
Imagine for a moment that we have all these options. I just lost a battle, what do I do? Fight again and try a different approach, move my troops differently, defend my crossbowman this time, use up all the will points to eliminate that mystic as quickly as possible, or lower the defence of that tank-ish knight with a special attack etc. Lots of possibilities, as you can see. Now back to reality. I just lost a battle in Legends of Eisenwald, what do I do? Reload the game, ask myself why I failed and SAVE-SCUM by using that knowledge to modify my army (shift their initial positions, give some weapons or armour to different people, go back to a village to buy a potion or recruit a different person). See the difference? It’s breaks the immersion if your character is a psychic who can predict what will happen next :)
So I’m not saying there’s no depth to the combat system. The problem is that the meaningful choices occur BEFORE the battle. Once you engage in combat, there’s very little you can do to change the outcome. And for me, that’s not much fun at all. I watched combat videos made by the devs to see if the situation changes in the mid- and late-game, but no, it doesn’t.
Also, as I already mentioned, the game doesn’t make the rules clear enough. Why does the spearman sometimes counterattack and sometimes he doesn’t? Is there any defence penalty from being surrounded? Why can I sometimes choose the direction of the attack and sometimes I can’t? And so on.
When it comes to the RPG elements, I didn’t play the game long enough to say anything about the story, but as I said, there are too few stats and skills for the game to actually FEEL like an RPG. Also, there’s no character creation whatsoever, which is sad. You can only choose the class and change the name so you don’t have to play as Heinrich.
Overall, it’s not a bad game and some people will find it pretty fun (might as well give it a try when it's on sale and, if you feel about the combat system the way I do, you can always get a refund...). Personally, I may play it for a few more hours, but I have to say I’m disappointed (I was waiting for this game when it was still in early access). Too bad, because it definitely had potential.

The Bad.
The writing is kind of rubbish, firstly a lot of the things that made the Thief world interesting seems to have vanished, there's no hammerites, no pagans, I did go to some keeper ruins but have yet to meet one and so far the game have not eluded to what happened to the most important factions in the game series.
The story itself is fairly weak, we never get a feel for Garret's relationship with his apprentice, we never get to see her training or what drove them apart, Garret seems to care a lot more about people than he did in the previous games, the game world seem to have moved 400 years ahead in fashion, no longer is the word in a medieval steampunk style, it now much more resembles the typical victorian steampunk you so often see, though still without the invention of gunpowder
The Good.
The gameplay is solid, it’s fun to sneak around and still everything within arm’s reach, the levels are well designed with tons of hidden loot,  the core gameplay of stealing stuff, then using the money you get from the stuff to by upgrades and gear so you can steal more stuff even more effectively is a good time. Tripping over a bottle on the ground you didn’t notice and alerting a guard is hearthstoppingly tense, and the game is full of small cool details like that.
The extensive difficulty settings are also excellent, not content with just the easy medium hard settings, you can extensively customize the difficulty, feel like the focus ability makes the game to easy, turn it off, long for the days of Thief 1's saving methods, you can turn that on, and so on.
The Ugly.
It’s the small things in this game that drives me up the wall, the silly story I can easily look beyond, but the game is held back by a lot of small bad design decisions.
For example the locations of loading points in the open world will drive you crazy, why the nearest merchant to my hideout is in its own little area with its own loading time in and out is beyond me. Using slow quick time events to open a window to enter into a new area only to realize you already roped that apartment and having to do another slow quick time event to get back out gets old real quick. The map could have used some more work, or at least the ability to place your own notes on it would be nice, for example you can replay old missions by reentering them at their starting point, which is great, if it wasn’t for the fact that their location isn’t shown on the map after you done them, so if don’t remember where it was it can be problematic. The hideout is a nice touch but serves no real purpose (an idea would have been to allow you do redo old missions from your hideout, thereby giving you a reason to return to the bloody thing and saving me the trouble of running around the city trying to find the damn mission entrances, but I digress).
Conclusion.
This is almost the worst kind of game to play, there’s an excellent stealth game in here, but playing it can sometimes fell like death by a thousand tiny cuts, it can be very frustrating to feel hold back by small weird design choices.
Still with all that said, it’s probably the best pure stealth game I played in recent times, a lot of my frustration stems from my love of the Thief series and its world, but if you are a fan of stealth it should still easily be worth your money.

TLDR; Free-build or guided decks, zero mandatory expense, grind to get digital cards or pay for them. Bugs include crash, freexe, temp exit to desktop (minimises), card mechanics.
Overall, this game is good if you want a preview of the mechanics of a new set before you commit to buying physical cards.
It starts you off with a handful of reasonably useful cards (via story mode) and you can grind your way up to a more comfortable collection for free. You are, of course, encouraged to buy cards directly but it is more than plausable to play the game without that -- it's just a bit of a grind at first until you get some more effective card combos together.
You get less commons per pack than with physical cards BUT to counter that there seems to be zero risk of excessive repeated cards, which is the main problem with buying packs of physical common cards. It caps at four as you won't need more than four even when building multi decks (shared accross decks.)
There is, unfortunately, no way to trade cards with other players.
Play against other players or  against bot AI. AI is low reward but easier to consistantly beat after a bit. Modes are solo bot (3 difficulties), multiplayer solo, two-headed giant.
Comes with a story mode which is great for seeing the new cards in action; you play a pre-built inflexable deck against another prefab deck.
Comes with a guide to basic mechanics called "skill quests" which reward you with some tokens for your trouble and are a garunteed win (provided you understand the mechanics and play smart) while they last.
Daily quests give you bonus tokens for meeting in-game goals (sac x creatures, ect)
Build a deck from the ground up with or without AI guidance, "auto-complete" feature and reasonably extensive search filters and deck wizzard for the less experienced.
Bugs: sometimes bugs out and goes to desktop for no reason, freezes have been reported and I have seen a full computer crash several times. AI is not always as clever as all that, sometimes getting its own units killed for no reason (Ravenous bloodletter being an example.) Some mechanical bugs have been noted with some cards as well. Alt-tab does not properly minimize the game; it re-opens after being minimised. You have to ctrl-alt-delete and bring up task manager if you want to minnimize it for a moment.
Personal opinion: This game makes me angry at times, especially in the early card-grind before you get anything all that good. What I hate most is losing in story mode (where you have zero deck controll) as this seems rather unfair to lose when you can't alter the deck. I also sometimes forget that I do not have all these cards in physical form :( so I get ideas for irl decks and can't use them. All that aside, this game has the deck building side of magic down pat and that's what I most enjoy about MTG anyway.

I'm not a fanboy of either Dragon Quest or Dynasty Warriors. I played a few Dragon Quest games before (remakes for DS) and one Dynasty Warriors game, over 10 years ago. I liked those games though.
I like the graphics for the most part and combat is nice too, though pretty mindless for the most part. Not really a problem for me, since I don't play these types of games very often. The story is typical Anime / JRPG stuff, nothing special. I liked most of the characters and their play style. However there are tons of small problems that keep me from loving this game.
Everything, outside of combat just takes so much time.
Creating or upgrading accessories is unnecessarily long, especially if you want to use the better recipes, which use another cheap accessory as a base. So you'd probably just sit around 5 minutes to get one item to +2. Luckily those items don't really matter to get through the story, since the game isn't really difficult, so I never upgraded anything.
Accepting or turning in quests is similar. Unskippable jingles and animations play when you turn in a quest, It's not really long when you look at them individually (5-10s each) but it sucks when you want to turn in multiple and just get back into the game.
Spending skill points as well, not a problem when you're just unlocking 1-2 skills. However there are a ton of characters and when you get the later ones, with ~100 points to spend, it just takes too long.
A small thing for me, you have to confirm almost everything and the game defaults to "No", so you can't even mindlessly mash a button, just to get through stuff.
The camera is a bit too close to you character during combat but there are mods to fix this. Same if you want to play at >1080p. I had problems at first with Windows 10 and an Nvidia graphics card but enabling Windows 7 compatibility in the launcher fixed this.
I would probably have recommended this game, because despite those annoyances I had fun. However, DQH2 was released a few weeks ago, and from what I have played they fixed almost all of the problems I had with the first game. Maybe just get the sequel if you can.

Story Missions dont vary much from each other but play out like a game of dynasty warriors game moving around the area to take out or protect key locations(kill this horde, defend is object from this 2-3lanes spawning hordes, kill these 3 miniboss at once etc.) but what makes they really different is the variety of different enemy types you’ll be facing, You could get mobbed by slimes in combination of golems + skeletons that try to take your objective or fight against a squad of skeletons backed by a giant sabretooth tiger with heal bot slims around, a squad of armor knight blocking your lane, it adds a really different kind of chaotic diversify to the game and when your against harder lvl enemies  Later levels where you meet Maya is when the game really takes a turn into a tower defence game where it shines when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan when you face afew higher HP mini boss demons at once and you got to act fast with every tool at your disposal,it's pure chaos and only you can bring order.
Characters within your party vary greatly from each other (expect the two main story ones you choose at the start of the game) as each bring different abilities that do different things in the pursuit of monster killing or supporting the party to kill monsters, you could have a AOE spitting mage with rods, DPSer with gantlet fists, or a Boomerang wielding status healer that take care of status stuff which are very specific to them. Party members can be lvled up with xp acquire from missions to get points to unlock new abilities, stat boosts and combo attacks as you progress which sets character apart from each other.  Each character’s appearance is customization(to a point) and has a specific weapon of trade they use that can’t be switched out for something outside it’s type say from a sword to a staff.
Monster coins  make you summon defeated monsters you killed during that current mission to fight alongside your party but with some limits(they cant follow you through the level so most will guard objectives,lanes,and killing other monster within range), with well slotted coins you could have your own hordes of skeleton knights, slimes and zombies, golems guarding a lane or useing healer slimes like a potion, just another cool layer added during combat.You can also increase your coin slots from Quests to have even more minions at your side as well as more stronger ones at once.
There’s alchemy system with recipes for mixing ingredients to make new items for bonus stats, theres also weapons and armor shops to buy new gear that scale as you progress through the story.
Overall the game sets itself apart with its enemy types, party member abilities,diffrent gameplay genres and monster coin mechanics, to where it doesnt play in the like regular Jrpg but a game with a lot of JRPG/Tower defence/musou  elements stuffed in and out actual combat with party member swapping, I recommend the game to any Musou/JRPG fan as well anyone looking to dip there toes into the world of Dragon Quest

A nice little platformer with innovative yet satisfying controls, and a lovely story that is told without words or heavy-handed metaphors, and yet you will completely understand it.
Some people have commented that you play a “good” dragon, but to be honest it is not so simple. You are called upon to kill enemies, but as a recent hatchling you don't really know who is good and who is evil. The enemies are just another race of beings, that happen to attack you rather than aid you. A deeper reading of the story reveals how morality is often something you are caught up in, that spins around you and presents you with challenges. In the end, you want to survive, but are you truly a hero?
The story is remarkably mature, as you see allies die, and of course you dish out much destruction. You need to kill animals to survive, but often they are cute little creatures that do not pose any real threat to you. You are, at the end of the day, a predator.
It's wonderful that such a little platformer can inspire such thoughts.
Be warned that the game itself is not that easy. It takes time to get used to the controls. Also, your game is saved only automatically, and if it saved you with little life energy left just before a difficult area, you will be a tight spot. But persevere, learn the enemy tactics, and you should be able to beat the game.
Finally, thank you so much, dev, for supporting Linux!

Dragon's Wake is a wonderful game and you should probably give it a shot.  It's an indie game, but it is a solid indie game.  It's not a long game, but it is fulfilling. This game was a joy to play.  The art was great, and the entire game looks adorableThe colors really help build the tone all the way through.  The music was great too, and it also added to the atmosphere.  The dragon controls really well, and I loved the upgrade system.  It was simple and effective, encouraging exploration to find each of the upgrades, and effectively putting the player in scenrios where they would have to upgrade a couple times so they can learn.  Most of this game is designed very, very well.  The visual storytelling in this game through both the loading screens and events depicted in the game iteself is very effective, far more than a game like FF13 where the writers felt the characters had to talk about everything rather than actually show it.  It was very well done, and it made the experience even better.
HOWEVER,
The final boss was aggravating.  It was a huge spike in difficulty that didn't match the rest of the game at all.  While most of the game emphasized movement, even in combat against normal enemies, the final boss gives so little options for moving and dodging.  The final boss moves far too quickly to dodge effectively, and it turned what should have been a triumphant and satisfying ending into a frustrating half-hour grind to memorize his patterns.  It was like taking someone who had only ever played Kirby's Epic Yarn and tossing them headfirst into Darksouls.
Overall, the pros far outweigh the one con.  The ending was good, and after seeing the achievement for finishing, it gave me reason to play the game again.  You'll see what I mean when you beat it yourself ;)  I can easily recommend this game to friends, and the price tag perfectly matches the time taken to finish, especially considering the replayability and difficulty of the final boss. Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! is a god-damned disaster. CSD 1 is one of my favorite games of all time, an awesome little thing that combined fun and satisfying progression with bite-sized mechanics and unexpected twists to create an experience that is still a blast 40 hours later. Not only selling the dream of being your own chef, setting your own menus and growing your own restaurant, it made the 'work' of cooking dishes challenging, stressful, and, most of all, fun. Balancing your menu with high priced vs high buzz (how many people come to your restaurant) items; strategizing which food to cook first based on how long you think it will take vs how complicated its recipe will be; weighing the options of buying new, low-cost foods vs spending the big bucks to upgrade your current ones; for such a simple seeming game, it was also rich with fun little puzzles like these outside the core cooking experience.
Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! takes nearly all of this away. Why? And what's gained in return?
First, let's talk about the 'additions' in the sequel (for nearly every new thing that's added, something gets taken away). Holding stations the big new mechanic, allowing you to pre-prep food, skip a long grill time, or serve side dishes. Holding stations are alright. Some foods are now prep-station-only, meaning if a customer wants it and they're none left in the prep station, well, you'll have to prepare some before you can serve them. This creates a new fun stressor to worry about: do you put in the hot dogs now, hoping that people will order them at rush hour but burning a hole in your pocket (and a space in your holding stations) if they don't? Or do you use it to make a cheap and easy side dish for quick money? While these questions are initially a lot of fun to try to puzzle out, you quickly gain enough prep stations to trivialize this mechanic. Not only that, but without holding stations you wouldn't have side dishes, and side dishes are, perhaps, the single worst addition to the entire game.
Side dishes are a new type of food that are only made in holding stations. At first glance, they're pretty cool: once they're in your holding stations, customers will automatically buy them if they get a great (or ok, I think) order. Getting a great order and a side dish nets you a 'delicious' order. All good, right?
Wrong. The problem with side dishes is that they introduce a new waiting mechanic. To understand why it's so fundamentally bad, let's talk about how CSD 1 handled waiting. In CSD 1, if a customer ordered a dish, you had a certain number of seconds to fulfill that order or they would leave in a huff, giving you a bad order in the process. These seconds were the same for each dish and each restaurant, and could only be upgraded by purchasing upgrades that lengthed them (or gaining stars for your restaurant, I think). Since the times were pretty short up until the end of the game, cooking food was a constant juggle of trying to correctly make the complicated recipes, do your chores, and still have time to get every order. This made the moment-to-moment gameplay in CSD frequently exhilarating, as you tried to work as hard and as fast as you could to get all the orders perfect.
CSD 2 throws out this mechanic entirely. Each day you have a base amount of waiting time (I think 16 seconds) that can then be augmented by side dishes. Each side dish adds a different amount of seconds to the waiting time, and by having multiple side dishes in your holding stations you can increase your waiting time to 50+ seconds with relative ease. This change completely destroys the manic gameplay integral to the original and dials down the challenge to basically zero. Yes, some dishes can ONLY be completed if there are side dishes out, but for the majority this isn't the case. Gone are the frantic dashes from one food to the next; now, I can take my time with each food, even during the height of rush hour because everyone's down to wait up to a minute for their food. It completely kills the challenge for me.
Another 'addition' is the YUM system, a leveling mechanic so poorly described (at least on release) and woefully unrewarding that it begs the questions of why it even exists in the first place. Now, experience is gained whenever you're cooking, if it's in the new Chef For Hire mode or the incredibly bare-bones Standard mode. It's entirely unclear what gains you experience, however; several times I have leveled up simply by waiting for a customer to show up in my restaurant, doing absolutely nothing.
Leveling up unlocks a number of items for another addition, the Restaurant Designer mode. After you ding, an unskippable animation of a crate rattling appears and an item pops out, frequently multiple times. A chair! A table! A lamp! All these can be used to design your restaurant, an ok idea on the surface that in reality completely destroys any sense of progression gained from leveling up. The problem here for me is that I don't really care about designing my restaurant, and if you don't either than there's basically no sense of progress *at all* anywhere else in the game.
You can also unlock food, I guess, but with nearly all of the 180 foods unlocked at the start and with no descernable differences beyond visuals between several of the foods, there's a clear amount of quantity over quality here. Nearly each recipe in CSD 1 felt distinct and fun to master; here, it's a wild west of foods with little indication of what foods are actually fun to play. Several foods also feel like complete missed opportunities: the entire cooking process for scrambled eggs, for example, involves putting pre-scrambled eggs on the stove. What about cracking the eggs? Scrambling them? What about any unique gameplay twist that makes preparing scrambled eggs different from any of the other side dishes you prep the exact same way on the stove? I cannot stress enough how many of the recipes here just feel like palette swaps of one another. And without any information (as of now) about how much buzz they offer and with no consequence to using the same food multiple days in a row, there's very little reason to branch out beyond what you've already got.
Not only are the foods blander, they're also mechanically less interesting: gone are the use of arrow keys in recipes. Now, this might seem like a trivial thing, but for me the arrow keys really helped sell the 'fantasy' of whatever recipe you were cooking. Chopping each vegetable in a soup recipe by hitting down three times made me feel connect to the action; same with hitting down to flush the toilet. Small, important details that helped bring me into CSD 1's world. CSD 2 does away with all that, replacing all arrow strokes with keys. 'F' for flush, 'L' for cut, etc. This not only makes these tasks more mundane but also helps all the recipes kind of just bleed together, since the range of things you'll be doing is actually much smaller than the first game’s.
Now, some of these terrible changes can be remedied. CSD 2 did launch in a tattered state, after all; crazy to think this was a fully-fledge release and not an Early Access title. Gone - but promised - is CSD 1 style progression, as well as better buzz implementation and the beloved emails. The developer seems dedicated to finishing the game, to which I have no doubt that he will, but it’s clear even from now that the game has some deep, fundamental problems. How do you reintegrate challenge when a major new mechanic purposefully removes it? How do you fix progression when the visuals don’t change and the recipes don’t gain difficulty? How do you make 180 foods distinct and interesting? Questions that I sincerely hope get answered sooner rather than later, but either way it’s going to be a long time before Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! is anywhere near as good as its predecessor.

The art is amazing and the sound, especially of the rain and storms is stunning (the first time I actually thought it was really raining outside).
The bad:
THe main campaign feels listless compared to the original, but when I look at it objectively I'm not so sure that's true as it has objectives just like last time, but it just feels like it is missing something.  There are currently no emails and that added a ton of flavor inthe last game.  No Iron Cook challenge nor Hungry Festivities, nor any replacements, but the cook for hire kind of replaces these.  There are still a few bugs being work on, and some content yet to be added.
Overall I have really enjoyed it.  I've put in dozens of hours already making it well worth the already low price.  And I still have plenty of content waiting to be unlocked.

When the enemy pulls back to make a punch, you press the block key.  Sometimes you need to press it two or three times.  Then you press one of two attack keys (which one doesn't really matter) a few times. You repeat this until  the enemy is dead, then walk forward on the bridge a little, meet another enemy and do it again.
I'm not just telling you the best strategy - I'm telling the ONLY strategy.  The game doesn't even let you attack until after you've blocked first.  You cannot move your character.  There's no strategy, no combos, no variation; just block, block, attack, attack, attack.  It's like Punch-Out, but without the dodging, stamina, unique enemy attacks, or any of the other things that made Punch-Out fun.
After doing the same thing a dozen or so times, I stopped playing.  I can't recommend this game to anyone, even if you got it for cheap in a bundle.

Karateka is a remake of an old school game, that I have never had the chance to play, but may check out now given the theme of this remake. That said, I have no basis for comparison to the original. It would seem some fans of the original did not like this remake too well. But this could very well be the same syndrome one gets when comparing a book to a movie adaptation, or anything similar.
In any case, I enjoyed the little bit I played of this. Karateka is very nice looking. You play as one of 3 characters: The hero of the game. A monk. And a oafish brute. You start as the hero, and when you die, the monk takes his place, and if the monk dies, the big brute takes his place. Each character has their own ending, and fighting style. So the objective to get the better endings would indeed be to not get killed.
Karateka feels very on rails. It is 2.5D, and you can only move forward. there is no jumping, or going back. Just a series of fights. One after another. That is pretty much what this game involves. The fights though are handled pretty nicely. It's not like a fighting game, but more like a QTE without the on screen button prompts, or a rhythm game, again, without any prompts. You block oncoming attacks, which wll be switched up with each opponent, and after succesfully blocking, do your own attacks. Or once in a while, the enemy may taunt you, in which you can attack them at that point. That's pretty much it. Very simple, but challenging at the same time.
There is no voice work. There are no subtitles. So the story is pretty much interpreted through actions. But it's pretty simple. A young girl is being held captive. And one of the three playable characters is going to go through an army of bad guys to save her. One♥♥♥♥♥kicking at a time.
I can't really recommend this one at the current price, given how short it is. But if you get a copy either through a bundle, or a nice discount, this is definitely worth playing.

You're one of three heroes who have set off to rescue a foxy chick. You get to use all three characters, one at a time, to beat the game. When one dies, the next one steps in to take his place right at the same spot. Health is sprinkled pretty generously throughout the game in the form of flowers. And even if you do die on the third character, you'll get a chance to exchange some of your points for an extra life with the last hero. Obviously, "mastery" of the game means beating it with fewer of the characters as miss foxypants prefers the second hero to the third, and the first hero to the second.
Gameplay is very simple. Run forward (there's no sideways movement, just forward) until you get to the next guard. When you fight the guard, listen for an audio cue that tells you the rhythm to block incoming attacks with, then counter attack as you wish. You occasionally fill your combo meter, which allows you to deal a not-all-that-special special attack.
If you want a quick game to kick out of your backlog, Karateka is a fine choice. It's totally a one-sitting game as you can beat it in half an hour. For that brief period of time, it's fun enough, and every time you think you've gotten it down, it throws a new tricky pattern at you, though it never gets too hard.

War. War never changes.
The Romans waged war to gather slaves and wealth. Spain built an empire from its lust for gold and territory. Hitler shaped a battered Germany into an economic superpower.
But war never changes.
In This War of Mine, war was waged over the resources that could be acquired. Only this time, you're in control of many players and fight to survive by raiding neighboring homes, churches, and other such buildings. Along the way you may have to kill. Innocent? Who knows? You're fighting for another day in this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a place. In this game maybe China would invade Alaska, the US would annex Canada, and the European Commonwealth would dissolve into quarreling, bickering nation-states, bent on controlling the last remaining resources on Earth. Who knows? Who cares? You need to worry about you and yours.
On November 14, 2014, the storm of world war had come again. In two brief hours, most of the planet was reduced to cinders. And from the ashes of nuclear devastation, you struggle to arise.
You were one of the few who were able to reach the relative safety. No, not in some large underground Vaults. You're thinking of a totally different game. You're not imprisoned safely behind the large Vault door, under a mountain of stone...you're out there in the thick of it, and you won't last long if you don't get your head straight.
Pros: War never changes.
Cons: No vault.
