Maplestory -- the mere mention of this game brings many feelings, anger, nostalgia, happiness are among the chief emotions -- the game that defined my childhood, how could I bring myself to criticize that? Or so you may think.
Some people have already pointed out that this game is completely only for money, like China and Britain after the Opium Wars, Maplestory makes its most aggressive, passionate, and downright obsessed players squander their money and their life away for this 2D childrens game. To which they will cry "IT'S NOT A GAME! IT'S... MY LIFE!!" Which is almost as equally depressing, although they may never see that. Pretty ironic, isn't it? They're looking at a screen of a character portraying themselves, but they become blinded to their own person.
Other people have consented to point out the critical flaws of the game, including disgusting balance. After all, a class rehashing some of the previous mechanics by subtly putting them in different job numbers can't result in a bad game, can it? And if so, what if we just make every job stronger than the last so everyone has to use more money to level it up to the level of their previous class? I mean, every single class might as well be the same right? In fact, there are two classes which were literally the same thing. Everything was the same, besides the addition of a storyline. Every skill. And I'm looking at you, League of Legends, don't pretend like you don't know what I'm talking about.
And the last group of reviewers have followed the age old tradition of ad-libbing several actions and words together to form a semi-coherent -- and, to their hope, funny and well upvoted -- thought. This is no insult, I have no doubt that the effects of Maplestory are nothing but as painful as having bleach poured down one's urethra, if not worse.
I'll admit, 5, 6, 7 years ago, sure, I'd recommend this game. I made friends, most of which whom were older and taught me things, very, very inappropriate things, strengthened my friendships in elementary school. These lessons of how friendship is important is clearly worth *something*, correct? I'd admired Tiger, FangBlade, sushixx, curryishot, dray86 at one point I won't deny that. Perhaps I learned to respect from this game, something people don't even know how to do to this day. However, I'd be remiss to recommend such a trash game to anyone now, not even to my worst enemy's juvenile brother so he can watch him grow up to become a Mapleslut, driven in life by only more Maplestory. Id est, I would not recommend, nor do, this to my worst enemy, or anyone, for that matter. Not that I haven't thought about it. Several times. But that'd run the risk of making Nexon more money. Which is a sin in and of itself, according to the word of God himself.
Let's go over some of the good things; the background music, maps, and storyline. The BGM... the power of music is strong, so much that even by listening to the songs, you want to play it again. Then you remember what a shtity game this is. And then you download it anyway and uninstall it again. That's not to detract from Studio EIM, take a listen to some of the BGM, it's pretty amazing how they can churn up as many decent pieces to contrast with how Nexon can pump out cancerous updates. The maps, the artwork, the backgrounds, everything has its own style, except the flying half naked 13 year old that transforms into an even more naked flying dragon Megawoman thing, I really don't get that one. Or that flying Power Ranger dragon superhero samurai guy who morphs into a bigger samurai dragon guy. Both of which are from the same place. I'd insult that space cowboy as well, but that'd feel like I'm insulting Cowboy Bebop. The storyline is alright, maybe it's just me, since I'm a sucker for storylines.
Finally, the things that ruined Maplestory: not just the pathetic money-grubbing attempts, but the updates. Big Bang? Sure felt like a big bang to the balls. RED? The color of the blood that I coughed after laughing so hard at N$X$N's feeble attempt at dragging people back into the game, like some deranged meth dealer. The level 200 to level 250 character level update was pretty ♥♥♥♥ing hilarious too. Just think about it, FangBlade, some idiot who put almost, if not more, than 3000 hours into this game, finally got level 200, and was the first one to do so. Not a bad accomplishment, even if you couldn't put it on a résumé, it's still pretty amazing that you were, or are, the best at a game, in North America or otherwise. However, Nexon is the biggest fan of crushing the balls of their fans. Like, just flat out obliterating them, they might as well be called "hacky sacks" at this point, the balls are done for -- you get my point. Nexon decides to change the level from 200 to 250, removing his number 1 status forever. No, it wasn't enough that people can now do what he did in less than several days, in comparison to his years, they can now even ignore him.
Anyway this is a pretty good game, I'd recommend it to anyone who wants the following:
1. The suffering of:
i. Their immediate family
ii. Close friends
iii. Anyone they may ever contact, ever
2. The deaths of:
i. Their wallets
ii. Job prospects, if you can only think about this game (after all, getting the urges to answer interview questions with "Maplestory", "Black Mage", or "Zakum", really don't cut it)
iii. Their social life
3. Renouncement of all teachings of Jesus Christ, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, or any deity, other entities, or lack thereof. Along with the admission of all things evil (as well as everything Pandora released into the world) into your soul.

And then, BOTs. Thanks to spinning, the Koenisegg Agera R is literally undrivable. But, you'll find out those BOTs will drive this car like a gust of wind, no crashing, no spinning and don't even slide! And like GRID, BOTs of GRID2 like crashing too. That Bruno Silva guy, before the race the radio will tell you he's so agressive and always crashing others, so he hit me, well, I can't blame anyone because they warned me the guy was dangerous. But when they tell me Eliminaciόn drivers are afraid of trade paint, those guys still crashed on me. My face was like "dafaq" as I was spinning. So since those BOTs made you so upset, why not spin them out or crash them out of track to take some revenge? No, you won't move them a little bit. If they crash you, you'll spin, and if you crash them, you'll spin too! And in two racing type the BOTs made themselves boss there. One of them is touge. In touge competitor will take penalty for hitting other driver. But in GRID2 it's directly disqualified. And here is the problem. If you crash them, you'll get disqualified, that's the rule. But if they crash you, you're still getting disqualified. Simple. The other one is drifting race. Drifting race is literally a series of jokes in GRID2. Just get behind one of your competitor and see how they drive and you'll find out that it's no even sliding, just driving fast through every corner like a normal race. And when you get to the finish you'll find out that they still have a decent score for that. Drifting itself is a joke in GRID2, drifting race is a series of jokes.
In career mode you can test drive your cars. But it's only one lap only in Indianpolis. So in real life it's reasonable because those race track will charge you for using their tracks. If you don't have much money you won't be able to go like 10 laps on the track. But come on! If you can't drive those racing car on the race track freely, why are you still playing it? Are we playing a race manager simulator rather than a  race driver simulator, if it ever is?
And, well, no Nürburgring, even worse.

Legends of Eisenwald plays a little bit like King's Bounty, but unfortunately lacks some of the polishing (and a lot of game balance). That alone made this game a lot more frustrating, when making things just a bit easier or just a bit more apparent would have tipped the balance.
The overhead map movement is an exercise in frustration because finding the correct path through the terrain isn't always immediately obvious. This led to a lot of pixel-hunting, something I thought we got rid of in the late 90s.
UI is a bit of a mess, as well. One commenter noted that upgrading was a bit of a chore, since there isn't a way to figure out what unit upgrades do; unlike your hero upgrades, there's no tooltip to explain what an upgrade does, so choosing and saving/reloading was the norm. I stumbled upon this completely by accident, but right-clicking the upgrade tree for your units shows a tooltip of their upgraded abilities. I have no idea why this wasn't included in a regular hover tooltip, and this could have more clearly been highlighted in the tutorial.
Finally, there are a lot of game moments where everything just feels unfair, without much warning. Spoiler alert: in the third act, you face zombies, which would be fine and dandy if I'd known that some units that are afraid of zombies will desert your army completely. I was put in an unwinnable situation since I'd chosen the ranged hero, and my whole front line disappeared. There isn't much build-up to this at all, and that alone put the stopper on any desire I had to play onwards.
All in all, not recommended.

At first, I wasn't too sure about the combat system. It seemed too simplistic (i.e., there weren't going to be enough tactical options). however, I ended up liking it a lot and found the beauty in it's simplicity. It's quite different from any other turn-based strategy game I ever played; sometimes your options are limited but that just has to be taken into account when planning your strategy (the worst thing is when you are forced to knowingly send one of your soldiers into a vicious counter-attack).
Unfortunately, you will sometimes have to endure walls of text. And let me be clear I have no problem reading text in my RPGs. When it's well-written, I like it just fine. But some of the many legends in Legend in Eisenwald (usually encountered as rumors in taverns) are… shall we say, needlessly verbose. They just go on and on and on. And while they are usually somewhat interesting and may even play an important part in the main story, I feel that many of them could be cut in half without losing anything substantial.
Some other things I wasn't crazy about:
*At the end of most chapters, you say goodbye to most, if not all of your soldiers and their gear.. That means all of the units that you worked to build into powerful army will be gone and you'll have to pretty much start over building your army in the next chapter.. leveling up peasants and buying basic equipment.
I understand that this probably done for game balance reasons (and in particular, to give you incentive to conquer enemy castles, which allows you to hire additional units)…. nevertheless, its very irritating to lose all your veteran soldiers and their gear, and the game usually gives very weak rationale for this (e.g., someone tells you that a large force will attract too much attention so you can only take two units… But then as soon as you get the next chapter, you'll likely recruit more troops ASAP). I would've preferred if the game was balanced to take more of my units with me… You spend a lot of time rebuilding your army in each chapter, and while that can be fun for awhile, it inevitably feels like busy work.
*Moving across some areas in the game can be pretty painful… I constantly experienced misclicking as it's seldom clear where you can and can't go on each area... Lots of twists and turns. It would have been nice if you could double click on a point on the map and have it plot a course to the destination… Instead, you have to actually see the place you want to go to, and since your field of view is so small, you will have to constantly rotate the camera to try to see whatever town or building you're trying to get to.
*There were a few instances where enemies respawned. I could understand if they were vampires or something, but no, there in one chapter I remember regular enemies coming back to life and retaking the castle.
*There were some instances in the game where my character makes some morally questionable choices that I would not have liked to do… There's perhaps a couple times in the game when you can make a choice, but for the most part your character is going to complete their quest by any means necessary. It's a bit frustrating in a role-playing game when things like this are decided for you… In the final chapter in particular, it seems my character acts based on a decision I made several chapters ago..
The final chapter dragged on a bit as you have to clear a bunch of castles, but I found the battles to all be rather easy (except the final battle which had an insanely powerful enemy).
Other than that, I really liked the game overall and would recommend giving it a shot if you want to try something different. The music is fantastic and the combat / character class progression system is simple, yet effective.

First and foremost, recommending this game.
Pros:
1. co-existence of variety and depth in combat mechanics; for example, weapon type diversification, unlike the almost purely visual differences in most other RPGs, carry significant inherent differences that makes weapon type choice a strategic decision; a multitude of functionally distinct units, troop count limitation and intentionally confining combat map mean that homogeneous unit composition will be countered hard, thereby forcing the player to build for complementing roles rather than legions of identical units.
2. Windy yet convincing plot, which tie with complex characters.
3. By layman's (mine) standards, highly authentic reenactment of medieval thoughts, beliefs, customs and trends (goes into a con later)
4. literally epic (purple text and expectedly powerful) loot for warrior, filling helmet, body and weapon slots (the big 3) by mid-game, with potentially 2 optional yet extraordinarily difficult encounters to test your mettle, resolve and tact.
5. free-rein editor to carve out your own designed scenarios
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cons
1. lose virtually all companions when progressing towards all but the final scenario
2. on all difficulties other than easy, upgrading unit classes take a long time, especially if your unit is the high power, high experience requirement type (cough, noble)
3. poor transitional optimization; when triggering dialogue, buying/selling an item, or exiting a shop, the wait time seems a bit too long
4. stringent location requirement for triggering events
5. not recommended if you are Jewish and sensitive about it (as employee of an accounting firm, I borderline feared for job security while reading some of the lines); while this is part of the reenactment and a very accurate one, I don't see this bit has to be mentioned.
6. excessive randomization in shop content, forcing me to scour the map for suitable companion equipment
Dishononored and Hitman are far better in this genre.

(At the time that this review is released, I will have NOT beaten Thief yet. I may change my feelings/opinions on it as I progress the game)
Thief is a good game for any of you stealth gaming enthusiasts.
Although it's story is NOT very interactive, and you don't get the same sort of emotion you would get if you played any games such as, The Walking Dead by Telltale, it is still an overall good game.
In a graphic perspective, the game itself is very nice when it comes down to details, shadows, and lighting, but other than that the gameplay feels at points either too jumpy, or too slow paced. At some areas it feels like you have no idea what is going on, and you just want to 'beat' the chapter.
As of playing this game, I can't help but feel the way I did when I first tried to get into the game, 'Dishonored'. I kept feeling like I couldn't comprehend what was happening no matter how much the story progressed, and in the end I just got tired of it and had to stop playing it. Thief feels relatively similar to Dishonored's gameplay, but are not nearly the same in a matter of combat, or storyline. The stealth in Thief, which is what is made out to be it's "core gameplay mechanic", works very well if you try to play as a thief who must hide in the shadows and stay hidden. This can make the game feel VERY slow after a while, and eventually I gave up on hiding, as it proved useless when no guards where around.
In the aftermath of all that, this game does have some pretty bad AI. The AI which ussually consists of guards or at some points, just average townspeople, which seem to have a pretty mental way of thinking. If you throw a bottle directly at them, they either start getting confused, or walk in the complete opposite direction of where the sound percieved of the bottle smashing was heard.
You may be thinking at this point, why am I not stating any real positive outlooks on Thief? Well, that is simply because their isn't many. Like I stated either this game more or less a lighting showcase with some stealth and parkour.
After defeating the first Chapter/Tutorial stage, you seem to notice a severe lack of things you could steal. At this point, it's more or less a parkour simulator with a few confusing stories and characters that I just don't seem to get attached to, or relate to at all. In fact, as of playing this game the only emotion I have felt is anger towards the AI for somehow not being able to spot you less than 2 inches away, while standing INFRONT of them... If your one of those people who want to look for a cool game that has action, "parkour" or stunts, and an interactive story, than this game is not for you. However, if you are looking for a linear game that focuses on one main topic and task, than this game is for you.
Overall, I would say this game would get 6.5. Although I put a some-what negative look on Thief, this game could be fun for anyone who may have enjoyed games such as, Dishonored and Metal Gear Solid, and I would recommend it to any new-commers to stealthy gaming industry. However, if you are a fan of the original Thief series, and not this decently okay reboot, then I suggest not getting this game. Although I have never played any of the original Thief games, I have heard from many fans of them that this game misses out on some of the key elements used in the original games, which leads many original fans to dislike the way this games story and gameplay was delievered.
Well that is it for my review of the game Thief, I hope you enjoyed reading this, and if you were wondering whether or not you wanetd to purchase this game I hope I helped you in making that decision.

I'm conflicted by this game. I really do want to like it more than I do. It's a good "Thumbs in the middle" type of game, but if I had to choose a side, I'd lean towards Thumbs Down.
The gameplay is fun enough, but it's also the main hangup of the game. The main game is just too easy. There are only a couple of battles that are the least bit tricky. Most of the game is easily cleared with a mindless hack and slash style and no need for strategy. If that's too tough for you, just about every character gets an AOE skill or two that can pretty much vacuum up all the enemies in front of them and spit them out on the ground so they're harmless and defenseless against a rinse and repeat of the same tactic. Bosses seem to offer little challenge, most can be dispatched with button mashing, a few require you to use a tailored strategy to beat them, but even this is overly simplistic. You basically need to do one thing aside from the usual mindless hack and slash to take them down, and they offer no real resistance. The post-game ramps up the challenge, but I really didn't enjoy the experience of feeling like I was playing two games here, one for the younger crowd and one for the older crowd.
The other complaint I have is with the shallow story. It feels like it was crafted for the instant gratificaton crowd, and I hate that. There are basically two things going on; Gathering your party members, and progressing through the storyline. They go hand in hand. The catch is that once you finish the former, you're also right at the end point of the game. Then, right to the post-game, which is just a mish mash of added quests and time rushes on boss fights to unlock their veteran form. I felt extremely disappointed when I realized I was at the end of the game, with no time to really try out the new characters in my party. It felt like I should have been halfway through, or at best 75%.
Again, it feels like a game that could have been so much better, but was rushed. Add to this things like the in-game achievements, most of which are just things you accomplish in the course of the game anyway (there's even one for each boss you kill along the way, and of course you get rewards for these "participation trophy" achievements), and you have a game that isn't going to appeal to most of the lifelong Dragon Quest fans who are used to an enriching storyline that could keep you hooked for days on end.

Dragon's Wake was a game I purchased because, one, it was on sale, and two, the idea of a game with a dragon main character is something I had been hoping for! The game itself is charmingly simple; I won't give any spoilers, but all the puzzles are simple to figure out and the success of discovery is a great feeling throughout gameplay. Without any words, the story is able to be told well, and I think that is a selling point in an of itself.
The game does have a few technical cons. At some points when I was changing screens, I found my dragon getting stuck in rock walls! (haha I did manage to get an acheivement for flying for ten seconds because of that). Sometimes, especially with a controller, the button presses don't seem to compute properly and I had a hard time breathing fire because of it, or beating the final boss. But even with those issues, I managed relatively quickly, and there's nothing I saw that would cause progess to be lost. Once you reload, the dragon loads in his proper place again and all is well.
I think the thing I was most impressed with was the flying, though. Not only does it seem far more real than any other game I play with similar mechanics, it has a puzzle solving charm to it all its own! Managing to fly for longer and longer periods of time seems like a key part of the dragon's growth as well, and I found myself jumping and flying around just for the pure fun of it a lot of times! It's very, VERY well worth it.
The money was well spent. I look forward to more innovative ideas and cute stories.

No storyline/campaign to speak of. I really wanted to like this game, as I loved the first one, but honestly, you're better off sticking to the first game. There is no incentive/reason to continue playing this game, other than obligation. The only back story you get is from the description of this game on the Steam page. Unlike the first game, there is no reason to do anything related to the campaign in the actual tower. There is no reason to change up your menu every few days, there is no reason to pay attention to the weather outside, there is no ability to spend money on things other than food (in the first game, you could pay money to decrease the number of chores/speed up the length of time chores took to complete), and there is no reason to put challenging items on your menu because someone will offer you extra money if you can pull off a combo with that item on your menu. All of these were in the first game, and are nowhere to be found in this one. The only thing they've improved is the range of food items available, but with no incentive to change the menu since menu items don't go 'stale', there's no incentive to try other food items out.
Secondly, some of the controls are incredibly clunky. It says there are ways to bind different keys to each individual dish, but either this hasn't been implemented yet, or it doesn't exist because I can't do so. There should be a way to change the sound and display settings while you are playing, instead of having to exit a game, go back to the main menu, and then change it. Not to mention the fact that the sound isn't even controlled by a slider, you have to left click to go up in increments of 5%, and right click to go down. Not to mention probably the most nightmarish store 'designer' system I  have EVER encountered. I could not have imagined a less intuitive system for decorating a restaurant if I had tried. Clicking on items to put in your restaurant doesn't work, you have to scroll towards the item that you want, and clicking somewhere will make it appear on the screen. If you want to deselect, don't try clicking anywhere on the menu, instead, right click. If you accidentally placed something in the wrong place, right click all the way out of the questionably named 'create' setting, and click on the 'edit' setting. Then, instead of clicking on the item in your restaurant you want to move, select the TYPE of item you want to move/delete, then, use your scroll wheel to scroll to the item. Also, this scrolling system doesn't rotate back around. If you want to remove a bunch of things, you have to go through that process again, and again, and again. There are also a bunch of bugs that need to be fixed with this system as well, including lights not replacing other lights, or random lights you haven't selected popping up and becoming a permanent, although unintended fixture of your restaurant that you can't remove.
Tl;dr there was so much more nuance and actually interesting aspects of the first game compared to this one. This game feels like one restaurant after another, with nothing to make it into an actual campaign. Can't increase your buzz, dishes don't have weather/time of day specifications, and dishes can be on your menu for however long you want. It's also clunky, and definitely NOT suited for keyboard and mouse, although I can't imagine it'd be easier for controller either. A very poor follow up to what was a brilliant first game. Hopefully a number of these issues will be changed later, but you shouldn't release a game that isn't finished.

I want to start this by stating I am enjoying the hell out of CSD2. A lot of the mechanics stay similar to CSD1 but have been streamlined in some great ways. For example, i’m a hunt-and-peck typer so using the keyboard--while optimal--is troubling at later levels so aiding the use of the mouse is huge.The game itself looks fantastic and runs just as smooth as the original. At this point i’ve played about 9hrs and I’m still going pretty strong.
That being said I feel like CSD1 was the primal cut off the cow containing all the sub-primals and secondary cuts of meat. Sure it takes some work to get the meat you want and there might be some cuts in there you don’t want or maybe don't use as much, but it’s there; All of the bone, fat, and gristle is there too. My example is the Iron Chef mode that I never touched (just didn’t click with me). CSD2 is a secondary cut from one of the CSD1 sub-primals since it has exactly what you would expect and has very little fat or gristle, but if you’re looking for more it’s just not there.
Want to specialize your kitchen? Just buy the food, your kitchen already has everything it would ever need apparently. Looking to gamble a little on a perfect day? You apparently left your computer in SherriSoda Tower so no email here. Screw up a bunch of chore tickets? No worries, the health inspectors are all on vacation. Rainy Day? Sunny day? Who cares? Weather is there but I can’t find any noticeable impact when I change my foods or move to a specific chef-for-hire location. In fact it seems like all attractors and detractors have been removed so there’s--as far as I can tell--no difference between foods other than prep, use of holding stations, and amount of money you put in.
On the whole it feels like the game is in some form of sandbox mode that strips out the fluff and just gives you the core gameplay loop. I’m enjoying the hell out of unlocking little bits for my CSD restraunt and new chef-for-hire menus but this doesn’t feel like a campaign. I know the email system wasn’t the most useful but it gave you a sense of scale. Right now I feel like each “day” is just another round of minigames.
I worry that in an attempt to cut the primal down to the perfect filet the chef cut too much off and didn't leave enough for the customer to enjoy.
TL;DR:
CSD2 is a blast to play but it feels like the “campaign” is only in name, no real direction or flavor text to speak of. The core gameplay loop is great and some mechanics have been changed for the better but I fear new players to the series may become lost.

First of all, I'm such a fan of the first CSD, that I created a Twitter account for the only purpose to follow the devs tweets. He seems to be a nice guy and he's putting a lot of effort to make this game awesome. Plus, he's keeping the community up to date about what he's working on.
Unfortunately, I need to be neutral about the game to give a review and possibly feedback to improve the game:
POSITIVE:
- Really gorgeous artwork! It makes you feel comfortable as soon as you launch the game.
- Awesome music! The jazzy and sometimes funny soundtrack is exactly how it should be. Don't know if it beats the main "Cook, Serve, Delicious" song from the first game, but still impressive :-D
- A lot of foods and drinks to choose from. There's a quite big amount of stuff you can buy to use in your own restaurant.
- You can play the whole game in co-op!!! This is the main reason why I bought the first one and absolutely wanted CSD 2.
- You got a lot of options regarding the controller you're using and how the buttons should be visualized ingame. Even if you're using a PS4 controller on your PC and Windows would identify the controller as an XBox controller, you can tell the game to show you the right buttons (X, square, triangle and O).
- You can design your restaurant, which is a cool new addition.
- The concept of the game itself is super fun.
NEGATIVE:
- What made the first game so awesome was the progression system. The more and better you played, the more stuff you could unlock that really made a difference. More prep stations, a small box to get tips from your customers, faster ways to clean the toilet and so on. Finally, at the end of the game, you had a really different restaurant than the one you started with. In CSD 2 you basically start with everything you had to work for in the first Cook, Serve, Delicious game. Which would be ok, if you could still unlock tons of other things you couldn't before, which isn't the case. The new design feature is great, but purely an aesthetic thing. So it's a good addition to the game, but doesn't help to get a feeling of progression at all. You also had an e-mail feature where you received new mails from different types of people after each working day. From chef cooks, weird spam mails, girls stalking you, to bonuses from good working days. This feature isn't there at all atm BUT should be introduced pretty soon. I don't know how much this will totally change the progression aspect, but I hope it will a lot.
- Run your own restaurant and/or work for others. It's great in theory, unfortunately not well executed for my taste. In the previous game you had to run and improve your own restaurant. Now you also have the choice to work for others. How the game is designed, it makes you feel like your restaurant isn't that important anymore and you could also skip that part. On the other hand, I like the fact being able to work for others, but only if there's a real advantage in doing so and if it would be a much more special experience. Right now it isn't. So I've got the choice between running my own restaurant and having nothing to do except buy some new foods to do the same thing and no real progression, or working for others and doing the same thing, except buying foods. In the first game you had really cool special events to work for others. They were fun and different.
- More foods and drinks, but not necessarily more fun. There's a big list of foods and drinks to buy and choose from. Being the fact that I can't feel the big difference in buzz they do for your restaurant and that there's no real progression, I don't really know why I shoud spend money on this. You can't even upgrade your food for better quality recipes like you could in the first game. On the other hand, I couldn't find other things to spend my money on neither.
- Different co-op experience. This isn't absolutely a bad point. In the first game both players had different jobs to do. The one took orders and the other one prepared the menus. If you wanted to change your task, just change the controller. In CSD 2 everyone can take an order and prepare food. There's no feeling of sharing tasks anymore, but now everyone is able to do both. Which isn't bad, but would be great if there would be an option to choose between both ways to play in co-op.
- The deadline for releasing this game was just too short. I worked myself in a gaming company and I'm aware that it's not always easy to keep deadlines. But hey, that's the advantage in being an indie developer: You don't need to argue with so many people that quality should be the very main priority :-D Some of the issues I and many others have with this game regarding progression, could maybe have been resolved if the game would've been completely finished.
- Loot boxes. This is just a detail, but still wanted to mention. When you level up, you get new items to change the aesthetics of your restaurant. How do you get them? In loot boxes. This is something I'm used to in games from companies I don't appreciate like f.i. UbiSoft and Electronic Arts.In a game like this, I would love to get the stuff in a more realistic/fitting way. You could get this information by mail from furniture companies or whatever other idea you have, making it feel a bit logical. Just not with randomly appearing loot boxes.
I don't want to give the impression that this is a bad game. It's good, especially for this price tag. But it just doesn't make me want to play the game constantly like the previous one did, because there's nothing I'm looking forward to unlock and no significant progress in the game. I also compare it a lot to the first CSD game, which some people may find unfair, cuase it's still a good game. But to me, if there's such a big difference in how the game keeps you in, I have to give this one a negative review and need to point out that you need to buy the first Cook, Serve, Delicious game! It's such a good game and the awesome dev will still get money for an awesome product! For sure I'll change my review if the next updates bring a significant progression system to the game that makes you feel like you're really improving your restaurant.

From the creator of Prince of Persia, a fighter remade from early days of computing, 1984. Objective is to rescue the princess held captive by the evil warlord. You get three fighters though the ultimate objective is to not have to use numbers 2 and 3. The first fighter is weak and that's where the challenge lies. Upon his failure he is replaced by a stronger fighter. Upon his death he is replaced by an even stronger fighter. The princess is happy to be freed but wants her true love, fighter 1 to rescue her.
Unlike the 1984 version this version is based almost solely on counters. By listening carefully to the musical score you can discern the number of attacks to which you must block. After successfully blocking the last attack you can counter, damaging the opponent and whittling away his health. There is a chi system that allows you to stun your opponent as well as a health recovery system after some but not all fights.
The game itself is quite short but the path to freeing the princess is challenging and the ambiance of feudal Japan is immersive. The game is also available on the IPhone but does support 1080P and controllers on the PC.

A depressing, heart-wrenching reminder of what man is capable of doing to his fellow man in times of utmost necessity.
Would you stick by your principles and morals whilst all around you abandoned theirs? Would you refuse to steal, or to kill? Would you stand by your guns and remain steadfast in your morality, your
, even whilst your family are freezing; starving; dying of disease?
Many wouldn't.
I didn't.
And that, I believe, is the true value of this game. It made me think, a lot more than any other game I've recently played. It made me sit down and think about what I was doing, and why I was doing it.
And it made me realise something:
These characters, these
represented by pixels on a screen, could be any one of us, given all the wrong circumstances.
With that knowledge also comes the understanding that, at some point in time, in some oft-forgotten conflict, a real human being decided they had no choice but to do exactly what you just did.
That broke me, personally, for a while.
It's depressing, it's soul-crushing, and yet it's somehow still so compelling.
It's us, as a species, trying to survive the torture that we create for ourselves.
War is hell.

A gamepad is absolutely a must for this game. 360-degree controls are nice, but moreover, certain missions (for instance, the final mission of the first set) almost require you to move diagonally while also switching colors, which requires three keyboard inputs. Due to how keyboards are designed (google "keyboard rollover" for details), three simultaneous inputs aren't always recognized.
The UIOP keys (used for color switching) aren't typically used often in games, so even specially-designed "gamer keyboards" may have problems with this (most prioritize isolating circuits on the left side for WASD-area movement).
If it was possible to rebind keys this wouldn't be an issue, but the developers - for whatever reason - have not implemented this option. UIOP is pretty weird to begin with, and even without key jamming I'd probably prefer them on 1234.
(to test your keyboard, google "Keyboard Ghosting Explained" and click the first link from Microsoft)
Ignoring this pretty major issue, the game is a fun little timewaster - nothing too complex, but (again, aside from the above problem) competently executed. But as it stands I can't give this game a thumbs up - we're nearly two decades into the 21st century, if you design a PC game, there's honestly no excuse for not allowing players to set their own controls.

Fun but lacking. It definitely adds some varitey to Civilzation 5 but at the end of the day it feels more like a really polished reskin/mod from the workshop than a full fledged sequel worthy of full price.
Pros
- Beautiful unit upgrades based off the type of "faction" you focus on
- More freedom in the tech tree (read: web) to go straight to what you want/need
- Espionage is more refined and a lot more engaging than in Civ 5
- Satellite Units add some extra tactical condierations
- Customizable starting bonuses*
Cons
- Wonders don't feel special...actually all buildings don't feel special, they are missing that visceral fun of having recognizable changes (e.g. Great Wall of China around the border of your nation,)
- Not a lot of personality from the small selection of nations (to be fair base Civ 5 didn't have that many more nations) but each nation feels the same, their personalities are further diluted by the customizable starting bonuses that can make a nation feel like another one
- Maps are a messy blur of blue and purple, resources are hard to distinguish from roaming aliens, city evolution looks don't change much
Overall if you LOVE the civ franchise it's not a bad game. But if you're a fan of Civ 5, this feels like a step backwards. Save your money and wait for a sale if you want to play this.

Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth, takes the Civilization franchise into the Final Frontier. Settling an alien world, with new choices, familiar themes, allies and adversaries, I found the AI to be more sophisticated than even Civilization V, with alien creatures capable of wiping out soldiers with a single strike in the beginning of your campaign. You must be on your guard as the terrain itself can be hostile, with miasma deposits that damage you when you get near. The research tree is much more extensive than previous Civilization games, and is more dynamic, as opposed to linear, with branches and leaves to the research tree. I found this game to be more difficult than V, but it has a decent tutorial system to help you through the transition. I think for hard core lovers of the Sid Meier's Civilization series, you will have those who love it, and those who hate it, due to the changes. I think it is a pretty fun game, even with it's new features.

So far so good. Game looks great and plays great (didn't even have the new driver installed and it played fine). Haven't played enough to get a real review on it but I just wanted to put out that it plays fine. Troy Baker has an amazing voice, not exactly the person I thought would do the voice of Pagan Min but hey it worked out in the end. Mouse sensitivity was a bit odd but I was able to change and now it fits me better. The, I forget what it is called so I will just call it this, mouse tagging was also a bit odd but I turned it off so now it is fine. Overall it is pretty good so far.
EDIT: OK, just beat the game and I have to say it is still good. I guess I will start off with the story.
Story: Not the best story I have ever heard but not the worst. Had to play as the voice of reason at times between the bickering children and they often got their feelings hurt. A lot of times the story didn't make sense, you come to Kyrat and suddenly you are the greatest warrior that ever lived. Far Cry 3 was similar in that aspect but they had the Tatau so it made up for it meanwhile Far Cry 4 doesn't. The story is important but not too important in a free roam game.
Gameplay: It plays like Far Cry 3 so if you liked Far Cry 3 gameplay then you will most likely like this one as well. They added a few new things that Far Cry 3 didn't have like Grappling Hooks, Beehives, etc. but for the most part it is just like Far Cry 3. Belltowers to climb in order to reveal the map and to get free weapons. Sneak in to take down an outpost, charge head on and take everyone out or just put down everyone from a distance. My favorite thing to do is come in with a Buzzer and a grenade launcher as my secondary and rain hell from above. Cars act pretty much the same, but they added a new feature where you can shoot from the car instead of getting out and shooting them it also has an auto drive feature so you can shoot without worrying about slamming into a tree. New Karma system which allows you access new perks and other things. You can also call in gunmen to help you out.
Location: It's alright but this might be a bit biased since I like city settings not forest/jungle settings. Lots of interesting places to visit with their own little theme. Kyrat is a large and open place to explore so it will be hard to get bored. The Himalayas is pretty fun to visit. They added snowstorms so you have to find oxygen tanks in order to stay alive. It also makes it harder to see and harder for the enemies to see you so you get a boost in your stealth. Haven't explored it too much so I haven't found everything up there.
Replayability: It has a lot of replayability. This game has a good amount of choices on what you should do. Side with this person and get this mission or side with that person and get that mission. I have only beaten it once so I haven't been able to see what all the different decisions will do but I plan on playing it several times in order to see what all the choices do.
Characters: MC isn't my favorite but not my least favorite. He comes off very awkwardly and bland. Don't really like the leaders of the Golden Path, one of them is stuck in tradition meanwhile the other wants to destroy it and move on often dragging you into their little spats. Hell I liked the villains more than the "good guys". Noore and Paul made me feel bad, Yuma made me feel pitty but the "good guys" made me feel nothing really, couldn't care less if they lived or died (except Bhadra, felt bad for her). Pagan Min, 7 words: best video game villian in my opinion. He beats Vaas in my opinion, dude is a riot. Couldn't stop laughing at the end and having Troy (♥♥♥♥ing) Baker as his voice actor is the cherry on top.
Wildlife: Eagles are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, straight up jerks. "Oh you minding your own business, just walking around? Caw caw ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥." A lot of the predators act the same as they do in Far Cry 3. Rhinos are rude, Elephants are pretty chill and riding them is fun. Terrified of swimming due to the Demon Fish and Honey Badgers are made of steel. Everything else just runs away like normal.
Weapons: A lot of Far Cry 3 weapons make a return and the weapon wheel is pretty similar except now you can't have 4 rocket launchers, only 3. You have to have a secondary which can be a pistol of choice, a sawed off shotgun, a crossbow or a grenade launcher. You can use your secondary in vehicles to avoid getting out to kill people. New throwing knife so you can take people down silently without a bow (or 360 headshot someone across the map). Grenade launcher mounted weapons and mortars which destroys everything in the way (I wasn't expecting that the first time I shot that thing). Attachments aren't really special, for example silencers, sights and extended mags. You can also give your weapon a new paint job just like in Far Cry 3.
TLDR: Game plays like Far Cry 3 so it is a lot of fun for me. Story is alright, not the greatest. "Good guy" characters suck, villains rule. Location is fine, but I am a bit biased on that. Wildlife is rude most of the time but they can be pretty cool. Far Cry 4 has the same weapons as Far Cry 3 but also has some of its own weapons. Also forgot to mention the game continues after you beat it so you don't have to worry about stopping before the last mission in order to continue playing.

I like so many others had been looking forward to the Thief relaunch for a long time with both great anticipation and daunting dread. Gaming has changed so fundamentally since the 90's that there was no doubt in my mind that any profit seeking entity would "modernize" the title with a heavy hand. Looking Glass Studios who created one of the most immersive gaming experiences in the orginal game
(not to mention System Shock 1&2 (especially 2)), left behind some great big shoes to fill in the form of fan expectations. Being Garrett lonewolf master thief observing from the shadows, taking his time and avoiding conflict by avoiding detection, the duality of being superior in ones element and weak, almost helpless out of it was what made the game. Garrett is no fighter any typical guard presents a monumental foe in a fair fight. That makes Garrett an atypical anti-hero, which was/is so refreshing and so risky, did Square Enix make Garrett more of a modern killing machine?
The Square Enix version. First of all I would like to say that I'm also a fan of several Square Enix titles and have many in my Steam library. I'll start by mentioning things I dislike in Thief:
-Bugs there are quite a few. A lot of people have performance issues. There are odd issues with the guards sometimes freeze in place making the game easier or impossible depending on where they freeze. Once you load the game they start moving again, sometime you dont know if the guards are really suposed to be moving or not so you are not getting the correct gaming experience... Another bug I had was when I saved while standing in a doorway with the door open when I loaded the game I was stuck inside the door unable to move, the savegame was useless. I also get strange flickering. There are many more bugs reported. So far it's playable though, still quite infuriating but nothing new in this industry that publishers force developers to launch an unfinished product. Lets hope for good and swift patches!
-Claw gadget for climbing. New maneuvering tool a claw thingie which pretty much has been made up only so that the there is some reason why you can climb in only the places where the level design wants you to climb. Hillarious when you stand on the street and there is some loot about 2meters up on a protruding piece of lumber on a wall of a house. There is no way for you to reach it even though the wall looks like one of those climbing walls on the playground and a soft gamer like me could easilly scale it IRL... Instead to get the loot you have to go around somwhere...
-Lack of jump sometimes makes for some ridiculous situations when for example a pipe on the ground can stop a strapping young master thief with the dexterity of a cheetah in his tracks...
-Rope arrow was kinda the ace inte sleeve before, didn't find a way to progress? Start looking for where a rope arrow might help. Rope arrows could be shot freely on wooden surfaces. Now there are blue tinted specific/obvious places to shoot the rope arrow. The whole thing is just another form of control from level design over the player...
-The levels are beautiful and I'm sure that designers have spent a lot of time on each and every room to make them individual. Even so I'd argue that the level design is lazy. The game tries hard to make it feel like you have options of how to progress. In truth you are being lead by leash all along.
-The main character has changed. Garrett the quintessential loner, introvert, sarcassm spewing, hater of establishment, outsider who likes it that way. Does the things he does because he feels like it not because others ask/tell him. He is equiped with unfaltering selfesteem and hes motivation is money or just pure challenge not helping and he most assuredly allways works alone! Not so in this time. Also the voice actor has changed (which I'm sure everyone is aware of), in a FPS the voice is kinda a big deal especially in a game where you didn't really interact with that many other characters.
-The story makes no sense... I feel as though they've tried too hard or something... In this case less would have been more... Any time there is amnesia involved (like pretty much every rpg ever) I feel like its a bit of a copout... While playing I really don't care about the story at all.
-Guard dialogues used to be great fun to listen to and still are in some cases, its just that the writing on average is not good and some of it is ludicrously moronic. Although I agree that this game is not "as" good as the older Theif games, by no means is it a bad game. And I don't see why people have to downrate or find every little thing they can nitpick about.
The entire game is in first person, you can look down and see your feet & hands, you can sneak around a corner and lean out from behind a box to check for guards, or you can run along the roof tops and not care one bit.
Although your not required to stealth through the game, it's hard... Not Impossible, but hard, to fight more then one enemy (it's better off to just run). Besides, why fight when they give you so many ways to knock out, kill, distract, or sneak around the guards?
You can...
-Shoot a torch out of a guards hand from the shadows (water arrows ftw)
-Toss a bottle / glass at a guards head to knock him out, or at a wall to distract a group of guards
-Sneak / run along the rooftops (guards won't follow you up there, these are no Assassin creed guards)
-Leave a body in plain site to creative a deversion
-Extinguish a lightsource or open a door that's in plain view of a guard (best to stay in the shadows)
-Or my personal fav, create sounds with your blackjack to draw a guard over
Every shadow is your hiding spot, and when you have none... there are occasional broom closets you can hide in to avoid a patrol or attempt to hide from an angry group chaseing after you. (although your likely to eventually be found if that happens)
Then we get to the sheen of this game, how good it looks.
I'm running it off of a widescreen TV in Big Picture mode (Hdmi cable from my laptop!) and I have most of the settings cranked up to max. Sure, there is a loading issue when you first enter a town "zone" (the town is split into ~3 main zones) as the entire zone needs to load a 2nd time before it plays at a nice smooth framerate.
It's obvious they spent extra time on every aspect of this game, cloth almost seems real (plus it makes reletively good cover from guard patrols). And every surface has a diffrent sound set for walking, running, dragging a body, etc. Not only do the diffrent surfaces change the sound set but they also help mask or unmask your presence. Carpt is your friend while broken glass, oil, water / wet surfaces, ploished stone, and more, all make you louder and in some cases can even give away your presence.
Bug wise, I have only found three problems with the game.
-Saving during / right after a scripted sequence can break the script when you reload that save. (Can be game-breaking on some levels)
-Occasionally a table or chair will be missing, or you can see a "crack" in the world.
-Scripted event characters (corpses & characters only seen during a realtime event) have an odd tendency to suddenly show up in the refrence pose (without an AI).
TLDR: Overall it's a damn good game, and I'm still playing it!

LoE is a turn based strategy game with rpg elements set in "fantasy Germany". It's a medieval low fantasy world where magic and the supernatural are present but pretty rare and low key compared to a more typical dnd-esque environment.
Combat works similar to the older Disciples games where you have front and back lines meant for melee and ranged/support units respectively. The initiative stat determines the order in which the units act. Unlike in Disciples, units in LoE can actually move though options here are limited to attacking the nearest unit or using an ability or potion. There's a good amount of tactical options in terms of how and when you attack (there's a wait command), how you use your abilities,   how you build your squad and such though, imo, gameplay here is not as detailed or engaging as in Expeditions: Conquistador or Battlebrothers for example.  For one terrain plays no role in LoE except in terms of unit positioning. There's no traps, obstacles, "high ground", no attacks of opportunity or flanking (except for a specific "rogue" unit). There's a few unit types that fight better in difficult terrain and mounted units have to dismount in forests and buildings but that's it and it rarely comes into play.
On the strategic level LoE plays similar to King's Bounty. You move around in real time fighting, trading, conquering, training, completing quests, etc. One nice part of LoE compared to Disciples or Expeditions: Conquistador is that each of your soldiers has their own inventory allowing you to customize their loadout with certain restrictions depending on unit type. Your men and women also level up and "evolve" into new units with a few branching choices available. You can pick between 3 hero characters representing the usual melee, ranged and support roles.
LoE allows you to capture castles and various other locations to earn money over time and you can leave units in castles to be trained and level up on their own. However LoE isn't really a strategy game like Heroes of Might and Magic and like in King's Bounty the world is fairly static in the sense that it generally waits for you to act rather than actively trying to destroy you although there are roaming enemies that will harras you and capture some of the locations. This means that once you have positive gold income you could technically place some units in a castle and just leave the game running for hours while gold and xp accumulate. This makes some of these strategic elements feel tacked on and redundant, like LoE is trying to stradle the line between King's Bounty and HoMM but doesn't quite make it. But in the end it doesn't really hurt the game and there's no actual need to grind this way.
Story elements seem to be very much derived from medieval folklore as well as pagan and Christian religions which adds to the game's down to earth, low fantasy feeling. The writing is pretty verbose and there's quite a bit of lore and stories to read in-game which can sometimes contain clues for quest solutions or secret items. Since the writing is so grounded in real life history and myths many fantasy geeks might find it too mundane or boring. Personally I found it charming and a refreshing break from the usual high fantasy stuff but I'm also someone who always reads in-game books and lore and enjoys text in general.
Overall while I certainly wish combat had a bit more going for it and the strategic level was either better fleshed out or further streamlined (basically either KB or HoMM style) it's certainly a fun game for fans of turn based tactics. Just keep in mind I said tactics, not strategy.

I want to give some insight about this game to people who played the first one.
I was one of those guys who watched the reveal trailer some time ago, then read all the news from the developer and even joined the Discord server to trace it even more. And i told myself that it looks like we're going to get exactly the same game like the original Cook Serve Delicios! but better and with more of everything: food to cook, new holding stations mechanic, unlockable restaurant customization objects and a ton of challanges in the Cook for Hire mode. Great!
But one thing changed in the sequel - the classic restaurant management mode. The simplest way to describe it is to call it a sandbox cooking mode as most of the managing is gone. We are free to experiment with the menu without strict goals and time limits and our restaurant grows as we serve food. Money is also much less important as it can only be spent on new dishes. We also can't see how different food is affecting our menu, what was the case in the first game. I cannot tell if those changes are for the better or worse, it's just a different approach - some might like it, others not. And I think it's the source of most of the negative reviews.
To sum up, I recommend this game. Even if you don't like sandbox games, you will have more than enough fun playing all the challanges, praising all the new food, art and improved cooking aspect of the game. Moreover, the developer announced that at least some elements from the original game are comming back in future updates, like the emails, plus he will support this game with even more content. Buy this game!

In addition to growing your own restaurant by purchasing new foods and adding unlocked cosmetic decorations, the game features a large number of established restaurants to try with a variety of menu items (180 different foods to prepare are in the game). Also, you can play cooperatively with a second player (one on the keyboard, another on the mouse or gamepad), which is very enjoyable and makes handling more hectic scenarios easier. The goal is to prepare orders by pressing keys in a specific order; some entrees (and all sides) can be prepped ahead of time in holding stations to complete orders more quickly, but food does eventually expire. The simple, intuitive gameplay gives way to chaos, as many complex orders come in at once. Chores (like refilling the drink machine, cleaning the toilet, or taking out the garbage) also must be completed, adding to the disorder. The game is very addictive, and once specific key combinations become memorized, fulfilling orders becomes fun and majestic. Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! is a very enjoyable sequel, adding new strategic options through the holding stations, lots of new foods and restaurants to prepare them in, and rewarding cooperative gameplay.

This isn't a perfect game. The difficulty curve is kind of all over the place and the game is not for everyone; it is *stressful.*
However, it is still a fantastically fun game. It's frantic and enjoyable and there's so many more recipes than the first. The campaign mode is a wonderfully welcome addition - it lets you play around with recipes you can't afford and gives you a set menu with specific challenges in it, and all the food is delicious.

I am really enjoying the sequel so far. I see a lot of people complaining about difficulty, which doesn't make much sense to me. As someone who played into the end game of the original, I would be incredibly bored if the pace and difficulty had dropped down in the sequel.
As a game that is meant to be difficult and realistic, I think that the sequel is great! There are way more foods, and chef for hire levels. I do miss some of the story from the original game, but the developer is constantly updating and adding content. I'm really excited to see what he does for his planned DLCs.
If you haven't played Cook Serve Delicious before, I would recommend playing through at least some of the original to get a feel for controls. The game definitely drops you right into some pretty intense gameplay, especially if you're a perfectionist!
10/10 would burn everything in rush hour again

I loved the first game and love this one as well. Most of my experience has been local co-op using an Xbox 360 controller.
If you're a fan of the original, this version will give you some big features you always wanted.
1) You can customize your restaurant layout.
2) So many more recipes! Many are mechanically similar, but you can decide which one appeals to you (i.e. steak fingers or chicken strips).
3) Save several menu presets.
4) High resolution assets / slammin' animations.
You'll also get some cool new features you didn't ask for:
1) Holding stations add another dimension to the game. Prep burger patties so when you get a hamburger order, you can immediately slap it together and toss it at a hungry exhausted customer. Prep side dishes to increase customer patience. But there's a catch - they spoil, and create chores.
2) The co-op has changed so both players expedite orders and cook simultaneously. Overall, this is a good thing, though it has some tradeoffs. There's a lot more stuff happening on screen. You may collide with your teammate and get confused. Splitting the screen space means your work area is smaller. You don't get to be lazy while your friend cooks for a round.
Mr. Galindo did right by fans of the series with this iteration. The changes make a lot of sense if you're familiar with the first game. There are a ton of foods, a ton of restaurant decorations - every time you do reasonably well you're showered with loot. There are too many subtle details to mention (after the first few loads of trash, you have to smash the trash into the bin. Dude!)
Features I'd like to see:
1) Boosters and detractors are invisible right now, but this should be added in a patch soon, I believe.
2) Restaurant layout presets would be really cool. When combined with the menu presets, it would be like owning several restaurants... or maybe the answer is to allow you to own several restaurants. However the UI sells it, I want to be able to create layouts without blowing up another one that I liked.

Cook Serve Delicious 2 is my current pick for GOTY. In my view Vertigo Games has taken the excellent gameplay of the first title and made it even better, with generally superior mechanics. There's nothing quite like the thrill of desperately trying to keep up with the pressure of a Rush Hour, when the music flares up and the orders start rushing in. The amount of content added in this game is immense, with quintuple the number foods of the first game and an enormous catalog of fixed levels to select. That's not even counting the campaign mode, which is currently unfocused but has wide latitude for the customization of your restaurant.
You play the role of a chef, with the basic gameplay being the completion of orders from customers and various chores throughout a working day. Chore tasks have a time fixed set of inputs based on chore type, however most food items are cooked to order, so you will have to check the bottom of the screen to figure out what to do. On paper every kind of food is straightforward if you follow the recipe faithfully, but if you want to cook at lightning speed each food is essentially a different minigame to master. Once things get serious you need accurate execution and quick thinking to succeed.
While the core gameplay above is the same as in the first game, this game has added extra depth to the system beyond the stunning number of foods. This game adds the feature of 4-8 holding stations (at the top of the screen) you can use to prepare food ahead of time, especially useful during the lulls before and between rush hours. This includes some of the entrees as well as side dishes, which are a new addition. Holding stations can be used for side dishes or a subset of entrees. In short, the situation might call for different strategy, which deepens the already busy moment-to-moment tempo.
There are major changes to the campaign. In the current game there are several different game modes corresponding to your desired experience.  The 'Zen kitchen' mode is available for someone wanting to chill out and not worry about rush hours, while the 'Stress kitchen' mode is available for someone who wants to turn things up to 11.  Of the two main modes, the 'Chef for hire' mode has you going to several preset restaurants with set menus.  The 'Classic' mode (and the similar 'Standard' mode) is the most similar to the campaign in the original Cook, Serve, Delicious.
The previous game's checklist of requirements to earn stars for your restaurant has been replaced simply by the need to gain experience, which can be done in any game modes. You randomly unlock decor for your restaurant and some new foods either by gaining levels, getting medals in the 'Chef for Hire' levels, or by completing various milestones in your restaurant. I confess that I had a surprising amount of fun messing around with the restaurant designer after I had earned a number of unlocks.  I will note that since food unlocks are random that if you have your heart set on some particular food you will likely be frustrated by how long it takes to unlock.
The campaign gameplay is also changed by an overhaul to how buzz works.  In the previous game, your buzz was determined by the properties of the foods you had in your menu, as well as by the number of perfect orders from the previous day.  Outside of the new game plus mode, this essentially put a cap on how high buzz could get.  The new system accumulates buzz over time, so that as long as you're avoiding bad orders you will inevitably push the pace to something challenging.  Note, however, that you can manually reduce the buzz and the number of prep stations if you want something more relaxed.
In conclusion, the game as it stands has a staggering amount of content (120 foods, 364 preset chef for hire levels), and offers a wide array of options depending on your skill level and goals.  People who want to mold their own restaurant over time have the option of investing time in the campaign mode, and people who want a more predefined set of challenges can try to get medals in the 'Chef for hire' mode.  I wholeheartedly recommend Cook, Serve, Delicious 2 to anyone looking for an intense experience.
(Note: this review has been updated to reflect the changes of the 1.1 update.  Right now the only area where the game the game clearly falls short is the ability to customize keybindings, which is in the works but not available yet.)

Karateka is basically Prince of Persia 3D meets Asian culture. Instead of 1 hour to beat the game, you have 3 lives, using 3 different characters, each one with unique abilities. Once your first character loses a match, you continue from the last checkpoint with the second, and then when it loses, with the third. If the third loses, it's game over.
It has the charm that all Jordan Mechner's games have: no dialogs, no narration, only cinematics and the game itself. It is more combat-centered than Prince of Persia, but it still has the same combat mechanics: side to side camera, block attacks until you see an opening to attack.
The story is basically the same: young princess guarded by old man's guards and the hero must get to her.
All in all it is a very good game but a little more of the same. More an Arcade title than other thing. It's even catalogued as "ARCADE" over at XBOX Live.
Anyway, it's worth the while and a good game to pass the time when you don't know what else to play.

I would rate TWoM about a 7 out of 10 - This could easily be a 9 or even 10 out of 10 however I have to deduct some points for reasons listed below.
Procedural - Well... to be honest this game can only be called procedural with the barest bones of random elements. Dont be fooled into thinking every play through will be 'completely' different. There are approx 20 different locations you can scavenge and they always look the same. They have the same layout, cabinets etc are always in the same place. Only the contents vary somewhat (a cabinet may hold food and wood in one play and parts and wood in another). As to what will happen when you go there: every location has one of two possible events/scenarios at that location. Pretty barebones with the random element if you ask me...
Also survivors - There are basically 5 main survivors you can control, but they are always the same and have the same strengths/weaknesses every time.
Overall content - There just isnt enough that you can craft, harvest or build. Not by a long shot. No matter what 'random' scenario you have in your game you will always end up visiting the same locations in roughly the same order (by order of threat) and always building and upgrading the minimal amount of upgrades in roughly the same order of priority.
Despite the poor amount of overall content and procedural randomness I would still recommend this game (during a sale) as it shines when it comes down to gameplay and emotional attachment of characters. Some decisions you make can really weigh on your mind haha.

This game is mainly resource management (including time management) but the main draw is its dark atmosphere and dynamic story telling. You control up to four people you can switch to and fro from while in your home base, that also have their own unique emotions and needs. Depending on how you react to different situations, and the sometimes immoral decisions youre forced to make while out looting, certain characters can become paralyzed from severe depression and eventually leave your group. Characters can also become injured or sick if your home is too cold, their basic survival needs aren't met like food and sleep, or theyre hurt during a looting expedition/turmoil amongst your own people.
In your base you can build animal traps for meat, gardens for vegetables and herbs (used for cigarettes and medicine), water filters, beds (essential for sick survivors to recover), a radio and guitar (increases happiness), a stove for warmth, various types of workbenches, moonshine fermenter (increases happiness) and alchohal distiller (for medicine). You can also create cigarettes (necessary to keep certain characters happy/great for trading), weapons, ammo and armor.
At night, you have the option to send a single person out to scavenge while the rest of your survivors stay behind to either guard or rest, which I normally do during the day so my people can guard at night. While out, you may come across other survivors that may or may not be friendly. If they're friendly, and you steal from them, your survivors may take a moral dump and become depressed so its best to avoid stealing until you become desperate. On the flip side, you may discover an opportunity to help someone in need and give your people a much needed boost.
All in all its a great game that I've spent 10+ hours playing, which I consider to be an achievement for this type of game, and I intend to keep playing for another couple run throughs. A solid 8/10

Shortest Summary; The game has loss it's support and is now "Down" in some sense. Fortunately though it's mechanic was well created. The game bases its blocking in a Forward fashion meaning you have to actual direct your blocks. And you cannot GO IN 1 versus 25 players and expect to live, you'll get swarmed all sides. Top this off, however - The gameplay is extremely skill based, like a Tekken in a Gang fight.
You actually have to figure out what the other is doing, and if he/she is blocking, use a Guard Breaker combination - If he/she is not, then launch for juggling - Like you would in Tekken. You can use the walls for your Jump combinations as advantage (Using Ridika for example), if not, pushing people off with harder pushback/knocback combinations can yield a fall death for your benefit as well.
To me, this was an ideal game I would've loved to play heavily - Unfortunately I play it very casually when I'm itching for a Good fighter game - This is not a "Pure Action" MMO you'll be seeking - It's more like Tekken, or Street fighter, on how  precise your choice of combinations string together, and what they may do with one another - And what combos are better for XYZ situations. Spy Chameleon- RGB Agent, going into this you have to have the mind set of a time runner, and leader board player. The game is devised up into many different levels and a large amount unlock to you as you progress so you don't get wall stuck on just one mission. As you progress through the nicely designed levels the game gets much harder. The game does have stealth, and in the earlier missions it is of heavy use, done right with the ability to change into four colors in order to blend into your background, red, blue, green, teal. Sadly there is no color blind option in the menu.
The issues come from as you progress through the levels, the game turns into less of a stealth based, and more of a time runner. Even through the clock runs up not down, every movement has to be perfect, ever time carried out flawless or else you will set off an alarm and be sent back. This is good for people who want a hard time runner, leader board challenge, but for the rest of us it kills the desire to play again. The game is not bad for what it does it does right, but its not so easy, and can get annoying very fast.

In some ways it's a mixed bag but so far the likes have outweighed the dislikes. Partly because the dislikes are relatively minor things like the voice of garret being done by a different guy who does an ok job but generally it lacks the cynicism of the world weary protagonist from the first three games.
Not a big fan of the focus mode but you can either opt to ignore it's existence or go into the options and turn it off alongside the glowy prompts. Other options include being able to turn off those consolised "vault here" button prompts that infest games all the way through on the assumption you cant remember how to open a door the same way you did a few minutes before.
Combat situations are horrible but it's not a game where you're meant to charge headlong sword swinging into every situation. Alert an enemy and you will probably find a sword shoved through your back if you're not careful. So with that in mind I have to say that I think the direction they took for combat was a good idea, as garret mentions in the prologue it's about not getting caught. This does mean that the people who slashed their way through dishonoured will probably loathe this title but thats their choice to ignore the core of the game where you're a sneaky thief.
I would like to have seen the hammers and pagans still at odds with each other, even the more mechanical minded factions could have a place in the barons city. Certainly the excuse of adding realism is blown out the water by the cutscene at the end of the prologue where guys in hooded robes are doing what guys in hooded robes usually do in games.
Lockpicking is done well, although it's less fiddly on a controller, and not having time stop means you will be working on a lock while hearing a patrol get closer, knowing that you're not quite hidden.
There is a fair bit of freedom of movement although for some reason the rope arrows cant just be shot into any wooden beam which does reduce options. The climbing gloves from DS have gone (a good thing as they were a fairly cheap mechanic) replaced with the claw which is basically another way of mounting walls.
No jumping is odd but at the same time it is there as long as you run towards an edge you will auto jump across a gap or vault a wall. Similar to the freerunning of the AC series in some ways but so far without the irritations of the game thinking it knows where you want to go better than you do.
The city looks lovely and they do look like they spent a lot of time/money getting the lighting right and while graphics should rarely take precedence over gameplay if the lighting was wrong here the game wouldnt play as well.
There are a lot of repeated conversations in the open city bits you use to get between missions which you noticed very quickly so thats a black mark for sure.
