Note: This game is no longer in development as it was halted 2 months after the game officially released. However there are a few community servers still running as of writing though most aren't online 24/7.
ArcheBlade is a competitive online multiplayer action game. Using a variety of characters, you fight against other players using a combination of attacks and skills to gain money to buy cosmetics.
The controls are simple enough, you have the usual WASD movement, block, and attack by initiating a handfull of combos using the left and right mouse buttons. Some attacks also require the CTRL key to be held at some point. Other than combos, each character has two single-button Rage skills which use a seperate metre that builds up as you fight; like Street Fighter.
While there are clear fighting game elements, its gameplay is more akin to Action MMORPGs such as Dragon Nest than your typical fighting game like Tekken and Street Fighter. Each attack animation is long and drawn out and each successive attack does their own thing, similar to skills in most Action MMORPGs with the difference being a timing requirement. So for example, a typical LMB LMB RMB chain would do a Attack -> Attack -> Skill combo. As far as I could tell, none of these skills could be cancelled so if you miss, you're stuck on an animation. There's also no parry/counter system so most of the combat is around keeping distance, baiting attacks and stun locking.
Obviously, you need to perform your combinations at the right time for it register which can be a problem on most servers due to latency. Living in the United Kingdom, I've found a few 50ms to 100ms servers to play on, all of which felt somewhat laggy. Most inputs took a noticeable time to register and it's hard to know if an attack would land as hitboxes are all over the place and don't seem to map accurately between the attack animation and target. With this, you often end up activating random attacks and missing your target as they skip across the map. For a game selling itself as a fighting game, it's a major problem and is mainly why I don't recommend this game.
Balance-wise, there are clear favourites and avoids in the community but for the time I've played, I can't say for myself how balanced each character is as they require in-game currency to unlock (though there is a "try before you buy" training mode against bots). There's also premium currency but that's no longer an option, instead discounted DLC is available which just buys everything in the market.
There are definitely different play styles among the characters where some can be good at one-on-ones, hit-and-run, group combat and ranged combat. There are some issues though with balance. Some skills are just generally better than others. For example, one of the ranged characters has a Rage skill which shoots an unavoidable laser at every opponent on the map taking out more than a third of their shield or health. Also as most characters are limited to close combat, running away from battle to grab health is also often way too easy.
Being a game that just released before it was abandoned, variety is also lacking.  There's only 3 maps that the community seem to play: Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch and Capture, and other than unlocking characters there's really no other gameplay-changing aspect to the game. Everything else is purely cosmetic and even then there's not much there.
That's about it for Archeblade. A game that showed a lot of promise but sadly died prematurely.

As a big fan of the first game I really, really wanted to like "Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!!".  However, I just cannot recommend buying CSD 2 at this time; it is obvious that the game needed some more time to bake.  At the game's current state it behaves more like a mini-game instead of an actual game.  Overall, the game feels either lazy or rushed.
The Good:
The new holding stations are a fantastic idea and really change how you think about recipes.  Being able to prep more complex dishes and prepare for "rush hour" really adds a new dimension to the game.
The game itself also looks quite a bit nicer than the first CSD and the amount you can adjust the eatery's background is appreciated.
The Bad:
Despite having many new foods, a lot of them are carbon copies of each other.  For example, pizza is split into actually making a pizza per customer or putting a random pizza in a holding station.  There's also four different "slices of meat" for side dishes and all that has been done is a simple color swap to differentiate them.  Seriously?  I never heard anyone complain about a lack of padding in CSD, I'm not sure why this laziness has infested the menu.
The controls have also been greatly simplified to an annoying degree, to the point where recipes no longer seem unique from food to food (likely to make the game easier to port).  For example, in CSD, to make soup, you had to press letter combinations to select ingredients and then press the "down arrow" to chop them.   This made the game more immersive and different foods stand out.  The equivalent in this game is you select ingredients you need from one page, HAVE to press spacebar to switch pages (even if you know the letter for the ingredient you want), select more ingredients, and then press "c" to chop.
All this game actually is now is typing.  No other part of the keyboard is incorporated.
The Ugly:
This  game is a minigame and not an actual game.  The first CSD had a full-fledged campaign.  Emails after every day would add life to the tower and alert you of upcoming events, mini-games like Iron Chef acted as the game's "bosses", and lastly you had clear-cut goals to follow that showed you exactly when you would progress and you knew you would unlock extra items to spend your money on such as dishwashers or trash compactors.
In this game every day acts the same.  There is no health inspector days.  You simply select the menu you're going to use that day and that's it.  Money you earn goes directly into buying more food.  There's nothing else to actually buy.
Secondly, the game has a terrible difficulty curve.  Part of buying new foods in CSD 1 was buying upgrades.  For example, you'd start out just making two types of hamburgers.  Then, upon buying upgrades for the food, you'd unlock different recipes to add to the mix.  This allowed you to slowly become more profecient at making the food until you were comfortable enough to move on.  In this game you just buy the food and you have every recipe unlocked.  Good luck learning difficult food like Ramen and Sushi without using practice mode - which is far more boring of a method than actually playing the game.
Lastly, the game explains nothing.  This is likely due to the fact that the game itself is so content-light.  The restaurant customization feature is a hot-mess, as are the menus (that currently don't even accept mouse support).  There's a ton of food this time around (some of it exactly the same or color swapped, as mentioned earlier) and has few ways to actually narrow down the list.  The story of the game and how you lost your first business is nowhere to be found; you are simply thrust into the main game immediately.
What a dissapointment this was.  I can only imagine the development process was to blame, as the game was already delayed and doesn't seem to be any better for it.

A decidedly interesting take on the Sid Meier's: Civilization formula - those of us fans to the genre will recognize it well yet will find ourselves feeling as though it is little more than a "fan-based complete revisionist mod" to the traditional Civ engines. It is an alien planet and, like SMAC, there is a native lifeform with which each empire ("Sponsor", in BE) must contend. Sponsors may decide on technologies and affinities that determine how well (or poorly) their cities and units contend with the local fauna and flora, and this in turn affects all sponsors' abilities to eventually deal with other sponsors. Basically, in your efforts to advance your empire, you can fight the planet, try to integrate with it, or capitulate to its biodiversity. The result of these principal decisions affect your ability to deal with the other empires on the planet making the same choices.
In short: This is like Civilization 5, except
you get to deal with other empires, you must first figure out your "stance" on the local ecology and how to deal with it. For instance, in my first couple of games, I "defended" myself against the local fauna to the point it became hostile and I was fighting as much against the planet as my "empire" neighbors. In my last (current) game, I avoided entirely ever attacking anything on the planet, and essentially now the planet is my ally. So basically, the "planet" is an additional player that does not happen to count toward victory conditions but must still be dealt with on some level.
Nifty, but again - not SMAC. In SMAC, the "indigenous lifeform detected" bits were as "barbarians" in the traditional sense except that you could utilize them as cultural or technological resources - as forests, for instance. In
the alien fauna and flora are of one mind, so you are either with them - wholly - or against them. Again, a separate "player" that does not count toward victory conditions. Neat concept, but by midgame your strategy is in-place and the planetary biology becomes fundamentally irrelevant. Essentially, the early game is dealing with the planet; by midgame you've conquered/joined it and it's then Civilization 5 (you vs. other empires) as usual. At that point, the local biology is just a glorified barbarian horde - with miasma.
What does this mean for game-play? As with all Civ games, there are a variety of options you can setup at the beginning to determine world type, biome sphere, victory conditions, etcetera. But at the end of the day (turn), you end up with the typical paradigm: Decent starting location, slow advance to establishing a few critically successful cities, then - shoot for your preferred victory condition. The mechanics of
are such that it discourages rapid initial advancement - no city spamming, for instance  - but once you have a decent foothold and a few good virtues (think Ideologies) you basically are invincible from negative effects. So, struggle with social choices, affinity choices, deal with the local biome . . . then
you're a God in a tech race toward victory. Only on the more difficult levels, where the AI has distinct advantages, is there a challenge, and even then it is really only a matter of time.
is a decent game, but it really feels like more a "community generated re-haul" of the original Civilization 5 game than a game in its own right. There are some unique innovations, such as the veteran option for units depending on your affinity/ideology choices. You do have some choices in how to progress militarily, economically, and diplomatically, but in my games I have observed these effects are much reduced toward the mid- and particularly end-game.  Despite the shortcomings I have listed, I still have to say I prefer this engine/version over the Civ5/GvK/BNR original if only for the reminiscence that smacks of SMAC (ahem) but it still lackluster in that attempt.

First of all, let's start with a premise: as it was obvious from the screens and video of the steam page, this game does -NOT- play as a classic Dragon Quest game. Instead, it's more like Hyrule Warriors and other similar titles, where your characters take on whole armies at the time.
Let's put a few positive and negative points:
+ Gameplay is pretty solid, fun and enterataining.
+ So many characters from the other Dragon Quest games! It's a huge cameo fest in there.
+ Nicely remastered music from the classic games!
+ They didn't forget to include metal slimes, and by all means, they are as elusive and infuriating as they are in the main serie (as well rewarding!)
+ Tons of side missions!
+ Cool animation scenes
+/- Once finished the main storyline, the difficulty increases by a surprising amount with all the extra missions
- The plot wasn't that much interesting, nor the dialogues. Very, very vanilla.
- Fairly vanilla also the main protagonists.
- ♥♥♥♥ING. PROTECT. MISSIONS. There are -tons- of those. And sometimes the AI can get dumb and not walking away from danger (when you're protecting a person).
+/- The voice of this game's BBEG was so darn annoying. Also his "I already did it!" got repetitive in the long run. On a good note, it makes easy to hate on him.
Stay away from this at all costs. Don't say we didn't warn you!!

Reviewing this because of the sudden wave of ridiculous bad reviews. The game is a musou, meaning you can expect soemthing along the lines of Dynasty Warriors with a Dragon Quest theme. The production values are very high, the game feels very polished, particularly as this genre goes, and despite never really getting into the main series DQ games, I've loved the aesthetic and presentation of this game so far. It's not an overly complex or difficult game, but offers exactly what you should expect from the genre: tons of enemies in large environments, and a bunch of characters with crazy flashy movesets to dispatch those enemies. Beyond that, there's a lite crafting system, and a bunch of equipment to mess around with the tweak characters to your liking and playstyle. Also, I've seen a few reviews that say it's poorly optimized, and that's just not true in the least. In fact, I'd say this is the one Tecmo Koei game that is incredibly well optimized on PC. Ran flawlessly maxed out at 1080p on my GTX 770 I was running when I got the game, and continues to do so on a 980 Ti. I would say the $60 price tag is a bit high, but I paid $40 for it, and didn't regret it in the least. And that's coming from someone who has only ever really been curious about the DQ series and played very little of it. If you are a huge fan of musous and/or Dragon Quest, I think you'll LOVE this game, and that's exactly who this was made for. For those people, this shouldn't disappoint.

I am currently playing this game but i am writing a review because of all the negative ones that are here.
This is a wave based hack'n slash game, it kinda feels like Dinasty Warriors but it's a bit different in the combat.
You have at your control at the same time a team of four characters which you can customize however you want. There is quite a big number of weapons for every character, and they look different bur they play the same almost all the time. There is a levelling system which works quite well, every level up you get on each character gives you point to upgrade that character, there are three special abilities for every character, they are not in categories, every one of them is pretty cool and unique. The graphics are perfect for this type of cell shading, obviouslt the character desing is great considering that Akira Toriyama made it, if you've seen or read Dragonball you will notice it, a lot and that to me is a huge pro. There are lots of different monsters and each one is pretty unique. During combat you will be able to summon monsters and that adds a lot of deepness in the gameplay. As an hack'n slash this is not the best one out there, i really prefer Bayonetta over this, but it is also true that is a different gameplay. The sounds are great, you can choose beetween japanese and english languages for the audio, musics are great and sound effects too. I am really in love with this game, i've actually played just a bit of Dragon Quest on the ps2, and this is not a turn based rpg so it is not really comparable.
I've read about performance issues, but running this on a 980 never have me a proble, 1080p 60fps maxed out, the framerate gets locked to 30 when you're doing a particular type of attack that i won't spoil.
Buy this game if:
You love hack'n slash games, you like Dragonball, you are not looking for the most deep story and you just want to kick asses.
Don't buy it if:
You hate hack'n slash, you hate anime, you want a deep rpg like the other games of this serie.

Incredibly good. Bought on sale based only on user likes. So I wasn't expecting much.
This is the kind of game that takes you out of your comfort zone. It is a memorable experience.
You can't save the game to "try something out". You just can't.
(Obviously when you leave the game, you can come back to the same day as you left).
And it is a hard game. So ... what happens when you have a hard game with no saving? Something near to life. So don't try it out If you just play games to have fun. This game is a life experience. Not exactly funny one.
I'm very experienced with management games, but I resorted on saving all the time, to get a 'perfect' management. In this game you HAVE to risk one of your characters, and that's a feeling I didn't have for years. Fear!
When you have a "save game" option, you don't fear much, or at all.
So, in short, this game brings this intense experience. Specially fear of making bad decisions and having to live with it. In other games, if one character died, I loaded the previous save game instantly. I just could not live with that 'mistake'. Here you would begin a new story. And that's a lot of time. So I had to live with some losses. That was quite an xp for me  =)
Also the game is very well polished. No bugs, nothing annoying. If I was the QA guy, I would have nothing to suggest.
R.I.P The Game

Bought this game today since it was on sale, and for 8 pounds it's pretty damn cheap. Was a big fan of the top down tank game on the old TV consoles (can't remember name lol) so this game sure brings back memories. Gonna try and give a list of pro's and con's for the game so you know what you get. I've played it for an hour so far, and played quite a lot of stages so I think I've got a good idea so far. Also I've played it with an Xbox controller if it makes any difference. Didn't try it with keyboard and mouse.
Anyway, PRO's:
-it starts slow and gets pretty fast paced and hectic as you get more weapons and upgrades
-the levels aren't too long and fast to complete if you pay attention
-weapons are pretty diverse and it's nice that they upgrade to stronger versions if you take more of them
-there's quite a few types of modes and a lot of level types (so far), so you won't get bored fast :P
-SPEED BOOST is life (the gold coin powerup), best powerup in the game so much fun
-it has bosses! didn't expect that, and took me a while to figure out, but yeah :P; they seem pretty diverse so far (i've only seen 3)
-it's nice that the environment is destructible, especially if you take the piercing rocket which just shoots through everything :P
And, CON's:
-there's a few glitches here and there, nothing gamebreaking or annoying so far
-would have preffered if you could choose the color of your tank
-enemies sometimes gank up on you if you stay in the same place too long (dunno if con but I hate it)
-aiming has to be too precise to hit things, maybe a little leeway would be nice
-needs more announcements when getting something (like an upgrade) or when needing to do something; at the moment it's pretty vague and you need to figure it out yourself by trial and error (i still don't know what all powerups do)
-i think the speed of the tank should be a bit higher (most fun when speed is high)
Can't think of anything else on the top of my head right now. I'm not good with reviews so don't mind me too much :P. It's just my thoughts so far.
I recommend the game for the price it's at, especially now that it's on sale. It's fun and fast paced, and if you're a fan of top down shooting games you'll love it :P.

The game is a survival game, set during a war (if you hadn't noticed).
For once, you're playing as the civilian victims, not the soldiers.
Struggling through the game, without access to anything from water to food, you have to scavenge to survive, and repurpose what you can.
As you slowly drag your way forward in this game, more and more options open up to you, but the game is brutal and punishing, offering little respite or help.
Some might be inclined to call this a rogue-like.
The music in the game is memorable, and the game paints a very vidid picture of an actual situation. The summer of 2015 will probably always be somewhat associated with this game for me.

Do not buy this game. As mentioned by many here the game is completely shallow and in no way compared to any 4x games out there. At the strategical level there is no empire building at all. You have one wandering party you control with simplistic recruiting. There are a few wandering mobs to fight.
At the tactical level there is no depth. Even ignoring the lack of spell effects and other graphical elements there is no combat gird that you can use. You have no control over where your units get positioned in battle and really it matters very little anyways as there are no deep game mechanics that make that useful (Like FF tactics os any RPG strat game).
You merely click on an enemy, and your character will walk the ENTIRE length of the combat field to that person and mindlessly attack. The AI is absent completely, and is why these features are not there. There is some very crude path-finding and a simplistic algorithm for targeting units which the AI uses and that is it.
Character customization is a farce. You can change the way your shield and weapon look. That is it. So don't get fooled into thinking you can customize your character.
Oh and by the way, you cannot level your character in this game. Its bugged right now, when you load up your game from a save it forgets all of your upgrades in the skill tree. So you will be a level 6 character with no skills. This game should not be on steam it makes me doubt every indy developer out there.

I'm very mixed about my review, especially since this game is in early access level and in the middle of being worked on. I really REALLY want to like this game and my pros almost outweigh the cons but after careful consideration Ive come to the conclusion that overall unless they make some drastic changes to the game, I wouldnt in good conscience recommend it. Now its not a very expensive game, so maybe its still worth trying it out and finding out if you can ignore the major cons that pushed the scales out of balance for me. My review is purely informative, though I have to admit the game's frustration level outweighed my objectionable standing.
While this game looks much like Heroes of Might and Magic and Kings Bounty in how the combat system looks and overall map systems are designed and played, the combat you would expect and how static buildings are handled are very different. If you are looking for another version of M&M or Kings Bounty, This game is not it.
Combat takes place with single units instead of mass groups, and limitations on how many units you can have are based on how many castles you own. The castles only other benefit is that if you are attacked while in a castle, before your army is engaged the opposing unit gets wounded based on its level and defense. Siege equipment is not present at this time in this game at all.
So far from I have seen, you have a starting base of six units you can have (including your hero) and you get an additional unit per castle you own. For example, if you have one castle you can support one hero, two foot troops, two archers, a healer, and a priest. Im going to break down what the units are like in Pros (because I do like their versions) and other ideas the game excelled and is severely hampered by below.
Pros and Cons:
Pros:
Makes great use of the German historical background and some of its mythos. It really tries to immerse you in that culture of the medieval dark periods in its campaign.
The art and music is by far enticing like few games out there and makes great effort to keep in the tradition of Germanic arms and equipment of the time period.
Equipment is very easy to understand in terms of bonuses they apply to your units.
The Tutorial slowly integrates you into the functions of the game rather well.
Units consist of Melee, Ranged, Healing, Buffing, and limited Magic classes that really well integrate into the historical setting.
Units promote into different options and provide interesting additions to your game, each unit can be customized with gear.
While combat is predominately a "Con" for me in this game (see below), it does make sense that the front line limits melee from engaging in the secondary and tirtiary line of defense. I sincerely wish games like King's Bounty and M&M had that limitation in their games as well.
The Journal is very useful though it could be better streamlined when giving you notes in "Additonal Information" on where to find quests..I stumbled around a lot trying to find some locations that are not immediately available unless you find yourself close to them.
Cons:
Movement in combat is a happenstance; Melee units are directed by the computer towards specific targets. a Melee unit cannot move just anywhere on the hex board, they may delay their action to move them to the bottom of the turn line once, but hereafter MUST engage in units directed by the computer with no other alternatives. If they do not have skills that they can use instead (for example, if you have a peasant that would most likely die if he engages with another by himself) he must engage since he has no other skills to avoid that engagement. A unit's only other move instead of to engage into combat (outside of skills like parry, counter strike, as an example), is to retreat one or two spaces from an already engaged fight.
Healers, Mages, and Ranged Units cannot move except to retreat from a melee unit. They can only do their functions such as attack or heal, they are rooted to the spot otherwise. There's no moving to a better position in this game at all, and when suggested to the developers that this is a weakness to the game, they were steadfast that this would never change, as it would require a complete rework of the programming.
This may be a condition of the early access situation, so this one is not a severe con since it can be reworked or streamlined, but it should be mentioned. Sometimes healers will not have certain targets available to heal, regardless of how wounded the unit may be. Ive contacted the developers on the topic and I was assured the game is working properly and that most likely the unit was trying to buff the units instead of healing them since as healers are promoted they get multiple spell options. This was not the case but by the response I was pretty sure there was no point in discussing the matter anymore (especially after the pointless conversation to cover movement in combat).
The Market has a major limitation in that you cannot take something that your units are wearing and swap it out for something else. In order to upgrade, you must first buy the item you want, leave the market, switch items, go back to the market and then sell the item.
In the second chapter of the campaign game, four different leaders ask you to destroy two of their opponents for them to help you. One of those leaders sits in the large town and is not accessable in order to destroy that opponent. You can take his castles and land holdings but it will not count towards destroying him unless you confront him as well. Once you declare war on him, he will no longer be accessable.
The campaign in the third chapter is rather punishing. You are limited to jump through obstacles that require you to wait on other enemy units (which I dont want to spoil it for you, so Im being perposefully vague here) and at the same time are run down by an impossible adversary that requires you to keep on the run. After trying to play that section as specified by the game by its rules, I finally gave up when that impossible adversary showed up.
In conclusion, at this moment while I believe the game has extreme potential, unless they make changes to the combat system I cant emphatically suggest or recommend such a game system...especially since a game like this is anchored around its combat system. The campaign is nothing without it. If changes occur during development of course Ill be happy to come in and redo my review when (or if) that happens.

As a big fan of the first game I really, really wanted to like "Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!!".  However, I just cannot recommend buying CSD 2 at this time; it is obvious that the game needed some more time to bake.  At the game's current state it behaves more like a mini-game instead of an actual game.  Overall, the game feels either lazy or rushed.
The Good:
The new holding stations are a fantastic idea and really change how you think about recipes.  Being able to prep more complex dishes and prepare for "rush hour" really adds a new dimension to the game.
The game itself also looks quite a bit nicer than the first CSD and the amount you can adjust the eatery's background is appreciated.
The Bad:
Despite having many new foods, a lot of them are carbon copies of each other.  For example, pizza is split into actually making a pizza per customer or putting a random pizza in a holding station.  There's also four different "slices of meat" for side dishes and all that has been done is a simple color swap to differentiate them.  Seriously?  I never heard anyone complain about a lack of padding in CSD, I'm not sure why this laziness has infested the menu.
The controls have also been greatly simplified to an annoying degree, to the point where recipes no longer seem unique from food to food (likely to make the game easier to port).  For example, in CSD, to make soup, you had to press letter combinations to select ingredients and then press the "down arrow" to chop them.   This made the game more immersive and different foods stand out.  The equivalent in this game is you select ingredients you need from one page, HAVE to press spacebar to switch pages (even if you know the letter for the ingredient you want), select more ingredients, and then press "c" to chop.
All this game actually is now is typing.  No other part of the keyboard is incorporated.
The Ugly:
This  game is a minigame and not an actual game.  The first CSD had a full-fledged campaign.  Emails after every day would add life to the tower and alert you of upcoming events, mini-games like Iron Chef acted as the game's "bosses", and lastly you had clear-cut goals to follow that showed you exactly when you would progress and you knew you would unlock extra items to spend your money on such as dishwashers or trash compactors.
In this game every day acts the same.  There is no health inspector days.  You simply select the menu you're going to use that day and that's it.  Money you earn goes directly into buying more food.  There's nothing else to actually buy.
Secondly, the game has a terrible difficulty curve.  Part of buying new foods in CSD 1 was buying upgrades.  For example, you'd start out just making two types of hamburgers.  Then, upon buying upgrades for the food, you'd unlock different recipes to add to the mix.  This allowed you to slowly become more profecient at making the food until you were comfortable enough to move on.  In this game you just buy the food and you have every recipe unlocked.  Good luck learning difficult food like Ramen and Sushi without using practice mode - which is far more boring of a method than actually playing the game.
Lastly, the game explains nothing.  This is likely due to the fact that the game itself is so content-light.  The restaurant customization feature is a hot-mess, as are the menus (that currently don't even accept mouse support).  There's a ton of food this time around (some of it exactly the same or color swapped, as mentioned earlier) and has few ways to actually narrow down the list.  The story of the game and how you lost your first business is nowhere to be found; you are simply thrust into the main game immediately.
What a dissapointment this was.  I can only imagine the development process was to blame, as the game was already delayed and doesn't seem to be any better for it.

I really can't recommend this game even though I am still playing it and have lots of hours invested.  It really is a solid match 3 game but the meta game is the problem.  If you do not invest money (probably lots), you will progress at a snails pace.  There are so many heroes, and for the most part you will get them at random meaning you will end up with lots and lots of poorly covered heroes.  The higher the rarity, the bigger the problem.  Also you will need roster spots to even recuit the heroes you have won.  These can only be bought with premium currency (which you do get from playing) which means you will often have to sell your hard earned covers or pay real money for roster spots.  This is especially bad early in your career.  Heroes are added every two weeks, so the problem is only getting worse with time, not better as you would hope.
The biggest problem with the game though, is lack of new content.  I could live with the above problems if new, fun stuff was coming out, but I am playing almost the same game as I was almost 2 years ago.  Boss battles were added, but they are rare and alliance based (so not much fun if you aren't on a good alliance).  There have only been 2 or 3 stories added since I started (not counting rare, short events that are only seen once or twice a year).  That means 75% of the stories are against the Dark Avengers which means you are fighting the same villians over and over.  And to compete in these events?  You need to beat each pin (battle) 4-6 times.
There is also PvP but that is against AI controlled player rosters.  As the heroes are not the most balanced in the world you tend to see certain teams and heroes a lot there.  And they almost always be of similar strength which makes it feel very grindy.  And both PvP and PvE are time based, there is no content that you can play at your own pace other than the short introductory stories that you can only play once.  So to get the good prizes you need to devote lots of time to them.  Whether a paying player or not.
So bottom line, don't play this.  The match 3 is fun and can get some people hooked.  Do yourself a favor and don't let that happen.  At least until they address the problems above which isn't likely to happen.

The original CSD is one of the most fun and underrated career sims I've ever played. It was fast-paced and stressful as hell, with very little margin for error, but the feeling of accomplishment after finishing up a perfect day was fantastic. My main "complaint" with the game was that the small variety of foods made the recipes old hat after a while. Sure, you had a system of menu rot to encourage you to switch out items, but you could rotate between 7 of your best-selling items and easily snag perfect day after perfect day.
I'm very happy to say that so far the ceiling is a lot higher in CSD2. There are 200 menu items, with more to be added later on, and the new Chef For Hire mode (honestly my favorite mode now) encourages you to step outside of your menu comfort zone by making you cook other restaurants' menus. Some of the more obnoxious things were taken out like the need for very strange keybindings and arrow mashing for chores/wine/etc. Customer patience seems to be a bit better from the get-go and can be improved by fixing side dishes. No health inspections anymore, thank goodness, and the robbery "minigame" is a lot easier to manage.
There are two new features that took me a while to get used to after playing CSD for so long. The first is the fact that your recipes are separated into pages now, so you add some ingredients, hit space, add more, etc. At first I wasn't a fan of this, but I love it now. The pages are color coordinated with the recipe card and it keeps you from having truly bizarre keybinds because you've got 5 ingredients that start with S on one page. I would like to see consistency across keybindings, but I hear the developer is working on that.
The second big feature honestly changes up the flow of the game and makes it a lot more fast-paced. You now have holding stations where you can prep certain food items. They fall into three categories: Holding station required, holding station optional, and side items. Prime rib, for example, is a holding station required recipe, so you have to prepare it before anyone can be served it. But once it's there, you have (I think) 6 servings to distribute, and you just have to finish each one off with seasoning. Burgers are holding station optional, and these types of foods give you some control over how fast things are moving. Ready to blaze through orders at rush hour? Prep a couple stations with 8 burgers each and all you have to do is assemble them for each guest. Need some more time? Leave them off the holding station and you'll need to cook each order individually, locking down that serving station for a little while so you can catch your breath. The final holding station items are sides, and when prepared, those increase guest patience (giving you more time to complete an order) and guests can add them to their entree for an upcharge. They'll almost always order a side if it's available, so it's good to reserve a couple holding stations for them.
These features have made gameplay more intuitive and a lot more fun, in my opinion. Once you learn to integrate them into your routine, it really does take some of the hassle out of things.
Now, all that said, the game isn't without its flaws. The progression system was completely restructured, so you're not purchasing upgrades but rather unlocking new things including new restaurants to work at in Chef For Hire mode, high end menu items, more serving/holding stations, etc. There's a lot less focus on building up your own restaurant in career mode, and it seems much easier to do so because you bring money in hand over fist if you have even a couple decent menu items, like the prime rib you unlock for getting a perfect day in Chef For Hire. The removal of those meta management systems changes the feel of the game, and if that was something you liked from the original, you might not enjoy the current incarnation of CSD2.
Additionally, though price is supposed to correspond with difficulty to prepare, there are some menu items that are incredibly easy but sell for a high price (like steak), and some that involve a lot of tedium but sell for less. This makes it a breeze to load up your menu with big ticket, easy to prepare items (just like CSD) and cruise to success.
BUT... you don't have to. You control the difficulty in many ways, and I really appreciate that in a game like this. Overall, I highly recommend CSD2 to fans of the original. If you never played CSD and you like fast-paced career sims that put you in the day-to-day chaos, give this game a whirl--I think you'll enjoy it.

Ghost Control Inc seemingly has everything going for it. It's a game where you essentially play team manager for Ghosbusters! And it has a nearly-perfect blend of tactics and management gameplay! What could possibly be more fun?
Unfortunately, the game is marred by several issues.
Firstly, the art direction is uneven at best. Most of the ghosts have very uninspired designs that won't stick in your mind like those of other franchises involving catching ghosts. Several of the ghosts are just recolors or slight redesigns of the lower level ghosts you fight early in the game, so they're both boring to look at and repetitive. This also makes it slightly harder to tell what you're figthing at times.
Secondly, the writing is just atrocious. This isn't a story-driven game by any means, but there's still quite a bit of text, both in item/ghost descriptions and in the dialogue where you're offered missions. It often tries to be humorous but falls incredibly flat, to the point where you'll probably stop reading it after a while. There are also many spelling and grammatical errors throughout the game. The dev team's native language is obviously not english, which explains this problem but doesn't excuse it, as they should really have hired someone who could do a better job localizing the text.
The poor writing also affects the central story, such as it is. Certainly, the real story of the game is just managing your team, but there is an attempt at a mounting threat, but it's very bare bones and unengaging, and marred by more failed attempts at humor. Again, a certain other ghost-catching series knew how to build up a supernatural threat...
Lastly, the game is just incredibly janky and buggy. Crashes are relatively common, items will sometimes not equip properly, the interface will ignore your input, performance will start chugging wildly after playing for more than an hour, certain items and features won't unlock when they're supposed to, and most importantly, saved games will load incorrectly, switching character positions and stats around willy-nilly. It's a very frustrating experience to try to play a full campaign, as the game becomes less and less stable the more you progress and save.
While I would love to recommend this game, I simply can't in the state it's currently in. Some of the problems are down to personal taste, but a buggy game that doesn't save your progress is something that no one should buy.

Fantastic game! Especially for free, or just $10 for all the DLC content (costumes and cosmetic items like different weapons skins); it's a steal for such a quality game!
It's gorgeous, runs well, features a great fully-3D combat system that applies across all characters, yet all the characters feel diverse thanks to their abilities, and there's a good mix of modes in here, including team stuff, command point capture, and free-for-alls.
It lacks a bit of polish and refinement though; It doesn't tell you which maps are tied to which modes; that seems to be important, necessary information. And there's just multiplayer and a basic training mode; you can't check out 90% of the arenas from there, and you can't even pick different characters to go up against, just some dumb little robots. Also, combat can break down when too many people pick projectile focused characters and spam attacks on others from afar. But those are small quibbles for such a great game from a small, rookie developer; and those cons immediately evaporate once you actually hop into a match and start playing against some people.
Just brush up a bit on stuff OUTSIDE of the game if you get frustrated. Nothing will stop snipers from being annoying, but there are certainly some good Beginner vids on Youtube. And the Wiki tells you which levels are FFA, 3v3, 4v4, 5v5, or 7v7. Though if you just want to know the Free-for-all Levels while starting out (and avoid potential "noob letting the team down" situations), they're "Training Room", "Summer Island" and "Naga's Pit".
Highly recommended! Such a great game!

This game is a black hole of time, but at least for me I don't mind, I often have fun with the game when I  play it, and I look forward to the daily rewards. Despite being a "match 3 game for kids and soccer moms", I think that it is an enjoyable game, and way more in depth than anyone cares to give it credit for. +Fun and enjoyable, plain and simple.

As for the common freemium complaint, for the most part I am free to play, only putting in a few dollars to get one extra space, or trying the VIP program. Another 3D fighting game, another time to screw things up with a poorly written review by myself. This game is most likely  the first fighting game I've ever reviewed so take this with a grain of salt.
Lets start with the game itself. ArcheBlade is a three dimensional, ffa (free-for-all) fighting game, one that I've recently found. The game is in my opinion a 3D, third-person, highly skill based Mortal Combat (I know that Mortal Combat takes a lot of skill as well). ArcheBlade is (dumb moment, you have been warned) free-to-play, but if a person wants to get all 14 characters early or get the all access pack you need to pay a petty amount of money (9,99€ for the all access pack).
And since I've mentioned the characters, lets get to them for a while. As stated before there are a total of 14 playable characters, each with their own playstyle and combos. At the start of the game the player will recieve a total of 3000 Meceta (gold) to buy characters. You can
buy two since each character costs abut 1400 Meceta, which in my opinion is somewhat boring, seeing as it takes quite some time to get enough Meceta points to buy another character.
Moving on to gameplay. As I stated before, ArcheBalde requires a
lot of skill, something that will be noticed when playing your first online match. There are no crosshairs that helps with aiming (except with one character whose name alway eludes me), no way to if an opponent is within range of your attacks, nothing that will help you if you are new to the game. It is with this I came to the conclusion that this is a an experiance based game, seeing as the only way to get better at this game is by actually playing it ,unlike most games nowadays which are based on the over-powered items you've recieved.
Now you may think: "Wow, no bad things to mention. That's amazing!" There are a few things I've noticed with this game, albeit not many since I've haven't playd for that long *sniff*. The first thing is that there is no matchmaking, as stated by so many others before me, meaning that you need to find an appropriate server yourself, which can reslut in joining a server on which you've got <500 ping. Another thing that I noticed is that some maps appear to be bugged (can't remember thier names though), which sort of ruined for a friend of mine when he was playing. The third thing might have been server specific, but I'm bring it up just in case it wasn't, and that was a bugged mini-map. Normally the player icon and enemy icons should be on the mini-map, but when I played they were in the middle of the screen instead.
So all in all, this is a game I recomend to those that enjoy ffa, pvp action in a sort of MOBA style, best enjoyed when playing with a couple of friends of the same skill. And one last note: this is not a p2w game as other reviewers have stated, a statement on which I agree.
Hope you found this useful and have a nice day.

While there are many upsides, they are upsides that the other Civilization games have. I would recommend other Civilization games, but for some reason.. Not this one, at all. All the good things I can say about Beyond Earth and Rising Tide, I could probably say the same in Civ4 and 5.
The biggest downside is moronic AI teammate and the diplomacy system. They will declare war on their own, only to negotiate peace on their own a moment later. That's all good and fine... Until your relationship with them take a huge nosedive because they tell you to "Don't trust them!" and promptly take away 2 points from their relationship with you. And then they go ahead and declare war on their own a few turns later anyway, repeating the cycle. There's batshit insane, and then there's Civ AI - I guess I should've seen this coming.
Common Resource have almost no meaning, especially after a certain point in the game where a common farm can outperform plantations et al.
Orbital Units are fun, but after they are launched, you can't move them at all. This includes a certain flying octopus. "Hey, flying alien monstrocity, you want to nudge over a hex so that you can eat that ship alive? No? Ok.". A lot of that make no sense.
Leashing alien was fun until the 5th time you leashed a scarab and realize how pointless it was. Would be fun if you can use aliens to "Promote" units, like giving Marines better movement or ignoring terrain cost for hills/forest that's under miasma... Or something. As-is... At least they are fun way to make energy. "Come here, lil monstrous faceripping alien. That's a good boy, now into the gene smelter with you!"
It's like... The game could've been so much more, but it's a lot less. A civ4 or 5 space mod might've done more, and that's the saddest part.
Nice graphics, though.

GhostControl Inc. is an excellent game about busting... I mean controlling ghosts.  I've played about 12 hours now, and I'm confident that I'll play at least a few dozen more.
The gameplay is heavily influenced by X-COM, which is of course a great thing to be heavily influenced by.  The graphics and sound are polished and attractive.  The writing is a bit hokey but solid, and I'm eager to see where it's all leading.
Combat can get a little repetitive, though.  I played for a while on Normal, then restarted on Hard because I often found myself just standing in one place and spamming attacks while the enemies flailed at me with little effect.  So far, Hard difficulty is making things rather more interesting.  I haven't reached the highest tier of enemies yet on either difficulty setting, though, so possibly I have some nasty surprises waiting for me.  I hope so!
Overall, GhostControl Inc. is very good, and a definite contender for my Game of the Month.

Very fun free version of magic. Sure you have to get through a tutorial meant for plebs, but not having to repurchase cards in a digital form is great.
Pros:
- Free digital version of magic.
- Tutorials explain the game well for newcomers.
- Time limits seem ok for the most part (always be ready to stop the timer!).
- Mechanics seem to mimic the card game well (a couple of bugs here and there).
- UI is clean and intuitive for the most part.
- Artwork, as in mostly all magic games, is phenomenal.
- Bug fixes/improvements are added to the game when there's an update (more in the cons section about this).
Cons:
- There's no cancel button on the "Joining Session" screen. Which only matters if you try to play two-headed giant in the wee early hours.
- There are a few more sever bugs that happen occasionally. game can get hung sometimes with no real way to get unstuck, but it doesn't happen often.
- Overall turn time is set a bit high in my opinion. Some players seem to try and get coins by joining matches and not doing anything on their turns to run other players out of the match. When a player concedes the other player gets the win and the coins. A work around for this is to disable your network adapter when someone seems to not be actually playing. Once you get a message saying the enemies been replaced by AI you just enable to adapter again.
- There isn't a way to communicate with other players in a match.
- Bug fixes/improvements are added to the game, but only every time they do an update. So far it seems they only update the game whenever a new Magic: the Gathering set is released.
- To veteran Magic players the game mechanics may seem broken at first, until you disable a ton of the automatic settings they have on by default (be sure to check the settings before you play a match if you know what you're doing!)

If you're old enough to remember the old Rollercoaster Tycoon games from the last decade or maybe even Theme Park (which was so long ago now I don't want to think about it) you'll be on familiar territory with Adventure Park.
Familiar but slightly disappointing territory.
It is, but a little historical context is important here. Let me take you on journey back to 2005.
We were listening to The Crazy Frogs Axel F on our I Pod, watching Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith at the cinema and secretly hoping that Santa would bring us a new Xbox 360 for Christmas.
One of the other things that I found myself doing back the halcyon summer of 2005 was playing an amazing game called Rollercoaster Tycoon 3.
A shiny new 3d graphics engine, terraforming, customisable scenery, Rollercoaster Tycoon 3 had it all and that's before you start building the facilities and the rides.
You'd build a few shops, a few rides, maybe place a fireworks display or two. Employ some staff to run it all for you and tweak your prices to pay for them.
Then you could drop back down into first person view and explore your own park, even take a ride on that huge rollercoaster you'd just finished building! Now lets go back... back to the future!
Yes and no..... mostly no.
In the sense that you get to build your own theme park, rides, stores and all, then yes, Adventure Park is like Rollercoaster Tycoon.
In the sense that it is executed as well or as much fun to play as Rollercoaster Tycoon then No, no it's not like the classic game at all.
Yes, compared to the classic park games, it looks "nice". The graphics are fairly well detailed (if not pretty) even when you zoom all the way in.
Then again, the hardware we're all running has come a long way since that Rollercoaster fuelled summer of                                    2005, so this is really a given.
At first I found the tiny map size to be another hindrance to my enjoyment of this game.
Then I began to realise that this isn't a huge issue as there isn't that much content to place on them anyway.
The star attraction of any game like this is usually the Rollercoaster design itself. Unfortunately here, your coaster construction options are limited.
Want loops, spirals, curved bends banking and twisting their way around the scenery of your park? then you're out of luck.
The track design here is strictly an up and down affair.
Whilst playing I began to notice that the game felt hollow, empty somehow.
I gave up with the clunky controls and left my second "upty, downy" coaster half constructed to ponder why. Then it occurred to me, the reason this game was lacking any sort of atmosphere was down to sound, or lack there of.
No people screaming as they hurtle around the (just up and down) track of your painfully built coaster. no chatter of people as they stroll between the burgerstand and toilets, no ambient sound at all,
Apart from the occasional squawk from a stray flock of birds lost in the souless emptyness that is your "fun" park and some slightly irritating music, all is silent.
There are many little annoyances in this game that by themselves wouldn't overly bother me, but taken all together they become a pretty big distraction.
I could point out a host of irritations here but I think I can some it up with the example you are about to read.
You can't sit down because you need to achieve a 3 star park before you can build benches.
Benches! Wow, We need to get the R&D boys on that! oh wait, their is no R&D, just the star rating system to unlock objects.
I know this is a game mechanic to incentivise continued play but benches.... really! Oh well, just keep walking...
For me, it's the nostalgia of building a theme park again that attracted me to Adventure Park, unfortunately nostalgia can only carry you so far.
After playing Adventure Park for a while I was left with an overwhelming desire to turn it off and play Rollercoaster Tycoon 3 instead.
Enjoyment can be found here, you just have to look really, really hard to find it.

DQH is a reasonably average game. I'm giving it a thumbs down because the combination of length and quality makes a $60 price tag absolutely laughable, and I don't feel I got my money's worth even having paid $30. If it ever goes to $15 or lower, that's a decent time to jump.
Provided you're using a gamepad, the controls and moment-to-moment gameplay are pretty good. Most of the characters (around 10) are fun to play, and the only control issues I ever ran into were problems with held buttons being released mid-animation. I actually think the game would've been bettered served by trying to be Zelda than Warriors - there's a series of Zelda-like one-on-one boss fights about three quarters of the way through the game that I found far more compelling than the rest of the game. The main problem with the other boss fights is that your AI partners are dumb as toast and get themselves killed by telegraphed AoE constantly. Since you only get 4 revives per mission, this is a major and frustrating problem. You do at least have healing items to save them before they get KOed, but these have to be recharged in an incredibly tedious menu every time you use them.
The other 40 or so story missions are almost entirely represented by the following: boss fight, defend the point, and kill everything. Boss enemies and destructable spawn points do a decent job of keeping things more interesting than they'd otherwise be, but the fact that there's only a dozen or so enemy models that are constantly recolored (and sometimes not even that) and renamed means even those get tiring. Speaking of things getting tiring, all characters have special moves that can only be used after building up "tension points" from attacking enemies. The animations associated with these are pretty cool the first time, but you're going to see your main ones 50-100 times in a campaign, and they never become skippable. "YOU ASKED FOR IT ... LIGHTNING SLASH!"
Monster summoning is basically the opposite of that, thankfully. There's a very short animation that doesn't cut out of the battle, you're constantly getting new options, and using them as defenders gives you new options about how to fight. It's the game's best idea.
Nearly all sidequests are pointless filler. A handful give you new combat scenarios, but the rest are all either "kill 100 of this enemy" or "get 5 of this item." Those types are particularly annoying because the game seemingly deliberately picks enemies and items that no longer appear in the story missions. You're forced to go back and grind - sometimes for a significant amount of time - to complete a mission that wasn't interesting in the first place. Worse, rewards are kept secret until you finish. You can at least guess about the ones that'll give you bigger item bags or more monster slots, but all the rest could be anything from a tiny amount of money to very rare crafting items.
The story is crap. Light and dark, tree named Yggdrasil, ancient baddie sealed away - it's nothing new and it won't keep you playing. The writing itself is fun at first, though. It's as punny as you'd expect from a mainline DQ game, but most of the characters can be described fully in one word. I'd be okay with that if they didn't talk so much, but alas, they do. One "joke" in particular about Luceus' strategies is rehashed in almost
. It's painful.
Performance and graphics are solid. A lot of the options are in the configuration launcher, but the feature set is reasonably complete. I never encountered any series framerate dips even when the screen was full of enemies and effects. Loading times are great (although this was on a SSD) and I never encountered any crashes outside of the widely-reported ones after the second boss. That those crashes are still in the game this long after release and with so many people reporting them at exactly the same spot (it seems to be luck if you get it or not) is definitely a point against the game, however.
No complaints about the sound. Most of the music and effects appear to be taken from previous DQ games and get the job done. The voice actors mostly have various British accents, as you'd expect, and largely do a good job. Some of the combat sound effects are pretty satisfying.
The game is loaded with minor annoyances that don't fit into any of the above categories, however. Shopkeeps have lines they say every single time you talk to them or visit certain screens and you're going to get incredibly sick of them. Equipment can only be sold one at a time regardless of how many copies you have. Taking on quests is incredibly slow because the game insists on playing short music clips every time you select or finish one. There's way too much text involved in using any of the ships services, and you're going to accidentally select a lot of things trying to mash through it. Level up skills are pretty boring outside of the three active abilities for most characters. There's a scrolling view of the ship that plays during loading, and the game always finishes that cutscene even if it takes several seconds longer than the actual load.
There's probably 15-20 hours of content here if you're not going all out on the sidequests. It's not a bad game, all things considered, but it's also not nearly good enough to justify its current $60 pricetag. Unless you're very into DQ and Warriors, in which case you probably already own it, I'd wait for a 75%+ off sale.

This game is quite unique in what it has to offer.
There is a depth to this game that is not initially apparent, I think. By sticking to a well-defined set of rules of limited engagement, the developers have effectively created their own version of tactical chess. Recall in chess, not every piece can move as it might like, but they have very restricted types of movement in how they can attack (a pawn can only move forward, usually one space, but must attack diagonally).
This game is similar except any movement is the result of an attack, and not purely done in and of itself. The movement, when it occurs, is well defined and can be anticipated. Having these kinds of limits makes this game distinct from other games like King's Bounty and Eador, Masters of the Broken Realm, which are both great games in their own right. In this respect, I would argue, less is actually more, in terms of the depth this game provides. I really thought Eador was extremely tactical until I played this game, and decided this one had a more "mature" type of strategy than the you-can-move 1, 2 or 3 spaces kind of games.
I believe the overwhelming reason to buy and play this game is to, in essence, play a new type of low-fantasy tactical chess based upon a 36-hex board. This game has all the tactical depth that chess does given in how it works. It may not be balanced, or fair, or even easy to grasp in terms of what this game really is, but it is a gem in its own right.

Having played for a little over five hours since yesterday, I've got to say I'm really enjoying this game.  Great combat system that feels more like battle chess than DnD.  The story is alright so far, the lore is interesting enough that I didn't just ignore all of the sidequests.  The day/night cycle was a surprise the first time I saw it, with shadows stretching and shrinking as the sun moved east to west.  Really cool, very beautiful.  I also enjoy that unlike some similar games, they give you full control of the camera's rotation, but keep the camera centered on your party, so your eye of God advantage is somewhat muted while you can still fully appreciate the visuals.
This being an early access game, there are a lot of bugs that make it difficult to advance the story.  So far I've made note of 22 major bugs that either cause ctd problems, or are effecting quests so that workarounds are required, or are completely disrupting advancement progress.  This is quite a large number of problems for a relatively short play time.  There are also many minor bugs as well, from corrupt textures and spelling errors to even some Russian dialogue that hasn't been replaced yet.
The dev posting on the game's steam forum mentioned that they aren't proud of the UI, but work is being done to improve it.  I'm really looking forward to seeing the work done to it, as its probably the game's largest non-technical weakness.  It's not very intuitive at all, the map is functional but clunky, quest markers sometimes mislead you and accidentally doing part of a quest out of order can make the journal quite confusing.
I bought it at the sale price, and I feel like I've gotten some very good value for my investment and recommend others who are interested to to buy it while it's cheap as well.  If I'd paid full price for the game, I'd honestly regret not waiting until it was complete.  I look forward to keeping track of the progress of Eisenwald as the game comes closer to a full release, as it has potential to be a dark horse that will really surprise and delight many old school fans of this genre.

Awesome arena multiplayer game! 9/10
Have you ever wondered what it would be like to be a Jedi Narwhal? Then this game is for you.
The game is like a mix of Super Smash Bros and  Nidhogg. Play it with friends (in local multiplayer) and enjoy the coordinated mayhem! Controls and physics are great (easy to pick up, but difficult to master). The goal of the game is to attack your opponent's heart whith your Starwhal's horn (only the tip of the horn does damage, hence the "Just The Tip" in the name of the game) while avoiding having your heart attacked. The game does a slo-mo anytime that a player gets his/hers horn close to another player's heart, so every attack or dodge feels epic (and this allows all players to really see what's going on and think about their next moves). You wil learn how to use your Starwhal to stab an opponent, pin him down, fling him away, bait him, etc. And all those actions are not predetermined moves, but rather actions derived from the mobility of your Starwahl and the physics of the game.
The game keeps getting more content and feels very stable, despite being in Early Access (I have not encountered any bug or glitch). untill now it lacks online multiplayer, so it's a local multiplayer experience only. But it's one of the best local multiplayer games I have ever played (next to Super Smash Bros. Melee, Castle Crashers, Battle Block Theater). If you have a couple of controllers and competitive people next to you, play this and enjoy a great experience. I find that even against the bots the game is awesome, as the AI is very good and seems to have some behavior variation.
I gave it 9/10 as the game is still in Early Access and thus, it lacks some options (like the ability to create custom games, choose songs, maybe a level editor, more content). But so far it feels that this is already a solid game that is in the phase of getting more content. I don't doubt that it would become a 10/10 when the final release comes out.

Downloading the Steam version, previously I've only played the Android version.
The game is a good time-sink. For those calling it pay-to-win; certainly you can buy most of the meaningful resources in the game, but you're not getting good value for your money, and you're kind of missing the point of the game.  $10 will save you, eh, maybe 5 hours of in-game effort, and because of the way the game groups people for the in-game competition, you don't get any actual advantage; you have better characters, but so does the group you're competing with.
Which does imply something of the issue: The whole game is a Red Queen's Race.  Enemies level up with your strongest three characters (as best as I can tell), so "Easy" missions will always be easy, and "Difficult" missions will always be difficult.  The RPG elements are mostly an illusion; mostly, because characters are separated out by their "Star" power, and each star-level has a power cap.  So once you develop a two-star roster, your one-star characters stop being useful (mostly); after you get a three-star roster, your two-star roster is less useful, and your one-star roster becomes, outside very specific situations, completely worthless.  If you're spending money to advance your characters, you're wasting your money.
Because the point of the game isn't to "win" - there is no winning.  It's a time sink, and a well-designed one; you'll be tempted to spend money every now and then to increase the size of your roster (which can be done without spending money, but more slowly and deliberately), to avoid having to make a painful choice between selling a new powerful character, or selling an old favorite character to make room.  If opportunity cost is painful for you, you probably shouldn't play this game; you'll be spending a lot of money.  (Disclosure: I've personally spent $20.  Not because I couldn't not, but because I like the game and like supporting developers.)
If, on the other hand, you're accustomed to trade-offs, this game could be a very satisfying way of spending free time.

Original review left below for posterity; TL,DR the new update 1.1 rectifies a number of the issues I had with the game at launch. While I still miss a couple of aspects from CSD1, the new additions provided give not just more flexibility for those who would want to play this as a relaxed game, but also for those who want to bring some of the CSD1 challenge back.
-----
Almost two months post-announcement, the 1.1 update for CSD2 was released, adding in a number of options for your restaurant. There are now 4 modes: Standard (the initial gameplay option available); Stress (maxes out prep and holding stations, max buzz of 150%), Zen (removes all rush hours); and Classic (brings back boosters and detractors as in CSD1). The other restaurants you can choose in the Chef for Hire mode are untouched, so for those who enjoyed the original setup they can continue as they were.
For all but Stress, you are also given the option of adjusting how many prep and holding stations you can have. Zen and Standard modes also allow the option of adjusting your Buzz levels (from 1% to 31% in increments of 5, and a max of 32%), and Zen also allows an option for infinite patience.
This - in theory - means you can have a Zen game to practise in a 'real world' kitchen with new menu items, a decent buzz level, but inifinite patience to allow you to get used to and perfect a recipe.
I've gone back and started afresh, deleting my (sparse) progress, and I definitely feel more inclined and exited in this game, utilising Classic mode and seeing all the Boosters and Detractors back into the game. Classic detractors like Menu Rot and Trashy Food are joined by things like Super Menu Rot, Micro Servings, and Pest Fest; similarly boosters such as Healthy Eats and Staple Food are joined by things like Instant Food, Stacked, and Green Footprint. As in CSD1, some boosters and detractors only activate with multiple foods with that same effect on the menu.
Thankfully one of the new detractors is a symbol informing people when a food is complex (Recipe Overload - loads of recipe types and/or allows for custom orders; Complex Bits - loads of ingredients and steps; Extra Prep - two cooking stages) which allows for some guidance towards which dishes should be avoided if you're new or needing practise. So long as you check the detractors (even if you're playing in a mode that doesn't utilise them) you shouldn't find yourself overloaded with options at the start.
The food catalogue now also has options to show the price (money you get per serving), description (name and cost for you to buy), and holding station options. Any food with no 'HS' indicator is a cook-when-ordered food; any with 'HS' in yellow and in a rounded triangle is HS optional (you can pre-prep to make serving for rush hours easier); and any with 'HS' in red and in a hexagon is HS required (i.e. these will be your holding station only foods).
We also now have options to buy equipment upgrades (accessed on the main splash screen for your restaurant). There are six items for upgrade - the dishwasher, trash service, bug lamps, toilet, rat traps, and roach spray. These do not appear to be tied to any progress levels, so you could reasonably get them very early on in the game.
And, finally, the emails are back. I'm only a few days in so I have not yet received anything of importance, but the charm and humour of some of the tower emails from CSD1 is back.
In short, I'd still like to see more options available, but as it stands with the 1.1 update I am happy to recommend this game to people :)

It pains me to give this a negative, as a day one Steam purchaser of CSD1 and someone who'd been following CSD2's development since announcement.
The good: the foods are visually stunning, and the chef for hire options in Teragon Tower highlight not only the new options for pre-designed set menus, but also offer options to test out new foods while getting paid to do so. You have a sushi restaurant, ice cream and desserts, pizza, breakfast, and more. The skills and progression is tied to you as the chef, and is more reliant on your skill and experience gained than seemingly-arbitrary requirements to play x number of days to progress. Experience can be gained from both your own restaurant, and the chef for hire options.
The so-so: The new layout also offers multiple and repeated use of keys for different foods. Back in CSD1 every ingredient or item had to have its own key option. In CSD2 items and ingredients are split into multiple pages, allowing the reuse of key bindings...but this can also cause a small issue if you're used to the CSD1 method and input what you *think* is the right combo, only to put an unwanted ingredient on the order.
The bad: No food progression. I know the idea of improved ingredients was nixed reasonably early on, but you can find yourself thrown into the deep end with a huge mass of ingredients to use. In CSD1, the initial purchase of ice cream gave you vanilla and chocolate ice cream, sprinkles, and cherries. Level 2 earned you mint choc chip, whip, and nuts; level 3 earned you butter pecan, strawberry sauce, and chocolate sauce. That totals four ice cream flavours and six toppings.
In comparison, in CSD2 your purchase of ice cream sundae gets you eight ice cream flavours, seven toppings, and three additions. There is no purchase or progression upgrade, so you get thrown all the options and seemingly told to deal with it, rather than being guided along and having options unlocked as you progress.
TL;DR: Due to having all options available for meals upon purchase (rather than offering upgrades and unlocks), the difficulty is much higher than CSD1. The chef for hire feature is a nice addition, showcasing new recipes and menu options. If you enjoy the general feeling of getting a perfect day, or having a huge array of food to choose from this may well be worth the purchase, but the lack of progression muddies the game.

This game is good, and it almost feels wrong to not recommend it, but a lot of what made the first Cook, Serve, Delicious! feel so right and so good is currently gone. Some of it has yet to be added, for sure, but some of it seems to just plain be missing. I will avoid talking too much about what's currently missing, as I trust the developer for sticking to his promise of adding these features soon.
The first and probably biggest problem I personally have with this game is that there's no real progression. You are introduced to new foods at a rapid pace, and barely get any time to get used to them before already being shoved onto the next set of foods. Rather than having a small set of foods that you upgrade to slowly introduce more elements to them like in the first one, you get to buy a massive amount of foods for your own restaurant that have all of the options unlocked from the begin. This doesn't really make me want to use the foods, it feels like after seeing every recipe card once you've already seen all there is to see of this food (which is both the case and not encouraging to use said food more). The new Chef-For-Hire mode has a similar problem, but at least it makes more sense here. Where's the upgrades, both for food and the restaurant?
The second problem is related to the first problem I talked about, and the Chef For Hire mode. Now, I have nothing against this mode existing, in fact, I think this mode is a really good idea and I'm glad something like this is in the game. The problem for me is that it feels like the mode is what the game is focused on. Instead of working on your own restaurant, gradually unlocking upgrades as you go (which was really the thing that made the first game so good in my opinion), you just go from one place to another, making foods you likely haven't even been introduced to or have had practice for, only to get some money and a gold medal for that specific level.
I feel like this mode needs to be secondary. Working on and upgrading your own restaurant is what the game should, at its core, really be about. It isn't, though. The game is at its core just making foods in other restaurants that you don't actually work on improving. Your own restaurant is as a result not really even upgrade-able. It feels like a side mode where you just practice on foods you unlocked instead of being an actually important thing in the game.
There's other problems I had with the game, for sure, but those were more minor than these two, and other negative reviews have summed these up better than I probably would.
Rest assured, this game isn't without positives. There's a lot of smaller improvements, and a couple pretty big ones. Biggest probably being the holding stations, but I don't really have anything to add onto this as everyone has already explained how much more depth these bring the gameplay.
If this game was its own thing instead of being the sequel to Cook, Serve, Delicious!, I probably would've recommended it, but as a sequel, this fails and it ignores most of what made the original so good for me. If you ask me, just buy the original instead.
