If you're into MOBA styled games like League of Legends and DotA2 but you're maybe looking for something less time consuming and more enjoyable in bursts give Battlerite a try. I would describe it as a Fighting game mixed with a MOBA. Its fun and highly competitive. There are no items, no towers to destroy, No RNG crits to get you salty and most importantly ALL SKILL. Every character has unique traits and it feels good when you find a character you click with to call your main. The  game breaks down damages and health bars to small numbers and has consistent damage on all your abilities. For example supports start with 210 health or so and thats consistent and then you can have an ult that does like 40-50 damage and it will always do that much. There is no math with calculating defenses from items or how much damage you have with your items. It adds another layer of skill cause you can figure out exactly how much burst you can do and how much you need to do to kill someone. The only problem I have with the game currently is a lot of characters feel extremely similar especially the earlier characters that came out. But I think thats getting fixed the new characters are a lot more complex and its good to see. I hope Stunlock continues to update the game and add interesting characters.

I literally can't think of another game with more hooks to try to get you to spend money than MPQ.
There are *multiple tiers* of in game currency that you can pay for.
If you want more characters ("covers"), you have to buy them. If you want to reliably upgrade the abilities of characters you do have, you have to purchase the upgrades. If you want to level up those characters without a crazy grind, you have to pay. If you want more character slots, you have to pay. If your characters take too much damage and you want to keep on playing, you have to pay for a heal. If you want to compete in PVP you have to pay for boosts.
Sure, *some* of those things you can grind for, but the results are often unpredictable. For example instead of an upgrade to an existing character you might get a new character cover. But if you don't have enough character slots you have to buy more. You can try to grind for enough currency to unlock more slots (prices for new slots increase depending on how many you already have), but you have a time limit on your covers, so if you can't unlock a new slot fast enough, the new character you earned just disappears. This is a deliberate time pressure to try to get you to just buy the slot.
You spend a bunch of time and currency investing in a character just to find out he has a level cap because he is a lower-tier character, and if you actually want to progress in the game you need higher tier characters. You can try and grind for the (exceedingly rare) chance to get a rare cover to drop, or you can spend money to get one as a sure thing. Again, the game is trying to pressure you into buying♥♥♥♥♥♥
You can try to unlock more rewards by competing in PVP and PVE events, but as soon as you get anywhere near the top bracket you'll find it is impossible to progress and get the real rewards without paying money because the other people at the top are paying for heals and boosts so if you aren't doing the same you can't possibly compete with them, so even the "free" rewards are effectively locked behind a paywall.
There is absolutely no skill involved in this game, it's all about how much money you are willing to spend. It's probably the most disgusting example of pay to win mechanics and "gambling" hooks in something purporting to be a video game I have ever seen.

Overall, I did somewhat enjoy Dragon Quest Heroes. It's an amusing way to kill an hour by well... killing hundreds of cartoony monsters. However, that's about all it seems to be good for. After playing for a while, I started to get bored faster and faster. My first play session lasted 4 or 5 hours, the 2nd one only around 2-3 hours, and every play session after that has gotten shorter and shorter. I feel like the game is just too shallow, even for a musou style game. Each level is small (even the biggest level I've done yet is still smaller than the average musou game level) and usually has either no strategic objectives other than the monster summoning portals (named Nightmaws) that you need to close or one or two people/objects you need to protect while you close the Nightmaws. The closest thing to "depth" that the strategy for defending objectives is would be the fact that as you kill monsters, they can drop monster medals which let you summon copies of that monster to defend a small area for you. Generally these monsters do a good job of defending, but can be overwhelemed quickly if you don't keep an eye on them. The number of enemies in each level also feels small compared to other musou style games but to keep the spirit of the Dragon Quest series, you have a party of 4 characters  that you bring to each level. Granted, you don't need to bring 4 people once you have finished the first few levels and unlock the ability to edit your party, but it just feels pointless to bring 4 people when 1 is more than enough. So with that out of the way, time for the pros and cons list.
(I will go over the two with asterisks in detail at the end of the review)
Now onto the last two things I want to discuss. The crafting system and the mini cutscenes and jingles.
The crafting system is fine in terms of functionality and UI, but the accessories you can craft are pretty much all completely worthless until much later in the game. The base effects of most of the lower level ones (based on what level you are before the materials for them start to drop) are not going to effect you in any way. For example, one gives you 40% resistance to sleep. That's all fine and dandy... but at the point in the game I got to before giving up, I only encountered 1 enemy type that can put you to sleep and had only actually been put to sleep twice. Ever. The only good thing about the crafting system in early game is that when you combine multiple of the same accessory to upgrade them, a new random stat is added to that accessory. If you are lucky and get one of the few stats that matter it's great, but more often than not you will end up with another worthless stat.
The last thing to mention is the unskippable mini cutscenes and jingles. An example of the mini cutscenes would be every time you load your game, you have to watch the camera fly down and zoom into the priestess at the cathedral. Not a big deal, but it takes a few seconds each time you load your game, and that adds up. Another example is every time you return to the Stonecloud after you finish a level. You beat a level, go to a loading screen, and then AFTER the loading screen, you have to sit around and wait for another few seconds while the camera cinematically shows you what the central room of the Stonecloud looks like (a room you spend 95% of your time in while not on missions). It adds up. An example of the jingles would be every time you turn in a sidequest. When you finish a sidequest, you have to report it to the questmistress. When you do, she congradulates you by putting a stamp over the quest description window for that quest and then clapping for a few seconds. You can skip her dialogue to a degree, but you can't skip the stamping or the clapping. Say it with me now: It adds up. Things like this also occur for various other events throughout the game such as when a new character joins your party or when you craft an item. To really drive this point home, let's say you complete 35 side quests. have recruited every character (6 mini cutscenes since some are recruited in groups), have loaded your save game 50 times, have completed 100 levels, and crafted 100 items. Now let's assume that each of those events has 3 seconds of unskippable cutscenes/jingles (3 seconds is about the average).  That adds up to 14.5 MINUTES of unskippable, repeated events that you will have seen dozens of times each by the end of the game.
So there you have it. The game is fun in short bursts and has great looking levels and spell/ability effects, but lacks any kind of depth in level objectives, has a mediocre at best crafting system, wastes your time with unskippable repeating mini cutscenes, has poor english voice acting, small levels, limited enemy numbers and variety, and a story we've all heard a thousand times. The only way I could recommend this game is if you have never played a musou style game before and want to get a taste of a dumbed down version that will require very little effort to learn and beat or if you are a parent who for some reason wants to introduce their kid to a colorful and cartoony musou style game (I won't judge). Aside from that, I cannot recommend this game.

GhostControl Inc. is an enjoyable turn based game with some management sim flavor. The closest game I can think of would be XCOM, but in GhostControl you are running a ghost hunting company (think Ghost Busters) instead of running a secret government agency tasked with defending earth from alien attack.
In GCE you'll have to manage your team, a base, and your car. You can recruit additional members for your team from your home office and must keep their sanity maintained, periodically visiting a hospital to "repair" that sanity. Your base is where you'll drop off your ghost goo and perform various other tasks. And while out roaming the town waiting for calls from new potential clients, you have to remember to keep the car gassed up with a few gas stations around the town.
*[While the game is actually quite enjoyable from my experiences thus far, there are a couple minor issues that can be frustrating. One such issue is the fact that every time you select a team member for their turn, their inventory screen pops up in the bottom middle of the screen blocking your view (they can be moved and if you remember to move them, and not close them, on your first couple turns it's easily fixed).]
*[Edit: 6/10/2014: This issue has been fixed and I haven't noticed any other real issues]
All in all though, a very enjoyable game. I'd give it a solid 8/10 from my experience so far.
*[Edit 2: 6/10/2014: As you can see from the comments to this review, the devs care a great deal about their game. I'd give the game at least a 9/10 now]

Definitely recommended for fans of card games or those looking to learn or get into Magic, or just play it casually for fun. There are some definitely frustrating qualities at times, but remembering it is free to play and has some inherent differences from the regular Magic format help to make it worthwhile.
+Multiple solo campaigns - 5 for Origins and 1 for each set thereafter, all free
+Lots of information in the tutorials and available as you play to learn
+Fully customizable decks - a huge improvement from past MTG games
+Generous free to play style, no alt account/login needed, earn 2-3 packs a day even casually
+Boosters only award cards you actually need to complete your playsets
+Variety of game modes including Story, Solo vs. AI, PvP, and 2-Headed Giant; all award coins for boosters
+Future MTG sets continue to be added as they are released
+/- Limits are placed on your playset by rarity: you can own 1 of each mythic, 2 of each rare, 3 of each uncommon, and 4 of each common. This means you can't play and won't see many of the decks common in actual Magic meta, but will see different strategies/tactics available that wouldn't be otherwise.
-Developers are not active on Steam community; they are (a little) more active on Reddit / other social media.
-There are generally no hotfixes; if something is bugged/broken, it will stay that way until the next set (~3 months)
-In-depth tutorial and first chapter are required prior to use of other modes; not geared toward vets
-Sets include only a selection of cards from each set, not the entire set (for that you want paper or MTGO)

Alright so I've never played any of the thief games before, so my opinion may not be helpful for you hardcore Thief fans out there. However I must say that this game is excellent. If I could sum up the experience of playing Garrett in one word it'd be ATMOSPHERE. This game has outstanding atmosphere accompanied by sound design and gameplay elements, I've not been so immeresed in a stealth game in years!
Thief is a balls to the wall steath game. Sure you could go in and try to kill/knockout everyone but that's not a challenge, and the game will let you know that. You're not rewarded for being a baddass night assasin; instead you're a ghost sneaking in and out without having to knock out guards or kill them truely leaving no trace of your having been there save for empty pockets and missing trinkets. Difficulty is extremely customizable, for example let's say you don't want to have access to a map, or maybe no ammo counters, or how about no visability meters, scratch that no hud at all, thief let's you do all that and more with extensive GUI/HUD options and difficulty options.
Optimization wise this game runs like butter, I by no means have a high end righ my graphics card is a GTX 650ti Boost SSC by evga, and I play on ultra maintaining around 30-45 fps. All settings can be changed outside of the game in the launcher and can be changed in realtime in game without having to restart the the game, Seperate audio sliders, Benchmarking tool you name it and this game pretty much has. My only real performance problem has to be with the cut scenes for some odd reasons the in engine renders are at a much lower fps than the actual game runs at. This is apperently a well known issue and is being addressed so hopefully we'll see a patch to reslove this issue.
In closing: Thief Looks great and plays tight, with outstanding atmosphere and immersive diaglogues and collectables be warned you will loose hours stalking the money lined pockets of watchmen and hunting down every last bit of loot available.

I bought the original game at release and loved it. I bought this game at release and I regret it.
This is not good enough for a full release. Not even close. This should have been an early access game, it is not finished and nowhere near it.
Starting with the positive things when compared with the original game:
- Holding stations. This is the greatest addition of the game, adding depth to the gameplay and making it feel just complex enough for a seasoned player
- High number of foods, restaurants, and chores
- Robberies are much more fun, as you can beat the crap out of the robbers rather than having to draw them
- Rush hour alerts in advance, giving us enough time to get ready and prep some food to respond to it in the best way possible
- Cook for hire mode, which is like the general game but with preset menus, with harder foods as you progress
Thumbs up for the artist as the assets look fantastic in general (if we exclude the refried beans and the rice, I can't even describe how terrible the beans look, they don't even fit on top of the nachos properly).
I could also list the ability to design your restaurant as a positive, but it is so unintuitive I can't be bothered to actually use it. Which brings me to the list of negatives:
- Menu UI. It looks like rushed♥♥♥♥♥♥and a huge downgrade from CSD1
- Tutorials. On the original game, they were integrated with the campaign, allowing you to feel the general game's mechanics as you play it. CSD2 has 7 different tutorials completely separate from the core game, 4 of which are utterly useless as they're just text. And none of them tells me what I'm supposed to do to run my restaurant.
- Talking about campaign, there isn't really one. You have your CSD restaurant, where you can customize the menu, and the other restaurants which are part of the Chef for Hire mode. By the developer's definition, this is a campaign because they're integrated into the same progression system. The campaigns I play usually have stories (not this one). There is no feeling of progression, because you just unlock items (at least I haven't unlocked any relevant stuff so far, all foods are unlocked). There is absolutely no direction on what to do. I know what I can do, but what am I supposed to do?
- Emails? Gone. They're supposed to be implemented in the future, but right now they don't exist
- Cooking competitions? Gone
- Catering events? Gone. Although to be fair, there is a high variety of restaurants which is probably a fair replacement
- Achievements?
EDIT: There are now 20 achievements, all with the same icon. There is much more that could be done in this regard and I hope that the dev revisits this in the future.

EDIT: This has been fixed - the option is now named "Start Game"
- Boosters/detractors which alter the gameplay if you do not know them from the original game, are present (according to the developer), but there is no information about it nowhere in the game. There are no options to filter by booster/detractor in a game with over 80 foods in the catalog. There are no search options in a game with over 180 foods in the catalog.
- Talking about "food catalog", some foods are locked. How to unlock them? By leveling up? By completing certain restaurants? By gaining medals? How would I know, the game doesn't tell me anything. How does my restaurant gain stars? Yeah, no way to know that either.
- Unlike in the first game, you're forced to switch pages to apply ingredients in other pages, even when their keybindings are unique
- The gold medal requires a perfect day, which is a ridiculous objective when compared with the other medals
- Foods feel much more generic. Each food felt unique in CSD1, while in this game everything feels like the same. Also, why would we need brisket slices, turkey slices, ham slices, and sausage slices? They're all sliced meat. They're all holding station foods. They're all entrees. They're all cooked in the similar forms, only being different in pressing a key for seasoning or pressing a key to inject sauce
- Chores feel much more generic. The only one having a twist to it is the one where you throw garbage, where you have to repeatedly tap a key to mash the garbage inside
This game feels like a barebones framework of what it should really have been. It may become great after an extra year's work on it. But it will also be having deep sales by then, so there's no point on buying it now. The dev's definition of a campaign mode is also ridiculous and one of my biggest gripes with the game. There is nothing relevant to work towards, there is no story to get me hooked.
If you're new to this CSD franchise, by all means buy CSD1. It's a fantastic game. It's polished, introduces you properly to the mechanics, has a story, and feels complete.
But I can't recommend this game in its current state. This game has none of that. The developer was clearly afraid of delaying the game further (as it was supposed to be released in 2016), which resulted in this precipitated mess of a release. CSD1 is the better game, by far. There is still time to change that, as the potential is present. But at this time, you shouldn't really buy this.

Given what I've played thus far, Thief is a game right up my alley. I jumped into this game on the hardest difficulty available, and am loving it. The emphasis on stealth and trickery as opposed to brute force is a delight not often experienced in modern gaming. This is a game I'd like to see further delved into, as there is tons of potential. While I am aware that it is a remake, I still hope for the addition of traps, misdirection (besides throwing a bottle) and subterfuge. Adding cinematic stealth kills (or takedowns) would've been nice as well.
The enemies aren't cheap or stupid like in most stealth games, forcing you to perform recon and planning around the situation. And believe me, planning is imperative, as you are not an indestructible force of death. Getting surrounded is usually a one-way trip to the reload screen. The Focus mechanic doesn't wreck the game by making it stupidly easy and performs well enough to make it a useful tool as opposed to either a liability or a dependancy.
All in all, a great experience for stealth game fans, both new and old. There are a few things I would chage with the platforming (Sometimes your character will happily jump to his doom, but refuse to step over a two inch ledge). Other than that, this game is a stellar example of the ingenuity that was so common before modern gaming.

When the game first came out, I rated it "not recommend" because it was unfinished and because it didn't have a campaign mode. I have since changed my recommendation because the developer listened to the community and announced a patch, coming in October, that will add a campaign mode back into the game.
That preamble aside, here's what you need to know about CSD 2 in its current state.
Compared to CSD 1, the day-to-day gameplay is unquestionably superior. Side dishes, holding stations, and dynamic chores add a lot of difficulty and strategy to the game. Foods can no longer be upgraded, and while many people do not like this change, I personally consider it a plus. When you buy a food, what you see is what you get, and you can set about mastering the food in its totality. The range of selling prices is much narrower now, which encourages the player to use more foods instead of upgrading a few to $25-$40 per plate and ignoring the rest.
However, it is crucial to understand that CSD 2 does not currently have a campaign. If what you loved about CSD 1 was the ability to manage your own restaurant and grow it from a swampy buttcrack to a pinnacle of 5-star majesty, that isn't here. Instead, the metagame centers around the chef-for-hire mode which consists of "levels" -- essentially, setups with a preset menu, buzz level, and number of prep and holding stations -- that you attempt to earn "medals" on, with a gold medal only being awarded on a perfect day. Your own restaurant is just a sandbox.
Is the chef-for-hire mode fun? Yes. But I played the original CSD for 70 hours, and I wouldn't clock half that many on CSD 2's new style of gameplay. I'm excited for the October update to bring back the campaign feel to CSD.

A very fun Hotline Miami-esque game that focuses on just the melee section of its predecessors.  It's about five hours long the first run through the game, but for most of the missions there is great replayibility if you want to go for zero death runs.  The graphics reminded me of a comic book, and it fit the cheesy theme really well. You're not going to get much out of the story besides a game that just relies on sterotypes to tell itself, but what more do you need for a cheap romp? The music is maybe not the best, but yet again it fits the comic book aesthetic.  The highlight of this entire game is honestly the difficulty curve that ramps up all the way to the end. This could be a textbook example of difficulty curve at this point.  It will introduce a new type of enemy or obstacle, let you experiment with different configurations of them, then mix them into the cycle of what the game will throw at you. Even the number of enemies and lengths of each room will increase over time in a pattern that builds tension then explodes with the final rooms of a stage.  As I progressed through the game, I never felt out of my depth or unprepared; I just needed to find the pattern that fit the problem.  One glitch that affected some of my time is the game seems not to display certain enemies till their attacking.  It mostly happened in large scale encounters but would almost always result in an instant death.
Buy, wait for a sale, or pass: Buy, the game is the equivalent of a fun yet stupid action movie, and it provides an evening or two of fun for a discount price.

This game isn't terrible. But it feels like there's so much wasted potential here. The game is lacking any sort of character to make it memorable. You open diplomacy with the other leaders, and they say the exact same thing every single time, whereas Civ V gave them some variety. The consequences of picking a different affinity to the other leaders are generic. Even having specific insults for each leader and sponsor would have made them stand out.
Like many Civ games, it is filled with quotes, but the quotes read when you discover new technologies are read in the same voice, and just seem silly or absurd. Why is it wrong that the world is unspoilt and beautiful? The thing that made Alpha Centauri so memorable is that the issues explored in that game are real philosophical and ethical debates. Yang may have seemed like a monster, but he was only acting according to the principles of utilitarianism. What motivates Kozlov's ideas of progress? You never really know.
The gameplay has never been balanced well, and there's nothing really to strive for. No must-have wonders, strategies to complement your sponsor's unique abilities, special terrain features like Kilimanjaro in Civ V or the Monsoon Jungle of Alpha Centauri, or any real military advantages. You get to make choices throughout the game about what new effect each building has, but for most of them there's either only one right choice in all cases, or it doesn't matter.
It's fun to play a few times to discover all of the features, and it's visually impressive, but it feels like a weaker version of Civ V. Get it on sale if you want to try it.

Ever since that fateful incident with my neighbor lady's cat and a vacuum cleaner (sorry Cinnamon!), I've tried to find a healthy outlet for my ghost busting fantasies. Until now it has been fruitless. UNTIL NOW. "Ghost Control Inc." provides such an outlet. Part management sim, Part XCOM combat/base strategy, this is a fun little distraction of a game. You name your starting character (My guy is Fat Indiana... you'll know him when you see him) and start your own paranormal cleaning service (I named mine the Ghost Murderers). Time passes as you sit in HQ, upgrading, hiring, firing, and managing equipment - that is until your cell phone rings and your services are required. Then you load up your vehicle, prep your team, and head out; make sure to beat the competition there.
Combat is deceptively simple. Your team opens doors, turns on lights, and encounters nasty ghoulies. Hit them with your lasers until they're worn down and lay down a trap. It's pretty satisfying to wreck ghosts in a fun, lighthearted atmosphere. Your team will suffer physical (and mental) wear-and-tear, so you'll have to swing by the hospital. Your car needs gas, so you'll get that too. And obviously as your business expands, the ghosts will amp up their game. You'll need to buy more equipment and hire new people.
If you like XCOM, if you're a fan of management games, or if you have fond memories of a certain iconic franchise, I can recommend this wholeheartedly. I've just got one question: who ya gonna call?
PS: Do NOT call the Ghost Murderers, they are highly unprofessional.

Bottom line: Very slow and grindy from the get-go.
Don't get me wrong I know exactly what I'm in for when I download something with the tag "free to play". I know that eventually I will come to point in the game where the progress slows down and I have to decide whether to commit my time or my money. I do not expect every f2p game to be PoE or DOTA2. But the thing that disappointed me with this game was how soon I got to that point.
In my experience these sorts of free to play games, the good ones, tend to be pretty fast paced at first to get you hooked and learn the ropes. Then as the pace of progression gradually slows down you can start to really appreciate and understand what you can accomplish long term, either through play or through paying. But Marvel Puzzle quest sort of just gives you one semi-fast prologue chapter and then says "now we grind".
I haven't even beaten the second prologue chapter yet and my best character (Iron-man) takes over an hour in real time to heal up to full health if he’s downed. The battles even against normal goons take a long time now. Even if the battle isn't hard they usually damage my heroes so much that I can't use them for a good while. And the reward for beating them are sometimes just these consumable boosts that do not progress your characters in any way which makes it feel like you won nothing for such a long battle.
My most dominating thought is "if it's this grindy in the prologue how bad will it be when I actually get to play the main PVE/PVP modes?" I don't know, maybe it's admirable how upfront this game is about what it is (i.e. a typical f2p game) but it's a huge turnoff for me and I guess for others as well.
I see the potential in this game, it has some pretty cool ideas and the Puzzle Quest match 3 battles are fun, but it got grindy way to fast. I enjoyed the previous puzzle quest games and hoped this could become my new "play a quick session every once in a while game". But it gives such a bad early impression that I’m pretty much done with the game, which is a shame honestly.

Aesthetics 5/10
I can definitely see what style Codebrush Games was trying to go for. Elements of fighting games are present, with an upbeat soundtrack and bright on-screen effects when things happen. The game also makes use of the Unreal 3 Engine, which has lent its prowess to action and adventure alike. I’ll admit that seeing “KILL!!!” up on screen is a pretty exciting feeling, but I can get that with just about any violent video game. All of the characters have a Soul Calibur-esque feel to them, and most of them tend to have distinct looks and movements. There are a couple characters however who are almost entirely the same, with some minor differences in weapons or effects. The characters also have this ‘action-figure’ look about them, as if they’re made of medium grade plastics.
This continues all the way to the facial features, which are emotionless and unmoving. The game utilizes a champion rotation for free users, where a selection of heroes are available per week, so a user can experiment pretty freely with what character they find visually pleasing. Players can also shell out real money for recolors and custom skins as well, however, there is no other way to personalize your character. The in-game animations seem alright at first, but they can be clunky and detrimental versus a moderately skilled player. I’ll go into more detail on that in the Gameplay section. The soundtrack itself is fast-paced and fits the maps, however they are completely repetitive and this is true for the main menu as well.
Social 4/10
The game is distributed through Steam’s platform, so players will have access to Friends Lists, chat-rooms, community pages and even guides. However, the in-game Social features are sorely lacking. There is no matchmaking, of any kind, as most matches are lobby based. Auto-balancing doesn’t exist either, so you will often run into issues with stacked teams and even one versus four games. This will throw the ball completely into an individual’s court if they want to even out the playing field. The game can work when you have a pool of friends, but the average player doesn’t have the time or patience to organize a full stack. If you decide to brave the community ‘matchmaking’, then there will always be the chance to go against more-experienced players or unbalanced characters. Some people think this is good training, but I think effective training requires a degree of humility. I ran into an awful lot of people who spoke broken English and other languages as well, so communication is a bit of an issue. A group of friends with shared interest in the game and a working VoIP program is recommended.
Gameplay 5/10
Archeblade is said to be a skill-based fighting game with team-based elements. There have been a wealth of fighting games released in the past, so you can feel free to imagine what that sounds like after factoring in the third-person view. The gameplay features combos and active-skills that have to be coordinated to beat opponents, but there is a sore lack of combinations that makes things pretty uninteresting. On top of that, some characters are completely unbalanced and have either super-powers or a lack of any strength of note. At most, the characters only have up to 5 attack combinations, so it’s not like you can play with combinations of combinations. The attacks themselves are slow and take anywhere from a second to hit to a fraction. The damage from them are also wildly spread apart between characters. In addition to the minimal influence of combos, this makes certain characters feel like a pop-gun would have more effect on the battle.
Currently, there are eighteen characters to choose from (either from the free picks or purchased from the store). These range from a monk with a penchant for greed, a swordsman who reminds me just a little too much of DotA’s Juggernaut, and an undead revenant with a poisonous touch. Some characters have near complete copies in terms of models, as I stated in an earlier paragraph. Certain characters are also very easy to win with, such as an ice elementalist who can stun-lock characters near-endlessly. Combine this with the characters that simply aren’t as good and you will get bored from the 5-10 second matches.
ArcheBlade uses controls that are very similar to third person shooters and Smite; WASD for movement, Spacebar to jump, left mouse button for primary attacks and right mouse button for secondary attacks. Guarding is also possible, but some matches boil down to whoever can guard and evade the longest. The weaker auxiliary skill is activated with Q button, and the ‘ultimate’ is activated with F. Both of these skills require a charge meter to be filled up so you pretty much have to engage in melee combat in order to be more threatening. The controls are pretty clunky, and the animations are woefully predictable. I understand that skill-based games require pretty concrete mechanics, but (personally) I find that a hint of randomness makes reactions and retaliation possible. Isn’t that just as skill-based as any other competition? Character’s also have the same movement speed as well, so that takes the idea of chasing a fleeing enemy out of play. Most characters have to get into melee range in order to attack as well, so the more ranged characters have a natural advantage.

I highly recommend this game to all Dragon Quest fans and lovers of action games. However, unless you have a rather powerful computer to play on, I must recommend you go for the PlayStation 4 version over this one.
This is my first "hack-and-slash" kind of game, and I love it. I'm not sure if I would particularly enjoy just any game of the genre, but the alure of Dragon Quest is enough to get me to try anything once, and this was impressive enough that I'm already sold on the upcoming DQ Heroes II. However, since I do not have much other experience with the genre, I'm not well equipped to compare or contrast it with other games.
I can, however compare this version to the PS4 version, which I owned until recently (and intend on purchasing again when I can get a copy of the Collector's Edition). The requirement for an i7 processor seems to be irrelevant - the one listed appears to be on the lower end of the i7 scale. I'm about 3 hours into the game and haven't had any problems with my i3-2120 @ 3.3GHz. (I'm not an expert, your results may vary.) However, I was a little dissappointed with the graphical requirements. I had to fiddle with the settings quite a bit to get the game to run at 60fps on my machine, and even now it occasionally dips around 30-ish at 720p. (I"m currently using an Nvidia GeForce 640GT.) I had to drop all the graphical settings between the low and medium settings to achieve even this resolution and framerate. It's not quite as pretty as the PS4 version this way. But I'll give it this: It looks much more beautiful and fluid than the Japanese-only PS3 release, which is locked to 1280x720 @30 fps, with much less impressive textures and shaders.
One last thing to note: While I didn't particularly expect it, I'm still disappointed by the lack of native DualShock 4 support. Even though Sony has released official drivers for it, I have yet to find a single game that supports the controller natively (without treating it as a generic DInput device). Though I was able to get around this inconvenience using an XInput wrapper (the one I use is called DS4Tool), it's still annoying, as I figured a previously PlayStation-exclusive title such as this would be a good candidate for DS4 support. Also, the rather basic-looking XBox button prompts do the job well enough but look like they were just thrown in without consideration for how they look with the rest of the HUD. They'r rather flat, with a boring font and light colors, and look rushed. (This is also the case for the PC port of the Japanese-only Dragon Quest X... Looks like a pattern to me.)
I'd give the game a 10/10 overall, 8/10 for the PC port specifically.

Runs like a dream on Integrated Graphics.
I've played this game on 3 sperate systems 4 if you include running it on Integrated Graphics for a month due to an RMA and the game has always ran very well.
It's hard to say I have had any issues with this game as it has just worked from the moment I bought it. Even on my i5 System this game easily had over 100fps on integrated playing at all Medium. To be fair to the game, even at all Medium settings 1080p this game still looked amazing and ran with little to no frame drops when running on iGPU. Solid running game and very well optimised. This game was clearly built with the lowest level of graphical horsepower provided and yet pushes that to the furthest it can. When I first loaded it and watched the "Intel HD Family" video splash I honestly thought this game would look like an end of life PS2 game. To be honest if the textures were a little sharper - You could easily confuse it for a PS4 Launch title. Especially with the grotesque amounts of Lense Flares present at any given time.
Yes this game has one - it is by far a little basic but with some racing games there is not much to be expected. As far as Career modes go this one is fairly simple. You are <Protagonist>. Your mechanic (I think - after 3 playthroughs I am still not sure) decides that after entering a few races yous can make this big racing tournament called
- World Champion Racing. Over the course of the first few "Seasons" you build a small tournament comprised mainly of US racers and tracks and get major attention from big brand sports entertainment and news outlets - Mainly ESPN. Over each season you gain tracks, racers and races from Europe, Japan and Dubai. Unlock high tier race cars and luxury sports cars all whilst chicking off "Objectives" for Sponsors (Similar to GRID but each Objective can only be finished once and new sponsors cannot be added until the begining of a new Season).
On a fundamental level - a racing game is all about how the game controls and how cars feel... That being said you will probibly need to get a pen and paper ready for when you play. Each car controls, drifts and drives differently from similar cars making some cars better for some courses than others. I
stick mostly to Drift class cars but even when I know some tracks have tight narrow corners I will take a heavy drift car over a lighter one as not to spin out going round the corner. Each car is different and each car is better at something than another car.
The HUD is fairly minimalistic compared to GRID. Where as GRID had a very blocky HUG that could take up a fair chunk of the screen on each part, GRID 2 loses all the clunky and chunky looking text and replaces it with a more clean looking UI. Most of the UI is transparent so you can see what you are doing in every POV. Compared to the first game the UI in GRID 2 takes up about 50% less space (judging by eye) and is far less distracting.
This however is a double edged sword. In GRID - if you had an issue with any mechanical part of your car you could just look at the speedometer to see what it was. If you felt your car had more of a pull to one side after a crash you could just look down and see if you had damaged your steering, whitch tire it was and how bad it was. With GRID 2 all of this is gone and replaced with a Triangle in the Speedometer that will flash yellow or red depending upon the damage. The only other clue you have is what your mechanic will say after a crash but if you miss that then you are out of the loop. THe Lense Flares (as previously mentioned) are also a major concern as the light shafts always comes from the Top Left which can obscure a timer or even make taking a corner much harder as you cannot see the brow of the hill - this part however is somewhat realistic to driving in real life and even though the game is not a Driving Sim (like Project Cars & Project Cars 2) I do like the added feel of realism at that point. Maybe they should have added a black outline to the timer or moved the timer position from Top Left.
Though the game is very enjoyable, very well optimised and can be replayed multiple times there is a few things missing from GRID 2 that were present in GRID that would have made this a more enjoyable experience, mainly the Damage HUD by the Speedometer. There is not an option to turn this on meaning you could potentially have serious damage to your car and not know until you get rear ended, spin out and total your car.
As also mentioned earlier the Lense Flares could be toned down a bit and the timer for Time Trials moved to a different location on the screen - just to make it easier to see in very bright parts of tracks or when driving towards the sun.

I've amended my CSD2 review to reflect recent game updates that addressed some of my prior complaints. E-mails have now made their return from the original game and offer a decent amount of amusing threads to pore over, and these messages sometimes contain extra decorative items for the player's restaurant. A higher degree of difficulty customization has been implemented while managing CSD itself, allowing players to choose the total number of available Prep/Holding Stations, lock their restaurant's daily Buzz to specific values, disable hectic Rush Hours or even enable infinite customer patience. Stress Mode offers the ultimate challenge, locking Buzz at 150% and maxing out both PS and HS slots.
While the UI is still far from perfect, it's been made more functional than it was at launch; players now have the option to toggle on/off different info labels for food icons in the Food Catalog, including the food's name, pricing and Holding Station requirements. Unfortunately these handy labels are not present while choosing your own restaurant's daily food offerings inside the Tower menu, which would've been even more helpful as an at-a-glance reference.
Interface issues aside, the core gameplay definitely feels like a meaningful evolution from the first game. The most substantial addition is the new "Holding Station" mechanic that allows preparation of large batches of entire dishes or individual ingredients in advance, as well as new Side Dishes that are ordered alongside main entrees and extend customers' wait timers. With effective use of the Holding Stations, it's possible to compose a daily menu of large-volume recipes that are all prepped ahead of time and ready to serve with a single keystroke, making heavy lunch and dinner rushes much easier to handle. I haven't had a chance to try CSD2's new co-op mode, but the idea of one player handling prep at the Holding Stations while the other cooks the finished recipes sounds very intriguing.
CSD2 still feels a bit thin on extra content right now, though the developer continues to roll out significant updates. Aside from growing your own restaurant, the campaign's other major focus are the new "Cook For Hire" levels that take place across several other restaurants located inside the Teragon Supertower. Each restaurant has a particular theme, such as Italian food or barbecue, and you can select from a list of daily shifts with different food options. Completing certain optional objectives during a shift earns a Bronze, Silver or Gold medal, and these can unlock additional recipes as well as other items for your restaurant. Speaking of which, CSD2 adds the ability to customize the look of your restaurant with hundreds of unlockable objects, wall and flooring options; this is a welcome addition after the very limited aesthetic options in the first game. The art style has also been given a nice overhaul with some truly mouthwatering representations of the different ingredients and recipes you can serve.
Overall I'm very pleased with the core gameplay and have high hopes for future updates.

Ok, so I'm not a huge racing game fan. I've never really been into need4speed, gran turismo, project gotham and so on. And having not lost the will to live whilst playing it I actually got ok at it and played it upto the point when the endurance races begun. Then my friend discovered it and finally here was a racing game that I could beat him at. So the Forza franchise will forever hold a special place in my affections. But sadly Microsoft have not ported any version of Forza to the PC, which sucks.
Step up Grid 2. Grid 2 has a feel of Forza about it. It looks beautiful, with graphics that are comparable to Forza 5. It boasts game play that can be exhillerating and infuriating during the same race. It also includes Brands Hatch and two F1 tracks in Yas Marina in the UAE and the Red Bull Ring in Austria. In short I have been looking for a racing game that I can find as enjoyable as I used to Forza. And although Grid 2 lacks the depth of Forza, I have found it every bit as enjoyable in the few short hours that I have played it, and for me there can be no higher praise for a racing game than that.
8/10 (would be 9/10 if it was Forza)

Dragon Quest VIII is probably one of my favorite games of all time, so when I heard that a Dragon Quest game would come to PC (Steam) I was hyped. After seeing the trailer I noticed that it wasn't the usual Dragon Quest gameplay, but more of a Hack-n-Slash/Tower defense game. Nevertheless I decided to buy the game since I liked the previous one so much.
At the beginning you can choose your main character (either male or female). The story deals with monsters and creatures turning against humanity, what's usually not the case in this world of Dragon Quest. The further you get into the story, the more allies you gain. Even getting allies from different dimensions/worlds, where characters of older Dragon Quest games come into play. It was funny to see Jessica and Yangus again after all these years, and also fun to get to know the characters from other Dragon Quest games.
While you go onto missions, you can always choose a team of 4 characters joining you. Having such a big roster of characters increases the variation in gameplay. Every character has its own spells and attacks and can be skilled in a different way. In addition to that most of them wield different types of weapons. Besides the main story, you can also do side quests and earn additional upgrades with it, use alchemy or collect mini medals.
The story itself was rather predictable, but it was still entertaining. The gameplay was getting repetitve, after 30 hours into the game. But all in all I really enjoyed the game and I'm looking forward to more Dragon Quest games on steam. 7/10

Dragon quest on steam what an epic time to be alive.
I never got the chance to play this on the PS4 due to not buying one but man I was close to missing out on one of Koei tecmos best games to date. Its your standard hack and slash Koei style at first glance but the fresh monster summoning mechanic and the crazy dragon quest monsters you have to fight make it 100times better.
Pros -
- The story is square enix all over but if you love there stuff your going to get sucked in.
- Combat is crazy good some might say repetitive but they must not be swapping it up enough.
- Monster towers is a great I dear can change the whole flow of the game where you use what you have to summon. There are 2 types - sentry to guard pathways and fend off everything that comes their way and then the saviour which will either attack the enemy's and vanish or add elements to benefit yourselves. (this feature alone makes me think a pokemon crossover would be biblical)
- Character selection - there is a lot of choice you will start the game and have to pick one main character out of 2 who will be your leader but once in battle you can chop and change between your 4 and they all have their own unique move sets.
- The soundtrack and general effects are some of the best, I personal eat this stuff up even the menu screen has the ultimate dragon quest jolly tune.
- Graphics have the nice DQ coat and the art style is what you would expect from a series of this calibre but don't be fooled the trailers do have a refined polish compared to the ingame look.
- RPG elements are just right it has a nice town hub to take side quests in, buy new weapons and armour you can even go to the tavern to pick new characters to take to battle and then you have the monster suppression list and they have even integrated the achievements in game which is a nice touch that most games usually don't bother with.
- Cut scenes are wonderful they always push the story forward and every time one comes about you know your getting close to finding a new character or fighting a epic boss monster and that refined polish make them look glorious.
- Controls are fine had no issues I used a 360 remote so not sure how the mouse and keyboard players will find it but from a 360 point of view tight and responsive.
- There are more pros with this game but ill be here all day listing them all so last pro would he helix what a legend.
Cons-
- Win7 compatibility mode, I can only play this while set to this mode it did only mean me having to go to the DQ config launcher but I feel this shouldn't be happening in 2015 I understand its a port but I doubt it will ever be sorted.
- Multiplayer has been left out on all levels, split screen or online would make this game gold standard its a real shame.
- Pricepoint does seem a tad to much would have been nice to see it at 40euro but I get that all Koei ports cost a bomb.
- Sink now im not sure if it because im in WIN7compat but the odd cutscene has gone out of sink and it can be a big gap if anyone else is having this problem you know it can be a good 4 to 6 second gap.
Overall Im really happy I picked this up, its cons don't overshine the pros and we need more collaborations like this, It really is a fresh take on both sides. Its a game thats good for all ages if you love dragon quest you will very much enjoy this and if you love DW,SW Toukiden this is another must have to the collection. If you've never tried either game go watch a review you'll know if its your sort of thing.

WTF?
In the challenges I saw that there should be more "entertaining" way to kill him. So I started to explore. Yeah, while I cannot bring my own explosives, they are lying around the street. I "just" have to memorize the timing of the clockwork cops walking around to be able to steal them.
In the previous episodes, when there was a crowded scene, using a sniper rifle from a vantage point would have been a natural solution to this. Not here -- I cannot bring my own rifle, and I have to get myself dirty with mingling in the crowd -- while I am surrounded by tall buildings. Two corrupt cops are guarding _specifically_ the apartment of a drug dealer, but if I put on the _clothes_ of the drug dealer, they not even getting suspicious. They let me through, no problem, and in the apartment -- a perfect vantage point to the target -- and wow, there is a sniper rifle! A bit of a problem: it has no silencer...
Staging ridiculous accidents, poisonings in thoroughly artificial manners are the cherry on the cake.
This is not the assassin game I used to enjoy, this is the parody of an assassin game, when you have to solve ridiculous riddles to stage hilarious situations in which the target comes out dead.
EDIT:
I managed to squeeze myself through it, on Normal difficulty, and I cheesed out the epilouge on easy. The game quite consistently sets up challenges which are a pain in the neck to complete and makes absolutely no sense. (I will not attempt to poison a highly trained assassin with rat poison, in the middle of her operation.) In Blood Money, collecting evidence was a way to clear my path. Now I have to pick up "evidence" (random files at seemingly random spots on the map). AI is hard and ridicolous at the same time; they can get suspicious of your disguise in seconds, but if you throw something, they always go and examine it. I was hiding behind the desk, a security guard was standing at the other side of the desk, I have thrown a vase past him from a distance of 1 m, and instead of investigating where the flying vase came from, he turned around and started to look at the vase.
Many maps are linear in the sense that you have to crawl through a given route -- many map does not have targets at all, you just have to get from A to B. Replayability is out of the window, performing these tasks are a chore and there is no variation or alternate solution.

Seriously, replay the previous episodes instead.

Mr. Shifty does a fantastic job of making you feel like a superhero. Blinking through walls, between enemies, and laying low wave after wave of goons with only your fists, a random broom you found and the head of a statue is exhilarating, but be warned: You might feel like a superhero, but you’re far from invulnerable. Mr. Shifty is brutal, and while it’s easy to get used to the mechanics, mastering them to really excel will take some time.
Mr Shifty wastes no times on origin stories or background, and instead drops you right into the action at the start of a heist. Your goal is to steal some deadly mega-uranium from Mr. Stone, a villainous criminal billionaire. There’s a lot of goons between you and your prize, but luckily, you’ve got just the skill set for this job.
In Mr. Shifty, you’re able to blink short distances, leaving behind a brief puff of blue smoke  a la Night Crawler. Unfortunately, whatever convenient plot point gave you this skill didn’t grace your with invulnerability or super toughness: One bullet, one laser beam or one particularly brutal punch is all it takes to stop you permanently.So, as Mr. Shifty, you’ll need to rely on hit and run tactics, using the environment and your enemies slower reactions against themselves and a dash of slow mo, activated after you get a high enough combo and a bullet gets close enough to you.
The combination of fast paced melee combat, hordes of enemies, and the ability to dart around the environment, through walls and doors, is an incredibly potent combination, and Mr Shifty will have you feeling like a superhero in no time. Of course, this will all end pretty darn quickly when you accidentally blink a hair to far away from a thug holding a shotgun to land the punch you intended for his face, and instead get a load of lead in your own.
You will die… a lot… in Mr. Shifty, particularly while figuring mechanics and what you can get away with out. It takes a few levels to get a good handle on how far you can blink, and your characters hit box, but once that clicks, the gameplay feels absolutely amazing. While there are more than a few moments where death is all but certain, there are plenty of checkpoints throughout the game, so it never feels like you loose all that much progress.
Another thing that Mr. Shifty does incredibly well is nailing the comic book aesthetic. Unlike the overly-gritty Hotline Miami Mr. Shifty has been compared to so often, the characters and environments are depicted with clear lines and bold colors. The main character has a particularly striking outline, which makes him clearly stand out from the many enemies you’ll be laying the smack down on.
My only complaint is that Mr. Shifty‘s narrative feels incredibly lack luster. Narrative clearly isn’t the focus of Mr. Shifty, but what’s there feels rather rushed, under-developed, and an excuse to include and explain game mechanics, rather than develop characters. This didn’t stop me from enjoying Mr. Shifty, but it did stick out to me.
It should also be noted that Mr. Shifty is clearly set up to be a speedrunner’s dream. Every level times you, and it’s very obviouslt that there are some very tricky manuevers that could be pulled to shave second off your time. The speedruns that are already out there of the game’s first/tutorial level (which has been available in beta) make we feel like I’m a sloth on a slow day.
Mr. Shifty is a fast paced, action game that will make you feel like a comic book hero.  Speedrunners will absolutely adore the game, and even if you’re not looking to break the record for fastest completion, Mr. Shifty is an incredibly fun, with engaging combat and mechanics.

I've been using the app for over a year and the only reason I haven't deleted it is because I've invested so much time in it. But I deleted The Quest For Stuff and that Simpsons one when they kept moving the goal posts further and further until you could only reach them if you paid for it. I'm going off track but it's kind of related.
Everything about this game is severely P2W, the majority of updates ove the past year has been catered to "the elite" so they can stay in their position by paying for it. When I first started playing they were still introducing third tier characters, when they introduced fourth level characters they were available in standard character packs as I managed a neat couple of drops.
Then things started changing, when fourth and fifth tiers started developing they dropped even fourth tier characters from standard packs. The drop level even for third tier dropped with standard packs and a legendary option was added, but to achieve this token you'd have to parcipate in PvP and PvE events with over the top achievements to get there. I work fourty hours a week, even devoting two hours in the morning before work, playing sporadically through my breaks and a couple of hours after work gets me nowhere, My points always end up halfway to where it's needed even with everything I put in. It seems like if I want to achieve anything in this game I need to quit my job and devote my entire life too it,
The P2W goes even further with later updates, not only can you upgrade tiers 2/3/4/5, if the character is already maxed out you can make them chanpions then up their levels even more. I've been playing for over a year and this game is still finding ways to punish me and reward the people who throw money at it even more,
Pro's\Con's:
There's a variety of characters, just be prepared to pay for them.
There's a variety of events, just be prepared to pay for them too,

Being a fan of the Dragon quest series I had hoped that this would live up to its expectation. I was utterly dissapointed, there are a few good points but the bad outwaeighs the good.
Summary of good Points.
1. No more turn based combat. -It is quite a contreversial change because of the JRPG genre usually focusing heavily on turn based but changing it to action was a good move it brought the game to life.
2. Crossover of all the charecters from the entire series. -The charecters from the ninetendo being introduced was exciting exhellerating even seeing some of my favourite charecter bought to 3D is still enjoyable.
3. Well done graphics. -Can't say I'm not impressed it is quite a big improvement.
Now on to the bad points.
1. The combat is repetitive. -Although the change from turn based fighting to action figthing was a good idea, it is not challenging at all. You know a few combo's and you can win the game easily without dying once. There was maybe 3 boss batlles where I had probelms but that turned around quickly  once I started to exploit their weakness. Be prepared for a lot of repetitive button mashing.
2. The crossover charecters feel dead. They have almost no emotional input towards the story except towards one of the  two main charecters and some banter but nothing interesting. (and to those who say that this game was made for family my argument is go play rogue galaxy it has is teen rated but my 8 year old cousin is playing that now and he is enjoying the experience.)
3. The poorly written story. -This game is too obvious on too many occasions. This story is the WORST in all of the dragon quest series games. You want a more linear, single plotted story line then you'll enjoy this but for people who actually enjoy the stories and takes on RPG's and sometimes different endings, you should stay away from this game you will find this boring very quickly. The charecters are overly positive and caused me to wonder what was going through their minds and then they blurt it out. The progression is stereotypical, as in the bad guy is evil older than 200 years and killed his people for no apperent reason than being evil. The supposed big reveal of the characters is not really a surprise you can see that coming from a lightyear away.
4. This game is not difficult. -As i said in point 1 this game is too easy there is no difficulty spike asside from a few varying challenges(3-4 of them) to my experience that is pathetic.
5. Linear level design. - Seriously this is a very qeustionable thing there is almost no exploration factor except maybe that you can revisit levels but that is not worth it because of the combat. Some of the previous games were open world you could explore and if you ventured to far your♥♥♥♥♥would get whooped, what happened to that aspect?
6. The crafting system. -First off i thought that this would be well done but apparently what you equip makes no difference to your appearence (except the weapons and shields). The alchemy pot has no waiting time that might be a good idea for impatient players but it removes the factor of exploration (refer to point 5). Secondly the drop rate of some of the rare items outnumber the drop rate of the basic items, so youll have all the rare stuf to craft the awesome items but then you need to fo and farm for the basics cause even the rare items need  the basic items (makes no sense and removes any further sense of progression)
5/10 Very dissapointing to me is not worth even the name of the excelennt franchise.

It's a fairly straightforward, simple-to-play, teleport around and beat people up game.  I played it with keyboard and mouse, while the game says it's best played with a controller, so I will chalk up the occasional mistakenly teleporting in the wrong direction to that.  Despite that happening every once in a while, I found the game to be very playable with a mouse and keyboard.
The core mechanic of teleporting around is very fun, smooth, and makes you feel like a badass.  You're limited to five rapid-fire teleports, but they usually regenerate pretty quickly.  If you burn through them all, though, it takes longer for them to regenerate.  You also get a short slow-mo ability that builds up as you attack.  Once it's full, getting nearly shot triggers it - sort of a "get out of jail free" card.
Despite all the pluses, the store page mentions some things that are exaggerations:
1. Shift through walls, through bullets, cover huge distances and be everywhere at once
You can definitely shift through walls.  Shifting through bullets takes...a lot of practice, but is possible.  Covering huge distances?  Not really.  You're limited to a short range with each shift, so to cover "huge" distances, you'd have to chain a lot of shifts rapid-fire, and you're limited to five.  Be everywhere at once?  Nope.  Not even close.
2. Use distraction, trickery, explore what's possible when stealth and action become one!
You *can* distract and trick enemies to some degree, and you can make clever use of your environment to kill enemies in creative ways.  Stealth, though, is next to impossible.  Most rooms are locked until all enemies are dead, so you can't truly stealth your way through this game.  Sometimes, the act of shifting destroys things that enemies hear, so sneaking through rooms can either be easy, difficult, or impossible.  There are no stealth takedowns in the game.
3. Toy with enemies, laugh as they use doors to enter rooms
If you take the time to stand there and laugh at enemies as they use doors to enter rooms, they're probably going to kill you.
4. Underestimate enemies, and cry as they use group tactics to outsmart Shifty
Group tactics?  Really?  Is that what it's called when they surround you and all fire at once?  Really, that's all they've got.  The AI is dumb.  They show no regard for their compatriots' lives and will fire or throw grenades at you even if you're surrounded by a bunch of their buddies.  You teleport away and then their buddies die for nothing.  They do not ever see or run from explosives.  They do not fire from cover.  They do come with different abilities, but use their abilities exactly the same regardless of whether they're alone or in a group.
Anyway, despite those flaws, the game is very enjoyable.  Definitely worth the $15 price tag.

e: ok, so for me, I played CSD1 by focusing my attention on the text of each individual order and pressing the necessary keys to satisy it, without looking away or having to change ingredient page. I did that by rebinding my keys so that the same ingredient was always the same key, regardless of which recipe, and it really worked. I like to call that the Mise en Place necessary before service - doing the prep, and getting your♥♥♥♥♥♥sorted beforehand. As far as I can see, you have no option to do this in CSD2. You can only bind to "universal" keys, which are position based. That would be ok except for multiple pages of position...
Bottom line is, if you loved CSD 1 and expect to jump right in to CSD 2 and enjoy it: you're not going to.
ee: there's a lot more that's wrong with this game, though, at a more fundamental level. In CSD1 you're running a restaurant, buying dishes you think you can make and saving up for progressively more dishes/upgrades/enhancements/etc. You're trying to make money because you want the next XYZ for your restaurant. I love that mechanic. (In fact I think it could have been made even stronger by the restaurant having ongoing expenses that you needed to meet, since otherwise there are no consequences for screwing up orders. But hey, that's CSD1, and why I put this in parens).
However, in CSD2, you do.... what? You pick a restaurant to work for, and you're just - boom - thrust right into it. Did you know you can or should make side dishes, on your first campaign mission? Do you even know that, actually, you have to prep ingredients for some (all the early) dishes in special holding stations before you can serve them? These are the kind of pacing problems that were alleviated in CSD1 by the fact that you, the player, were deciding exactly what dishes to serve, and before you bought those dishes or put them on the menu you got to try them out. By contrast, CSD2 drops you in at the deep end. This is an unfortunate, incredible step backwards. It's made all the worse by CSD1 handling the progression so well, and by CSD2 simply not letting you bind your keys in the same way you could in CSD1.
While this game is very good, I finished it  in around 4 to 5 hours, so. buy it at your own risk. The game I still consider Worth the price but it runs a thin line.

I hate writing reviews for games like this. Not because I don't like the game or because I don't have any strong feelings for it, but because it's so difficult to sell what's so good about it without also spoiling the very magic you're trying to praise. So brace yourself for an incredibly vague read; charting the virtues of a game whilst also avoiding any meaningful details of it in the process.
Eurgh...
By now, hearing the words "a first-person horror game on Steam" typically elicits a weary sigh or some heavy eye-rolling as the most horrifying thing about them will be the prospect of actually having to endure their insultingly abysmal content. But the thing that makes IMSCARED different from all the "me, too" genre fluff is it values atmosphere and thoughtfulness above cheap jump scares and poor attempts at sensationalism. This is the thinking-man's horror game.
Actually, I say horror, but first and foremost it's more accurate to call it a puzzle game based in a psychological horror setting. It's a game that's never abundantly clear, and always leaves you guessing. In fact, from the very start, it states that it intends to deceive you whenever possible, and it absolutely lives up to that declaration. It operates on levels beyond what's merely contained within the game and will cause you to pause often as you try to figure out your next step and apply the solution.
There are hints of a story, but it's never explicitly stated, and in a way could probably be considered one of the biggest puzzles of the game as information is gradually drip-fed to you throughout the various everyday (and sometimes otherworldly) environments you'll explore. Aesthetically, it closely resembles - and I think largely tries to ape - games like the original Doom, but also draws heavy influence from another genre masterpiece, Silent Hill.
As with the best horror games, the thing that most unsettles you isn't the blood and gore or the scary monster jumping out at you - it's the anticipation that gets you; the moments in between where your mind is doing most of the work and your worst enemy is really your own imagination. This is where the game excels, and I think strikes a near-perfect balance of building tension before delivering some kind of release in one way or another.
I do have to make one pretty major criticism, though. It's all but impossible to say without "spoiling", so I'm just going to say it... The game likes to close itself a lot. And I don't mean it crashes, I mean, at certain points the game will just shut down before having to be opened up again. And, actually, quite a lot of the time you'll need to do this manually to progress. The first few times I had to do it I thought it was a really clever and interesting novelty. But by the end of the game, when I was closing it over and over again every couple of minutes, I was thoroughly done with the concept; a classic example of a really great idea being overused and losing all of its impact, and, eventually, its good will. As a result, while I'm very glad that I played this, at the same time, I'm almost just as glad that I never have to play it again.
It may only take a couple of hours to complete, and the asking price may be a little questionable for some? (though I personally think it's fine), but even with its increasingly flawed progression mechanic, I still think this is a title worth experiencing that offers something genuinely unique and stands head and shoulders above the vast majority of its genre peers.

TLDR: The debut title from Team Shifty, Mr. Shifty, delivers a compelling and stellar experience. Many indie games fail to captivate such great charm and quality as well as Mr. Shifty does. Everything from the audio to the visual style is well thought out and complements each other perfectly. The gameplay involves a badass-but-not-overpowered teleporting mechanic which is required and exploited throughout the game in many exciting ways. Enjoy punching everyone to death as you fight your way through the most adrenaline-filled heist in a video game. Mr. Shifty will almost certainly be the most empowering and exciting top-down-puncher you will ever play.
Mr. Shifty is a top down beat-em-up set in a comic-book styled world. It's set presumably during modern times with the layout and style of the environment. The flagship mechanic in this game is the teleportation ability that Mr Shifty possesses. While we don't know why or how he can "shift," I'm glad he can. The game is set across 18 increasingly difficult stages which are different sections of a really big building. This game reminds me of Neon Chrome, which is also an enjoyable (but not as badass) top down shooter about ascending a tall tower.
- Mr Shifty opts for a sleek comic-book visual style. The game is 3D but in a top-down perspective, which helps give you an advantage over your enemies. The "shift" effect is nice and so is the visual feedback from punching. I really like the overall stylised look of Mr. Shifty, it's full of detail yet simplistic enough to not feel convoluted or messy. Overall, Mr. Shifty delivers striking and wuite appealing visuals.
- There's only 7 songs in the game which isn't very many. You will hear songs repeating quite a lot and it loses it's charm after a while. That being said, the music is very good and fits very well with the game. Definitely a job well done on the OST. Now the sound effects, those are awesome. The sound of punching has a lot of weight to it while still sounding stylised and comical, matching with the comic-book visual style. Punching enemies out of windows and hearing them scream as they fell to their death was admittedly pretty funny. I was happy to find that all the sounds have great bass to it, making good use out of my subwoofer to make the ground shake. Overall, Mr Shifty delivers a great audio experience.
- Mr Shifty has a very smooth difficulty curve, ensuring that you'll always be faced with a sufficient challenge from the opponents to match your ever-improving skills. And this game never fails to make you feel like an utter badass. The constant adrenaline high this game provides will make it hard to stop playing. I just wished this game could've gone on for longer; I was just left wanting more (and I mean that in a good way). The controls are spot-on and Mr Shifty is as competent as your fingers permit. Mr Shifty squeezes the full potential out of your controller's haptic abilities. It really makes a difference as you'll feel all the action, from subtle vibrations of smashing a goon in the face, to the violent rumbles of explosions.
In Mr. Shifty, you must ascend a tower going from floor to floor. Each floor usually has an objective, and these range from retrieving an item or simply just staying alive and finding the exit. As you progress you will encounter new enemies, and new obstacles like missile turrets. All enemies are weak and easy to dispatch, dying in 2-3 punches, however the difficulty usually comes from the sheer number of enemies, and the fact that they possess firearms. You can never use a gun, instead you must use your fists or any object you can find. And how does a purely melee character stand a chance against dozens of weaponised goons? With your shiftiness of course! The main mechanic of Mr Shifty is the short-ranged teleportation ability, and this is what makes you a badass.
Aside from smashing enemies, there are also other clever and intuitive gameplay elements. You can use your teleportation ability and add a little boom to it: pick up a proximately mine off the floor, teleport through a wall, throw it at a group of enemies, and teleport a safe distance away. Of course you need to get the timing right and not get shot, but pulling this off is just awesome. There are even some small puzzles where you need to manipulate your abilities in unique ways, and I really enjoyed those segments.
- The goal from the start of the game is to steal a Mega Plutonium from the tallest and most guarded facility in the world, Olympus Tower. You're probably the only person capable of achieving that, thanks to your ability. You have the help of a friend, Nyx, who aids you by giving you hints and finding routes with "minimal" resistance. The antagonist is a rough man known as Chairman Stone ("He's an evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" according to Nyx) and he resides at the top of the building. There's an interesting twist towards the end of the game but not much story actually develops. It would be nice to know the backstory of Mr. Shifty (maybe there'll be a prequel?) but overall, the story is sufficient.
- Mr. Shifty is pretty much devoid of any bugs, save for some inevitable ragdoll spazzing, but that's not necessarily a bad thing ;)
The performance is quite good, but in the more serious action involving lots of explosions and ragdolls flying, the frames can suffer quite a bit.
- The user interface is very well done and the menus are simple, clear and easy to navigate. Cut scenes could do with the option to skip them though (after already beating the game). The controls feel natural enough so you barely even have to learn to play, you can just jump in straight away. One little thing I appreciated is that if you died after a cutscene, you won't have to watch it again, thank goodness! The user experience of Mr. Shifty is under appreciated, it's good enough that you won't even notice it, it just feels right. Team Shifty definitely nailed the UX.
- This game took me just over 4 hours to beat, however I got all achievements and played through 3 times, which gave me 16.7 hours. If you're aiming to get all the achievements, this could easily last you up to 15 hours (trying to beat the last few levels without dying will take you a while). Aside from that, the replayability is quite low; there's no secrets or additional endings, no special unlockable powerups, and no extra difficulty modes or anything like that. There's no reason to play the game again other than for achievements.
- I would love to see a level editor, but currently Mr Shifty doesn't have any mod support or a level editor.
- I heard the game will get leaderboards in an update later on, so that sounds pretty good. Post-release content is always welcome.
Absolutely, you won't find another top-down game anywhere near as awesome as this. Just don't expect a long game with great replayability.
Overall, Mr. Shifty offers some of the most intense and exciting gameplay in a top down game. If you're looking for an adrenaline rush like Hotline Miami, the I very highly suggest Mr. Shifty. I give this game a 8/10 - An empowering game full of style and charm.

Well this one's actually tough to rate, on the one hand feels like a civ total conversion mod, on the other there are plenty interesting things that kept me going which a mod probably coudln't easily pull off, like the affinity system and the tech web. The game feels like there's more choice of customization, although the unit customization was effectively just picking from a pair of upgrades every once in a while. Choice for which technology to research is however more open than ever. And the diplomacy system is a welcome change from the standard trade/declare war/ask for alliance I've been used to in Civ games.
However the game didn't stray enough from the basic civ gameplay, sure you have new features but there's just not enough for them to provide a whole new and unique experience. If you played a lot of civ 5 before, it's likely going to feel more like a reskin, you're probably going to use alot of the same basic strategies of how to develop cities and so on, though there is novelty in the new decisions to make, the quest system and the new technologies, so there might be enough to keep you interested too.
In the end, if you never played a civ game or did so only casually and like the genre, go for it.
