Let me preface this review by stating that I loved the first Cook, Serve, Delicious!  I have an 80 day normal save and a 15 day extreme mode save with 150% buzz.  Never finished the game as it got a bit repetitive for me but I still enjoyed it immensely and will be using it as a basis to review this game.
The positives the sequel brings are pretty evident;  The food looks unashamedly glorious as does most everything else, the UI looks clean and the animations are swell.  There's enough restaurants to fill a metropolis and a variety of dishes that would intimidate even an emperor.  However, I find that the game makes these advances by sacrificing the variety of many of preparation the previous game possessed.
Many of the dishes in CSD1 felt totally unique.  The bananas foster required patience and timing, the stacked enchiladas frantic repetition, the soup and kebab mind-bending combinations of ingredients, all of this interlaced with the manual actions of knife-chops, drink pours and dish scrubs.  A few were copy pastes of each other, but the most complex ones stood out to me and tended to be the most rewarding to make.  So much of this flair is absent from this game:  Pick an ingredient and it's on your food, that's it.  Just slap on ingredients, cook a little and add more later, serve now or serve later.  Foods take all ingredients and either one or two motions or all motions to make, severely neglecting the complicated processed of chopping, mixing, pouring and heating that come with them.  There are a few exceptions, but many of these are the same dishes from the last game, and these are few and far between in the vast sea of otherwise similar foods compared to the rather diverse preparation CSD1 had.
I don't mean to undermine CSD2's new mechanics:  The introduction of holding stations is brilliant and adds unprecedented depth to your gameplay.  CSD1 focused on simply maximizing buzz and getting perfect orders, but trying to serve side dishes and drinks with every meal, being able to prep dishes ahead of time and needing to deal with dishes getting stale is a HUGE advancement in terms of depth.  Although many dishes play out the same, the huge range of complexity allows you a ton of flexibility in deciding how difficult you want your experience to be, whether it be from menu to menu or restaurant to restaurant.  For what it has lost in variety, I'd argue CSD2 now makes it up with complexity and depth.
Alongside a plethora of different menus and buzzes to cook from with the restaurant system are new options for how you want to tackle the game;  You can play with normal buzz modifiers, ramp up the difficulty to max or just sit back and tap away at your own pace.  Even though a lot of the restaurants and foods play out similarly there is variety to be found in how difficult it can be to juggle the tasks each menu presents with however many stations, and being able to choose your own pace with your own hand-picked dishes is excellent as well.
The game is missing quite a bit of the miscellaneous gameplay and management the old one had.  The catering and cooking challenges are nowhere to be found as are special events like health inspections or VIP customers (if they're in, the game hasn't given me any indication of it yet.  Let me know if I'm wrong), and restaurant progression and buzz management is heavily neutered.  In lieu, you're presented with a massive menu and a plethora of locations, an ultimately distilled experience focused on getting out as many dishes as you can along with drinks and sides as opposed to maximizing customers with brain-melting recipes.  If you came looking for more of CSD1, you'll find the soup, salad and dessert to have been replaced by a load of breadsticks, but damn if they aren't good breadsticks.
As of the 1.1 patch pushed out two months after initial release this review has been changed to a thumbs up, with most of the bugs I was concerned with fixed and new features adding in some extra kick.  It's a shame it didn't come out sooner but I'm happy it got through in the end.

For people who are interested in game design,
is a very interesting game to study. The player is dropped into the game world with little, if any, instructions or hints. They must experiment with the mechanics to discover their behaviour and relationships.
While players looking for a fun, familiar puzzle game won't find it here, players willing to dig deeper and figure out how the game works for themselves will be rewarded. Once past the initial confusion, the game's minimalist approach is refreshing. Each new discovery or "aha" moment is totally worth it, because you will have earned it by yourself.

Edit 2: now that we're able to rebind keys, I'm able to play this game again! It makes more sense now.
Edit 1: I need to edit my review. I've been waiting since the game came out for an update where I can change the key binding but we still have yet to get such an update. There are some recipes that just don't make sense with the original binding and unfortunately I can't play any more levels until I can change them, which is really disappointing because as a huge fan of the original game, I want to like this game more.
I like the new mechanics of this sequel! The holding station is an interesting concept. And I like the multiple "pages" in a recipe (i.e. the hot dog buns being on the first page and the condiments on the second). It allows for fewer unique ingredient keys which makes the process of assembling the food a lot smoother.

I really want to like this game. Teleportation is totally my superpower I would pick to have. The premise is awesome. The opening seen of X-Men with Nightcrawler is one of my favorites. This game should have been on my list of favorites...
Unfortunately, there are a couple of serious gameplay problems that ruin it for me.
1. You die in one hit. You can play perfectly for minutes doing masterfully with jumps and teleports and punches and throwing things, and then one random bullet from off the screen and it's a total do over. This is somewhat offset by a bullet time mechanic that builds via meter, but it's automatically activated, and it often goes off at totally useless times, making it very random and unhelpful most of the time. It would be so much better if this mechanic was manually operated, and I could turn on slow motion mode when I needed it.
2. It's very repetitive. You can punch, and you can teleport, and throw random objects. There's no powerups, no new skills, no variation on the basic punch attack. The enemies are slightly different variations on each other, so you run around punching guys, and then go to another room to punch guys, then another room to punch guys. There's a few variations to the rooms (like turrets) but for the most part after you've played it for 10 minutes, you know what the rest of the game is going to be like (at least as far as I could stand it). If you like mashing the same button with no variation except the amount of frustration you feel caused by #1, then this is your game.
It feels more like a demo than a complete game. More variation on the attacks, more unique weapons (the trident was awesome), being able to manually control your own super powers instead of it being poorly automatically activated by the game, enemies that actually require some skill and not just mash buttons, etc. It's very sparse, which is a shame, because the premise and the little execution it offers is so good. Too bad, so sad.

Take your time, don't rush it, and this game will grow into you like a seed in the soil. It is extremely difficult to win (I only completed one or two of the challenges), but once you get the grip of it, you're up to a rewarding experience.

IAMSCARED is not like other games. It’s “meta” and it’s spooky. I can see how the designer was aiming to create a unique experience, and I commend him for this, but in the end I think he was only partially successful in the execution of his goal and in creating a game I wanted to play. I ended up just watching my friend play through most of it and if it was only me I would have given up before I finished.
My thoughts (very mild spoilers ahead):
* The meta-puzzles (puzzles which require you to look outside the game itself) are clever and out of the ordinary.
* The more traditional puzzles are all pretty simple. The answer is usually obvious although sometimes you might have a hard time because of the game controls or because you can’t find something.
* For the most part the game succeeds in creating an eerie atmosphere. The sound, the way the environment looks, the creepy messages and enigmatic characters….
* As others have pointed out, part of the scare factor is a result of your annoyingly small field of vision. You can only see like five feet in front of you so it’s easy to run into something surprising.
* Related to the limited field of vision, the game has a lot of jump scares. These are fun at first but get old fast, especially if you are caught by the monster and have to replay the same part again and again. This is frustrating; but more than that it can destroy the scare factor.
* The controls! You need to use the WASD keys to move around (this alone is almost a deal breaker for me) and the game is not very responsive, so your movements are jerky. It’s also easy to get stuck in a corner or at the edge of a wall (this is  just a result of poor game design/programming). It’s particularly frustrating in parts where you’re being chased and need to run.
*The graphics and the environment: I have mixed feelings. I see what the designer was going for with very basic, very retro graphics. The game’s look reminded me of EGA computer games and also the LSD: Dream Emulator on Playstation. So this gives the game a dream/nightmare vibe and it fits well with the “deconstructing the game” aspect of IAMSCARED. On the other hand, this really goes beyond artfully pixelated and sometimes just feels insufficiently detailed (get close enough to something and you’ll see it’s just colored blocks).
* More than the graphics, I disliked the low level of interactivity. 90% of the objects you see (bookcases, cabinets, tables, shopping carts) are just decoration you can do nothing with. You’ll spend a lot of the game going up to things and trying to interact with them only to find out “nope.”
*Related to the simple puzzles and the static non-interactive environment, there are a lot of times when it seemed like I reached a dead-end and needed to do something (like find a key or a secret passage or something) but the answer was that I needed to trigger something like a “cut scene” and then when I came back the way would be clear.
*The story: again mixed feelings. In the game you’ll encounter one or two important characters. You’re given vague hints as to what their story is, but it’s left pretty fuzzy. On one hand, this is good because you need to fill in the blanks yourself and it’s open to interpretation. On the other hand, maybe there’s just not enough there.
*That leads into my final gripe which is that there’s no pay off. Towards the very end, the game throws up such a barrier it’s almost like the designer doesn’t want you to finish the game. And the ending(s?) are kind of anti-climactic; it made me question whether it was even worth it.
TL;DR: All-in-all, if I put aside the annoying controls, I’d say I got something out of IAMSCARED and enjoyed the unique meta-puzzles but so many things frustrated or bored me that I would never have finished the game on my own.

People say "You need to experience this game for yourself." They behave in an obtuse manner, as if there is some grand secret there, something that is wonderous that is just hidden away.
They're lying. There isn't anything here.
The game is garbage. You plant seeds. They grow. There are some mechanics related to them - the pink seeds can be harvested for more seeds. The bush sprouts heart flowers which can be collected when you go into the void. The orange block's growth is dependent on whether it has space to grow horizontally. The red one explodes outwards in blocks and will throw you into the void if you stand too close.
Your goal is to get to the void star blocks - not the one on the bottom, but ones which are off isolated on far edges of the screen. These turn into keys when you step into them, but unless you have brought your blocks up adjacent to it, you'll have no way out.
Once you grab your key, you can go back to the start and go back into the main world, where you can plant seeds and grow to reach other areas with bits of esoteric poetry hanging in the sky.
There's a hidden block with three little stars in it which spawns a three keyhole exit. Bringing three keys to it will let you unlock some secret levels which can then be navigated to completion.
There are a number of levels in the game, and they all LOOK the same, but are functionally slightly different. The void doesn't absorb you in some. You can't destroy blocks in others. The list goes on.
The way they describe it, it seems like an unlocking, unfolding type game, but it isn't. It is just the very basic growing mechanics which the game is obtuse about. That's the limit of the discoveries in the game.
It is boring. And it is a waste of time.

In my opinion, excessive RNG battles does not equate to welcome difficulty.  In this game, you are given a random sequence of seeds that will grow in a completely random way.  Yes, there are ways you can abet the enemy of randomness by planting them strategically, but unlike something like Tetris, where the player's strategy and direct control ultimately allows them to conquer the RNG, this game turns up the randomness times 10, and when the RNG beats you, it beats you HARD by throwing a wrench in your plans that you can't do anything about.  Imagine if Tetris occasionally gave you an awkward shape that has 20 squares in it.
The discourse around this game will scoff at you and tell you that you just aren't artsy/smart enough, and you should go back to playing your easy games like CoD and AC, you non-progressive little pleb.  I think this is just an unfortunate legacy from older players whose nascent years were the 80s and 90s, when publishers had to convince us that excessive trial-and-error punishment and RNG-derived difficulty were good things.  If you are fine with (or enjoy) such game design, then you will actually find a really neat puzzle game underneath these things that I hate.
I definitely would have given this a thumbs up if it weren't for how punishing the RNG is, because the concept of the puzzle itself is fun, discovering the mechanics was fun, and the aesthetics were cool.  It definitely isn't worth 6 dollars in my eyes (good thing I got it in a bundle), but I could universally recommend it more if it were around a dollar.

Eidos Montreal had all the experience they needed for developing Thief through the making of Deus Ex: Human Revolution. Although the new Thief was a bit harder to create since the last game of the series was released in 2004 and they had to keep the new game's atmosphere as close to the older ones as possible.
Starting with the story it's not what you will remember after you have finished Thief. You will be expecting most of the plot twists and towards the end the story seems a bit far fetched. The City is divided in different areas or districts. The problem is that those districts are divided into smaller areas as well so there are frequent loading screens. Also the city offers an illusion of an open-world environment but the truth is that you can't go everywhere you want to. But even in a smaller area there are many paths you can follow to your destination whether it is on the rooftops or the roads.
The biggest problem of the game is it's AI. It may be easy for enemies to spot you but it is really easy to escape and hide. Just hiding in some shadows or climbing on a roof does the trick. Also their reactions to noises, torches of fires going off or when finding bodies are really bad. They may look around for a while and then go on with their patrols as if nothing happened.
Leaving the games problems behind, the stealth mechanisms are really great. Garrett has a lot of tools and his trusted bow at his disposal which he can use to avoid his enemies or dispose of them. The City is filled with loot to steal and a lot of them (especially unique loot and collectibles) are really hard to find so that offers a good challenge. You will have to find safe combinations, secret passages behind bookcases and items hidden behind paintings. Sneaking around the city and searching every corner and every house for loot is really fun.
If it's hard for you to find loot you can use the Focus ability which highlights objects you can take or use and enemies. The thing is that Focus makes the game a lot easier so try to avoid using it as much as you can. Garret's abilities can be upgraded by buying (or findind) Focus points and you can also buy new tools or equipment upgrades from merchants around the city.
The game's graphics are great. Especially the character's faces which are really epxressive. The animations are smooth. As for the music, it gets a little annoying at times. For example when you are trying to sneak around somewhere and you hear music pounding in your ears. The voice-acting is good as well with Garrett's voice standing out.
If the bad AI is not a really big problem for you then Thief can give you a really great time. There are a lot of secrets to discover and finding them using Thief's stealth mechanincs is a real pleasure.

The early access version of this game is much more playable using keyboard and mouse than using a gamepad, at least for me.  With all that said, it looks like all the right stuff is there in the game.  The controls are easy to get used to and there is a definite beauty found in the thought 'less is more'.
The music is amazing and transitions from area to area.  The control is tight.  Death is a part of this game, but the balance between what you can randomly acquire on your misadventures versus what you can build up between deaths is very nice.  Because there is a balance between the two, I hesitate to call this a 'roguelike', where accomplishment is >90% the skill and randomness of a run.  With all that said, sitting down and blowing stuff up is fun!  Looking forward to more content and challenges ahead.
Some improvements I'd like to see (skipping content requests and keeping everything vague to try to avoid spoilers):
- More granular randomness:  the current level seems to be generated in sections.  Think of rooms and once you see the same room fifteen times you have figured out all its secrets.  However, you can to a great degree predict which enemies will be where and the game becomes a grind rather than engaging.
- More AI depth... combined arms.  So, when enemies are grouped it's really easy to blow them all up as a group.  They spawned as a group, they die as a group.  That's awesome.  In keeping with simple AI, allow units in groups to work together.  Maybe a big enemy throws a small enemy at or behind you.  Maybe a fast moving enemy picks up one or two small enemies and brings them with as a sort of earth-shattering kaboom.  Perhaps the likelihood of bots to work together increases with the amount of resources you spend between deaths or uses some other measure.  Whatever these combinations are, still keep it simple so that the learning curve doesn't become a cliff.
Bottom line: for an early access game, what is delivered is rather well polished and full-featured.  Everything in this review is subject to a LOT of change as the game is still in early access.

This game is unfortunate that it suffers for being a reboot of one of the greatest and most important series of games of all time. Thief is a very good stealth game on its own but as a reboot, it is a terrible Thief game. What made the original Thief games great was thrown out the window for linear-looking levels, weird A.I and lots of problems and bugs for some Steam users who preordered the game although I was fortunate not to have to deal with it. And don't get me started on the story. There's potential but the execution was bad. And the last third act leading to the ending was a complete disappointment. Without Stephen Russell in the role, Garrett's voice sounds pretty flat most of the time.
However, Thief The Reboot FELT like a Thief game and that's where this reboot excels. Stealing here is as fun as it was in the original games, maybe even better. The tension as you're opening a drawer to pocket a bit of loot is there and the glee as you watch your loot count rise brings back memories from the old games. Challenge Mode is brilliant, that's where the replay value for this game is. Its more tense and more exciting than the base game itself. No need to worry about the story or anything, just focus on good ole stealin.
Not a great game but not a terrible game either. Thief 2014 will probably be remembered years from now as a missed opportunity but hopefully, it will ignite an interest for more returns to the Thief universe. But it looks like we'll have to wait some more for a more triumphant return of the Master Thief.

I knew the game would be a different experience, and hard hitting, from watching other people play the game on Youtube. But boy, did I get myself into some state playing the game.
Sitting there, playing God to survivors just trying to make it through a war, is a lot harder than I had originally thought. The choices you make DO matter so much in the end. Whether or not you give food to one character, whether you steal from others, rat out your neighbours to the local militia, or even worse, kill someone. Any morals you are firm in before starting this game, prepare yourself to throw it away. As you become desperate in the latter days, you become so desperate that you have to steal, or kill in self-defense, and yet, you feel so guilty for it afterwards.
There are an immersive cast of characters, including your own made characters later on in the game. Some are far more useful than others, though have contrasting personalities. One can be completely against murdering someone, and yet another couldn't give a toss if you murdered someone for your own gain.
The visual art style and soundtrack in this game is AMAZING. It gave me the sense of being there in that shelter, shivering or starving to death. When going through dangerous places, every little sound give me the creeps, kept me on my toes the entire time, just as a game should do.
If I could fault it on anything, it'd have to be the controls and the tediousness of playing the game for awfully long. At first, not being an overly avid keyboard/mouse player, I found it a little difficult and almost tedious at first with the click to move function, especially when dragging the screen at first (until I realised I could simply move the mouse to the side of the screen to move it.) Playing the game for incredibly long like I did on my first playthrough over a span of a week or so became more of a chore as I continued on. Yet, nonetheless, the game had me immersed, and kept me coming back.
Overall, I became incredibly fascinated and enlightened by This War of Mine. If you are looking to buy this, I wouldn't hesitate. Getting this in the Autumn sale was probably the best thing I had ever done!

I've played this game for roughly two years on the iPad & iPhone, and although I've taken a few breaks, I generally play it every day.  I find it to be a somewhat repetitive but still enjoyable game.  Mechanically the battles are done using a match-3 mechanic, like a bejeweled game.  It's not hard, but I'd say it's more challenging than Candy Crush or other similar games.  The tricky part is that there's a paper-rock-sissors element to the characters, and you need to match enough a certain color gem to enable a hero's power to be used.  Like many other free-to-play games, there are two currencies, one common and another rare.  (plus a third, command points, which was recently introduced and can unlock much stronger four or five star characters).
The real key to success in this game is patience and persistance.  It's somewhat pay to win, but the truth is that I'd say it's pay-regularly-to-frequently-win, or play-frequently-and-do-ok. If you just keep plugging away, your characters will continue to improve, and you'll stay reasonably competitive for a long time.  It's fairly easy to play entirely for free, though I'll admit I found there was a point somewhere around the mid-two-star level where I coughed up some actual money in order to not lose characters. In retrospect, this was unnecesary, but I didn't realize it at the time. I'd recommend reading through some of the great guides on the marvel puzzle quest forum for advice on which characters to keep and which to get rid of.
I think the most fun part of this game, over time, is that the developers truly seem interested in keeping it alive and interesting. I like how they keep introducing new mechanics.  I feel like sometimes they don't entirely think through the result of their actions on the way that people play the game.  For example, right now with new command points, rewards for people like myself working on their four-stars is definitely skewed to PvE rather than PvP.  I don't know if the developers did this intentionally, or just don't realize it.  But whatever. It's still fun, and somehow it's more fun for the fact that they're not entirely polished and thoughtful in their actions.   Some people get bent out of shape about this, but I actually think the chaos that comes with each new game mechanic or meta-change keeps things fresh.
I'd recommend it for the tablet or phone.  It's the perfect game to play once or twice a day over lunch break.

Typical puzzle game with a twist. Each super hero has special abilities that are charged up by matching gems of each color. For instance, a super hero may have a power that requires 12 "red" gems to charge, so you must match 4 sets of 3 red stones, then that power becomes available to use. There are some interesting strategic combinations that affect the outcome of the game, and the Marvel characters are beautifully rendered.
It doesn't take long, however, before you doubtlessly realize that you have hopelessly screwed up your game, either by buying heroes when you should have been buying hero slots or leveling up your existing heroes. This will basically make the game a fun sucking grind early on. The obvious solution would be to start over from scratch. This is easy... if you are playing this game on a phone. If you are playing on a PC, you're basically screwed, because the developers haven't bothered to allow players to reset their progress on PC (at least not a way that's as easy as "start new game").
Go ahead and look up how to reset the game, and you will find a lot of conflicting opinions, and very little that is likely to work, since the solutions are all from 2013. The quick and expensive way to make your game playable again is to buy tokens to fix your FUBAR game save... so, of course, that's where they want you to go... when phone users can just delete their file and start over from scratch.
This game is hopelessly flawed on PC. It's literally stops being fun as soon as you hit the brick wall of battles the game says "are trivial" difficulty. Unfortunately, it's yet another underwhelming Marvel title on PC. Stick to the phone if you're going to play it at all.

The game has a simple premise:  The character you control is a clockwork postal bird, kind of like a parrot.  The objective is to get from one cage to another to deliver the mail, avoiding anything spiky along the way that will kill you, and don't fly off the screen either.  Your flight direction is predetermined, but you have the ability to click and drag your clockwork bird to teleport in order to avoid hazards.  Pulling this off successfuly is another matter.  It becomes more difficult as each level progresses.  Just when you think you've avoided a set of spikes, a steam jet can change your direction and now you're flying in a direction you don't really want to go.  To add to that you have gates that slam together, pinwheels that spin around, and the screen is constantly moving you ever onward, and not always just left to right.  Sometimes the scrolling direction changes.  There's no health meter or hit points.  Touch something sharp and you're dead.  Fall behind and you're dead.  It will test your reflexes and mouse skills, and patience as levels become increasingly difficult.
The levels themselves are fairly short so it's an easy game to play for a while, put down, and come back to.  As you play you can collect gears on each level and gain a "flawless" status for completing a level without dying and collecting all 3 gears on the same pass.  You can die as much as you like (there's achievements based around the number and types of deaths) or you can restart a level and try to get a flawless status.  There's really no difference between dying and chosing restart from the menu except that restarting will reset your death counter so you can attempt a flawless pass.  The teleportation mechanic itself is very straightforward.  It's just click, drag, and release.  It's extremely easy to learn.  There's 60 levels.  It's already challenging by level 10.  Expect it to be hard to master.
Visually the theme is black and red, and I mean that - just black, and just red.  Well, a little variation on the red, but mostly just red.  The environments are steampunk inspired, with spikes, lots of metal framework, spikes, gears, spikes, steam pipes, and did I mention spikes?  Yeah, you'll want to avoid those.  It's very minimalist and simplistic, which actually helps with the gameplay.  There's no cluttered textures or anything that will visually distract you from what's important.  The high contrast keeps you focused on the hazards and your bird.
The soundtrack seems to be Hungarian, or at least the title song is.  It's fairly light and completely non-distracting, giving an upbeat air to what would otherwise seem like a completely hellish environment.  Again, going with the theme of sharp contrasts, it fits right in.
Performance concerns should be a non-issue due to the visual simplicity, and there's no real benefit of playing this on a super-high resolution.  You can play it at 1024x768 just fine.  It'll play just fine on your custom gaming rig or the "old family computer".
An often overlooked concern with video games... this game is a very good choice for colorblind players.  The high contrast between the open spaces and solid objects means that those who cannot see the full spectrum won't have any trouble distinguishing between the two.
Final word:  If you want a simple game that's easy to learn but provides a fairly steep challenge you can't go wrong here.

Playing The Red Game after its successor, Green Game: Timeswapper may make this review a bit skewed. The core objective in both games are the same - navigate the Bird through some obstacle-ridden scenes to the target cage, and collect all three cogs if possible. How to do that differs significantly though - in Green you only control the environment, while in Red you control the Bird directly - drag and drop to teleport it to another area of the screen.
That's our first problem right here - while the control method is intuitive, it doesn't make much sense as you're only ever teleporting the Bird. So why not only point to the destination? Because then the game would be so easy, of course. Needlessly complicating the control method to increase difficulty is a pretty bad design choice, I believe, and additionally, the controls are not really accurate.
Combine that with the other glaring issue (also present in Green), that the game is unable to detect collissions accurately, and you have a recipe for disaster. But... no. Even like this, Red manages to be fun and entertaining, if sometimes infuriating for the wrong reason. The level design is more consistent than in Green, fewer clever tricks but also (much) fewer lame filler levels. The visuals and the music are similarly fetching, and up to level fifty-something, I was having a great time. And then the rotating levels came in. Quickly rotating screen + sloppy controls + bad collision detection = why am I still playing this game? Listening to my inner completionist, I suffered through most of these levels, but at the end level 60 just proved to be to much of a waste of time, not to mention the slowly developing nausea. Too bad.
At the end, there's much to like about The Red Game, but obviously, I'm recommending it with quite a bit of caution. It's not for everybody.

The trailers made it look like Dragon Quest meets Dynasty Warriors, and while this is technically the case, most missions put more emphasis on a system that works more like  tower defense than anything else. Overall, I'd say that the game is worth around $10-15, a far cry from the $60 they're now charging, which essentially amounts to a whopping $3/gameplay hour for a boring, repetitive disappointment.

It's a nice little “puzzle” game where you have to help a mechanical bird to fly from one point to another on the level and pick some stuff on the way. The twist is in the unique controls which let you teleport a bird into any empty from obstacles place on the screen by dragging it there with a mouse. However, you can't stop it or directly control flight direction of the bird, so don't leave it alone for too long since it may crash into spiky objects and... break, I guess. It's mechanical, so it can't actually die. The level scrolls on its own too, so if the bird will go off-screen it will “break” too.
However, these unique controls are both blessing and woe of this game. They feel out of place since they were developed for a touch-screen in mind and mouse is different. It feels clunky and hard to control.
There are only two audio tracks in the game. One in the menu and one on the levels. They ain't bad. The one in the menu is actually a song “Maszynka do Świerkania” by Czesław Śpiewa. Wait a bit in the menu and listen. You may like it. At least I do.
Can't say it does or doesn't worth a full price. Clunky controls are quite disappointing. Also, achievement hunters will be annoyed by that “die 5000 times” achievement. Even with 60 level in the game you have to be terribly bad at it to die that often naturally. So, if you want 100% in achievements that might be frustrating. I'd recommend installing some auto-clicker application and start a level with an obstacle which will kill a bird in front of a cage. Then just leave it clicking to make it fly and die repeatedly and go to sleep.
BTW, the whole “don't die” mechanic is not for a hard challenge, but only to screw your “flawless” achievement in case you won't figure out how it works. Only death counter on the level counts towards “flawless” playthrough and it's easy to reset it with a “Reset” button in the pause menu. Don't forget to press that button every time you die.
I recommend give it a try, but it might be better to pick it up during a sale or in a bundle. It's short and a bit clunky.

The Splinter Cell franchise has not only been known for its weird name, but its innovation in the fields of stealth games. Each title in the series brings something new to the table, and this one is no different.
This game has a gigantic amount of strategy and options of play within it, so much so you don't really have to play stealthily most of the time. Each playthrough will no doubt have you testing out new ways to get the job done, coupled with the amount of levels makes this aspect one of the best features about this game. The game rewards you well for playing nicely.
You will have to think smart more and more as you progress through each challenging level, as they get tougher and tougher to pull off. Each and every level is extremely fun and challenging to play through, and require a good bit of thought to get through.
The dialogue between characters is very well done and you will talk to a lot of enemies and learn intel or just their general personality which is always entertaining. The game also has its fair share of funny moments as well to lighten the mood, which is gladly welcomed.
If singleplayer wasn't enough, multiplayer co-op is also in, adding even more fun and tactical thinking with your friends. There is also an online versus mode to try too.
The soundtrack as well is also very fitting for the game and never fails to immerse you into the experience.
At full price or not this is definitely worth your time, and is a great starting point for perhaps those new to stealth games or some such.

Despite all the negative things that were said about Hitman : Absolution, I can safely say that this is a great game. And that's from a guy who played Hitman ever since the Codename 47 era!
So, here's an objective review about this game, not biased by any of the post-previous entries expectations, but from someone who wanted to spend good time on an entertaining stealth-action game.
First, the graphics are insanely good! It's the first think that struck me when I first played it. For a 2012 game, they are more than decent, and I think they still are for today's standards. Hitman : Absolution is pretty to look at AND it runs smoothly. This is something today's games have hard times to achieve, so I thought it was good to mention it.
The light effects and reflections are very good. See the screenshots in the Steam store? Well, the actual game just looks like that! And speaking of graphics, I find Agent 47's face extremely well detailed and designed. They really nailed the character and you can read in his eyes how brilliant he is as a cold-blooded killer.
As for the gameplay, it's interesting to note that not all levels contain targets to assassinate, which is one of the reasons why other players disliked Absolution. I think the fact a lot of levels are classic action-stealth and "go through that area undetected" kind of gameplay, isn't a reason to bash this game. The developers wanted to try something new, and they did an great job with it. Those levels are really well designed and amusing, and there's, as usual, several ways to progress without being seen.
Keep in mind that there's still a whole lot of levels with bad people to eliminate in tons of different ways, so your average Hitman gameplay isn't absent from this title, by far.
About the story, well... I enjoyed it, really! In my opinion the plot was a bit weak in the previous games (apart from the first), but this time they worked on a very polished storyline and wonderful cutscenes that almost watch like a movie. The voice acting is excellent (especially the french one, which I played with) and the bad characters really are hateful. Unlike previous games in which they were introduced with a short speech, in Absolution you actually get to see them in action and what their motivation and personnalities truly are. It justifies their assassination a lot more and makes you closer to Agent 47, story-wise, I believe.
The game length and replay value are excellent. The levels are numerous, and many of them contain several areas. You can count a good 15-20h to finish the campaign the first time, and roughly between 50h and 100h to unlock all challenges. You may add to this a fairly entertaining Contracts Mode which offers virtually endless content, and you will get the most replayable game of the franchise (I haven't played the last HITMAN 2016 game though).
Finally, to mention a few negative sides, I'd say that the PC version crashes, unfortunately, a bit frequently. It occurs when you restart a level too often, sometimes it just gets stuck on the loading screen, and you must close the game manually. It's a bit frustrating, but it wasn't gamebreaking. Apart from that, I didn't have any other problem with crashes and bugs.
The other negative bit would be the Contracts Mode management being a bit clucky... if not non-existant! Okay...a pretty biassed review here: I played the **** out of the first cook, serve, delicious, and heavily participated in a private beta session. Though this was at the time pretty much all mechanics were in place, I have seen the game become better a lot. And it was already a great game.
So what's this one's about? Quick management skills and typing lessons, if you want to hear the abstract truth. Yes, it's themed like running a restaurant. Yes, it has lots of cooking in it. But when it all comes down to it, it's a matter of mashing the correct button sequence as fast as possible while choosing which buttons you mash. You can play the game with a mouse or game controller as well; this experience is a bit different, but I'm not sure how well it fares in the later levels.
Games play out as follows: you have a bunch of lanes on the left of the screen. Here you'll get your requests for meals or for chores to keep your restaurant clean and operational. They'll be patient, but up to a certain degree. Meaning: taking too long on one task means that you'll have less time to spend on other customers or chores.
Luckily, you'll get help. Where in C.S.D.1 you could just wait for the masses to come in, here you can prepare some dishes in advance in so-called holding stations. These allows you to either reduce the complexity of orders or increase the overall patience (as well as get extra income). However, the food in the holding stations can both run out and go stale, so while being a great help, it's not something you can forget about. Nonetheless, these stations are a great addition in four different ways:
Aside the holding stations, the main draw to this game is local co-op. I've played this with my girlfriend, and was amazed how little we were actually in each other's way. With so many tasks, we almost immediately went with what we thought had to be done and rarely needed to speak to each other (though it obviously adds to the fun).
Speaking of my girlfriend: she's not much of a gaming enthusiast. This is one of the exceptions she absolutely adores.
Does it has drawbacks? Not to my taste. Of course there were nitpicks and things I would've liked, but with this INSANE food selection and beautiful graphics, it absolutely scratches the itch of my addiction of having to handle way too many tasks at once and mentally assigning priority in milliseconds. I do have to warn you: this game gets pretty hard once you level up. 'Chef for hire' is a recurring theme of the original where you spend days on premade menus. It's brought more to the front now, with LOTS more restaurants with about a dozen levels on each one. I haven't seen the later levels, but I've got reasons to believe it gets much wilder than on its predecessor, and that was pretty wild as well.
Should you get it? As stated in the start, I'm biassed. For me, the answer will always be yes and twice on Sunday. But I like games that are unique, weird and require skills of an uncommon kind. Aside from the first game, I honestly don't know a single game that's even remotely like this (the "closest" I can think of is rocksmith, and that's really not very close :P ). I like the theme, I like the graphics, I like the idea, the gameplay, the sounds and music, the co-op...I'd say "everything", but I haven't even started decorating my restaurant with all the loot I got from serving customers.
So my bottom line becomes: the game is perfect...and has restaurant decoration on top of that. :P

So far, Botlike is an interesting sidescrolling platformer with randomized and roguelike elements. It combines move and shoot elements from games like ARES with pseudo randomized levels, coming across as easy to control with levels that feel fairly fresh while still allowing you to 'learn' the level. It also includes passive buffs similar to Risk of Rain, a permanent upgrade system a la Rogue Legacy, and enough weapons to choke and elephant. Classy.
After receiving a copy from the dev, I sat down and played about 30 minutes of the game. The controls felt fairly responsive, though I feel as if the timing of the double jump in relation to some of the platforms for 'secret' chests may be a little restrictive. Moving and aiming feel fairly natural and simple with a somewhat simple WASD + Mouse setup, though jump on both spacebar and W feels a bit odd. Apart from the aforementioned oddness with jump timing, everything felt good with the controls.
Graphics are shiny. There's plenty to look at in both enemy selection and environments so far. Cool lighting effects and fun pixelated graphics. Naturally there's a limited enemy selection and environs, but I expect that to change over the course of development.
The user interface is intuitive for the most part, but there's a few elements that are missing or lack information for the player. The combo system and the passive system come to mind for the latter, and any information related to the stats for the former. The devs say changes to fix these are on the way.
The music was enjoyable, though not entirely memorable yet. It didn't get repeitive or boring in the 30 minutes I played, but I don't yet find myself whistling it.
As for the most important part, gameplay, I kept wanting to go back in. Every time I died I checked to see if I could buy something before diving back into the game. Learning different areas and looking for secrets. While there's no overarching goal yet that I've seen, it was fun seeing how long I could last, how high I could get my multiplier up, and what guns I got. There's enough variety to keep me entertained at this stage. The passive items are also fun and similar to Risk of Rain; they give you a hint as to their function, but you still have to work at it to figure out what they do. It was fun to simply buy them or get drops as opposed to just the latter.
Overall, Botlike feels like a fantastic start to the game. There's definitely a good base here, and I want to see how it grows.  The devs have already been responsive to the few things I've mentioned both in video and in their discussion boards, so I feel as if there's a definite future for this game. I'd highly encourage taking a look and potentially jumping on it to help them work on bugs, balance, and improvements in the future.

I feel weak and powerless against more than two enemies and it makes me want to flee and rethink my strategy, really adding to the intensity of the game when you are fleeing and tests you patience and skill while you wait for the perfect opportunity to slip by unnoticed,  I enjoy the large variety of different arrows at Garrett's disposal. Beyond Gravity is an interesting number, a find courtesy of steams lovely little coupons.
I honestly have to say this is one of the simplest, sometimes infuriating and yet most enteraining little games I've played in a long time. The controls are literally just one button; Either your space bar or left click, that is it. You use these simple controls to guide your crashed astronaut (Jeff) through a series of different planets, by literally planet hopping, trying to avoid the occasional fire balls hitting you in the face and squishing you and collecting screws to repair your spacecraft, (I'm assuming anyway).
Among that, it offers some quaint little upgrades, visual ones included, stereotypical system for a ported pad game, but in all, it's an addicting little thing that is brilliant if you enjoy the 100% of achievements and such.
The system of only being able to work on 3 achievements at a time was one I've not seen before but came to enjoy quite a bit as it didn't have you trying to do about 20 different ones at any given time, it also actually felt rewarding with having to collect them at the end of a round that you had just earnt certain ones within.
The graphic style is another thing I have to give it credit for as it's one I'm particularly partial to personally. However..
There is one background throughout the entirety of the game along with one soundtrack which is all nice and dandy for a short while, but you soon find yourself diving into the options to turn it off and play some music of your own just to numb out the sound from the game as it really does grate on your nerves after a while. Along those lines, it also doesn't offer much if any replay value once you've unlocked all the goals, aside from fully upgrading everything and occasionally opening it up to just play something fun that doesn't require much brain power at all. Other than that, it's fantastic and gives a good 4ish hours of play.

I've spent my fair share of time playing this game, I love the mechanics.  The combo system is a little picky in the sense you have to really pay attention to your clicking finger and don't rapid click or you'll end up locked in the animation you don't want.
So the premise of this game is... I don't really know, it's based off of some manga somewhere and there is a good side and a bad side and some kingdom with undead pop stars, Money Monks, murderous sexy insurance brokers, some guy with a big sword and a deathwish and uh...some hedonistic narcissistic jerk who is a good guy (But he's fun to play).  Honestly I could care less about the story... it seems like a fascinating world I'm sure with a huge variety of characters though you'll never really get to know most of it just by playing the game.
I love the Arena style combat, the gameplay is solid and based off the Unreal Engine which is always a good choice when dealing with network based games.  Each character has enough difference between them with similar playability that makes them each familiar but interesting.  I'm a bit of a fighting game nerd, so it's important to note that different character match ups can end up with different results... however this game seems to be balanced that you are not likely to be stomped by a person who is just clicking haphazardly...  But yes, sometimes you will fight some characters which will be at an advantage to yours while you will be at an advantage over others.
The group combat is really what shines the most here, while with any game where the fighters are different enough that 1v1 with every match up combination may not be completely balanced (not impossible... but when you play as other characters you tend to avoid certain other ones) and usually (depending on server) like in other team versus games you'll find that you can only play characters that arn't picked yet so you won't fight a legion of mini-skirt wearing insurance hipster brokers.  The combat gets crazy, and often chaotic but at the same time if you pay enough attention and you're not taking on 3 rivals (in most cases) by yourself you can actually survive if you manuever enough.
This is a freeium game, though I can't say paying really puts you that much ahead like in other games.  However it's worth shelling out a couple of bucks here and there if only to unlock alternate outfits or get some gear...not that it helps you too much.  If you're bad at using your character... you're still going to be bad at using your character.  Whatever advantages you have at low levels when you level up enough you'll be fighting in a pool with players who have dealt with you and your character a thousand times before and will deal with you again.
The Graphics and Sounds are nice, though honestly it's definitely for anyone that loves that super shiny anime look.  I'm just happy it's simple enough to be playable and clean enough to not look like crap while playing.  Though uh... everyone is bit unrealistically shiny but I'm sure people could chalk that up to the anime look.  The music is repetitive and catchy but play enough hours and it will be stuck in your head for days... Days...... DAYS...
The only problem I really have with this game, is really the most crippling part.
Content.
I still feel like I'm playing the base demo of the game, even after messing around with it for a year I'm still stuck with the same old same old.
I can't completely blame the developers for this, what they have is the potential for a really great game - but just as they mentioned back in May they just arn't making ends meet.  It's sad to see this game potentially just eventually dry out and fade off considering even what was highlighted to come.
So really.  I recommend this game, infact- I've been recommending this game.  It's freaking Free to Play and it's not total crap.  Give it a shot, tell your friends, make some D*mn youtube videos of playing it.  There are a ton of POS games out there that get way more money and recognition than this one.
And if you like it, shell out the 5-10 bucks or whatever and show your support.  This is seriously a game that has potential and is only falling short because of the lack of funding.

Cons:
Bad plot.

What is "Beyond Gravity"?
Beyond Gravity is a very simple game set supposedly in space but with gravity none like it would be found in space. You take the role of an astronaut who crashes against a planet and has to jump from planet to planet, avoiding fireballs and collecting screws and cogs for no reason other than to buy upgrades for himself in his spaceship.
If you lay all the horrifying failures in the story aside, however, you are treated with a simlistic yet for a while fun game that tests mostly your hand-eye coordination. Unfortunately you will notice that the game is as simple as a Flash game - which is not fair maybe to Flash games since there are some quite complex ones - or a mobile game - ditto - where you just tap to jump. That is all there is essentially.
The game is fun for a while, and the rewards and achievements surely add to this, but it lacks content. There only is the probably endless mode. As it is, it is a game to get a fast and easy 100 percent achievements, but it is not a game I would recommend paying a lot for. I had maybe one to two hours of fun with it, and another hour of just playing it for the final few achievements.
The graphics are simple but fitting, the sound also is neither good nor bad. The controls are very simple - mouse only and there you need only the left mouse button. You need to move the mouse only for menus.
Recommended:
If you like a no-brainer game or want easy and fast 100% achievements. The felt worth for this is at maxmimum around 1.50 USD.
I would say, if you have it you can try it, but if you don't have it there is no real reason to buy it. So neutral again, with a negative tendency however. Although I don't want to condemn it - there surely is a populace that enjoys such games -, it is nothing I can wholeheartedly recommend either. I apologize here to the developer, if he reads this, and want to encourage him to add a few more game modes, like maybe a challenge mode or so, to add some more value.

username: Thief 2 is the best stealth game
text:
Like I said in my review for the first game, I love this series. It takes inspiration from the Thief games and gives you an interesting , modernized, espionage setting to play in. Although I love the first one to death, there are a few flaws with it. For one thing, it's a bit more linear than what I expected. There are alternate routes to take, but usually there is only one and it's obvious. Second, the game forces you to take out guards almost every level. Lastly, ( I just realized this after I wrote the review), shadows work weird. Even in pitch black, a passing guard can still detect you if he's close enough. Im not talking right up his♥♥♥♥♥close, I'm talking you have to extend your arm to touch him close.
This game fixes all that. Each level has multiple approaches in each segment, half of the missions can be ghosted, and you can pick the nose of guard if you are in complete shadow. Not only that, the story has a little personal touch to it to make it not only about the mission. It's interesting enough and probably the second best story of the series behind Double Agent.
The gameplay is outstanding. Each mission is highly different and unique. A linear cargo boat (which still has alternate routes), a bank, and my favorite, a North Korean missle base with which has the most infiltration options  out of all the levels and can be ghosted. New additions such as the OCP, which is attached to your handgun and lets you disable lights without destroying them. Excellent for perfect stealth playthroughs. Also there is now a new meter called the sound meter. It works exactly like the light meter. Now you don't have to guess how much noise you are making and it evn tells you how much noise the enviroment is making. A few more features have been added but I'd rather you expierence them for yourself.
Last but not least, the graphics. Now, I'm no graphics ♥♥♥♥♥, but when a game does a great job, it needs to be brought up. This game has one of the best lighting engines I've ever seen. I saw the trailers, the "mostly positive" reviews, and the cool trailers, and was expecting a simple, fun, casual game to play with my friends. Instead, the tutorial treated me to a forced stealth mission, which was probably the ♥♥♥♥♥iest "stealth" I've ever seen in a video game. After a few times of getting inevitably cased on the large, flat, open platforums with guards just walking back and forth, the game just teleported me past them. Later, in my fancy airship house, I had the worst time trying to navigate up the wierd 2D staircases and such. My screen was flooded with a million menus, all of which were rather un-responsive to trying to close out of them. Then I got my first "real" quest: kill mushrooms. My options: 1: a really slow and low-damage poke, 2: some move that sounded complicated and I never even used. 3: a jump-dash that did damage, but was super hard to aim and usually does more damage to me than the enemies, or 4: a double-slash on a large crowd of enemies that killed most of them instantly. Basicly, the whole fight was running up to mushrooms and pushing the "kill them" button. And it wasn't fun to do cool combos, cause my other moves sucked and the mushrooms dropped a ton of mana potions, and the move didn't even cost that much mana. Later, I got lost (like as soon as the game stopped railroading me) and found two areas full of enemies way stronger than me who just insta-killed me. Finally found one of those odd menus with way more stuff than I needed, but this one had a "teleport to places you don't even know what/where they are," and I chose the mushroom one because it was the first one, and killing mushrooms sounded like a new-player thing to do. Found another quest: kill more mushrooms. While looking through my stats, I noticed that for leveling up, they had a convenient button of "auto-assign points." This sounded good to me: it would probably have some cool algorithm to balance strength, dex, and int, while still prioritizing luck (my class' main attribute). Nope, it wanted to dump every point into luck. I also noticed that after another one of my quests, "drink instant-level potion" I still had the potion in my inventory. I used it about 6 more times or so before it dissappeared, which could be either due to durability (which was not listed anywhere in its description) or a glitch. In short, the only thing I could really grasp about the game was "kill mushrooms," which, as great fun as that is, doesn't make a game. Despite the "massive multiplayer" part of it, I didn't see a single other person on. My friend was trying it out too and we planned to meet up, but his game crashed, had trouble loading, and stopped itself because it "detected cheating" (and no, he wasn't cheating). I really wasn't expecting to be blown off my feet, but when your menus are more difficult than your enemies, then you're doing something VERY wrong.
Some nice music in the game, good controls, but crude animation and drawings reminiscent of a free flash game you would find on newgrounds in the mid 2000s detracts from the experience.

Starseed Pilgrim is a quirky puzzle action game. It starts out being quite obscure with its rules, and the process of discovering them (without outside help) is both frustrating and rewarding. I should note here that discussion about the game has grossly overstated the way that reading about the game before playing it will ruin your experience. ALL good games are better if you discover what's in the game
, rather than
of it. Starseed Pilgrim isn't special in this regard. It's just got weird rules. Pretty much all puzzle games do. It's the weird miscellaneous genre. Anway...
Sooner or later you find that randomness holds significant sway in this world, and accumulating resources increases your chances of success. So after you get a grasp of the initially mysterious mechanics, luck and grinding play a large role.
The game's structure is an interesting effort toward combining a system of 'endless' randomly-generated puzzle-action (like Tetris, Panel de Pon, and Puyo Puyo) with crafted puzzle-platformer challenges (like Loderunner, Lup Salad, or Braid). This mixture could be improved by aiming more toward the side of crafted stages.
It could do with more of a sense of progression. The unchanging atmosphere is austere, thanks to minimal low-res pixel art graphics, and ambient music with chords as sound effects. There are rhymes written in the background of the hub world, which tell a whimsical tale about an environmental space disaster or something.
The game's strength is in that feeling of mastery through discovery as you uncover its rules. I recommend it for that, despite the weak payoff of optimising and employing your grinding strategy.

So I feel obligated to review this game under two different paradigms. To explain, I have been a Dragon Warrior/Dragon Quest fan for as long as I can remember. one of the first games I had ever played was Dragon Warrior 1, and when I beat it I slowly began to move onto each indivdual one as they were released. I have played pretty much every western released Dragon Quest game out there spinoffs and all , and as a series the game holds a very special place in my heart. That being said I want to write this review in two sections, one for people who are new to the series, and one for long time fans such as myself.
For New Players : The game has quite an interesting story, the only thing you will find confusing is the random characters from other games, but they do quite a decent job of making it interesting in and of itself as a game. The combat looks a lot more simplistic than it can be in actuality and it was one of the things that shocked me, in a good way. I didn't expect it to have such a natural feel to it once you get a grasp. I played with the more complicated setup of controlling everything individually and it felt very fun. So far the game seems to have quite a bit of content packed in to optimize your characters however your style of play might be. There is some pretty neat crafting and skill tree systems that actually can effect quite a bit. plenty of quests and side missions scattered in the game and overall very fun. even a pet system of sorts. They also took aa good bit of time to make (most) of the characters unique from eachother, at least once you start getting the later ones. One thing that threw me off at the start was the controls assume you have a controller during instructions, you will have to open menu with esc, then go to misc > settings > keyboard to see how to play with a keyboard. Honestly the one thing I felt that could have seen more attention from the developers is the control scheme itself while intuitive when you get the hang of it, it does noot give the best inctructions on navigating. I started off on a keyboard and pulled out a controller because it didn't feel right. But honestly overall if you are looking for a fairly well polished game with plenty of content to burn through it is very fun as a standalone game if you have never played Dragon Quest. one thing that should be noted is that this is the first Dragon Quest game that isn't a JRPG/turn based strategy game.
For Long-Time Fans : Wow. I came into this game with so much joy. its been a long time since a dragon quest game came out new in the west and it far exceeded my expectations which were admittedly low with it not being turn based. as a game in itself it is enjoyable but for me it just offered so much more than that. all of the classic sounds and music just hits you with instant nostalgia. every moment offers you a memory of this or that and for me it just was amazing. It is packed with all sorts of references to the main series from the Imp Pets who dont have enough MP for their spells to the legacy characters to the bosses. it had its own characters and story as well that really makes it interesting at least for me. It feels like a more action packed version of all the hours of grinding that I was familiar with, and it has plenty of classic stuff that makes it well worth it. P.S. If nothing else, if you want Square Enix to release more DQ games in the west, BUY THIS GAME. The trailer didn't do it justice and maybe just maybe you will be shocked at how fun it is for a whole new style, like I was.

A man is driving down the road and breaks down near a monastery. He goes to the monastery, knocks on the door, and says, “My car broke down. Do you think I could stay the night?”
The monks graciously accept him, feed him dinner, even fix his car. As the man tries to fall asleep, he hears a strange sound.
The next morning, he asks the monks what the sound was, but they say, “We can’t tell you. You’re not a monk.”
The man is disappointed but thanks them anyway and goes about his merry way.
Some years later, the same man breaks down in front of the same monastery.
The monks accept him, feed him, even fix his car. That night, he hears the same strange noise that he had heard years earlier.
The next morning, he asks what it is, but the monks reply, “We can’t tell you. You’re not a monk.”
The man says, “All right, all right. I’m *dying* to know. If the only way I can find out what that sound was is to become a monk, how do I become a monk?”
The monks reply, “You must travel the earth and tell us how many blades of grass there are and the exact number of sand pebbles. When you find these numbers, you will become a monk.”
The man sets about his task. Forty-five years later, he returns and knocks on the door of the monastery. He says, “I have traveled the earth and have found what you have asked for. There are 145,236,284,232 blades of grass and 231,281,219,999,129,382 sand pebbles on the earth.”
The monks reply, “Congratulations. You are now a monk. We shall now show you the way to the sound.”
The monks lead the man to a wooden door, where the head monk says, “The sound is right behind that door.”
The man reaches for the knob, but the door is locked. He says, “Real funny. May I have the key?”
The monks give him the key, and he opens the door.
Behind the wooden door is another door made of stone.
The man demands the key to the stone door.
The monks give him the key, and he opens it, only to find a door made of ruby.
He demands another key from the monks, who provide it.
Behind that door is another door, this one made of sapphire.
So it went until the man had gone through doors of emerald, silver, topaz, and amethyst.
Finally, the monks say, “This is the last key to the last door.”
The man is relieved to no end.

I did not have a history with Top-Down Shooters (also known as Twin Stick Shooters) until Hotline Miami. Since then I have started to enjoy them more, especially with Nuclear Throne. I usually saw them as cheap little games that had very little to offer, but those aforementioned games and a few others (Enter The Gungeon) have put them back on the map. However, those heavy-hitters are already so good that one might find it difficult to break some new ground. And yet, Mr. Shifty comes and seduces with a mechanic that just feels perfectly at home with this viewpoint: a “blink” or “teleport” ability, that you might know from Dishonored’s Corvo, X-Men’s Nightcrawler or a few MOBAs that borrow it from WarCraft III’s Warden hero.
Empowering and beautiful; blinking from one bad guy to the other and punching them to death is exhilarating, thus Mr. Shifty is completely acing it in the gameplay department. There is a teleportation bar that empties upon each blink to prevent the player from abusing it, but it recharges fast enough to get in a quick rhythm without needing to ever stop. The necessity to abide to a rhythm pushes to enter the game’s flow, while leaving some room for extra quick manoeuvers. Marvelous. The enemies react immediately, but teleporting confuses them just long enough to get behind them.
Unlike all the other Top-Down Shooters, Mr. Shifty is actually not a shooter. It is possible to throw some (lethal) items, however our protagonist only resorts to melee items (broom, staff, keyboards) and never picks up a firearm. The genre might thus drift closer to a Beat ‘em up, except that enemies thankfully die quickly. Without any item, the punches are powerful and give an excellent feedback to the player. So while Hotline Miami was an obvious comparison as it is a leviathan of the genre, both games play extremely different. And that might be where Mr. Shifty starts to break down a little bit: while Hotline Miami offered a variety of weapons that changed the approach to the game, Mr. Shifty’s formula of move-punch-move-punch eventually becomes repetitive.
Variety comes from the enemies and their little quirks: some can dash, some will blow up after dying, some have spread weapons, some can throw explosive, and so on. Furthermore, while Hotline Miami was focused on the combat, Mr. Shifty makes use of its protagonist’s ability to manoeuver at high speed by throwing tons of traps at the player. Lasers and homing rockets will offer different sort of challenges. And talking about challenge, while the beginning of the game is fairly easy, it gradually ramps up and the latter levels will require quick thinking and quick reflexes to surmount the odds.
There are dozens of goons to fight, and yet Mr. Shifty dies in a single bullet. Hitting many enemies in a short span of time will fill up a slow-motion bar, however it is sadly not delivered to the control of the player. A bullet close to the protagonist will active the slow-mo, and while this can sometimes allow for a last-second save, it can often be triggered by a grazing bullet that would have never have hit the player, and thus waste the precious ability that would have seen a better use in the next difficult room. The save system is fair, but sometimes stretches the number of fights to survive before the next checkpoint. Repeating fights can become tiresome, since you mostly have the same approach each time. Each green door loading a new area is a checkpoint, and each elevator is the beginning of the levels. Sadly, even though the levels can be quite long, quitting the game and coming back brings back to the latest elevator rather than door. There are about 15 levels, and the game can be finished in 5-7h with no incentive to come back. While I mentioned the slow-motion, I will add that semi-destructible environments (cool physics overall) and a big sequence of levels taking place in a single building reminded me of another game: F.E.A.R. The same criticism can be aimed at both games, seeing the same thing over and over becomes dull despite the amazing core gameplay. Only the last level managed to excite me again with its chaotic redesign of the levels.
Finally, while Hotline Miami had a well-paced mysterious and hypnotizing story enhanced with ground-breaking music, Mr. Shifty does not deliver on both accounts. A more memorable music with a strong identity would have also helped set the levels apart. Moving on to the technical aspect, the controls can be rebound and work perfectly fine both with controllers and keyboard & mouse. The clean style of the graphics easily conveys all the necessary information (and destructible walls and items gives a lot more punch to the punches!), however the framerate can sometimes tank really hard when a lot of explosion are taking place with many enemies on screen as well. It happened rarely enough not to be an issue, but the game does not succeed to maintain a high framerate all throughout its length.
In conclusion, Mr. Shifty suffers from the comparison to Hotline Miami. The envelope is far less attractive, and the restriction to not use firearms but only punches and thrown items ends up becoming more repetitive in the long run. Traps and many types of enemies manage to keep the interest up, however there is not enough variation in the visuals as most floors of the building to scale look the same. So while Mr. Shifty is a good game, it clearly lacks a lot to be considered a masterpiece. Still, the essential is that the core gameplay is a brilliant success, and definitely worth a recommendation. Quick successions of fast-paced high-skill manoeuvers to punch, teleport, then punch again feel amazing.

As the first expansion to Sid Meyer’s Civilization Beyond Earth, Rising Tide is not only a great addition to the game, it is an essential addition that completes the experience of colonizing on other planets.
The premise, well… after the initial wave of great colony ships departed Earth – we finally managed to screw things up and Earth is no longer viable as a home planet with resources diminishing quickly – more ships depart for the new found home planet.

New factions arise and take the place of governments and countries. And of course, as a species we aren’t all that good at learning from our mistakes and play nice, we land on the new planet to wage war on the local dominant species (technically we’re the aliens not them) an insect-fish hybrid, and of course ourselves.
The local species are truly a peaceful lot that operate within a hive-mind. They’re actually quite peaceful and won’t attack you until you attack them. If you screw with one though (remember hive-mind?) you’ve basically declared war on the whole family.
In addition to getting along (or not) with the locals, there’s still that tricky bit of maintaining relations with other factions. Each faction’s leader is… how do I put it… very culturally distinct and iconic (I tried…) and has their own views on how cities and the planet should be run – through careful economic superiority, scientific breakthroughs or martial warfare. Play nice or risk having war declared on you… or vice versa.
One of my favourite aspects of the game is the number of upgrade and research options. The scientific web might be daunting to look at at first, but completing research unlocks new units and gives you options to upgrade old ones.
Depending on your line of research, you can also develop hybrid units that merge the local species with humans and tech to produce awe-inspiring troops – if it isn’t for war, what is it good for?The character models give the units lots of well… character. Here’s a good rundown on the different affinities – Harmony, Supremacy and Purity.
Finally, sending your troops out to explore can provide great benefits – especially when you come across a ruin or a dig site and uncover an artifact. Artifacts allow you to discover new tech and benefits – basically another reason to go stir “alien” nests.
Like most Civilization games, some might find the turn-based gameplay slow… but hey they built a whole franchise that way. Prepare to spend many, many immersive hours on Rising Tide.
Rising Tide, more than an expansion, feels to be the missing element that Civilization: Beyond Earth lacked. I wouldn’t call it an add-on as much as an essential.
