Have you been looking for a new real time strategy game lately to scratch that strategy itch you've been having? Well look elsewhere, because Citadels is a dreadful and incomplete mess. The game was created by an unknown and inexperienced development studio called Games Distillery. Currently a different studio called Big Moon was hired to add further playability and stability to the game. In the future, at best you can only hope for a polished yet dreadful entertainment product (without the entertainment value).
Citadels attempts to accomplish what so many other strategy games have already done before, and it accomplishes those things poorly. Citadels most closely resembles a stripped down Age of Empires title. Everything from base building, combat, and resource gathering are implemented poorly. There is no strategy involved at all because combat boils down to spamming units. You can literally spam the most basic miliary unit available and win every time. The utter lack of military units available leaves no room for strategy, tactics, or planning at all.
The game has a boring campaign that currently can't even be finished entirely, and a few lacklusted skirmish modes with terrible AI. There is only one map available per skirmish mode and no matter the difficulty you choose you cannot lose due to the incompetent AI. Citadels is only a singleplayer game so these are your only options. There is no map or scenario editor or multiplayer of any kind. The poor quality of this title combined with the utterlack of content at a $40 price point is downright theivery. Avoid at all costs.

Not as easy as it looks...... Fight for your life in Call of Tomsk-7, a simple side-scrolling shooter. I really enjoy this Match-3 game, between PC and Tablet I've put in well over 100 hours into it. Got every single reward from the tutorials, placed well in a few Story events (which are an interesting system of different timed thematical storyline events that spit out rewards every day or three) because I have pockets of time through the day which this fills nicely. Even dabbled a bit into the Versus system, where you fight other players' teams for rank and rewards, but the AI controls the opponent teams since Match-3 gameplay doesn't lend itself well to a realtime PvP system at all.
My roster's not as developed as long-time players yet, I have a bunch of 2-star heroes, a number of 3-stars with 1 or 2 powers, and a couple 4-stars from event rewards that I lean heavily on. (Star basically = rarity/power rating, with 1 stars being the lowest and 4 being the highest with a 5 now just released in an update). Enemies in story fights seems to scale according to your overall roster level, which is neat, because it allowed even my newer PC account to jump right in to a story event and place high enough to get top tier rewards.
The game is F2P with microtransactions, but the MT's are so RNG based that you don't really get to P2W very effectively unless you spend a ton, I think, and even then you can win loads of the same MT items just from several hours put into the story events, or by focusing your free time into an event that you think you can do well in.
Yet I hesitate to give this game a positive recommendation. I like it, but one thing really irks me. As a microtransaction-based game, it's unforgivable in my eyes that the accounts from different platforms play together but people cannot access their mobile account on PC and vice versa. If you are making a microtransaction game, especially since I noticed the mobile version already has Google+ and Facebook integration, you have to have this basic functionality since the game's pricing model is based on constantly spending money.
So while I like the game, I will not give it my recommendation until this is implemented as I feel that this is a necessary step for them to earn my thumbs up. They apparently have manually merged some accounts "in the past" but have since stopped doing so for everyone else.

My favorite game on Steam BY FAR!! (I started playing during its launch week already, and played almost 700 hours by now!) This seems to be Magic's answer to Hearthstone, which forced Wizards to FINALLY make an absolutely free Magic The Gathing game. Here are Pros and Cons:
Pros:
+ The best (free) Magic The Gathering Game ever created.
+ Finally FREE DECKBUILDING with A LOT of different cards! (Pretty much about 1.000(?) with the upcoming new expansion in a few days.)
+ The crucial bugs it had were FIXED already long ago! :) (At least for the PC version.)
+ It even has Two-Headed-Giant! (2vs2 mode) But this one is probably a bit buggy, see Cons.
+ Nice single player Campaign / Story Mode included, but quite short.
+ You can get 100% of the cards without paying anything this time!! I did never pay any money on this game and got EVERYTHING very fast; even always had enough Gold before each upcoming expansion already to buy all cards instantly!! :) (But with more expansions in the game, it obviously takes much longer now for new players. See Cons.)
+ "Intelligent Boosters": This means you dont get a card more often than it can be included in a deck, but get others you don't already have instead! So you only need 80 boosters for each expansion (for Oath only 60 cause it's a smaller set), and then you have every card!! :)
+ Good balancing: You can only get each Common up to 4 times, Uncommon 3 times, Rare 2 and only 1 copy of each Mythic Rare. Some players see this as a Con, but the game is well balanced and interesting!
+ Enough players only to (almost?) always find an enemy for PvP.
+ You can also play/farm vs the Computer and still get easy Gold for this, too!
Cons:
- Farming the Gold for all cards is boring (even though it's easy vs the AI) and will take months for new players now, because so many expansions are in the game now. (A few "Starter Cards" from old sets, plus "Origins", "Battle for Zendikar", "Oath of the Gatewatch", "Shadows over Innistrad" and in a few days also "Eldritch Moon".)
- Not 100% of the paper magic cards from each set make it into the game, but a bit less! (They select them for the game balance, though. :) )
- Two-Headed-Giant Mode was very buggy the last time I tested it, but this was MONTHS ago.
- "Ranked"/PvP system is very minimalistic, no "real" Ranking Ladder.
- Very few cards (less than 1%) interact wrong with others, but really most problems have been fixed.
- Some players seem to have issues.

While many would describe Hitman: Absoultion as the "black sheep" of the series, I find the time I spend with it thoroughly.
I agree that stripping away alot of the Stealth and Sandbox Aspects of the franchise were a step in the wrong direction, but still a curageous step that hadn't been taken before - what I mean by that is, that with the more action-based approach you get to see a side of Hitman Games you wouldn't normally get to explore in the older/newer entries and that is very much to be respected. Also Absolution has an amazing Soundtrack in my opinion, of course that's a feature of the entire franchise itself, but the suspense carried by the music here is something not many, even action-oriented games, match.
As for the story I also like the more personal approach to Agent 47 as a protagonist here, you learn alot about him and have him interact with the world and others way more often and in depth then he does in the other games where he is strictly bound by his current contract and Diana's guidance. Furthermore our "villains" in this story are very fleshed out, well voiced and feel more like Antagonists that you want to track down and take revenge on, a feat that the previous games didn't accomplish that well, with previous villains being pretty forgettable in my opinion.
The newly integrated challenge system also met mixed receptions, but for me they offer more additional hurdles to overcome or new ways of playing and navigating the levels. Combined with them serving as a sort of "checklist" for the missions, they are fine in my book, a welcome addition to the franchise.
Overall, I would definetly recommend Hitman: Absolution to a majority of people, from the casual trying to find an entrance point into the Hitman Franchise to even the most seasoned fan of stealth games. Maybe it is the "worst" Hitman game, but that sounds way more negative than it actually is. This game is still a solid adventure with lots and lots to do and huge replay value - if I had to give Hitman: Absolution a school-type mark: A (if viewed as a standalone experience) or B (If viewed in the context and compared to the other games of the franchise)
I am aware that many, also many die-hard Hitman fans, dislike this opinion, but there really isn't a "bad" Hitman Game.
I spent lots and lots of time with most entries of the series, know the lore and universe inside-out and in the end, being the "worst" of probably the best series of games ever made still puts you miles ahead of many, many other games.
Definetly recommending Hitman: Absolution, despite it's mixed reception with parts of the community.

The launch of Thief is very interesting. From what I've seen, this game is getting really mixed reviews from steam, to metacritic, to youtube, and the community seems very split on whether they think the game is good or not. I don't believe the answer is binary in this case.
Before I got the game I thought that the gameplay was horrible and antiquated and wasn't planning on getting it. I saw some early footage and none of it appealed to me, however I decided to pick it up after watching a few gameplay videos on youtube. Once I played the game, my perception changed as I actually enjoyed the experience.
The game is not bad, but I could definitely see why people wouldn't like it. The arguements that the game is linear, an on-rails experience, repetitive once you reach latter stages of the game, etc. are not unfounded. Despite all this, I have to disagree that it is less valuable of an experience because of these things. Some of the positive things I have to say about this game is that the attention to detail on the setting and ambience make it look beautiful, the mechanics are great, the story is not the best but it's not the worst either, and it is a fun experience.
Maybe it's just people have different tastes and the review system is flawed because it can't cater to everyone's individual preferences, but my needs were met with Thief. It's not bad but it's not for everyone, just don't go in thinking it's revolutionary or it will bring a strong sense of nostalgia. The truth lies somewhere in the middle.

If you like the type of a game where you want to throw your pad at the wall out of anger and then pick it up 2 mins later to continue playing this might be perfect for you.
TL;DR
If you plan to get the game for some single player racing - don't
If you plan to get the game for some multi player racing - don't
Unless you are a fan of GRID games and can get it for like 5$ max, you can buy it if you want to.
Good things:
1. Graphics and optimisation
The game looks really nice, even compared to new games and it's so well optimised that a decent pc can run it at medium-high or high settings with 60+fps. Night races are good looking and occasional eye catchers like jets or baloons are a nice thing.
2. Driving model
It's not a simulator, but still, driving model is very nice and somehow addicting, it's just fun driving in this game.
3. Multiplayer part 1
If you can get few friends to play with you, the game can be really fun.
Meh things:
1. Sounds
Sound is okay-ish, cars sound good, there is also some music. Nothing too impressive, but not bad either.
2. Career mode
At the beginning it's fun, but after some time it gets so boring and repetitive you completely space out when you want to do it. For the occasional races it's much better to create your own cup.
3. Amount of cars
Well, there are many known cars, both old and new ones, but still, feels like more wouldn't hurt and well...who wouldn't want more cars?
4. Racenet
Sometimes connecting to racenet takes a while - it's not a super long time, but still few seconds. It can be annoying when you have to do it multiple times.
Bad things:
1. AI
People responsible for creating AI for this game should be tied to a pole and hit with rotten tomatoes for every ruined race. The AI is just made to irritate the player as much as possible, it's the cause of failing like 80 out of 100 races. They block your line on purpose, won't let you pass on straights unless the track is wide, block you on the corners while they're slow as snails, block the hell out of the road on first corners, brake early, sometimes they crash with each other and they even ram you off the road. They feel like they have only two states - either you don't exist for them on the track, or you do, but they are so agressive it's ridiculous. Driving among them feels like defusing 5 bombs at the same time - you never know which one will do what. They can easily do the pit maneuver on you, but if you try to ram them out of anger, their cars behave like they weight at least 4 tons. It's worth noting that if you manage to pass an AI car, they seem to slow down. They also don't get any penalties...oh those penalties...
2. Penalties
So what about the remaining 20 out of 100 causes of faling the races? 6 of them are crashing the car or going off the track by yourself and ridiculous penalties you get for cutting the track are the other 14.
Sure, there definitely should be a way to punish the player for cutting the track, but the system in this game...it's crap.
Penalties slow you down to 50 km/h for a short duration, which is decided by how much you've cut the track...well that's all in theory, in practice you get 5 seconds of penalty for slightly-yet-completely-acceptable cutting when you go over the white line by few centimenters or sometimes even not go over it at all. That type of penalty completely ruins your lap or race and all the fun in trying to get the best time as possible by creating the fastest racing line by yourself. This penalty system was a failure from the very beginning, sadly there's nothing that can be done about it. A simple time penalty PROPERLY calculated would be much better.
3. Weekly challenges
While they are a good way to earn money in the game, it's extremely frustrating. In theory you can compete with other players in the world for the best time while getting paid for it - sounds nice? BAM, in reality you get the two problems from above and sometimes some ridiculous requirements for platinum. I'm 99% sure nobody checks if those times are possible to beat, just some AI(ugh) system sets it. I'm not the best driver there is, but good enough to be really fast with practice, and sometimes even when you practice one challenge over and over and over again until there's nothing that can be improved, you're still not getting that platinum. Weird thing is sometimes it's so easy to get platinum you can get it on the first try, even with some racing errors.
4. Multiplayer part 2
Well. we know how multiplayer racing games are - there are many good, clean racers and also there are the ones that crash other players and ruin the fun - this game is no different. Who knows, maybe those crashers are people who got angry at the AI? You can kick crashers if they get enough votes to kick...yeah, "if" is the keyword.
There is voice chat, which people with always-on-and-over-sensitive microphones love. You can mute them, no problem, but only if you're in the lobby before the race. Yep, even while you've crashed or abandoned the race, all you can do is listen to whiny comments or weird music or some other sounds.
There is no text chat, which should be available in a pc game, but when you think about it - maybe it's better you don't have to read about who did what with your mother, but then again, they can crash into you instead, so I don't know really.
There is also a small problem with lags. Sometimes you will get pushed out of the track and the other person might not even know about it and vice versa. The only solution to this is to keep a safe distance.
And while we talk about multiplayer races...
5. "Rewards" from racing...
...or rather lack of them. If you are racing in an expensive rental car, it won't matter if you finish 1st or 8th - you won't earn anything, instead you lose money for repairs after every race. I call it investing in the races to get better and have a laugh about it, but really I'm laughing through tears.
So in the end very few pros and many cons. Shame really, this game had potential to be really fun, but too many things are just bad. I wouldn't recommend buying it, there are so many better alternatives.

This game is GORGEOUS. I'm only partway through it, but it has revolutionized my idea of visual novels. To be fair, I've only just recently gotten into the genre, and so I've only read maybe ten (free ones, so not even the Expensive Art) or so. But this style--this relationship between the art and the text, the way that relationship is so *interactive*--is incredibly compelling. And the colors! The playful dialogue! I feel like this visual novel has soul, like the dev really enjoyed crafting it. That makes it a pleasure to read and watch.
The character designs are beautiful, and there is just the right amount of intrigue. The story doesn't hold back information the audience can piece together on its own; it KNOWS you probably already have connected the dots, and then it goes deeper, and takes you on a more thrilling, engaging ride.
This is the art of the story. As a visual format, it reminds me of a playful version of those medieval or Celtic texts with the beautifully detailed illuminations and illustrations gilding the written word. Except here, there is more of a balance, and maybe even a slight dominance of the visual over the written (but not too distractingly so). This is such a pleasure to play, and I look forward to finishing it.
Thank you for sharing it with us for free!

I really enjoyed the BattleLore and Memoir 44 games and was glad to see the game on Steam and for under $5 no less.
It is well worth that price.  It is very polished with high res graphics and a simple and easy to use UI. So far I found no bugs or gameplay issues.  The single player campaign is keeping me busy and the AI does a good enough job to keep it interesting.
The base game only seems to have two factions each of which had about 5 or so unit types – but there is already an add on DLC with more units and maps.
For those not already familiar with the BattleLore mechanics I’ll go over the basics.
In each battle you have a number of spend-points to choose which unit types to field. You then assign them to available start spaces across the three sections of the board (left, right and middle).
Each round you select a card that states which areas of the board you wish to activate units in. You have a set number of cards that can be used once before resetting. Each card mixes a number of available units in one or more sections (for example, activate two units on the left and one in the middle or activate 3 units on the right, etc.)  There is also a card for activating a specific unit type (Melee, Range or Mounted) and one for resetting your hand.  You then move and/or attack with the units you activated.
Units all have special abilities which range from stuns to poison to things like flanking and double shot.  In addition to units base abilities, you can play Lore cards which are gained one per round and are basically like spells and each gives you various offensive or defense boosts or some other boon.  Each card costs Lore which is accumulate 1 per turn and can also be generated by attacks that miss or thorough other card effects.
Each mission/battle has different victory conditions that require different tactics. For example in one mission you need to protect the sheep units on the board over six rounds, another mission may have you trying to end your turn in certain hexes or sometimes you just need to kill off the enemy.   These varying victory conditions help keep the battles form becoming too repetitive.
The game has a campaign and Skirmish mode (multiplayer vs UI) for single player and also offers PvP multi-player which I have yet to delve into. The PvP multiplayer supports internet, LAN and hot seat. There are 5 different battle maps included in the base game – each with different objectives (capture the flag, control areas, etc.).
Although perfectly fine as is, some things I would like to see to make the game more enjoyable IMO:
-	Some kind of colored “bases” to help tell the units apart a bit better when zoomed out.   It’s minor but often archers and melee can look the same.
-	A map/scenario maker would do much to make the game’ shelf life longer –but would probably diminish the value of DLC a bit if players could make their own.
-	Some kind of visual means to show line-of-site.
-	A campaign mode where losses are kept and reinforcements can be available and your units gain experience and are maintained from battle to battle.
Overall a well done game and if you like 15-20 minute tactical turn based combats, enough variance to keep each battle a bit unique, a bit of luck thrown in and not a ton of micromanagement then you will likely find this game well worth the minor investment.

For the meager asking price, I definitely recommend giving this a try!
This is a very simple and fun activity to pass the time. I say activity because I can't really call it a game. There is no "win" condition, you can just keep on going until you miss. There are, however, a good number of goals, earned by completing randomly assigned tasks. You can only work on three at a time, but completing each gives you an in-game bonus and a Steam achievement.
Each round, you begin with the character's spaceship crash-landing and him ejecting to the next closest planet. Each planet spins and you click your mouse to pause its rotation. When you release the mouse, the character jumps off, hopefully aligned in a trajectory which will end with him on the next planet in line. As you go, you can collect nuts and bolts, which act as currency for the game’s shop which is stocked with a number of upgrades and customization items. These are found in-game only; no micro-transactions!
The best ideas are the simplest, and this game is concrete proof! Best arcade game idea I've ever seen, truthfully, and the fun lasts for hours. A+

I bought this game as a preorder, because I thought it will be good.
Good graphics, nice optimization (Intel HD4600 playable on FullHD) sound is unfortunately worse than GRID 2 (I don't know why), driving model is good, but still quite arcade. Something near TOCA Race Driver 2/3. The feel of driving cars is nothing as good as in Shift 2/Project CARS or Raceroom Racing Experience. Cockpit view is ugly and unusable (GRID 1 and Dirt series have better). Inconsistent AI during races and also with something called "catch up", which I hate. The singleplayer has very long championships and is quite boring. Default chase cams are quite unpredictable, use some modded cams instead for competitive play. Too little people online and too much online achievements that are almost impossible to achieve now (like win 100 races and level up car to lvl 100). Car upgrades do literally nothing (see youtube comparison). Used cars vs bought cars... Only advantages of bought cars: 1. you can paint it 2. you can tune it. The tuning of everything other than Gear ratio is really subtle, barely noticeable in most cars. Limited multiplayer garage space with a +5 space DLC... you can't even buy a single car in all car classes, so you are stuck with money you can't spend. Constant disconnecting from Racenet, even during online race, and recently Racenet is barely working. Buying DLCs is pointless because almost nobody has them in multiplayer, so you are doing it basically only for the achievements and curiosity. DLC championships don't save in the middle like in singleplayer, you have to go through it as a whole during single seating. Weekly challenges are a really nice addition, these are the reason I still play this game from time to time. But sometimes there is a challenge with a Platinum or even Gold medal set too high, so nobody can even come close to it. Oh, and I like the drift events, they are really cool to play. There are bugs which will never be fixed, like a ghost car with an irritating constant booming bass sound. Or a ghost car which is enabled even if you disabled it. Or a massive lag when restarting drift race.
Overall I don't recommend this game, it doesn't feel like a true standalone game, rather like a big addon to GRID 2.
Choose free-to-play Raceroom Racing Experience instead. The feel of driving a car there is really satisfying, and the sounds + Force Feedback are amazing. Plus that game in constantly updated. And these things are something GRID Autosport doesn't have now. GRID Autosport feels abandoned now, and that is sad.

Get ready for a completely biased review!
I'm a board gamer at heart. I was following BattleLore Second Edition on Fantasy Flight Games' website since it was first announced and picked it up from my FLGS (friendly local game store) as soon as it was available. It is a fantastic game! One of the things that I love is that the units and factions are consistent with other games set in this Terrinoth universe, like Runewars and Rune Age. All three are great games!
Unfortunately, it's hard to find other people to play the board game with. I had been wanting to make a Vassal mod for it for a while, but never got around to it. And then ... FFG announced the digital version! Now I can finally play other people!
Okay, so all of that was background on who I am in relation to this game and why I like it. Unfortunately, it's kinda failing in the one thing I was excited about: multiplayer. Not that the multiplayer mode doesn't work, but that there still seem to be very few people on when I'm on. Realistically, all that means is that I need to reach out to others in the community and schedule a time to play instead of just hoping we're all on at the same time.
However, I was able to play against my brother using this game and that was phenomenally fun! So I think the potential for great multiplayer games is there, we just need more people playing!
One thing that makes this game interesting is the fact that it is a port of a board game. Board games tend to be simpler than video games because humans are responsible for all the upkeep so there can't be too much going on lest you make the games take too long. Unfortunately, the digital version takes that even farther. In addition to keeping track of all of your dice rolls for you, many of the abilities have been altered. Basically, abilities from dice that you have an option of triggering in the board game version are mandatory in the digital version.
Two examples: 1) Blood Harvesters have a 1/6  chance to deal one damage to themselves to cause one damage to the target, but while you can choose not to activate that in the board game (for instance, if it will kill your Blood Harvester), it is automatically activated in the digital version; 2) when a Poisoned unit is attacked in the board game, the attacker may commit any lore results rolled to deal damage to the poisoned unit, but in the app, there is no choice, even if your attack only generated a single lore and youd rather save it for lore cards.
Other changes include the Greyhaven Battlemages whose shield ability is no longer tied to combat results but to movement (which makes them too powerful, in my opinion).
But the changes are not all bad. For the app, they have streamlined the command card mechanic so that you have a small pool of cards you can refresh rather than drawing from a deck. This gives you more strategic control over your characters compared to the random draw of the board game. (Although I prefer the randomness of the board game with the deeper tactics of unit abilities.)
The graphics for this game are great! I mean, I only paid $10 for it and for that it's fine. Because the alternative is to pay $80 for the board game that comes with unpainted miniatures.
Speaking of the board game's core set, the units available is one screaming difference between the physical and digital versions. In the core set, you get a single legend unit for each team. With a 50-gold game, you could muster 6 of them, but since there is only one in the core set for each side, to get 6 for a single faction requires almost $500! For $10, you can field any combination of units you desire. That's quite a treat to me! Of course, that only matters in multiplayer missions, not in the campaign.
But one thing I LOVE about multiplayer is that I have the option of playing against the CPU in multiplayer battles. Why is this huge for me? Because I am an Uthuk Y'llan fan! :Uthuk: You see, the campaign is played from the point of view of the Daqan Lords (the humans) and you fight against the Uthuk Y'llan. I, however, love the Uthuk Y'llan, so I'm glad there is a way for me to play solo with my favorite faction. Good job, FFG!
The campaign was actually quite fun, for me. It is very scenario-driven, which makes things very interesting.
I'm done rambling. Hopefully I've answered some questions others have not. But the point is htat I LOVE this game and I highly recommend it! (And the board game, too!)

Beyond Gravity is yet another mobile device game ported to the PC, where the simplicity of it all is quite straightforward. The story, or semblance of it, is that you're an astronaut sleeping while cruising through space on a ship when it's attacked by asteroids, making it crash onto a planet. From there onwards, your main goal is to get as much screws as you can as you jump from planet to planet using the Space-Bar or Left Mouse Button. During your travels you'll come up with challenges - some easy, some hard - that once completed, net you more screws. that can be used to upgrade your astronaut with all sorts of help, from a magnet for greater pickup distance, to a triple jump. Each challenge getting completed also nets you the corresponding achievement. This all reminds me of a Miniclip game called "Rocket Man" where you jumped from cloud to cloud, although all you have to do is take care of jumping rather than aim any angles - the planet's rotation does the angling for you. The music isn't much, just some looping drivel that isn't intrusive, but you -will- experience cutoff once it loops.
Overall a stomachable game, but one you'll easily forget once you're done with all the challenges and getting all the upgrades. Recommended you get it with a 50% coupon to avoid any feelings of ripoff.

Barring a few hiccups (such as the ten-foot tall toolbox in the entrance to the bath house; the occassional guard getting hung up on geometry... or another guard; how finicky some of the targetting can be), this is a great port of a great game. I can confirm that controllers/game pads have limited functionality, so I went the mouse/keyboard route for input. It took a while to get used to those controls, but was pretty smooth sailing after a calibration period. Two exceptions: the camera is a bit wonky (frustrating at times, but mostly okay) and lockpicking isn't as much fun.
Sam is back to work his magic on a dozen or so black-ops missions that can be accomplished with discretion or force. Or some mix of the two. This time around, our favorite uber commando is dealing with information warfare. Though the game was made more than 10 years ago (as the somewhat sluggish response time will remind you), the story is still relevent today (and shockingly accurate about potential flashpoints). Several levels will beg for multiple play throughs, particularly if you're inclined towards extreme styles of play. For example, finishing the Korea-based levels with a pure stealth approach was rewarding as well as challenging. Playing those levels again in 'assault' mode was a very different kind of fun. And carthatic.
TLDR: 8/10, two thumbs up. Good story, especially if you're into action/thrillers. Incredible stealth/infiltration game in general, possibly the best installment in the Splinter Cell franchise. Very much worth playing.

This game has given me a full appreciation for chefs, short order cooks, and everyone else in the restaurant business. Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! by Vertigo Gaming, Inc., allows you to virtually experience the rush and adrenaline of preparing food at a restaurant, and let me tell you, it is much harder than it seems. You have to juggle a constant stack of food orders, impatient customers, and maintenance facility issues, and the fast pace, high pressure, and intense fun that results is both enjoyable and rewarding. Combine that with sleek, bright graphics, and you have a game worth playing.
Something about this game that I really appreciated was the high level of detail and intricacy in every aspect of the cooking process. In other words, you do more than fry burgers all day. You can create your own menu of entrees, sides, and drinks (sides and drinks also boost customers’ patience levels) that customers can pick from, which leads to a huge variety of recipes and ingredients that must be mastered. In addition, different foods require different preparation processes; for example: a small group of meals must be made on a “holding station,” which makes multiple batches of the same food item but takes a longer time to cook. However, once the batch is ready, any customer who comes in and orders that food item can be served immediately. Another advantage of hot stations is that you can use them to make any food item before the restaurant even opens, which can ease a lot of stress at the start of the day. Besides food, there is a plethora of tasks to perform, such as filling drinks, cleaning the bathrooms, exterminating vermin, and even putting out stove fires. Instead of a mundane job consisting of repetitive, boring tasks, this game is filled to the brim with dynamic variety and energy.
One of the unique aspects of the gameplay is the use of keyboard typing for making meals. Each ingredient is added by typing a specific key, and your customer satisfaction decreases if you press the wrong key or type out of order. I have personally not seen many games utilize the keyboard for the main controls, so I thought this was both clever and inventive. On the other hand, you must click on the customers to prepare their specific orders, and once you have clicked on someone, you must fully complete their order before clicking on the next person. Sometimes the food item takes a long time to cook, and this can cause you to lose other customers even if you type as fast as humanly possible. When I played the first few times, I was extremely frustrated by this. However, once I familiarized myself with the menu, I could remember which orders took longer and, therefore, needed to be started early or spaced out.
At first glance, Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! may look like your basic, simple cooking role-play game. But once you play your first round, you immediately realize that it is a challenging test of skill, time management, and memory. I love how the controls utilize all your fingers with keyboard typing instead of just your hand with a mouse, and how the flexibility and variety of the menu constantly forces you to reshape and re-sharpen your skills. So if you want high-key fun, check out Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! I promise the game will be as exciting and energetic as its title.

Grid 2 is an arcade racing game developed and published by Codemasters and is a sequel to the populair Race Driver: Grid game.
In Grid 2 you race in real world locations and cities such as Miami, Chicago, Paris, Barcelona, Côte d'Azur, Dubai, Japan and many more.
In the singleplayer mode it's all about the World Series Racing (WSR) and you must work your way up by beating racing clans and prestige drivers in career club events, receiving fans and earn faster cars varying from Tier 1 to 4.
There are many racetypes such as Time Attack, Elimination, Drift, Checkpoint, Faceoff, Destruction Derby (free dlc) and Race of course.
The multiplayer mode behaves almost the same except that you do not earn fans but money per race in order to buy and upgrade your cars. Besides Online Events there are also game modes such as Global Challenge and Rivals for more entertainment.
The DLC content packs for GRID2 are also great, giving you more cars and some of them have extra racetracks to challenge your competitors.
Grid 2 is one of my first race games where I feel very comfortable to go online with. Every car feels different and the racetracks are very memorable for me. Although Codemaster left the well known cockpit view from the first game, Grid 2 is still very enjoying and true must have for people who love arcade racing!

- The UI, while slick-looking (as long as you're playing fullscreen), is horrendously unintuitive at times -- now that boosters and detractors are in the game you can't actually view them from your active menu, you have to back out and find them in the food catalogue.

- There's next to no real

from this one, it hurts.

Indie developers pride themselves on breaking our expectations of game mechanics by flat-out doing things differently. Sometimes it works, too. However, there are occasions when the function of design contribute to the value and purpose of the subject. Instructions are integrated with the level design and after several sessions I was able to make just the barest sense of them.
Experimental games have limited credence with me. Structure has its benefits, and so do clear instructions. Released in 2013 on the now thriving Indie scene available on Steam, Starseed Pilgrim is an exercise in minimalist presentation and resource management. In this game you are a ‘symphonic gardener’, but so help me I wasn’t able to determine what the tools were, much less how they functioned beyond movement and block removal/placement.
The entire game is presented in a single screen with visual and audio indicators of your degree of success. Our nameless, 8-pixel tall caretaker is constantly pursued by an ink-black space that results in a reset of your garden when caught. A numeric counter of–your hearts, as it turns out–ticks down to zero over a fixed period of time, and your only hope is to grow more and collect them… I think.
Logic puzzles are a hobby of mine, but only when they make sense. Crazy, right? A legend of your inventory and their attributes would have improved my understanding greatly… not to mention more accurately phrased goals and consequences.
I have over the years enjoyed a few artistic interactive experiences in the past, and that’s usually all they are. If you’re feeling rebellious and anxious with mainstream, this is your bag – or, garden. For my entertainment, too much pruning of useful information took place here.
What’s fun: Discovery of unique mechanics is fascinating. Graphics and audio are refreshingly simple.
What’s not: Ironically, graphics and audio communicate function and mechanic far better than the handful of words that appear during play.
Recommendation: Know your mark before you buy. This is an information-sparse puzzler with perplexing logic. If this style of play interests you, it’s worth every bit the asking price.

I cannot recommend this game in its current state. It lacks depth, interesting game mechanics and overall it is just boring to play. The game is buggy and poorly explained, and if you were waiting for a Formula 1 simulation based game you'll need to keep waiting.
Review –
Pitstop Challenge is a F1 simulation game based around Pitstops. You join a team, get a crew together and race around the world in 19 locations. The problem is that all these features are poorly implemented. You have no association with the team, your contract states nothing and it is just a lump sum of money in order to progress through the game with. Your crew is bland with zero customisation, you can make certain crew members specialise in certain parts of the pitstop but due to the control scheme it doesn’t really come together. You never get to see areas outside your Pitstop, you can be in Rome, Australia or China, yet the inside of the pitstop never changes.
The biggest problems are the controls and what you can control. The only thing you can decide on is what tyres to choose, you can go between different versions of wet and dry tyres. There may be more later on but after nearly 2 hours of gameplay this is all I’m given, first impressions are everything. Maybe an option to not fill up the tank completely, maybe tell the drive to be more aggressive, just something to increase what the game has to offer.
The controls are terrible, straight up terrible. Every time you call your car in you have to reallocate your crew members to assigned positions, this takes around 1minute to do, and you’ll do this several times a race, which makes it come monotonous. Why can’t I have pre-assigned positions? Why must I click on my crew member, then the jack, then on the predefined location on the ground? This step should be more automated as the control you have is meaningless anyway.
My biggest frustration was during the ‘tutorial’ level. It is done poorly and doesn’t explain how anything works; my first pitstop took over 2minutes as I worked out the buttons that were never explained to me. The game also has bugs, causing my crew to walk around sporadically, refuse to go to their locations or buttons straight up missing. During the tutorial the game told me to ‘click here’, this button had disappeared from the game and not until I relaunched the game was I able to continue.
This game is not in a playable state, what we have here is a pitstop game, which is unique, but is bare bones and has obvious flaws that should have been fixed. The only challenge in this game is trying to actually play the damn thing.
P.S. It's come to my attention through a YouTube comment that the Shanghai track I pick is actually the Bahrain circuit, apparently this is a common bug/feature as it happens in my let's play/gameplay video also with the Australian track.

Maybe I'm just shouting into the wind here, but as someone who hasn't followed the Civilization series religiously, I think this is actually a decent standalone game.  I think perhaps C:BE gets an unfair rap for being 'more of the same' when it would be considered at least competent when examined in isolation from games like Alpha Centauri or Civ 5.
The game is not without issues.  Long loads, framerate drops, and network game issues were frequent on my system before the most recent updates.  Interactions with other national leaders can paradoxically show some underlying RNG (can't explain the number of out-of-nowhere face-heel turns otherwise) and yet can become rather predictable as well once you've played a number of games to completion.  The Rising Tide DLC does help significantly with the somewhat one-dimensional diplomacy system and a couple other issues.
On the other hand, I found this game much easier to micro-manage than previous Civilization games I've played.  The affinity system lent uniqueness to colonies and added replay value.  Tech progression felt easier to visualize and had real consequences (colony health and certain resource production become big drivers of difficulty if you don't plan ahead).  Native mod support was a nice touch as well.  This game is a great time waster.
All in all, I give C:BE a 7.5/10 - not flawless, but not the awful trash that a lot of reviews make it out to be either.  If you're a fan of resource management/turn-based strategy, then it's worth the sale price.

On the other hand, throughout the whole game I didn't give a tiny rat's a** about the game's storyline... All in all, I enjoyed the game greatly thanks to its fun gameplay and I would definitely recommend it to a friend!

This game is pretty.  The art style is pleasant to look at and contrast is high enough that you know what you're looking at.  In complement, the music is well-done also.  It isn't too loud or detracting from the story or sounds.  I also appreciate that all the dialogue was voice acted.  However, I think that the story isn't fleshed out nearly enough.  The concept has tons of potential but the tiny plotline doesn't do justice to the relatively large amount of exposition thrust in there.
Embers of Magic is a classic example of a story that isn't compelling simply because the reader (or player in this case) is confused by the things people say that have no visible reasoning, like the bit about the Lilies that cause the ship to fly.  How do they work?  Why can't the people take more than a required amount?  All we know is that they are needed and that Anne nearly gets arrested bringing them back.  Like I said, confusing.
Building on the concept of plot structure, this story is all exposition.  There is no conflict (aside from the police bit and a couple of other moments, but they aren't the main drama), so the story plods along and ends rather abruptly.  My reaction to the ending was one of confusion and a "well, guess that's over".  (Side note: the achievement for ending the game doesn't trigger when you actually end it, which was why I initially didn't think it was over.)
Overall, while the game looks and sounds very nice, the story is lacking and far too short for the world it is trying to express.  If there were to be revisions or patches, I would recommend the devs simply keep writing and just add more to the story.
ALL THAT SAID, HOWEVER:
I will still recommend this game because it has significant potential to become much greater.  Perhaps if a big enough audience can build up, we can show the devs that we are further interested.

PC VERSION:
WOW! I have been waiting for "Fantasy Flight Games" who make some of the best strategy and card tabletop games to make a PC game for BattleLore!
I am really really really enjoying this immersive yet relaxing great game!
Here is what I like about it:
1) It seems like a great adaptation of FFGs great selling boardgame version, as it is hex based, turn based and has the pc versions of the board pieces, but has a better look than most hex based games as well as board games adapted to teh PC.
2) It is very challenging, and what makes it unique is that you have to issue orders that limit what yu can do with how many units and where, i.e. you cannot just zerg. On the "Silverloft" mission, it took me several attempts to win and thus the legendary battle of Silverloft will long be remembered by those who fought it.
Another example of the above would be a mission I initially rolled my eyes at as I thought "defending sheep" would be boring...NOT SO! The freaking sheep would either run towards the enemy or away just like the fickle creatures thay are, and my poor troops had to deal with both their unpredictable behavior as well as fighting off the enemy wanting to kill them. it took me a couple of tries to win.
3) Unit type tactics are biggies, i.e. do I put my archers in front, back? Shoudl I keep my Cav in reserve etc etc.
4) Interesting objectives, i.e. taking and defending magic portals, defending a towns buildings from getting burnt down, etc etc and of course classic battle types.
5) interesting yet simple story, as the narrator and the text which are part of the storyline and mission descriptions including the artwork are simple yet interesting.
6) Do not expect Dawn of War or Total War, this is a turn based game where the intensity of making the right decisions, when, where, and how to make them is as intense and exciting as a real time strategy game like those I just mentioned.
7) Small maps, that feel big...I always wondered when looking at the boardgame version how good the pc version would be on what "seems" to be a small map...actually the maps are the perfect size, neither too big or too small as they are battlefield maps, and you also have the strategic map provide to you so you can decide your over campaign moves as opposed to your battlefield tactical moves.
8) I usually do not like hex based and/or turn based games, but this one I really really like, as it is very original. Do not let the pictures and/or store videos fool you, this is a very challenging game that has a perfect complexity.
9) I am usually turned off my artwork incorporated into a game instead of game graphics, but the artwork used on the strategic map is perfect in its adaptation and use.
The only thing I do not like is the design of the red units, i.e. the Uthoks...as IMHO their flesh color is too human and they run around in tarzan type barbarian jungle cloths, i.e. loin cloths. I do like the mobile ythok unit designs though and of course I really like the classic armor look of the blue guys, i.e the Daqan.
10) It is a $9.99 game that gives you the playability of a more expensive game, i.e. once you finish the campaign, there is muliplayer and additional DLC.
I highly recommend it, if you like turn based games and look forward to those special Friday or Saturday night game nights with your friends, now brought straight from the tabletop to your PC!

If you really MUST pick one between Grid Autosport and Grid 2, go for Autosport to avoid all those pile of SHXT arcade drifts.
IN TRUTH THOUGH, even Autosport has less realistic handling physics than GRID 1 (acceleration/braking is better in AS though, without being exaggerated). Handling in GRID 1 was so good that it could rival the top ultimate sim games (e.g. rFactor) in not all but at least few aspects (despite it was never meant to be full-sim).  GRID AS, despite its richer content, failed to recapture the handling magic of GRID 1, and the driving experience is too detached and easy(simplified) in typical modern Codemasters way. (same for Dirt RALLY, yes people gonna hate me for saying this but it's FACT).
IF SIM is what you have in mind, FORGET AUTOSPORT. At least GRID 1 one aspect close to sim level which makes it worth considering, but AS doesn't. I'm still waiting for GRID 1 v2 dear Codemasters.

To keep it short and sweet: Battlerite is a phenomenal entry into the multiplayer video game genre. It's like FPSes, fighting games, and MOBAs turned into the greatest Reese's Peanut Butter Cup of all time. Well, maybe not ALL time. But it's still pretty good. It's hectic but also razor-sharp, forcing you to make tactical decisions at every turn, and there's no fiddly mechanics like last-hitting to get in the way of gameplay.
The core mode of the game is a 2v2 or 3v3 battle arena, where characters from different classes battle it out in a no-respawn deathmatch. While the huge menu of abilities available to each character is dizzying (at last count, each character has 5 normal abilities, one ultimate ability, and three empowered abilities), it starts to fall into patterns fairly quickly, which means that time spent on one character translates to a baseline level of experience on another character. Having such a broad palette of options means that fights are brain-intensive, as you've got a whole bucket of tools and dynamic situations that demand different applications of those tools.
There's also enough difference between characters that you can pick one that suits your style. For instance, to look at melee characters, while Raigon is a leaping, aggressive swordsman, Thorn is an ominous grappler who keeps dragging enemies back to his clutches, and Bakko is a disruptive tank. Blossom is an elusive healer, while Pearl's bubbles and silences are a persistent frustration to her enemies. It's the part of fighting games that gives them a distinctive flair, without all of the complex execution (with the exception of games like Rivals of Aether or Fantasy Strike).
Matches are quick, you learn quickly, and you can measure your progress in competitive play--which, wonderfully, uses team-based MMR and creates new MMR for each team, so you can team up with better friends without worrying that you're dragging their competitive MMR down.
Battlerite is where it's at.
